cmp/1.title: The Dance That Shows the Way
p: In a dark, crowded hive, a worker bee has just come home. She cannot speak, so she does something else. She begins to dance. Within seconds, other bees press close around her, feeling every step with their antennae. A few minutes later, some of them are flying out of the entrance, heading straight for a field of flowers they have never seen.

This strange behaviour was first worked out by Karl von Frisch, a German scientist who spent years watching bees through glass-sided hives. He found that bees do not simply wander and hope for luck. When a scout finds good food, she goes back and tells the others exactly where to look. In 1973, his research earned him a Nobel Prize.

The message depends on how far away the food is. If the flowers are close, within about fifty to seventy-five metres of the hive, the bee runs in a small circle. This is called the round dance. It tells the others only one thing: there is food nearby, so start searching.

For longer distances, the bee does something far more precise. She walks in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then loops back and does it again. This is the waggle dance, and every part of it carries information. The speed at which she repeats the dance shows the distance. The slower the dance, the farther the food.

Direction is harder to show, because the dance happens on a vertical wall of wax inside the hive, and there is no sun to point at. So the bees use gravity instead. If the straight run points straight up, the food lies in the same direction as the sun. If the run leans twenty degrees to the right of vertical, the food lies twenty degrees to the right of the sun. Later experiments showed that the bees which follow a dance can even allow for the wind on their way.

Von Frisch did get one thing wrong. At first, he believed that bees measured distance by the energy they used on the flight. It turned out to be different. Bees judge distance by how much of the scenery rushes past their eyes. In one test, bees were fed forty-one metres from the hive, but the last six metres were covered with a busy pattern. These bees performed the waggle dance, as if the food were much farther away. Their eyes had been tricked.
So the next time you see a bee on a flower, remember that she may not be there by chance. She may have arrived because of a dance.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
q.e: The whole passage explains the round dance and the waggle dance, which are used to tell other bees where food is.
o: A. How bees fly long distances without rest, and how they find their way home
B. How bees make honey inside the hive
C. How bees use dance to share the location of food
D. Why Karl von Frisch won a Nobel Prize

q.q: Karl von Frisch won a Nobel Prize in 1973.
q.e: Paragraph 2 says his research earned him a Nobel Prize in 1973.

q.q: Bees use the round dance when the food is far from the hive.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says the round dance is for food that is close, within about 50 to 75 metres.

q.q: The waggle dance shows the other bees the distance and the ____ of the food.
q.e: Paragraph 5 explains that the angle of the straight run shows the direction of the food.

q.q: According to the passage, how do bees show direction inside the dark hive?
q.e: Paragraph 5 says there is no sun inside the hive, so the bees use gravity instead.
o: A. They use gravity as a guide
B. They follow the light from the entrance
C. They point toward the sun
D. They use the smell of flowers

q.q: Von Frisch was right from the start about how bees measure distance.
q.e: Paragraph 6 says he first believed bees measured the energy of the flight, which was wrong.

q.q: Young bees learn to dance before they learn to fly.
q.e: The passage never talks about when young bees learn to dance.

q.q: In paragraph 4, the word "precise" is closest in meaning to:
q.e: The waggle dance gives exact information about direction and distance.
o: A. simple
B. loud
C. exact
D. slow

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 3?
o: A. The round dance shows how many flowers there are.
B. Bees run in circles to show the direction of the sun.
C. Bees dance in a circle when they are tired of searching.
D. A small circular dance tells the other bees that food is nearby.
q.e: Paragraph 3 explains the round dance: a small circle that tells the others only one thing, that food is close to the hive.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 5?
o: A. Bees use the wind to find the hive again.
B. Bees use gravity inside the hive to show the direction of the food.
C. Bees show direction by comparing the dance with the sun on the hive wall.
D. Bees can only show direction when the sun is shining.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says the dance happens on a vertical wall with no sun to point at, so bees use gravity: straight up means the same direction as the sun.

q.q: In the test described in paragraph 6, why did the bees dance as if the food were much farther away?
o: A. The busy pattern made more scenery rush past their eyes.
B. They were tired after a long flight.
C. They wanted to hide the food from other bees, and so they made the pattern busy
D. Von Frisch had moved the food further.
q.e: Paragraph 6 says bees judge distance by how much scenery passes their eyes. The busy pattern tricked them into thinking the food was farther.

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
o: A. Bees find flowers mainly by sight and so they do not need to communicate with each other.
B. Bees tell each other where food is by dancing, and scientists have slowly learned how the dance shows distance and direction.
C. Bees dance only when they come home with a lot of food, and the dance tells nothing about direction or about distance.
D. Von Frisch won a Nobel Prize because he learned to talk to bees in their own language.
q.e: The passage describes how bees use dances to share the distance and direction of food, and how Von Frisch and later scientists worked this out.

ps.e: In a dark, crowded hive, a worker bee has just come home.
ps.b: অন্ধকার, ঠাসাঠাসি মৌচাকে একটি কর্মী মৌমাছি এইমাত্র ফিরে এসেছে।

ps.e: She cannot speak, so she does something else.

ps.e: She begins to dance.

ps.e: A few minutes later, some of them are flying out of the entrance, heading straight for a field of flowers they have never seen.
ps.b: কয়েক মিনিট পরে তাদের কেউ কেউ প্রবেশপথ দিয়ে উড়ে বেরিয়ে যায় এবং সোজা এমন এক ফুলের মাঠের দিকে ছুটে যায় যা তারা আগে কখনও দেখেনি।

ps.e: This strange behaviour was first worked out by Karl von Frisch, a German scientist who spent years watching bees through glass-sided hives.
ps.b: এই অদ্ভুত আচরণটি প্রথম বুঝতে পেরেছিলেন কার্ল ফন ফ্রিশ, একজন জার্মান বিজ্ঞানী, যিনি কাচের দেয়ালওয়ালা মৌচাকের ভেতর দিয়ে বছরের পর বছর মৌমাছিদের লক্ষ করেছেন।

ps.e: He found that bees do not simply wander and hope for luck.
ps.b: তিনি দেখলেন, মৌমাছিরা কেবল ভাগ্যের ওপর ভরসা করে এদিক-ওদিক ঘুরে বেড়ায় না।

ps.e: When a scout finds good food, she goes back and tells the others exactly where to look.
ps.b: যখন কোনো স্কাউট মৌমাছি ভালো খাবারের সন্ধান পায়, সে ফিরে এসে অন্যদের ঠিক কোথায় খুঁজতে হবে তা জানিয়ে দেয়।

ps.e: In 1973, his research earned him a Nobel Prize.
ps.b: ১৯৭৩ সালে তাঁর এই গবেষণা তাঁকে নোবেল পুরস্কার এনে দেয়।

ps.e: The message depends on how far away the food is.
ps.b: বার্তাটি নির্ভর করে খাবার কত দূরে আছে তার ওপর।

ps.e: If the flowers are close, within about fifty to seventy-five metres of the hive, the bee runs in a small circle.
ps.b: ফুলগুলো যদি কাছে থাকে, অর্থাৎ চাক থেকে প্রায় পঞ্চাশ থেকে পঁচাত্তর মিটারের মধ্যে, তাহলে মৌমাছিটি ছোট একটি বৃত্তাকারে ঘোরে।

ps.e: This is called the round dance.
ps.b: একে বলা হয় গোল নাচ (রাউন্ড ড্যান্স)।

ps.e: It tells the others only one thing: there is food nearby, so start searching.
ps.b: এটি অন্যদের শুধু একটি কথাই বলে: কাছেই খাবার আছে, তাই খোঁজা শুরু করো।

ps.e: For longer distances, the bee does something far more precise.
ps.b: দূরের পথের জন্য মৌমাছিটি এর চেয়ে অনেক বেশি নিখুঁত কিছু করে।

ps.e: She walks in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then loops back and does it again.
ps.b: সে সোজা একটি রেখায় হাঁটে এবং শরীর দুপাশে দোলাতে থাকে, তারপর ঘুরে পিছনে এসে আবার একই কাজ করে।

ps.e: This is the waggle dance, and every part of it carries information.
ps.b: এটিই দোলন নাচ (ওয়াগল ড্যান্স), এবং এর প্রতিটি অংশ কিছু না কিছু তথ্য বহন করে।

ps.e: The speed at which she repeats the dance shows the distance.
ps.b: সে কত দ্রুত বা ধীরে নাচটি পুনরাবৃত্তি করে, তা থেকে দূরত্ব বোঝা যায়।

ps.e: The slower the dance, the farther the food.
ps.b: নাচ যত ধীর, খাবার তত দূরে।

ps.e: Direction is harder to show, because the dance happens on a vertical wall of wax inside the hive, and there is no sun to point at.
ps.b: দিক বোঝানো আরও কঠিন, কারণ নাচটি হয় মৌচাকের ভেতরে মোমের একটি খাড়া দেয়ালে, আর সেখানে সূর্যের দিকে ইশারা করার কোনো উপায় নেই।

ps.e: So the bees use gravity instead.
ps.b: তাই মৌমাছিরা এর বদলে অভিকর্ষ ব্যবহার করে।

ps.e: If the straight run points straight up, the food lies in the same direction as the sun.
ps.b: সোজা রেখাটি যদি একদম ওপরের দিকে যায়, তাহলে খাবার সূর্যের যে দিকে আছে সেই একই দিকে।

ps.e: If the run leans twenty degrees to the right of vertical, the food lies twenty degrees to the right of the sun.
ps.b: রেখাটি যদি খাড়া দিক থেকে ডানে বিশ ডিগ্রি হেলে থাকে, তাহলে খাবার সূর্যের ডান দিকে বিশ ডিগ্রি সরে আছে।

ps.e: Later experiments showed that the bees which follow a dance can even allow for the wind on their way.
ps.b: পরবর্তী পরীক্ষায় দেখা গেছে, যেসব মৌমাছি নাচ দেখে বেরোয় তারা পথে বাতাসের প্রভাবও হিসাব করে নিতে পারে।

ps.e: Von Frisch did get one thing wrong.
ps.b: ফন ফ্রিশ একটি বিষয়ে ভুল করেছিলেন।

ps.e: At first, he believed that bees measured distance by the energy they used on the flight.
ps.b: শুরুতে তিনি ভেবেছিলেন, মৌমাছিরা উড়তে কতটা শক্তি খরচ হয় তা দিয়ে দূরত্ব মাপে।

ps.e: It turned out to be different.
ps.b: দেখা গেল ব্যাপারটি অন্যরকম।

ps.e: Bees judge distance by how much of the scenery rushes past their eyes.
ps.b: মৌমাছিরা দূরত্ব বিচার করে তাদের চোখের সামনে দিয়ে কতটা দৃশ্য ছুটে চলে যায় তা দিয়ে।

ps.e: In one test, bees were fed forty-one metres from the hive, but the last six metres were covered with a busy pattern.
ps.b: একটি পরীক্ষায় মৌমাছিদের খাবার দেওয়া হয়েছিল চাক থেকে একচল্লিশ মিটার দূরে, কিন্তু শেষের ছয় মিটার ঢেকে দেওয়া হয়েছিল ব্যস্ত নকশায়।

ps.e: These bees performed the waggle dance, as if the food were much farther away.
ps.b: এই মৌমাছিরা দোলন নাচ নাচল, যেন খাবার আরও অনেক দূরে।

ps.e: Their eyes had been tricked.
ps.b: তাদের চোখ ধোঁকা খেয়েছিল।

ps.e: So the next time you see a bee on a flower, remember that she may not be there by chance.
ps.b: তাই পরের বার যখন কোনো ফুলে একটি মৌমাছি দেখবে, মনে রেখো, সে হয়তো কাকতালীয়ভাবে সেখানে আসেনি।

ps.e: She may have arrived because of a dance.
ps.b: হয়তো একটি নাচের কারণেই সে সেখানে পৌঁছেছে।

cmp/2.title: The Banana That Almost Disappeared
p: If you bought a banana last week, there is a very good chance it was a clone. Not a copy of one banana, but part of an enormous family of plants that are almost exactly the same. That fact sounds harmless. For the people who grow bananas, it is a serious worry.

The story begins before the 1960s, when the banana that filled the shops was not the one we eat today. It was called the Gros Michel, and it was the main banana in the world's shops until the 1960s. Farmers planted it in huge fields, row after row, with every plant nearly identical. This looked efficient. Then a fungus arrived.

The disease is known as Panama disease. It lives in the soil and enters the plant through its roots, blocking the tubes that carry water and food. The leaves turn yellow, the plant wilts, and it dies. The fungus can stay in the soil for decades, and no chemical has been able to stop it. During the 1950s and 1960s, it spread through plantations, and the Gros Michel was nearly wiped out as a crop.

The industry needed a replacement quickly. It found one in the Cavendish, a banana that could resist that early form of the disease. Growers switched, shoppers accepted the change, and the problem seemed to be over.

It was not. Today, the Cavendish makes up about 47 per cent of the bananas grown in the world. For the bananas sold abroad to rich countries, the figure is closer to 99 per cent. And, like the Gros Michel before it, the Cavendish is made up of plants that are nearly identical. When one plant is weak against a disease, they all are.

A new danger has already appeared. A strain of the same fungus, called TR4, was first found in the early 1990s in Taiwan, Malaysia and Indonesia. The Cavendish has little defence against it. Another disease, called Black Sigatoka, can cut the harvest by 35 to 50 per cent if nothing is done, and farmers sometimes spray their fields more than fifty times a year to hold it back.

Scientists are searching for answers. Their main idea is simple: bring more variety back into the banana. Wild bananas grow in many places, and some may carry natural protection against disease. If researchers can find it, they may be able to build a new generation of bananas that are tougher.
For now, your breakfast is safe. But the next time you peel one, spare a thought for a plant whose greatest strength, being the same everywhere, may also be its greatest weakness.

q.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
q.e: The passage shows that both the Gros Michel and the Cavendish are at risk because the plants are nearly identical.
o: A. Bananas taste better than most other fruit
B. A banana crop that is too uniform can be easily destroyed by disease
C. The Gros Michel is still the best banana in the world, and farmers have never stopped growing it
D. Farmers should stop growing bananas

q.q: Panama disease spread through the leaves of the plant.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says the fungus lives in the soil and enters through the roots.

q.q: Chemicals have not been able to stop Panama disease.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says no chemical has been able to stop it.

q.q: Farmers replaced the Gros Michel with a banana called the ____.
q.e: Paragraph 4 says the industry found a replacement in the Cavendish.

q.q: Which share of bananas sold to rich countries is the Cavendish?
q.e: Paragraph 5 says for bananas sold abroad to rich countries the figure is closer to 99 per cent.
o: A. Over 50 per cent
B. 47 per cent
C. 35 per cent
D. About 99 per cent

q.q: TR4 was first found in Europe.
q.e: Paragraph 6 says TR4 was first found in Taiwan, Malaysia and Indonesia.

q.q: Scientists have already created a banana that is safe from every disease.
q.e: The passage says researchers are looking for answers but does not say they have a finished solution.

q.q: What does the writer suggest in the last paragraph?
q.e: The writer says that the plant's strength, being the same everywhere, may also be its greatest weakness.
o: A. The Cavendish has no strengths of any kind to offer farmers
B. Bananas will soon disappear from the shops everywhere
C. Being the same everywhere can make a crop vulnerable
D. Wild bananas are always better to eat than farmed ones

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 3?
o: A. Farmers stopped growing the Gros Michel because shoppers disliked its taste and its colour.
B. A disease in the soil spread through the plantations and almost destroyed the Gros Michel.
C. A new chemical was invented that saved the Gros Michel.
D. The leaves of the Gros Michel turned yellow because of bad weather.
q.e: Paragraph 3 explains that Panama disease lives in the soil, kills the plant, and nearly wiped out the Gros Michel.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 5?
o: A. Banana growers earn more money from the Cavendish than from any other fruit, so it is safe from disease and from every danger.
B. Most shops now sell a different kind of banana, because the Cavendish has been replaced for good.
C. The Cavendish solved the banana problem for ever, and no disease can harm it now.
D. The Cavendish now dominates banana growing, but its plants are nearly identical, so one disease could threaten them all.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says the Cavendish is about 47 per cent of world bananas and 99 per cent of those sold abroad, and that identical plants share the same weakness.

q.q: According to the passage, why can one disease be so dangerous to the Cavendish?
o: A. The plants are almost identical, so what harms one can harm all.
B. The plants grow very slowly, so a disease has a long time to spread.
C. Farmers do not spray the fields, so every disease spreads easily to the plants.
D. The plants grow only in poor soil.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says: "When one plant is weak against a disease, they all are," because the plants are nearly identical.

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
o: A. Because bananas grown for sale are nearly identical, they are easily threatened by disease, and scientists are looking for more variety.
B. The banana is the most popular fruit in the world, so farmers make a lot of money from it.
C. Panama disease is harmless to modern bananas, which grow well in all the fields of the world.
D. Scientists have already made a banana that no disease can harm, and every farmer in the world now grows only that one kind.
q.e: The passage explains that identical banana plants are vulnerable, that the Gros Michel was lost, that the Cavendish faces new diseases, and that scientists want more variety.

ps.e: If you bought a banana last week, there is a very good chance it was a clone.
ps.b: গত সপ্তাহে যদি তুমি একটি কলা কিনে থাকো, তবে খুব সম্ভাবনা আছে সেটি ছিল একটি ক্লোন।

ps.e: If researchers can find it, they may be able to build a new generation of bananas that are tougher.
ps.b: গবেষকরা যদি সেটি খুঁজে পান, তাহলে হয়তো তাঁরা আরও শক্তপোক্ত একটি নতুন প্রজন্মের কলা তৈরি করতে পারবেন।

ps.e: For now, your breakfast is safe.
ps.b: আপাতত তোমার সকালের নাশতা নিরাপদ।

ps.e: But the next time you peel one, spare a thought for a plant whose greatest strength, being the same everywhere, may also be its greatest weakness.
ps.b: কিন্তু পরের বার যখন একটি কলা ছিলবে, তখন এমন একটি গাছের কথা একটু ভেবো যার সবচেয়ে বড় শক্তি, সব জায়গায় একই রকম হওয়া, হয়তো তার সবচেয়ে বড় দুর্বলতাও।

cmp/3.title: The City That Fell Back in Love with Bikes
p: Imagine a city where there are more bicycles than people. Copenhagen is that city. About 560,000 bikes move through its streets, and only around three in ten residents own a car. To visitors, it looks as if the Danes were simply born on two wheels.
They were not. In fact, the story is much more interesting than that.

By the 1930s, Danish cities were already full of bicycles. Rich and poor rode them, and so did postmen and home helpers, and nobody thought it was strange. This lasted for roughly fifty years. Then, around 1960, life got better. Families had more money, and cars became a symbol of success after the hard years of the Great Depression and the Second World War. Buying a car felt like a step forward.

Within a few years, the city paid the price. Streets filled with traffic. Famous places such as Nyhavn were crowded with parked cars. Accidents and pollution grew. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, the share of people on bicycles dropped to an all-time low of about ten per cent. Many people thought the bicycle was finished.

Then came 1973. The oil crisis suddenly made petrol hard to get. Denmark introduced rationing and car-free Sundays, and on those Sundays the roads were left to walkers and cyclists. At the same time, a young environmental movement was asking uncomfortable questions about what cars were doing to cities.

Cyclists began to organise. The Danish Cyclists' Federation grew quickly, and its members held demonstrations asking for safe space on the road. When the city planned a new motorway across the lakes, there was a huge public protest. In 1983, the federation made a point in a rather funny way. It gave the head of the city's traffic department a "Cyclist Award". The prize was a two-metre piece of kerbstone, a reminder that Copenhagen still lacked proper bike lanes.

Over time, the message was heard. Planners began to design streets for cars, bicycles, walkers and public transport together. Today, Copenhagen has about 350 kilometres of cycle tracks that are separated from traffic by a kerb. Since 2009, it has been building cycle superhighways, long routes designed for people who travel between five and fifteen kilometres to work.

Is every figure perfect? Not quite. Different studies count cycling trips in different ways, so the exact share of people who cycle to work or school depends on who you ask. But the main lesson is clear. Copenhagen did not become a cycling city by accident. It became one because ordinary people asked for it, and because the city finally listened.

q.q: Which sentence best describes the main message of the passage?
q.e: The passage shows that cycling fell, then came back because of the oil crisis, protests and new planning.
o: A. Danish people naturally prefer cycling to driving
B. Cars are the best way to travel in big cities
C. Copenhagen became a cycling city after people pushed for change
D. Cycling was only popular in Denmark before the 1930s, and it has fallen since then

q.q: More than half of Copenhagen's residents own a car.
q.e: Paragraph 1 says only around three in ten residents own a car.

q.q: The share of people cycling fell to about ten per cent in the late 1960s and early 1970s.
q.e: Paragraph 4 gives this figure as an all-time low.

q.q: In 1973, a crisis involving ____ led to rationing and car-free Sundays.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says the oil crisis made petrol hard to get.

q.q: Why did the Danish Cyclists' Federation give a two-metre kerbstone to a city official?
q.e: Paragraph 6 explains the kerbstone reminded the city that it still lacked proper bike lanes.
o: A. To celebrate the opening of the new motorway
B. To thank him for building new bike lanes in the city
C. To pay for the repair of a road in the city
D. To show that the city still had no proper bike lanes

q.q: Copenhagen has been building cycle superhighways since 2009.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says: "Since 2009, it has been building cycle superhighways".

q.q: Every study agrees on the exact share of people who cycle to work in Copenhagen.
q.e: Paragraph 8 says different studies count trips in different ways.

q.q: In paragraph 5, the word "rationing" means:
q.e: Rationing means giving each person only a limited amount of something that is short.
o: A. limiting how much of something each person can have
B. making something cheaper for everybody
C. banning something completely for everyone in the town
D. selling something to other countries

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 4?
o: A. As cars took over the streets, traffic, accidents and pollution grew and cycling fell to a record low.
B. The city built new bike lanes in order to reduce pollution, and cycling soon rose to a record high.
C. Most people in the 1960s decided together to sell their cars, so the streets became quiet.
D. Famous places were rebuilt so there would be more room for bicycles and for people to walk.
q.e: Paragraph 4 describes streets filling with traffic, parked cars, more accidents and pollution, and cycling dropping to about ten per cent.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 7?
o: A. Cyclists stopped asking the city for any new roads and routes, because they were already satisfied.
B. Planners began to design streets for all kinds of travel, and Copenhagen built many protected cycle routes.
C. Copenhagen built more cycle tracks than any other city in the world, according to the passage.
D. The government banned all cars from the city centre for good, and then built the cycle routes.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says planners started designing streets for cars, bicycles, walkers and public transport together, with 350 km of cycle tracks and superhighways.

q.q: According to the passage, why did cycling become less popular after about 1960?
o: A. The government forbade cycling anywhere in the city.
B. Families had more money, and cars became a symbol of success.
C. There were not enough roads left in the city for bicycles.
D. Bicycles became too expensive for most families to buy.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says families had more money and cars became a symbol of success after the hard years, so buying a car felt like progress.

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
o: A. Cars caused cycling to disappear completely from Copenhagen for good, and it never came back.
B. The oil crisis was the only reason that Copenhagen became a cycling city, and people played no part.
C. Copenhagen became a cycling city because ordinary people campaigned for change and the city eventually listened.
D. Danes are born with a natural love of cycling that other people do not share, so no campaign was needed.
q.e: The passage shows that cycling fell, then returned because of the oil crisis, protest, and planners who listened to ordinary people.

q.q: Most Copenhagen cyclists wear helmets when they ride to work.
q.e: The passage does not mention this.

ps.e: Imagine a city where there are more bicycles than people.
ps.b: এমন একটি শহরের কথা ভাবো, যেখানে মানুষের চেয়ে সাইকেলের সংখ্যা বেশি।

ps.e: Copenhagen is that city.
ps.b: কোপেনহেগেন হলো সেই শহর।

ps.e: About 560,000 bikes move through its streets, and only around three in ten residents own a car.
ps.b: প্রায় ৫,৬০,০০০ সাইকেল এর রাস্তায় চলাচল করে, আর বাসিন্দাদের মধ্যে প্রতি দশজনে মাত্র তিনজনের মতো গাড়ির মালিক।

ps.e: To visitors, it looks as if the Danes were simply born on two wheels.
ps.b: দর্শনার্থীদের কাছে মনে হয়, ডেনরা যেন জন্ম থেকেই দুই চাকার ওপর চড়ে বড় হয়েছে।

ps.e: They were not.
ps.b: তারা তা হয়নি।

ps.e: In fact, the story is much more interesting than that.
ps.b: আসলে গল্পটি তার চেয়ে অনেক বেশি আকর্ষণীয়।

ps.e: By the 1930s, Danish cities were already full of bicycles.
ps.b: ১৯৩০-এর দশকের মধ্যেই ডেনমার্কের শহরগুলো সাইকেলে ভরে গিয়েছিল।

ps.e: Rich and poor rode them, and so did postmen and home helpers, and nobody thought it was strange.
ps.b: ধনী-গরিব সবাই সাইকেল চালাত, ডাকপিয়ন ও গৃহসহায়কেরাও চালাত, আর এটিকে কেউ অদ্ভুত ভাবত না।

ps.e: This lasted for roughly fifty years.
ps.b: এই অবস্থা চলেছিল প্রায় পঞ্চাশ বছর।

ps.e: Then, around 1960, life got better.
ps.b: তারপর, ১৯৬০ সালের দিকে, জীবনযাত্রা উন্নত হলো।

ps.e: Families had more money, and cars became a symbol of success after the hard years of the Great Depression and the Second World War.
ps.b: পরিবারগুলোর হাতে বেশি টাকা এলো, আর মহামন্দা ও দ্বিতীয় বিশ্বযুদ্ধের কঠিন বছরগুলোর পর গাড়ি হয়ে উঠল সাফল্যের প্রতীক।

ps.e: Buying a car felt like a step forward.
ps.b: গাড়ি কেনাকে মনে হতো এগিয়ে যাওয়ার একটি ধাপ।

ps.e: Within a few years, the city paid the price.
ps.b: কয়েক বছরের মধ্যেই শহরকে এর মূল্য দিতে হলো।

ps.e: Streets filled with traffic.
ps.b: রাস্তাগুলো যানবাহনে ভরে গেল।

ps.e: Famous places such as Nyhavn were crowded with parked cars.
ps.b: নিহাভনের মতো বিখ্যাত জায়গাগুলোও পার্ক করা গাড়িতে ঠাসা হয়ে গেল।

ps.e: Accidents and pollution grew.
ps.b: দুর্ঘটনা ও দূষণ বাড়তে লাগল।

ps.e: In the late 1960s and early 1970s, the share of people on bicycles dropped to an all-time low of about ten per cent.
ps.b: ১৯৬০-এর দশকের শেষ এবং ১৯৭০-এর দশকের শুরুর দিকে সাইকেল আরোহীর অনুপাত নেমে এসেছিল সর্বকালের সর্বনিম্ন প্রায় দশ শতাংশে।

ps.e: Many people thought the bicycle was finished.
ps.b: অনেকেই ভাবতে শুরু করল, সাইকেলের দিন শেষ।

ps.e: Then came 1973.
ps.b: তারপর এলো ১৯৭৩ সাল।

ps.e: The oil crisis suddenly made petrol hard to get.
ps.b: তেল সংকট হঠাৎ করে পেট্রোল পাওয়া কঠিন করে তুলল।

ps.e: Denmark introduced rationing and car-free Sundays, and on those Sundays the roads were left to walkers and cyclists.
ps.b: ডেনমার্ক রেশনিং এবং গাড়িমুক্ত রবিবার চালু করল, আর সেই রবিবারগুলোতে রাস্তা ছেড়ে দেওয়া হতো পথচারী ও সাইকেল আরোহীদের জন্য।

ps.e: At the same time, a young environmental movement was asking uncomfortable questions about what cars were doing to cities.
ps.b: একই সময়ে একটি তরুণ পরিবেশ আন্দোলন গাড়ি শহরগুলোর কী ক্ষতি করছে সেই নিয়ে অস্বস্তিকর প্রশ্ন তুলছিল।

ps.e: Cyclists began to organise.
ps.b: সাইকেল আরোহীরা সংগঠিত হতে শুরু করল।

ps.e: The Danish Cyclists' Federation grew quickly, and its members held demonstrations asking for safe space on the road.
ps.b: ডেনিশ সাইক্লিস্টস ফেডারেশন দ্রুত বড় হয়ে উঠল, আর এর সদস্যরা রাস্তায় নিরাপদ জায়গার দাবিতে বিক্ষোভ করল।

ps.e: When the city planned a new motorway across the lakes, there was a huge public protest.
ps.b: শহর যখন হ্রদগুলোর ওপর দিয়ে নতুন মোটরওয়ে বানানোর পরিকল্পনা করল, তখন বিশাল গণপ্রতিবাদ হলো।

ps.e: In 1983, the federation made a point in a rather funny way.
ps.b: ১৯৮৩ সালে ফেডারেশন বেশ মজার এক উপায়ে নিজেদের বক্তব্য তুলে ধরল।

ps.e: It gave the head of the city's traffic department a "Cyclist Award".
ps.b: তারা শহরের ট্রাফিক বিভাগের প্রধানকে একটি "সাইক্লিস্ট পুরস্কার" দিল।

ps.e: The prize was a two-metre piece of kerbstone, a reminder that Copenhagen still lacked proper bike lanes.
ps.b: পুরস্কারটি ছিল দুই মিটার লম্বা একটি কার্বপাথরের টুকরো, যা মনে করিয়ে দিত যে কোপেনহেগেনে তখনও ঠিকমতো সাইকেল লেন ছিল না।

ps.e: Over time, the message was heard.
ps.b: ধীরে ধীরে বার্তাটি শোনা হলো।

ps.e: Planners began to design streets for cars, bicycles, walkers and public transport together.
ps.b: পরিকল্পনাকারীরা গাড়ি, সাইকেল, পথচারী ও গণপরিবহনের কথা একসঙ্গে ভেবে রাস্তা ডিজাইন করতে শুরু করলেন।

ps.e: Today, Copenhagen has about 350 kilometres of cycle tracks that are separated from traffic by a kerb.
ps.b: আজ কোপেনহেগেনে প্রায় ৩৫০ কিলোমিটার সাইকেল পথ আছে, যেগুলো কার্ব দিয়ে যানবাহনের পথ থেকে আলাদা করা।

ps.e: Since 2009, it has been building cycle superhighways, long routes designed for people who travel between five and fifteen kilometres to work.
ps.b: ২০০৯ সাল থেকে এটি সাইকেল সুপারহাইওয়ে বানাচ্ছে, অর্থাৎ এমন লম্বা পথ, যা যারা কাজে যেতে পাঁচ থেকে পনেরো কিলোমিটার যাতায়াত করেন তাদের জন্য তৈরি।

ps.e: Is every figure perfect?
ps.b: প্রতিটি সংখ্যাই কি নিখুঁত?

ps.e: Not quite.
ps.b: ঠিক তা নয়।

ps.e: Different studies count cycling trips in different ways, so the exact share of people who cycle to work or school depends on who you ask.
ps.b: বিভিন্ন গবেষণা সাইকেল যাত্রা বিভিন্নভাবে গণনা করে, তাই কাজে বা স্কুলে সাইকেলে কতজন যায় তার সঠিক অনুপাত নির্ভর করে আপনি কাকে জিজ্ঞেস করছেন তার ওপর।

ps.e: But the main lesson is clear.
ps.b: কিন্তু মূল শিক্ষাটি স্পষ্ট।

ps.e: Copenhagen did not become a cycling city by accident.
ps.b: কোপেনহেগেন কাকতালীয়ভাবে সাইকেলের শহর হয়ে ওঠেনি।

ps.e: It became one because ordinary people asked for it, and because the city finally listened.
ps.b: এটি তা হয়ে উঠেছে কারণ সাধারণ মানুষ তা চেয়েছিল, এবং শহর শেষ পর্যন্ত তাদের কথা শুনেছিল।

cmp/4.title: An Animal with Nine Brains? Not Quite
p: Meet an animal that has three hearts, blue blood and arms that seem to think for themselves. It sounds like something from a film, but it is simply an octopus.

Start with the heart. An octopus does not have one, it has three. The biggest pumps blood around the body. The two smaller ones push blood through the gills, where the animal collects oxygen from the water. Hearts, in other words, are not the only strange thing about this creature.

Then there is the blood. It is blue, not red. Our blood is red because it uses a chemical with iron in it to carry oxygen. The octopus uses a different chemical, one with copper in it, and that chemical turns the blood blue. It works especially well in cold water where there is not much oxygen, which is why one Antarctic species carries even more of it than the others.

The most surprising part is the brain, or rather, the brains. Only about ten per cent of an octopus's nerve cells are in its head. Around sixty per cent are in its arms. Scientists say that each arm effectively has its own little brain. That is where the popular idea of "nine brains" comes from. It is not exactly true, but it helps us picture how independent those arms can be. An arm can even sense light when it is too dark for the eyes.
All this brain power is put to use. Octopuses have good memories and can tell people apart. They solve puzzles. Some have been seen using tools.
Changing colour is another talent, but it comes at a cost. Changing the colour of the skin uses a lot of energy, so an octopus does not do it for no reason.

You might think an animal this clever would live a long time. It does not. Most octopuses live for about a year. A Giant Pacific octopus may reach five years, which is exceptional. Most die soon after reproducing.

It is a short life, but a remarkable one. For scientists, the octopus is a reminder that intelligence can look very different from our own, and that it may have evolved in a body that is completely unlike ours.

q.q: What is the best title for this passage?
q.e: The passage describes the octopus's three hearts, blue blood and spread-out brain.
o: A. Why octopuses live in cold water
B. The unusual body and brain of the octopus
C. How octopuses protect themselves from enemies
D. How scientists train octopuses

q.q: An octopus has three hearts.
q.e: Paragraph 2 says it has three hearts, not one.

q.q: Octopus blood is blue because it uses a chemical with iron in it.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says the chemical contains copper, not iron.

q.q: About sixty per cent of an octopus's nerve cells are in its ____.
According to the passage, what can an octopus arm do in the dark?
q.e: Paragraph 4 says an arm can sense light when it is too dark for the eyes.
o: A. Change colour
B. Open a container
C. Make blue blood
D. Sense light

q.q: Changing colour costs the octopus a lot of energy.
Giant Pacific octopuses are the cleverest of all octopuses.
q.e: The passage only says they can live up to five years, not that they are the cleverest.

q.q: Why does the writer say "nine brains" is "not exactly true"?
q.e: The writer explains that most nerve cells are in the arms, so the idea is a helpful picture, not a literal fact.
o: A. Because octopuses have no brain at all, only nerve cells in their arms
B. Because octopuses have only one heart and one brain
C. Because the arms have nerve cells but are not truly separate brains
D. Because scientists have never been able to count them

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 3?
o: A. Octopuses need blue blood because they live deep in the sea, where the water is very warm.
B. Octopus blood is red, like ours, but it carries much more oxygen to the arms and the brain.
C. Octopus blood is blue because it uses a chemical with copper, which works well in cold water.
D. Blue blood is the reason why octopuses are so intelligent, since it feeds the brain more quickly.
q.e: Paragraph 3 explains that octopus blood is blue because a copper-based chemical carries the oxygen, and that this works especially well in cold water.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 7?
o: A. Giant Pacific octopuses live longer than any other animal in the sea, and they die very old.
B. Octopuses are clever, but most live only about a year and die soon after reproducing.
C. Octopuses stop growing after one year.
D. Octopuses live a long time because they are so clever.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says that although octopuses are clever, most live about a year, and a five-year life is exceptional.

q.q: About sixty per cent of an octopus's nerve cells are in its arms. According to paragraph 4, what is the result of this?
o: A. The octopus has nine real brains.
B. The octopus needs a larger head.
C. The octopus cannot move its arms quickly.
D. Each arm effectively has its own little brain.
q.e: Paragraph 4 says that, because so many nerve cells are in the arms, each arm effectively has its own little brain.

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
o: A. Octopuses are unusual animals, with three hearts, blue blood and arms that act almost independently, and they show a very different kind of intelligence.
B. Octopuses are intelligent only because they have so many hearts, and for no other reason that scientists have found, and they cannot learn.
C. Octopuses are dangerous animals that attack divers in cold water, and they are hard to study because they hide.
D. Octopuses are the longest-living animals in the sea and they grow slowly.
q.e: The passage describes the octopus's hearts, blood, brains and intelligence, and ends by saying intelligence can look very different from ours.

ps.e: Meet an animal that has three hearts, blue blood and arms that seem to think for themselves.
ps.b: এমন একটি প্রাণীর সঙ্গে পরিচিত হও, যার তিনটি হৃদয়, নীল রক্ত এবং এমন কয়েকটি বাহু আছে যা যেন নিজেরাই ভাবতে পারে।

ps.e: It sounds like something from a film, but it is simply an octopus.
ps.b: শুনে মনে হয় কোনো সিনেমার গল্প, কিন্তু এটি আসলে কেবল একটি অক্টোপাস।

ps.e: Start with the heart.
ps.b: হৃদয় দিয়েই শুরু করা যাক।

ps.e: An octopus does not have one, it has three.
ps.b: অক্টোপাসের একটি হৃদয় নেই, আছে তিনটি।

ps.e: The biggest pumps blood around the body.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে বড়টি শরীর জুড়ে রক্ত পাম্প করে।

ps.e: The two smaller ones push blood through the gills, where the animal collects oxygen from the water.
ps.b: ছোট দুটি রক্তকে ফুলকার ভেতর দিয়ে ঠেলে দেয়, যেখানে প্রাণীটি পানি থেকে অক্সিজেন সংগ্রহ করে।

ps.e: Hearts, in other words, are not the only strange thing about this creature.
ps.b: অর্থাৎ, হৃদয়ই এই প্রাণীর একমাত্র অদ্ভুত বিষয় নয়।

ps.e: Then there is the blood.
ps.b: তারপর আছে রক্ত।

ps.e: It is blue, not red.
ps.b: এটি লাল নয়, নীল।

ps.e: Our blood is red because it uses a chemical with iron in it to carry oxygen.
ps.b: আমাদের রক্ত লাল, কারণ অক্সিজেন বহন করতে এটি লোহাযুক্ত একটি রাসায়নিক ব্যবহার করে।

ps.e: The octopus uses a different chemical, one with copper in it, and that chemical turns the blood blue.
ps.b: অক্টোপাস ব্যবহার করে ভিন্ন একটি রাসায়নিক, যাতে তামা আছে, আর সেই রাসায়নিকই রক্তকে নীল করে।

ps.e: It works especially well in cold water where there is not much oxygen, which is why one Antarctic species carries even more of it than the others.
ps.b: এটি বিশেষভাবে ভালো কাজ করে ঠান্ডা পানিতে যেখানে অক্সিজেন কম থাকে, আর সে কারণেই অ্যান্টার্কটিকার একটি প্রজাতি অন্যদের চেয়ে আরও বেশি পরিমাণে এটি বহন করে।

ps.e: The most surprising part is the brain, or rather, the brains.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে বিস্ময়কর অংশ হলো মস্তিষ্ক, কিংবা বলা ভালো, মস্তিষ্কগুলো।

ps.e: Only about ten per cent of an octopus's nerve cells are in its head.
ps.b: অক্টোপাসের স্নায়ুকোষের মাত্র প্রায় দশ শতাংশ থাকে মাথায়।

ps.e: Around sixty per cent are in its arms.
ps.b: প্রায় ষাট শতাংশ থাকে বাহুগুলোতে।

ps.e: Scientists say that each arm effectively has its own little brain.
ps.b: বিজ্ঞানীরা বলেন, প্রতিটি বাহুর কার্যত নিজস্ব একটি ছোট মস্তিষ্ক আছে।

ps.e: That is where the popular idea of "nine brains" comes from.
ps.b: এখান থেকেই "নয়টি মস্তিষ্ক" কথাটির জনপ্রিয় ধারণা এসেছে।

ps.e: It is not exactly true, but it helps us picture how independent those arms can be.
ps.b: এটি পুরোপুরি সত্য নয়, কিন্তু এটি আমাদের বুঝতে সাহায্য করে বাহুগুলো কতটা স্বাধীন হতে পারে।

ps.e: An arm can even sense light when it is too dark for the eyes.
ps.b: এমনকি যখন চোখের জন্য খুব অন্ধকার, তখনও একটি বাহু আলো টের পেতে পারে।

ps.e: All this brain power is put to use.
ps.b: এই সমস্ত মস্তিষ্কশক্তি কাজে লাগানো হয়।

ps.e: Octopuses have good memories and can tell people apart.
ps.b: অক্টোপাসের স্মৃতিশক্তি ভালো এবং তারা মানুষকে আলাদা করে চিনতে পারে।

ps.e: They solve puzzles.
ps.b: তারা ধাঁধার সমাধান করে।

ps.e: Some have been seen using tools.
ps.b: কয়েকটিকে হাতিয়ার ব্যবহার করতেও দেখা গেছে।

ps.e: Changing colour is another talent, but it comes at a cost.
ps.b: রং বদলানো আরেকটি দক্ষতা, কিন্তু এর একটি মূল্য দিতে হয়।

ps.e: Changing the colour of the skin uses a lot of energy, so an octopus does not do it for no reason.
ps.b: ত্বকের রং বদলাতে প্রচুর শক্তি লাগে, তাই অক্টোপাস অকারণে এটি করে না।

ps.e: You might think an animal this clever would live a long time.
ps.b: তুমি ভাবতে পারো, এত বুদ্ধিমান একটি প্রাণী দীর্ঘদিন বাঁচবে।

ps.e: It does not.
ps.b: কিন্তু বাঁচে না।

ps.e: Most octopuses live for about a year.
ps.b: বেশিরভাগ অক্টোপাস প্রায় এক বছর বাঁচে।

ps.e: A Giant Pacific octopus may reach five years, which is exceptional.
ps.b: একটি জায়ান্ট প্যাসিফিক অক্টোপাস পাঁচ বছর পর্যন্ত বাঁচতে পারে, যা ব্যতিক্রমী।

ps.e: Most die soon after reproducing.
ps.b: বেশিরভাগই বংশবৃদ্ধির কিছুদিন পরেই মারা যায়।

ps.e: It is a short life, but a remarkable one.
ps.b: জীবনটি ছোট, কিন্তু অসাধারণ।

ps.e: For scientists, the octopus is a reminder that intelligence can look very different from our own, and that it may have evolved in a body that is completely unlike ours.
ps.b: বিজ্ঞানীদের কাছে অক্টোপাস একটি স্মারক যে বুদ্ধিমত্তা আমাদের থেকে সম্পূর্ণ আলাদা দেখতে হতে পারে, এবং তা এমন এক শরীরে বিকশিত হয়ে থাকতে পারে যা আমাদের শরীরের থেকে একেবারেই অন্যরকম।

cmp/21.title: When the Reef Turns White
cmp/21.src: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority; NOAA
p: Picture a diver swimming over a reef in the middle of a warm summer. Below her, the coral should be glowing in shades of brown, green and gold. Instead, patch after patch is a ghostly white, as though someone had poured bleach across the seabed. Nothing has been painted. Nothing has been poisoned. The reef is simply starving.

To understand why, it helps to know what coral actually is. Corals are animals, not plants, and they live in a partnership. Inside their soft tissue are tiny algae called zooxanthellae, which use sunlight to make food and share most of it with their hosts. In return, the coral gives the algae a safe place to live. The algae also provide the colour. A healthy reef is bright because of the guests living in it.

The partnership has one weakness: it works only within a narrow range of conditions. Corals already live close to their upper temperature limit during an ordinary summer. When the water becomes hotter than normal for long enough, especially during a marine heatwave, the stress builds up until the coral expels its algae. Once they are gone, the white skeleton is visible through the transparent tissue, and the coral loses its main source of food. This is what scientists call bleaching.

Heat is the leading cause, but not the only one. Water that is too cold, a sudden fall in salinity after heavy rain, pollution, or even long exposure to air at very low tides can all produce the same result. The common thread is stress. The coral reacts by sending its partners away.

Here is the important part, and the reason the story is not completely grim: bleaching is not the same as death. If the water returns to normal temperatures quickly enough, the algae slowly move back into the tissue, the colour returns, and the coral recovers. The danger lies in time. A coral that stays bleached for too long, or that is hit again before it has recovered, may simply starve. Storms such as cyclones can add to the damage.

Even then, a reef can come back, although the process is slow. In places where there is little further disturbance, a reef usually re-establishes itself within ten to fifteen years. That is a long time to wait, and it is useful only if the next heatwave does not arrive too soon.

This is exactly what worries scientists. On Australia's Great Barrier Reef, mass bleaching was recorded in 1998 and again in 2002. More recently, the gaps between events have become much shorter. Serious episodes were recorded in 2016 and 2017, followed by widespread bleaching in 2020 and 2022. In 2024, the reef experienced its fifth mass bleaching event, and this time every region was affected. A smaller event followed in 2025.

Notice something about that list. Some of those years, such as 2022, were La Niña years, which are usually cooler. Bleaching happened anyway. The pattern suggests that the old idea of a reef having a quiet decade to heal is slowly disappearing.

None of this means the reef is lost. Many corals survive each event, and recovery is real. But the margin for error is shrinking. For the reef, the question is no longer whether another heatwave will come. It is whether the corals will have enough time to recover from the last one.

q.q: What is the main purpose of the passage?
q.e: The passage explains the cause of bleaching, shows that recovery is possible, and then focuses on the shorter gaps between events.
o: A. To argue that the algae in coral are harmful to the reef
B. To prove that coral reefs are already dead and cannot be saved
C. To describe the best methods for diving on reefs and taking photographs
D. To explain how coral bleaching happens and why repeated events are a concern

q.q: Corals are plants that depend on sunlight.
q.e: Paragraph 2 says corals are animals, not plants.

q.q: Coral bleaching can be caused by water that is too cold.
q.e: Paragraph 4 lists cold water as one possible cause.

q.q: When the algae leave, the coral loses its main source of ____.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says the coral loses its main source of food.

q.q: What usually happens if the water returns to normal temperatures quickly enough?
q.e: Paragraph 5 says the algae slowly move back and the coral recovers.
o: A. The reef moves to deeper water
B. The coral dies slowly
C. New algae of a different type take over
D. The algae return and the coral recovers

q.q: A reef that is left alone usually re-establishes itself within ten to fifteen years.
q.e: Paragraph 6 gives this time range for places with little further disturbance.

q.q: The Great Barrier Reef was bleached only in warm El Niño years.
q.e: Paragraph 8 notes that 2022 was a cooler La Niña year, yet bleaching still happened.

q.q: What does the writer suggest about the gaps between bleaching events?
q.e: Paragraph 7 says the gaps have become shorter and the final paragraph worries about recovery time.
o: A. They are always exactly ten years, so reefs can plan for them
B. They are getting shorter, leaving corals less time to recover
C. They no longer matter, because corals now recover in a single year
D. They depend on cyclones only, and not on the heat of the sea

q.q: Scientists have proved that bleaching can be stopped completely by planting new corals.
q.e: The passage does not mention planting new corals.

q.q: In paragraph 9, the phrase "margin for error" most nearly means:
q.e: The writer means that there is less and less safe space before damage becomes permanent.
o: A. the amount of room to make mistakes safely
B. the cost of repairing a reef after a storm
C. the edge of a reef where the sea becomes deeper
D. a list of mistakes that divers have made on reefs

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 3?
o: A. The partnership works only in a narrow range of conditions, so very hot water makes coral expel its algae and turn white.
B. Coral turns white only when the water is polluted by farms and cities, and heat has no part in it, according to scientists who study reefs.
C. Coral skeletons are naturally transparent and can be seen through the tissue.
D. Bleaching is a natural process that happens in every summer, and it does little harm to the reef.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says the coral and algae partnership has a narrow limit, and heat stress makes the coral expel the algae, which is bleaching.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 8?
o: A. The Great Barrier Reef was bleached in every year since 2002, and none of it has recovered.
B. The old idea that a reef gets a quiet decade to heal is disappearing, because bleaching has happened even in cooler years.
C. Scientists can now predict exactly when and where bleaching will occur, so reefs can be protected from it every year.
D. La Niña years are always safe for coral reefs, because the water stays cool all year.
q.e: Paragraph 8 notes that bleaching happened even in La Niña years, so a quiet decade to heal can no longer be taken for granted.

q.q: According to paragraph 3, why does a coral expel its algae?
o: A. Because it no longer needs sunlight to live on the reef.
B. Because the algae have grown too large for the coral to hold, so the coral pushes them out into the sea.
C. Because the water around it has become too salty.
D. Because it is stressed by water that stays hotter than normal for long enough.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says that when the water is hotter than normal for long enough, stress builds up until the coral expels its algae.

q.q: In paragraph 5, the writer says "bleaching is not the same as death". What does this mean?
o: A. Dead coral cannot be bleached, because it has no colour.
B. A bleached coral has usually already died, and cannot recover at all.
C. Bleached coral can still recover if conditions improve in time.
D. Corals never die from bleaching, however hot the water becomes.
q.e: The paragraph goes on to say that if the water cools quickly enough the algae return and the coral recovers; the danger is staying bleached too long.

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
o: A. Coral reefs will recover naturally in ten to fifteen years, whatever happens to the climate around them.
B. The Great Barrier Reef has been completely lost, and no coral is left to save.
C. Coral bleaching is caused mostly by heat, and although coral can recover, heatwaves are now coming so often that recovery time is shrinking.
D. The Great Barrier Reef has been completely lost, and scientists say that no coral is left anywhere on it that could be saved.
q.e: The passage explains bleaching, shows that recovery is possible but slow, and warns that events are now closer together.

ps.e: Bleaching happened anyway.
ps.b: তবুও ব্লিচিং হয়েছে।

ps.e: The pattern suggests that the old idea of a reef having a quiet decade to heal is slowly disappearing.
ps.b: এই ধরনটি ইঙ্গিত দেয় যে, সেরে ওঠার জন্য প্রাচীর একটি নির্ঝঞ্ঝাট দশক পাবে এই পুরোনো ধারণাটি ধীরে ধীরে মিলিয়ে যাচ্ছে।

ps.e: None of this means the reef is lost.

ps.e: For the reef, the question is no longer whether another heatwave will come.

cmp/22.title: Why Cities Run Hot
p: Anyone who has walked home through a big city after a hot day knows the feeling. The sun went down hours ago, yet the pavement still seems to give off heat, and the air between the buildings is thick and warm. A few kilometres away, in the fields outside the city, it is already pleasantly cool. This difference is not your imagination. It has a name: the urban heat island.

According to the United States Environmental Protection Agency, daytime temperatures in cities are typically one to seven degrees Fahrenheit higher than in the surrounding countryside. That is roughly between half a degree and four degrees Celsius. At night, the gap is somewhat smaller, at around two to five degrees Fahrenheit, but it matters just as much, because the body gets less relief from the heat of the day. The effect is strongest in large, dense cities and in humid regions.

Why does it happen? The reasons are mostly about what cities are made of. Natural land is covered with soil, plants and water, all of which cool the air. Plants release moisture and give shade. Water evaporates. A city replaces much of this with hard, dry surfaces. Dark roofs and roads absorb sunlight instead of reflecting it, and on a warm day an ordinary roof can become up to sixty-six degrees Fahrenheit hotter than the air around it. Tall buildings and narrow streets trap heat and block the winds that might carry it away. On top of this, cars, air conditioners, factories and buildings all release waste heat. Calm, clear weather makes everything worse.

The consequences go beyond discomfort. Hotter cities use more electricity, because every household turns on the air conditioning at once. The EPA estimates that demand for electricity rises by between one and nine per cent for each two-degree rise in temperature. When that electricity comes from burning fossil fuels, the result is more pollution, and hot, sunny weather also helps ground-level ozone to form. Dirtier air makes the heat harder to bear.

Then there are the human costs. In the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recorded an average of 702 heat-related deaths each year between 2004 and 2018. The people at greatest risk are not random. Older adults, young children, people on low incomes, outdoor workers and those with chronic illness or certain medications are all more vulnerable. Some cannot easily avoid the heat, whether at work or at home.

Even rivers and streams suffer. When rain falls on a hot road, it runs into drains heated by the pavement, and that warm water flows into nearby streams. In some places, temperatures have surged by as much as eighteen degrees Fahrenheit above those in forested areas, which can harm fish and other wildlife.

The encouraging news is that cities are not helpless. Planting trees and other vegetation provides shade and releases moisture. Green roofs cover buildings with plants. Cool roofs and cool pavements use light-coloured or reflective materials that bounce sunlight away instead of absorbing it. Planners can also adapt their cities to heat in other ways, from smarter growth to careful layouts. None of these is a magic cure, but together they give cities a real set of choices.

What stands out is that the heat island is not a natural disaster. It is a product of design choices, which means it can also be changed by design. A city that is willing to plant, paint and plan with heat in mind can make summer easier for its residents, especially for those who suffer most.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
q.e: The passage explains the causes and effects of urban heat islands and then describes solutions.
o: A. Why rural areas have more heat-related deaths than cities, and what can be done about it
B. How to design an air conditioner that uses little power
C. The history of city planning in the modern world
D. Why cities are warmer than the countryside and what can be done about it

q.q: Urban areas are warmer than outlying areas only at night.
q.e: Paragraph 2 says daytime temperatures are one to seven degrees higher and nights two to five degrees higher.

q.q: Dark roofs and roads reflect more sunlight than natural land.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says dark roofs and roads absorb sunlight instead of reflecting it.

q.q: Between 2004 and 2018, the CDC recorded an average of ____ heat-related deaths each year in the United States.
According to paragraph 4, what happens to electricity demand as temperatures rise?
q.e: The EPA estimates demand rises between one and nine per cent for each two-degree increase.
o: A. It stays the same
B. It falls
C. It depends on the season only
D. It rises

q.q: Older adults and outdoor workers are among the groups most at risk.
q.e: Paragraph 5 lists them as more vulnerable.

q.q: Cool roofs are always more expensive than ordinary roofs.
q.e: The passage says most solutions are not expensive but does not compare the cost of cool roofs and ordinary roofs.

q.q: What does the writer mean by "the heat island is not a natural disaster"?
q.e: The final paragraph says it is a product of design choices, so design can also change it.
o: A. It cannot be measured, because the heat changes every day
B. It is caused by human design choices and can be changed
C. It happens only in rural areas, where there are few buildings
D. It is not harmful to people, who soon get used to it

q.q: In paragraph 5, the word "vulnerable" is closest in meaning to:
q.e: The paragraph describes groups who face greater danger from heat.
o: A. easily harmed
B. very rich
C. unusually strong
D. carefully trained

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 3?
o: A. Cities are hotter because hard, dark surfaces absorb heat, there is less shade and moisture, and buildings trap and release heat.
B. Cities are hotter because of the heat from the sun alone, since cities receive more sunlight.
C. Cities are hotter because more people live in them than in the countryside, and the people give out a great deal of heat.
D. Cities are hotter because they are mostly built in warm regions of the world, near the equator.
q.e: Paragraph 3 lists what a city is made of: dark surfaces, fewer plants and water, tall buildings, and waste heat.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 7?
o: A. Only planting trees can reduce the heat island effect in any city, and no other method works.
B. Cities cannot do anything about heat, because buildings cannot be changed once they are built.
C. Cool roofs are better than green roofs in every city and every season of the year.
D. Cities have several useful ways to reduce heat, and none is a cure by itself, but together they help.
q.e: Paragraph 7 lists trees, green roofs, cool roofs and pavements and planning, and says that together they give cities real choices.

q.q: According to paragraph 6, why does the water in nearby streams become warmer?
o: A. Factories pour hot water into the streams from their machines.
B. Streams in cities are always shallow, so they heat up quickly.
C. Rain runs over hot roads into drains heated by the pavement.
D. Rain falls from warmer clouds that form over cities.
q.e: Paragraph 6 explains that rain falling on a hot road runs into drains heated by the pavement, and that warm water flows into streams.

q.q: In paragraph 8, the writer says the heat island "can also be changed by design". What does this mean?
o: A. The problem cannot be solved, because cities are already built.
B. Only architects can solve the problem, because they design the buildings and make the choices.
C. The problem was created by design choices, so different design choices can reduce it.
D. Nature will solve the problem if cities are left alone for many years.
q.e: The writer says the heat island is a product of design choices, which means it can also be changed by design.

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
o: A. Heat islands are a natural disaster that cities cannot control, so people must simply accept the higher heat.
B. Cities are hotter than their surroundings because of how they are built, this harms people and the environment, but cities can reduce it.
C. Air conditioning is the best solution to the heat island effect in all cities, because it cools every street and building.
D. Hot weather is harmful only to older people, so cities do not need to change how they are built or planned.
q.e: The passage explains what the heat island is, why it happens, its costs, and the ways cities can respond.

ps.b: এর কোনোটিই জাদুকরি সমাধান নয়, কিন্তু একসঙ্গে এগুলো শহরগুলোকে সত্যিকারের একগুচ্ছ বিকল্প দেয়।

ps.e: What stands out is that the heat island is not a natural disaster.
ps.b: যে বিষয়টি চোখে পড়ে তা হলো, তাপদ্বীপ কোনো প্রাকৃতিক বিপর্যয় নয়।

ps.e: It is a product of design choices, which means it can also be changed by design.
ps.b: এটি নকশাগত সিদ্ধান্তের ফল, অর্থাৎ নকশার মাধ্যমেই একে বদলানোও সম্ভব।

ps.e: A city that is willing to plant, paint and plan with heat in mind can make summer easier for its residents, especially for those who suffer most.
ps.b: যে শহর গাছ লাগাতে, রং করতে এবং গরমের কথা মাথায় রেখে পরিকল্পনা করতে রাজি, সে তার বাসিন্দাদের জন্য গ্রীষ্ম সহজ করে তুলতে পারে, বিশেষ করে তাদের জন্য যারা সবচেয়ে বেশি কষ্ট পায়।

cmp/23.title: The Night Shift of the Brain
cmp/23.src: Abel, Havekes, Saletin and Walker; PubMed Central
p: Most students know the temptation. The exam is tomorrow, there is still a whole chapter to revise, and the clock says midnight. Staying awake looks like the sensible choice. But a growing body of research suggests that, for memory at least, it may be exactly the wrong one.

Scientists have long suspected that sleep does something useful for learning. In recent decades, they have started to understand how. The evidence points to two separate jobs. Before you learn something, sleep seems to prepare the brain to take in new information. After you learn it, sleep helps to strengthen the memory so that it lasts. Researchers call this second job "consolidation".

Start with the first job. In one human study, a single night without sleep reduced the activity of the hippocampus, a part of the brain that is central to forming new memories. Volunteers who had been kept awake found it harder to learn, and their brain scans reflected this. A short daytime nap, however, restored much of the lost ability. The effect was linked to a lighter stage of sleep that produces quick bursts of brain activity known as spindles.

Now consider the second job, which is better studied in animals. When a rat explores a new maze, certain brain cells fire in a particular order. During later sleep, the same pattern appears again, but this time compressed into a much shorter time, in some reports about twenty times faster. It is as if the brain were replaying the day at high speed. These replays seem to occur together with short waves of activity in the hippocampus called sharp-wave ripples. When researchers removed the ripples, learning suffered.

Humans show similar signs, although the evidence is less direct. People who spend more time in deep, slow-wave sleep after learning usually remember more the next morning. When scientists gently boosted the slow waves with stimulation, recall improved. In other experiments, a smell or sound that was linked to what people had studied was presented again during deep sleep, and their memory of that material became better. Older adults, who have less deep sleep, showed weaker overnight improvement.

It would be easy to turn all this into simple advice, "sleep more and you will remember everything". The researchers themselves are more careful. Much of the detailed evidence comes from rodents, and most of the human findings show a link rather than proving cause. The replay seen in rats is also quite weak, with only a small fraction of brain cells taking part. And there are puzzles still to be solved. Studies in rodents often highlight one stage of sleep, while studies in humans focus on another, and nobody can yet explain why.

So what should a tired student do? The research does not give a recipe, but it does suggest a direction. Learning is not finished when you close the book. Part of it happens afterwards, in the dark, while you are doing nothing at all. Cutting that time short to cram a few more pages may cost more than it gains.

q.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
q.e: The passage describes how sleep helps before learning (encoding) and after learning (consolidation).
o: A. Sleep appears to support both learning new information and keeping it in memory
B. Students should never study at night, because sleep is more important than exams
C. Memory has nothing to do with the hippocampus or with the sleeping brain
D. Rats are better at learning than humans, so human memory is not worth studying

q.q: A short nap can restore some of the ability to learn that is lost after a night without sleep.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says a short daytime nap restored much of the lost ability.

q.q: The replay of brain activity in rats happens at the same speed as in waking life.
q.e: Paragraph 4 says the replay is compressed, in some reports about twenty times faster.

q.q: In one type of study, smells or sounds were presented during deep sleep, and memory of the ____ became better.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says memory of that material became better.

q.q: Why are the researchers careful about turning the findings into simple advice?
q.e: Paragraph 6 explains the limits of the evidence.
o: A. The experiments were all done on humans, but the groups were very small
B. The studies were done a century ago, so the methods are out of date
C. Much of the evidence is from rodents and shows a link rather than proof of cause
D. Sleep has been proved to have no effect on memory in any study

q.q: Older adults, who get less deep sleep, showed weaker overnight improvement in memory.
Taking sleeping pills improves memory in students.
q.e: The passage does not discuss sleeping pills.

q.q: What is the writer's attitude toward cramming late at night?
q.e: The final paragraph says cutting sleep short to cram may cost more than it gains.
o: A. Completely neutral, since it neither helps nor harms learning
B. Strongly in favour of it, because students always remember more
C. Cautious, suggesting it may cost more than it gains
D. Convinced that it never works, whatever the student does

q.q: In paragraph 2, the word "consolidation" refers to:
q.e: The paragraph describes it as strengthening memory so that it lasts.
o: A. a type of exam that students take at the end of the year
B. making a memory stronger and more lasting
C. forgetting information that is no longer needed
D. learning a new language at an early age

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 2?
o: A. Scientists have always understood exactly how sleep works in the brain, so there is nothing left to learn.
B. Sleep helps learning in two ways: it prepares the brain to learn and it strengthens memories afterwards.
C. Learning is possible only when the brain is fully awake, and sleep can only get in the way.
D. Sleep is useful only after you have already learned something new, and it does not help before.
q.e: Paragraph 2 describes two jobs of sleep: preparing the brain before learning and consolidating memories after it.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 4?
o: A. During sleep, a rat's brain seems to replay what it learned, much faster, and stopping this harms learning.
B. Rats dream about food after exploring a maze, so they sleep badly and learn nothing new.
C. Rats forget their mazes when they sleep, so sleep harms learning rather than helping it.
D. Rats sleep much longer after exploring a maze than after rest, and this is the only change that scientists found.
q.e: Paragraph 4 says the pattern of activity from the maze reappears in sleep at a much higher speed, and removing the ripples made learning suffer.

q.q: According to paragraph 3, why did the volunteers who stayed awake find it harder to learn?
o: A. They were too hungry to concentrate on the test.
B. They had been given less time to study the material.
C. They were taking naps during the day, which made them tired when they came to the test.
D. The activity of the hippocampus had been reduced by a night without sleep.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says a night without sleep reduced the activity of the hippocampus, which is central to forming new memories.

q.q: In paragraph 7, the writer says "Learning is not finished when you close the book." What does this mean?
o: A. Books are not the best way to learn, so students should use videos.
B. Students should never stop reading, even when they are tired.
C. Students should study for more hours each day to remember more.
D. The brain continues to work on what you studied afterwards, during sleep.
q.e: The next sentence says part of learning happens afterwards, in the dark, while you are doing nothing at all.

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
o: A. Students should never study late at night, because any lost sleep ruins the memory for the rest of their lives, in every case.
B. Research suggests that sleep helps both learning and memory, but the evidence is not yet complete, so it should be taken carefully.
C. Scientists have proved that sleeping for longer always improves memory for every person, young or old.
D. Sleep affects memory only in animals such as rats, and it has no effect on learning in humans at all.
q.e: The passage explains what sleep does for memory, then warns that the evidence is incomplete, and ends with a careful suggestion.

ps.b: আরও কয়েক পৃষ্ঠা মুখস্থ করতে সেই সময়টা ছোট করে ফেললে হয়তো যা পাওয়া যায় তার চেয়ে বেশি হারাতে হয়।

cmp/61.title: The Slow Emergency
p: Few medical emergencies arrive without warning, and fewer still announce themselves so quietly. Antimicrobial resistance, the process by which bacteria evolve to survive the drugs designed to kill them, has no single dramatic moment. There is no outbreak map to watch, no ward closed overnight. Instead, there is a slow accumulation of cases in which a treatment that should have worked, did not.

The scale is difficult to grasp. The World Health Organization reports that bacterial resistance was associated with more than 4.7 million deaths worldwide in 2021. The word "associated" is chosen with care. It signals that resistance played a part in these deaths, which is not quite the same as saying it was the only cause, and the figure should be read with that distinction in mind. Nevertheless, it points to a burden that health systems cannot ignore.

At its heart, the problem is one of natural selection operating at an unnatural speed. Whenever an antibiotic is used, most of the susceptible bacteria die, but any that carry a mutation allowing them to survive are left to multiply in the space that has been cleared. The more frequently the drug is used, and the less carefully, the more often this selection takes place. This is why the WHO describes misuse and overuse of antibiotics as one of the main drivers of resistance, whether the medicine is taken for a viral illness against which it has no effect, or stopped halfway through a course.

Yet it would be a mistake to place the whole responsibility on patients and doctors. The WHO identifies a wider set of conditions that allow resistant bacteria to flourish: poor access to clean water, sanitation and hygiene; inadequate infection control in homes, hospitals and farms; limited access to vaccines, diagnostic tests and medicines; weak enforcement of the laws that regulate how drugs are sold; and a shortage of new antibiotics in development. In other words, resistance is not only a clinical problem but a social and economic one. Where infections spread easily, more antibiotics are needed, and where the rules on selling them are weak, they are more likely to be used without proper advice.

This is also why the response promoted by the WHO is deliberately broad. Its global action plan for the years 2026 to 2036 is built around what it calls a "One Health" approach, which treats human, animal and environmental health as parts of the same system. The plan sets six objectives: raising awareness and changing behaviour; strengthening surveillance and laboratory networks; preventing infections in the first place; ensuring fair access to medicines together with their appropriate use and safe disposal; encouraging research and innovation; and building the governance and financing needed to sustain all of the above. Countries are expected to turn these principles into national plans, which are then monitored every year.

The targets, however, remain modest in some respects and distant in others. In 2024, the United Nations General Assembly agreed to aim for a ten per cent reduction in deaths associated with bacterial resistance by 2030. A more concrete goal concerns how antibiotics are chosen. The WHO groups them into categories, and the "Access" group, which contains first-choice drugs with a lower risk of promoting resistance, is meant to account for at least seventy per cent of all human antibiotic use by 2030. The current picture falls short. In 2022, Access antibiotics made up only about fifty-three per cent of global use. The "Watch" group, which carries a higher risk of resistance and should be used more selectively, accounted for roughly forty-five per cent, and in nearly a third of countries it represented more than seventy per cent of all antibiotics used.

What these figures cannot show is how quickly things might change. The numbers describe where the world stood in particular years, and they do not forecast what will happen if the targets are missed. Even so, the direction of the evidence is clear enough. Every effective antibiotic is a limited resource, and every unnecessary prescription spends a little of it. The danger is not that medicine will suddenly stop working, but that, year after year, it will work a little less reliably than before, until the routine operation or the ordinary infection once again carries a serious risk.

q.q: Which statement best expresses the central argument of the passage?
q.e: The passage presents resistance as slow-moving, driven by several social and medical causes, and requiring a broad "One Health" response.
o: A. Resistance affects only hospitals in rich countries, so poorer regions face no serious risk
B. Antibiotic resistance is mainly caused by careless patients who do not finish their courses
C. New antibiotics will soon solve the problem, so the world need not change how it uses medicine
D. Antimicrobial resistance is a gradual, multi-factor problem that requires a broad, coordinated response

q.q: The WHO says bacterial resistance was associated with more than 4.7 million deaths in 2021.
The writer argues that the 4.7 million figure shows resistance was the only cause of those deaths.
q.e: Paragraph 2 warns that resistance was one factor among several and that the figure should not be read that way.

q.q: The WHO global action plan is built around a ____ approach, which treats human, animal and environmental health together.
According to the passage, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a condition that helps resistant bacteria to spread?
q.e: Paragraph 4 lists a shortage of new antibiotics as a problem, not an excess.
o: A. Too many new antibiotics being developed
B. Limited access to vaccines and diagnostic tests
C. Poor sanitation
D. Weak enforcement of the laws on selling drugs

q.q: In 2022, "Access" antibiotics made up more than seventy per cent of global antibiotic use.
q.e: Paragraph 6 says they made up only about fifty-three per cent, short of the seventy per cent target.

q.q: The United Nations has set a target of eliminating antibiotic resistance completely by 2030.
q.e: Paragraph 6 says the target is a ten per cent reduction in associated deaths by 2030.

q.q: What does the writer mean by "every unnecessary prescription spends a little of it" in the final paragraph?
q.e: The writer describes antibiotics as a limited resource whose effectiveness is reduced by unnecessary use.
o: A. Prescriptions are expensive for the patient, so every extra one costs the family more money
B. Doctors should be paid less when they prescribe, because each prescription wastes their time
C. Each unneeded antibiotic uses up some of the drug's future effectiveness
D. Antibiotics should only be sold in bulk, so that pharmacies can control how much is used

q.q: Vaccines are more effective than antibiotics at preventing resistance in every case.
q.e: The passage mentions limited access to vaccines as one factor but makes no comparison of effectiveness.

q.q: In paragraph 3, the phrase "natural selection operating at an unnatural speed" suggests that:
q.e: Heavy use of antibiotics speeds up the survival of resistant bacteria, a natural process happening unusually fast.
o: A. scientists are changing the bacteria on purpose in order to test new kinds of medicine
B. evolution is happening faster than usual because of human behaviour
C. nature has stopped working in hospitals, where living things no longer change at all
D. bacteria are becoming extinct because antibiotics are killing every kind of them

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 4?
o: A. New antibiotics are the only solution to resistance, so the wider social and economic conditions need no attention at all.
B. Resistance is caused mainly by poor hygiene in hospitals, and it affects no other part of society.
C. Resistance is a social and economic problem as well as a medical one, because many wider conditions help resistant bacteria spread.
D. Patients and doctors are the only people responsible for resistance, so nobody else needs to act.
q.e: Paragraph 4 says it would be a mistake to blame only patients and doctors, and lists wider conditions, concluding that resistance is also a social and economic problem.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 6?
o: A. The targets have already been met in most countries, so the problem is now under control.
B. The "Watch" group of antibiotics is now rarely used, because doctors have stopped prescribing them.
C. The United Nations has set no targets for antibiotic use, and leaves each country to decide alone.
D. The targets are modest, and current antibiotic use is still far from the goal for the first-choice drugs.
q.e: Paragraph 6 explains the targets and then shows that in 2022 Access antibiotics were only about fifty-three per cent of use, below the seventy per cent goal.

q.q: According to paragraph 3, why does careless use of antibiotics lead to more resistance?
o: A. Careless use makes the medicine more expensive, so fewer patients can afford to finish it.
B. Each use kills the susceptible bacteria and leaves resistant ones free to multiply.
C. Antibiotics cause bacteria to change on purpose, so that they can defend themselves.
D. Patients stop trusting their doctors, and so they take the medicine in the wrong way.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says that when an antibiotic is used, susceptible bacteria die but those with a surviving mutation multiply; the more often and carelessly this happens, the more often selection occurs.

q.q: In paragraph 2, the writer says the word "associated" is "chosen with care". What does the writer mean?
o: A. The WHO wants to avoid frightening the public, so it uses a softer word on purpose.
B. The deaths were caused by something other than resistance, which was only a coincidence.
C. Resistance played a part in the deaths, but the WHO does not claim it was the only cause.
D. The WHO is not certain that the deaths happened, because the records are incomplete.
q.e: The next sentences say that "associated" means resistance played a part, which is not the same as saying it was the only cause.

q.q: Which of the following best describes the writer's attitude to the global response to antibiotic resistance?
o: A. Completely satisfied that the targets will be met, and confident in the plans of every country
B. Uninterested in the problem, and unwilling to say whether the plans can work or not
C. Angry and critical of every country, with no praise for any of the plans or the people
D. Concerned but balanced: the plans are broad, yet the progress so far falls short
q.e: The writer describes the broad plans fairly, but points out that targets are modest or distant and current use falls short, ending with a serious warning.

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
o: A. Antibiotic resistance is a quiet but serious threat, caused by many factors, and the global plans so far are broad but still short of their targets.
B. Antibiotics have stopped working completely, so doctors in every country now have no way to treat any infection at all.
C. The WHO has solved the problem of resistance with its plan for 2026 to 2036, and no more action is needed.
D. Only patients who misuse antibiotics are responsible for resistance, so the global plans are not needed and should be dropped by every country.
q.e: The passage covers the scale of the problem, its causes, the WHO response, the gap between targets and reality, and the risk if nothing changes.
