ps.e: The WHO groups them into categories, and the "Access" group, which contains first-choice drugs with a lower risk of promoting resistance, is meant to account for at least seventy per cent of all human antibiotic use by 2030.
ps.b: ডব্লিউএইচও এগুলোকে ভাগে ভাগ করে, আর "অ্যাকসেস" গ্রুপ, যাতে আছে প্রথম পছন্দের এমন ওষুধ যেগুলোতে রেজিস্ট্যান্স বাড়ানোর ঝুঁকি কম, ২০৩০ সালের মধ্যে মানুষের মোট অ্যান্টিবায়োটিক ব্যবহারের অন্তত সত্তর শতাংশ হওয়ার কথা।

ps.e: The current picture falls short.
ps.b: বর্তমান চিত্র এর থেকে কম।

ps.e: In 2022, Access antibiotics made up only about fifty-three per cent of global use.
ps.b: ২০২২ সালে বৈশ্বিক ব্যবহারে অ্যাকসেস অ্যান্টিবায়োটিক ছিল মাত্র প্রায় তিপ্পান্ন শতাংশ।

ps.e: The "Watch" group, which carries a higher risk of resistance and should be used more selectively, accounted for roughly forty-five per cent, and in nearly a third of countries it represented more than seventy per cent of all antibiotics used.
ps.b: "ওয়াচ" গ্রুপ, যাতে রেজিস্ট্যান্সের ঝুঁকি বেশি এবং যা আরও বাছাই করে ব্যবহার করা উচিত, ছিল প্রায় পঁয়তাল্লিশ শতাংশ, আর প্রায় এক-তৃতীয়াংশ দেশে এটি মোট ব্যবহৃত অ্যান্টিবায়োটিকের সত্তর শতাংশেরও বেশি ছিল।

ps.e: What these figures cannot show is how quickly things might change.
ps.b: এই সংখ্যাগুলো যা দেখাতে পারে না তা হলো, পরিস্থিতি কত দ্রুত বদলাতে পারে।

ps.e: The numbers describe where the world stood in particular years, and they do not forecast what will happen if the targets are missed.
ps.b: সংখ্যাগুলো বলে নির্দিষ্ট বছরগুলোতে বিশ্ব কোথায় দাঁড়িয়ে ছিল, আর লক্ষ্য পূরণ না হলে কী ঘটবে তার পূর্বাভাস দেয় না।

ps.e: Even so, the direction of the evidence is clear enough.
ps.b: তবুও প্রমাণের দিকটি যথেষ্ট পরিষ্কার।

ps.e: Every effective antibiotic is a limited resource, and every unnecessary prescription spends a little of it.
ps.b: প্রতিটি কার্যকর অ্যান্টিবায়োটিক একটি সীমিত সম্পদ, আর প্রতিটি অপ্রয়োজনীয় প্রেসক্রিপশন তার একটু একটু করে খরচ করে ফেলে।

ps.e: The danger is not that medicine will suddenly stop working, but that, year after year, it will work a little less reliably than before, until the routine operation or the ordinary infection once again carries a serious risk.
ps.b: বিপদ এটা নয় যে ওষুধ হঠাৎ কাজ করা বন্ধ করে দেবে, বরং এই যে বছরের পর বছর এটি আগের চেয়ে একটু কম নির্ভরযোগ্যভাবে কাজ করবে, যতক্ষণ না নিয়মিত অস্ত্রোপচার বা সাধারণ সংক্রমণ আবার গুরুতর ঝুঁকি বহন করে।

cmp/62.title: Who Owns the Signal?
p: Every time a phone finds the quickest route across an unfamiliar city, it relies on a chain of decisions that began with an accident of listening. In October 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, and across the world radio operators tuned in to its regular beeps. At MIT, scientists noticed that the pitch of the signal rose as the satellite approached and fell as it moved away, a familiar effect of motion on waves. The significance was not that the satellite could be heard. It was that, if its path was known precisely, the change in the signal could be used in reverse: a receiver on the ground could work out where it was.

This insight turned out to be the foundation of satellite navigation. In 1959, the United States Navy launched Transit, a forerunner of the modern system, which could fix a position to within roughly twenty-five metres. By present standards that sounds crude. Nevertheless, it demonstrated that navigation from orbit was possible, and the armed services began to develop their own competing versions. The turning point came in 1974, when the Air Force's NAVSTAR system was created to merge these separate efforts into a single military programme. A prototype satellite followed in 1978.

From the beginning, however, the system raised a question that engineering alone could not answer: who should be allowed to use it? The answer built into the design was a compromise. The signal was divided into two kinds. American and approved allied forces received a stronger, more precise version, while commercial users received a deliberately degraded one, a practice known as selective availability. Accuracy, in other words, was treated as a strategic asset, to be rationed according to who was asking.

It took a tragedy to change the political climate. In 1983, a Korean airliner, Flight 007, strayed into Soviet airspace and was shot down. Partly in response, President Reagan promised that the coarser civilian signal would be offered to the world free of charge, once the system was fully working. That day was still twelve years away. In the meantime, the military value of the technology was proved in combat. During the Gulf War in 1991, when only nineteen satellites were in orbit, GPS provided between nineteen and twenty hours of three-dimensional coverage each day. It was heavily used, even though it was not yet complete.

Full operation came on 27 April 1995, with twenty-four satellites serving both military and civilian users. Yet the pledge was only partly fulfilled, because selective availability remained in force. Civilian receivers were allowed to work, but they were not allowed to work well. This changed in the year 2000, when President Clinton ordered the deliberate degradation to be switched off. Seven years later, President George W. Bush went further by agreeing to remove the ability to restore it from the requirements for the next generation of satellites. The system's owners, in effect, had given up the option of reversing course.

What makes this history instructive is the gap between the original purpose of the technology and its eventual role. GPS was designed for military navigation. Its civilian value, from aviation to mapping to the phones in our pockets, was largely a by-product, one that could be encouraged or restricted by decisions made in Washington. The long delay before the full signal was released suggests that the choice was not obvious to those who made it. Security concerns pointed one way, and the growing commercial potential pointed the other.

The story does not end there. The programme approved in 2000 for a third generation of satellites led, in 2008, to a contract with Lockheed Martin, and the first of these new spacecraft reached orbit in 2018. The technology continues to improve, but the central lesson has not changed. A navigation signal that billions of people treat as a natural feature of the world is, in fact, the product of political decisions about access, and those decisions were far from inevitable.

q.q: What is the main point of the passage?
q.e: The passage traces both the technology and the political decisions about civilian access.
o: A. Selective availability was never removed, so civilians still receive a weaker signal today
B. GPS was invented to help tourists find their way, and the military only used it afterwards
C. The history of GPS shows that decisions about who could use it were as important as the technology
D. Sputnik was the most important satellite ever launched, and GPS grew directly from its design

q.q: MIT scientists noticed that the pitch of Sputnik's signal changed as it moved.
Transit, launched in 1959, was accurate to within about twenty-five metres.
The practice of giving civilians a less precise signal was known as ____ availability.
What event led President Reagan to promise a free civilian signal?
q.e: Paragraph 4 says he promised this partly in response to the 1983 incident.
o: A. The war in the Gulf, which showed that civilians needed a precise signal
B. The shooting down of Korean Air Flight 007
C. The creation of NAVSTAR, which led the president to open the system
D. The launch of Sputnik, which made the United States promise free access

q.q: GPS became fully operational with twenty-four satellites in 1995.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says full operation came on 27 April 1995 with twenty-four satellites.

q.q: Selective availability was ended in 1995, as soon as GPS became fully operational.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says it remained in force until 2000.

q.q: What does the writer suggest in paragraph 6 about the "long delay" before the full signal was released?
q.e: The writer says security concerns pointed one way and commercial potential the other.
o: A. The delay was caused by lack of satellites only
B. Engineers could not solve the technical problem of the signal
C. Nobody cared about civilian users
D. The decision was difficult because of competing concerns

q.q: Lockheed Martin built every GPS satellite launched before 2000.
q.e: The passage only mentions Lockheed Martin in connection with the 2008 contract.

q.q: In paragraph 5, the word "degradation" most nearly means:
q.e: The signal was intentionally made less accurate for civilian users.
o: A. a careful repair of a damaged part
B. the replacement of old equipment
C. a gradual improvement in accuracy
D. deliberate worsening of quality

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 3?
o: A. The system was designed to be used equally by everyone, with no difference in accuracy for any person or for any country.
B. GPS signals were first sent by civilians, and the military joined the system many years later.
C. Engineers could not agree on how accurate the signal should be, so the design was never completed.
D. The system was designed with a compromise: a precise signal for the military and a deliberately less accurate one for civilians.
q.e: Paragraph 3 explains that the signal was divided into two kinds, with a deliberately degraded one for commercial users, called selective availability.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 5?
o: A. GPS became fully operational in 1995, but the civilian signal stayed deliberately degraded until 2000, and later steps made restoring it unlikely.
B. GPS was fully free for civilians from the first day of full operation in 1995, with no limits at all on its accuracy.
C. President Bush brought back selective availability, so the civilian signal became worse again after 2000.
D. The satellites stopped working in 2000, and the civilian signal was lost for several years after that, until new satellites were launched.
q.e: Paragraph 5 describes full operation in 1995, the continued degradation, its end in 2000, and the decision seven years later to remove the ability to restore it.

q.q: According to paragraph 3, why was the civilian signal made less accurate?
o: A. The satellites were too old to give a better signal, and could not be replaced in time.
B. Accuracy was treated as a strategic asset, to be rationed according to who was asking.
C. Civilian receivers could not handle a strong signal, so the signal had to be made weaker.
D. Commercial companies asked for a weaker signal, because it was cheaper for them to use.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says accuracy was treated as a strategic asset, to be rationed according to who was asking.

q.q: In paragraph 5, "the system's owners, in effect, had given up the option of reversing course". What does this mean?
o: A. They had changed the satellites' orbit, so the signal could no longer be made worse.
B. They had decided to close the system, so that nobody would be able to use it again.
C. They had made it practically impossible to go back to the old restricted signal.
D. They had started to charge for the signal, and so lost the right to restrict it.
q.e: By removing the ability to restore the degraded signal from the next generation of satellites, they gave up the chance to return to the earlier policy.

q.q: Which of the following best describes the tone of the passage?
o: A. Analytical and thoughtful, treating GPS as the result of political choices
B. Angry and accusing towards one president, whom the writer blames for every problem
C. Humorous and informal, with jokes about the engineers who built the system
D. Admiring of the military throughout, with no criticism of any decision it made
q.e: The writer explains events and concludes that the technology is the product of political decisions about access, in a calm and analytical way.

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
o: A. GPS stopped improving after the year 2000, because no new decisions were taken about it.
B. Satellite navigation was invented by the Soviet Union after Sputnik, and the system is still controlled by that country today.
C. GPS began from a chance observation of Sputnik, was developed for the military, and became free for civilians through political decisions made over many years.
D. GPS was made available to everyone from the very beginning, with the same accuracy for all users, whether military or civilian, in every country.
q.e: The passage traces GPS from Sputnik to military use, to the slow decisions that gave civilians a good signal.

ps.e: In the meantime, the military value of the technology was proved in combat.
ps.b: ইতিমধ্যে এই প্রযুক্তির সামরিক মূল্য যুদ্ধক্ষেত্রে প্রমাণিত হলো।

ps.e: During the Gulf War in 1991, when only nineteen satellites were in orbit, GPS provided between nineteen and twenty hours of three-dimensional coverage each day.
ps.b: ১৯৯১ সালের উপসাগরীয় যুদ্ধে, যখন কক্ষপথে মাত্র উনিশটি উপগ্রহ ছিল, জিপিএস প্রতিদিন উনিশ থেকে বিশ ঘণ্টা ত্রিমাত্রিক কভারেজ দিয়েছিল।

ps.e: It was heavily used, even though it was not yet complete.
ps.b: এটি ব্যাপকভাবে ব্যবহৃত হয়েছিল, যদিও তখনও তা সম্পূর্ণ হয়নি।

ps.e: Full operation came on 27 April 1995, with twenty-four satellites serving both military and civilian users.
ps.b: পূর্ণ কার্যক্রম শুরু হয় ১৯৯৫ সালের ২৭ এপ্রিল, চব্বিশটি উপগ্রহ নিয়ে, যা সামরিক ও বেসামরিক উভয় ব্যবহারকারীকে সেবা দিত।

ps.e: Yet the pledge was only partly fulfilled, because selective availability remained in force.
ps.b: তবুও প্রতিশ্রুতিটি আংশিকভাবে পূরণ হয়েছিল মাত্র, কারণ সিলেক্টিভ অ্যাভেইলেবিলিটি বলবৎ ছিল।

ps.e: Civilian receivers were allowed to work, but they were not allowed to work well.
ps.b: বেসামরিক গ্রাহক যন্ত্রগুলোকে কাজ করতে দেওয়া হতো, কিন্তু ভালোভাবে কাজ করতে দেওয়া হতো না।

ps.e: This changed in the year 2000, when President Clinton ordered the deliberate degradation to be switched off.
ps.b: এটি বদলায় ২০০০ সালে, যখন প্রেসিডেন্ট ক্লিনটন ইচ্ছাকৃত মান কমানোর ব্যবস্থাটি বন্ধ করার নির্দেশ দেন।

ps.e: Seven years later, President George W. Bush went further by agreeing to remove the ability to restore it from the requirements for the next generation of satellites.
ps.b: সাত বছর পর, প্রেসিডেন্ট জর্জ ডব্লিউ. বুশ আরও এগিয়ে গিয়ে পরবর্তী প্রজন্মের উপগ্রহগুলোর প্রয়োজনীয়তা থেকে তা পুনরায় চালু করার সক্ষমতা বাদ দিতে সম্মত হন।

ps.e: The system's owners, in effect, had given up the option of reversing course.
ps.b: ব্যবস্থাটির মালিকরা কার্যত পেছনে ফেরার বিকল্পটিই ছেড়ে দিয়েছিলেন।

ps.e: What makes this history instructive is the gap between the original purpose of the technology and its eventual role.
ps.b: এই ইতিহাসকে শিক্ষণীয় করে তোলে প্রযুক্তিটির মূল উদ্দেশ্য এবং এর শেষ ভূমিকার মধ্যকার ব্যবধান।

ps.e: GPS was designed for military navigation.
ps.b: জিপিএস তৈরি হয়েছিল সামরিক দিকনির্ণয়ের জন্য।

ps.e: Its civilian value, from aviation to mapping to the phones in our pockets, was largely a by-product, one that could be encouraged or restricted by decisions made in Washington.
ps.b: এর বেসামরিক মূল্য, বিমান চলাচল থেকে মানচিত্র তৈরি, এমনকি আমাদের পকেটের ফোন পর্যন্ত, ছিল মূলত একটি উপজাত, যাকে উৎসাহ দেওয়া বা সীমিত করা যেত ওয়াশিংটনে নেওয়া সিদ্ধান্তের মাধ্যমে।

ps.e: The long delay before the full signal was released suggests that the choice was not obvious to those who made it.
ps.b: পূর্ণ সংকেত ছাড়ার আগের দীর্ঘ বিলম্ব ইঙ্গিত দেয় যে যাঁরা সিদ্ধান্তটি নিয়েছিলেন, তাঁদের কাছে পছন্দটি স্পষ্ট ছিল না।

ps.e: Security concerns pointed one way, and the growing commercial potential pointed the other.
ps.b: নিরাপত্তার উদ্বেগ একদিকে টানছিল, আর ক্রমবর্ধমান বাণিজ্যিক সম্ভাবনা টানছিল অন্যদিকে।

ps.e: The story does not end there.
ps.b: গল্পটি এখানেই শেষ হয় না।

ps.e: The programme approved in 2000 for a third generation of satellites led, in 2008, to a contract with Lockheed Martin, and the first of these new spacecraft reached orbit in 2018.
ps.b: ২০০০ সালে অনুমোদিত তৃতীয় প্রজন্মের উপগ্রহের কর্মসূচিটি ২০০৮ সালে লকহিড মার্টিনের সঙ্গে একটি চুক্তিতে পৌঁছায়, এবং এই নতুন মহাকাশযানগুলোর প্রথমটি ২০১৮ সালের মধ্যে কক্ষপথে পৌঁছানোর আশা করা হয়েছিল।

ps.e: The technology continues to improve, but the central lesson has not changed.
ps.b: প্রযুক্তিটি উন্নত হতে থাকে, কিন্তু কেন্দ্রীয় শিক্ষাটি বদলায়নি।

ps.e: A navigation signal that billions of people treat as a natural feature of the world is, in fact, the product of political decisions about access, and those decisions were far from inevitable.
ps.b: যে নেভিগেশন সংকেতকে কোটি কোটি মানুষ পৃথিবীর একটি প্রাকৃতিক বৈশিষ্ট্য বলে ধরে নেয়, তা আসলে প্রবেশাধিকার নিয়ে রাজনৈতিক সিদ্ধান্তের ফল, এবং সেই সিদ্ধান্তগুলো মোটেও অনিবার্য ছিল না।

cmp/63.title: The Sea That Was Spent
p: Of all the environmental disasters of the twentieth century, few can be seen from space as clearly as this one. The Aral Sea, which sits between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, was once the fourth largest lake in the world. It was fed by two great rivers, the Syr Darya and the Amu Darya, which flowed across the dry plains of Central Asia and pooled in a wide basin. Today, much of it is gone. What remains is a set of smaller, separated waters, and a wide, dry lakebed.

The cause was not an act of nature. In the 1960s, the Soviet Union began a major scheme to divert water from the rivers that fed the lake, in order to irrigate the arid land of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. The aim was to turn desert into fields, above all for cotton. On the terms it set for itself, the plan worked. Crops were grown on land that had been desert. But a lake is a balance of inflow and evaporation, and once most of the inflow was taken away, there was little to stop the water level from falling.

The decline was dramatic. By 2000, the lake was already a small fraction of its extent in 1960. It had divided into two parts: the North, or Small, Aral and the South, or Large, Aral. The southern part later split again into eastern and western lobes, and by 2001 the link between north and south had been cut altogether. Even then, the retreat did not stop. Between 2005 and 2009, a drought reduced the flow of the Amu Darya to the eastern lobe, and the shoreline moved back by large distances. In 2014, the eastern lobe of the South Aral disappeared completely.

The consequences spread far beyond the water itself. As the lake shrank, the remaining water became saltier, and it was polluted by fertiliser and pesticides washed in from the fields. The fisheries that had supported local towns collapsed, and the communities that depended on them collapsed with them. The fishing communities were left with no sea to fish in.

Worse followed. The exposed lakebed was contaminated with agricultural chemicals, and wind lifted dust from it and carried it across the region. The dust was a hazard to public health. It was also salty, and when it settled on farmland it damaged the soil, so that farmers needed ever larger volumes of river water simply to wash the salt away. This created a vicious circle: the water taken from the rivers to grow crops made the lake smaller, and the smaller lake produced the dust that made more water necessary. Meanwhile, the sea itself had once softened the local climate. Without it, winters became colder and summers hotter and drier.

It would be easy to describe the story as one of pure failure, but the picture is more mixed. In 2005, Kazakhstan completed the Kok-Aral dike and dam, which separated the North Aral from the South. The effect on the northern part was striking. Water levels rose significantly between 2005 and 2006, with smaller increases in the following years, and, in the words of NASA's summary, the dam "has led fisheries in the North Aral to rebound". For the people of the northern shore, this was a rare example of a damaged environment being partly repaired within a few years.

The success, however, had a price. The dam also limited the flow of water into the South Aral, which meant that the larger, southern part of the lake was effectively left to its fate. In other words, the rescue of one part of the sea was achieved in part by giving up on another. Seasonal variation continued to affect what remained, and levels fluctuated from year to year between 2009 and 2018, with the effect of spring snowmelt making a visible difference in some years.

What does the Aral Sea teach us? Perhaps, above all, that large-scale environmental decisions are rarely reversible and almost never free of trade-offs. The irrigation scheme brought cotton, but it cost a sea. The dam brought back fish, but it closed off the south. A lake that had existed for a very long time was largely taken apart within a single human lifetime, and the efforts to repair it have been limited, partial and, so far, incomplete.

q.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
q.e: The passage traces the human causes of the lake's shrinkage, its consequences and the mixed results of the dam.
o: A. The Aral Sea has completely recovered, and all the damage has now been repaired
B. Human decisions to divert water caused severe environmental damage, and partial recovery has involved trade-offs
C. Cotton farming is always harmful to the land, and no country should ever grow it
D. The Aral Sea was destroyed by a natural drought that nobody could have prevented or reduced, and so no person is to blame

q.q: The Aral Sea was once the fourth largest lake in the world.
The Soviet Union diverted river water in the 1960s to grow crops such as cotton.
In 2014, the eastern lobe of the South Aral ____.
According to paragraph 5, why did farmers need more river water over time?
q.e: Salty dust degraded the soil, so ever-larger volumes of water were needed for flushing.
o: A. The rivers had become saltier, and so the farmers had to find other rivers
B. The lake had become too deep, so the water had to be taken away
C. Salty dust damaged the soil and the salt had to be washed away
D. The cotton plants grew faster, and needed much more water to do so

q.q: The Kok-Aral dam was completed in 2005.
The dam improved conditions in both the North and the South Aral.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says it limited flow into the South Aral.

q.q: The disappearance of the Aral Sea has increased the number of earthquakes in Central Asia.
q.e: Earthquakes are not mentioned in the passage.

q.q: What does the writer mean by "a vicious circle" in paragraph 5?
q.e: The water taken for crops shrank the lake, which produced the dust, which required more water.
o: A. A circular lake whose shape slowly changed as the water went down
B. A solution that works well, and so is used again and again
C. A political agreement that goes round in a circle between countries
D. A problem that makes itself worse by feeding on its own results

q.q: In paragraph 2, the word "arid" is closest in meaning to:
q.e: The land was dry, which is why irrigation was needed.
o: A. crowded
B. wet
C. cold
D. very dry

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 4?
o: A. The shrinking lake damaged the fishing industry and the communities that depended on it, and the water became saltier and polluted.
B. The fishing industry grew because the lake became smaller, and fish were easier to catch.
C. The lake became larger because of the fertiliser and pesticides that flowed into it from the farms, and fishing improved.
D. The remaining water became fresher and easier to use, so fishing became more successful.
q.e: Paragraph 4 describes the water becoming saltier and polluted, and the fisheries and communities collapsing.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 7?
o: A. The dam saved the whole of the Aral Sea, including the South Aral, and all its fish.
B. Seasonal changes ended in 2009, and the lake has not changed in any way since that time.
C. The dam was a failure that helped nobody, and the North Aral is now as dry as the South.
D. The dam helped the North Aral, but the rescue came at the cost of leaving the South Aral to its fate.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says the success had a price: the dam limited water to the South Aral, so one part was rescued by giving up on another.

q.q: According to paragraph 2, why did the lake's water level fall once the rivers were diverted?
o: A. The rivers changed direction naturally.
B. Less water flowed in, while evaporation continued.
C. Rain stopped falling in Central Asia.
D. The lake was drained by farmers directly with large pumps
q.e: Paragraph 2 says a lake is a balance of inflow and evaporation, and once most of the inflow was taken away there was little to stop the level from falling.

q.q: In paragraph 8, the writer says "The irrigation scheme brought cotton, but it cost a sea." What does this mean?
o: A. The sea was moved to a new place, where cotton could be grown
B. Cotton was more valuable than the sea, so the loss was small
C. The price of growing cotton was the loss of the Aral Sea.
D. Farmers sold the sea to buy cotton from other countries
q.e: The sentence contrasts the benefit (cotton) with the loss (the sea), so the cost of the scheme was the Aral Sea itself.

q.q: Which of the following best describes the writer's attitude to the story of the Aral Sea?
o: A. Balanced: it recognises a partial success while stressing the heavy costs of large decisions.
B. Cheerful and hopeful that everything has been repaired, and that no further harm will come.
C. Uninterested and neutral about the damage, offering no view on who should have acted.
D. Completely critical, with nothing positive to say about any of the repair efforts.
q.e: The writer calls the story "more mixed", gives the dam as a success, but notes its price and ends by saying such decisions are rarely reversible.

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
o: A. The Aral Sea was largely lost because river water was diverted for farming, which caused many harms, and the repair efforts have been only partial.
B. The Aral Sea is the largest lake in the world, and it is shrinking only because of cotton farming.
C. The Aral Sea shrank because of a natural drought that lasted for many years, and nothing could have been done to prevent it or to repair it.
D. The Aral Sea has been fully restored by a dam built in 2005, and fishing has now returned to every part of the lake.
q.e: The passage describes how the sea shrank, what followed, the partial recovery in the north, and the lesson about trade-offs.

ps.b: ২০০৫ থেকে ২০০৯ সালের মধ্যে একটি খরা পূর্ব খণ্ডে আমু দরিয়ার প্রবাহ কমিয়ে দেয়, আর উপকূলরেখা বহুদূর পিছিয়ে যায়।

ps.e: In 2014, the eastern lobe of the South Aral disappeared completely.
ps.b: ২০১৪ সালে দক্ষিণ আরালের পূর্ব খণ্ডটি সম্পূর্ণ অদৃশ্য হয়ে যায়।

ps.e: The consequences spread far beyond the water itself.
ps.b: এর পরিণতি পানি ছাড়িয়ে বহুদূর ছড়িয়ে পড়ে।

ps.e: As the lake shrank, the remaining water became saltier, and it was polluted by fertiliser and pesticides washed in from the fields.
ps.b: হ্রদ ছোট হওয়ার সঙ্গে সঙ্গে অবশিষ্ট পানি আরও লবণাক্ত হয়ে ওঠে, আর ক্ষেত থেকে ধুয়ে আসা সার ও কীটনাশকে তা দূষিত হয়।

ps.e: The fisheries that had supported local towns collapsed, and the communities that depended on them collapsed with them.
ps.b: যে মৎস্যশিল্প স্থানীয় শহরগুলোকে টিকিয়ে রেখেছিল তা ভেঙে পড়ল, আর তার ওপর নির্ভরশীল জনগোষ্ঠীগুলোও তার সঙ্গে ভেঙে পড়ল।

ps.e: The fishing communities were left with no sea to fish in.
ps.b: জেলে সম্প্রদায়গুলোর কাছে মাছ ধরার মতো কোনো সাগরই আর রইল না।

ps.e: Worse followed.
ps.b: এর চেয়েও খারাপ ঘটনা ঘটল।

ps.e: The exposed lakebed was contaminated with agricultural chemicals, and wind lifted dust from it and carried it across the region.
ps.b: উন্মুক্ত হ্রদতল কৃষিজ রাসায়নিক দ্বারা দূষিত ছিল, আর বাতাস সেখান থেকে ধুলো তুলে পুরো অঞ্চলে ছড়িয়ে দিল।

ps.e: The dust was a hazard to public health.
ps.b: ধুলোটি জনস্বাস্থ্যের জন্য একটি বিপদ ছিল।

ps.e: It was also salty, and when it settled on farmland it damaged the soil, so that farmers needed ever larger volumes of river water simply to wash the salt away.
ps.b: এটি লবণাক্তও ছিল, আর যখন তা কৃষিজমিতে জমত, মাটির ক্ষতি করত, ফলে কৃষকদের শুধু লবণ ধুয়ে ফেলার জন্যই নদীর ক্রমশ আরও বেশি পানির প্রয়োজন হতো।

ps.e: This created a vicious circle: the water taken from the rivers to grow crops made the lake smaller, and the smaller lake produced the dust that made more water necessary.
ps.b: এটি এক দুষ্টচক্র তৈরি করল: ফসল ফলাতে নদী থেকে নেওয়া পানি হ্রদকে ছোট করল, আর ছোট হ্রদ সেই ধুলো তৈরি করল যার কারণে আরও পানির প্রয়োজন হলো।

ps.e: Meanwhile, the sea itself had once softened the local climate.
ps.b: এদিকে, সাগরটি একসময় স্থানীয় জলবায়ুকে কোমল রেখেছিল।

ps.e: Without it, winters became colder and summers hotter and drier.
ps.b: তা ছাড়া শীত হয়ে উঠল আরও ঠান্ডা, আর গ্রীষ্ম আরও গরম ও শুষ্ক।

ps.e: It would be easy to describe the story as one of pure failure, but the picture is more mixed.
ps.b: গল্পটিকে নিছক ব্যর্থতার কাহিনি বলে বর্ণনা করা সহজ হতো, কিন্তু চিত্রটি আরও মিশ্র।

ps.e: In 2005, Kazakhstan completed the Kok-Aral dike and dam, which separated the North Aral from the South.
ps.b: ২০০৫ সালে কাজাখস্তান কোক-আরাল বাঁধ ও বাঁধ-প্রাচীর সম্পূর্ণ করে, যা উত্তর আরালকে দক্ষিণ থেকে আলাদা করে দিল।

ps.e: The effect on the northern part was striking.
ps.b: উত্তর অংশের ওপর এর প্রভাব ছিল চোখে পড়ার মতো।

ps.e: Water levels rose significantly between 2005 and 2006, with smaller increases in the following years, and, in the words of NASA's summary, the dam "has led fisheries in the North Aral to rebound".
ps.b: ২০০৫ থেকে ২০০৬ সালের মধ্যে পানির স্তর উল্লেখযোগ্যভাবে বাড়ল, পরবর্তী বছরগুলোতে ছোট ছোট বৃদ্ধি ঘটল, এবং নাসার সারাংশের ভাষায়, বাঁধটি "উত্তর আরালের মৎস্যসম্পদকে ঘুরে দাঁড়াতে সাহায্য করেছে"।

ps.e: For the people of the northern shore, this was a rare example of a damaged environment being partly repaired within a few years.
ps.b: উত্তর তীরের মানুষের জন্য এটি ছিল ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত পরিবেশ কয়েক বছরের মধ্যেই আংশিক মেরামত হওয়ার একটি বিরল উদাহরণ।

ps.e: The success, however, had a price.
ps.b: তবে এই সাফল্যের একটি মূল্য ছিল।

ps.e: The dam also limited the flow of water into the South Aral, which meant that the larger, southern part of the lake was effectively left to its fate.
ps.b: বাঁধটি দক্ষিণ আরালে পানির প্রবাহও সীমিত করে দিল, যার অর্থ হ্রদের বড়, দক্ষিণ অংশটি কার্যত তার নিয়তির হাতে ছেড়ে দেওয়া হলো।

ps.e: In other words, the rescue of one part of the sea was achieved in part by giving up on another.
ps.b: অন্য কথায়, সাগরের একটি অংশকে বাঁচানো হয়েছিল আংশিকভাবে আরেকটি অংশকে ছেড়ে দিয়ে।

ps.e: Seasonal variation continued to affect what remained, and levels fluctuated from year to year between 2009 and 2018, with the effect of spring snowmelt making a visible difference in some years.
ps.b: মৌসুমি পরিবর্তন অবশিষ্টাংশের ওপর প্রভাব ফেলতে থাকল, আর ২০০৯ থেকে ২০১৮ সালের মধ্যে পানির স্তর বছর থেকে বছরে ওঠানামা করল, কিছু বছরে বসন্তের বরফগলা পানির প্রভাব দৃশ্যমান পার্থক্য তৈরি করেছিল।

ps.e: What does the Aral Sea teach us?
ps.b: আরাল সাগর আমাদের কী শেখায়?

ps.e: Perhaps, above all, that large-scale environmental decisions are rarely reversible and almost never free of trade-offs.
ps.b: সম্ভবত সবচেয়ে বেশি এই যে, বড় মাপের পরিবেশগত সিদ্ধান্ত খুব কমই ফেরানো যায় এবং প্রায় কখনোই বিনিময়-মূল্য থেকে মুক্ত থাকে না।

ps.e: The irrigation scheme brought cotton, but it cost a sea.
ps.b: সেচ প্রকল্প তুলা এনেছিল, কিন্তু এর দাম ছিল একটি সাগর।

ps.e: The dam brought back fish, but it closed off the south.
ps.b: বাঁধ মাছ ফিরিয়ে এনেছিল, কিন্তু দক্ষিণকে বন্ধ করে দিয়েছে।

ps.e: A lake that had existed for a very long time was largely taken apart within a single human lifetime, and the efforts to repair it have been limited, partial and, so far, incomplete.
ps.b: যে হ্রদ অনেক দীর্ঘকাল ধরে ছিল তা একটি মানুষের জীবনকালের মধ্যেই বহুলাংশে ভেঙে ফেলা হলো, আর তা মেরামতের প্রচেষ্টা হয়েছে সীমিত, আংশিক এবং এখনও পর্যন্ত অসম্পূর্ণ।

cmp/5.title: The Elephants That Talk Below Our Hearing
cmp/5.src: Cornell Lab of Ornithology; McComb et al.; Foley, Pettorelli and Foley
p: An elephant standing quietly in the grass may look as if it is doing nothing at all. But scientists who study elephants have learned that it may be in the middle of a conversation. Elephants make many sounds that we can hear, such as trumpets, rumbles and roars. Yet some of their most important calls are too low for human ears.

Sounds below about 20 hertz are called infrasound. People cannot hear them, although we sometimes feel a deep rumble in our chest, like the bass at a concert. Elephants can make calls that are even lower than this. These sounds travel very well, because low sounds lose less energy as they move through the air. An infrasound call can carry across the open grassland for several kilometres, so an elephant that is far from its family can still be heard.

Elephants may also listen with their feet. When an elephant makes a deep call, some of the energy goes into the ground and creates tiny vibrations. Researchers have found that elephants can pick up vibrations through their feet and trunks, and they seem to react to them. Scientists think this may help elephants to sense the calls of others that are far away.

Elephant society is led by females. A herd is usually a family: a mother, her sisters, her daughters and their young calves. The oldest and most experienced female, called the matriarch, leads the group. She decides where to go, when to rest and when to run. Male elephants leave the family when they are teenagers and then live alone or in small groups.

Why does the matriarch's age matter? In Amboseli National Park in Kenya, researchers played recordings of calls from elephants of other families. Families led by older matriarchs were better at telling friends from strangers. When the caller was an unknown elephant, these families moved closer together, as if preparing to defend themselves.

Memory also helps in hard times. In Tanzania, a severe drought in 1993 killed many young elephants. Families that were led by older matriarchs, who had lived through an earlier drought, lost fewer calves. Scientists think these experienced females may have remembered where to find food and water when everything nearby had dried up.

Sadly, this knowledge is at risk. Hunters who kill elephants for their ivory often choose the largest animals, because they carry the biggest tusks, and these can include the oldest females. When an old matriarch is killed, her family loses its leader and, with her, a lifetime of knowledge.

So the next time you see an elephant standing quietly, remember that silence may not be silence at all. Elephants are talking, listening and remembering, and we are only beginning to understand the conversation.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
q.e: The passage explains elephant calls, then shows why experienced matriarchs are valuable.
o: A. How elephants find food and water in the wet season
B. Why male elephants prefer to live alone far from the herd
C. How ivory is sold around the world and why it is banned
D. How elephants communicate and why their older females matter

q.q: Humans can hear all of the sounds that elephants make.
q.e: Paragraph 1 says some elephant calls are too low for human ears.

q.q: Low sounds lose more energy than high sounds as they travel through the air.
q.e: Paragraph 2 says low sounds lose less energy as they move.

q.q: An infrasound call can carry across open grassland for several ____.
q.e: Paragraph 2 says an infrasound call can carry for several kilometres.

q.q: According to paragraph 3, how may elephants pick up the calls of distant elephants?
q.e: Paragraph 3 says elephants can pick up vibrations through their feet and trunks.
o: A. Through vibrations in their feet and trunks
B. By watching the sky for clouds and birds
C. By listening to the songs of birds nearby
D. By smelling the wind carried across the land

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 4?
q.e: Paragraph 4 explains that a family of females and calves is led by the matriarch.
o: A. Young calves decide where the whole herd will go, because they are the fastest walkers.
B. Male elephants lead the largest herds, and the females follow them across the land.
C. Elephants never live in groups or families, because each animal looks for its own food.
D. Elephant herds are family groups led by the oldest, most experienced female.

q.q: Male elephants stay with the family for their whole lives.
q.e: Paragraph 4 says males leave the family as teenagers.

q.q: Why did families with older matriarchs move closer together in the Amboseli study?
q.e: Paragraph 5 says they moved closer together when the caller was an unknown elephant.
o: A. They were afraid of the researchers and went away
B. They heard the call of an unknown elephant
C. They wanted to rest
D. They were looking for water

q.q: What can we understand from paragraph 6?
q.e: Families led by older matriarchs lost fewer calves, and scientists think experience helped.
o: A. Drought did not affect the elephants in Tanzania at all
B. Calves can find water without help from their mothers
C. Experience of an earlier drought may have helped some families to survive
D. Younger matriarchs are always better leaders than older ones, in every kind of weather

q.q: Scientists have proved that elephants can predict thunderstorms with their feet.
q.e: The passage does not mention thunderstorms.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 7?
q.e: Paragraph 7 says the largest and oldest females are often killed, so families lose their knowledge.
o: A. Ivory hunting can take away the oldest and most knowledgeable elephants.
B. Old matriarchs are not important to the family.
C. Elephants with big tusks are always healthy and strong.
D. Hunters only ever choose young elephants for their ivory, and so the older ones are safe.

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
q.e: The passage covers infrasound, feet, family leadership, memory and the danger of hunting.
o: A. Elephants are the largest land animals and they eat a great deal of food every day, so they walk far to find it, in groups.
B. Elephants use calls that humans cannot hear, and the oldest females lead their families with knowledge that is now at risk.
C. Elephants are in danger only because of drought and the lack of water in the places where they live.
D. Elephants talk only when they are afraid or in danger.

g.infrasound: অতি নিম্ন কম্পাঙ্কের শব্দ (যা মানুষ শুনতে পায় না)

ps.e: An elephant standing quietly in the grass may look as if it is doing nothing at all.
ps.b: ঘাসের মধ্যে চুপচাপ দাঁড়িয়ে থাকা একটি হাতিকে দেখে মনে হতে পারে সে কিছুই করছে না।

ps.e: But scientists who study elephants have learned that it may be in the middle of a conversation.
ps.b: কিন্তু যেসব বিজ্ঞানী হাতি নিয়ে গবেষণা করেন, তাঁরা জেনেছেন যে সে হয়তো একটি কথোপকথনের মাঝখানেই আছে।

ps.e: Elephants make many sounds that we can hear, such as trumpets, rumbles and roars.
ps.b: হাতি অনেক শব্দ করে যা আমরা শুনতে পাই, যেমন ডাক, গুরুগম্ভীর আওয়াজ ও গর্জন।

ps.e: Yet some of their most important calls are too low for human ears.
ps.b: তবুও তাদের সবচেয়ে গুরুত্বপূর্ণ কিছু ডাক মানুষের কানের জন্য খুব নিচু।

ps.e: Sounds below about 20 hertz are called infrasound.
ps.b: প্রায় ২০ হার্ৎসের নিচের শব্দকে বলা হয় ইনফ্রাসাউন্ড বা অতি নিম্ন শব্দ।

ps.e: People cannot hear them, although we sometimes feel a deep rumble in our chest, like the bass at a concert.
ps.b: মানুষ এগুলো শুনতে পায় না, যদিও আমরা মাঝে মাঝে বুকের ভেতর একটি গভীর কম্পন অনুভব করি, যেমন কনসার্টের বেস সুরে।

ps.e: Elephants can make calls that are even lower than this.
ps.b: হাতি এর চেয়েও নিচু ডাক দিতে পারে।

ps.e: These sounds travel very well, because low sounds lose less energy as they move through the air.
ps.b: এই শব্দগুলো খুব ভালোভাবে ছড়ায়, কারণ নিচু শব্দ বাতাসের মধ্য দিয়ে যাওয়ার সময় কম শক্তি হারায়।

ps.e: An infrasound call can carry across the open grassland for several kilometres, so an elephant that is far from its family can still be heard.
ps.b: একটি অতি নিম্ন শব্দের ডাক খোলা তৃণভূমির ওপর দিয়ে কয়েক কিলোমিটার পর্যন্ত যেতে পারে, ফলে পরিবার থেকে দূরে থাকা হাতির ডাকও শোনা যায়।

ps.e: Elephants may also listen with their feet.
ps.b: হাতি তাদের পা দিয়েও শুনতে পারে।

ps.e: When an elephant makes a deep call, some of the energy goes into the ground and creates tiny vibrations.
ps.b: হাতি যখন গভীর ডাক দেয়, তার কিছু শক্তি মাটির ভেতরে যায় এবং ক্ষুদ্র কম্পন তৈরি করে।

ps.e: Researchers have found that elephants can pick up vibrations through their feet and trunks, and they seem to react to them.
ps.b: গবেষকরা দেখেছেন যে হাতি তাদের পা ও শুঁড় দিয়ে কম্পন ধরতে পারে, এবং তারা সেগুলোতে সাড়া দেয় বলেও মনে হয়।

ps.e: Scientists think this may help elephants to sense the calls of others that are far away.
ps.b: বিজ্ঞানীরা মনে করেন, এটি হাতিদের দূরে থাকা অন্য হাতিদের ডাক অনুভব করতে সাহায্য করতে পারে।

ps.e: Elephant society is led by females.
ps.b: হাতির সমাজ নারী হাতিদের দ্বারা পরিচালিত হয়।

ps.e: A herd is usually a family: a mother, her sisters, her daughters and their young calves.
ps.b: একটি দল সাধারণত একটি পরিবার: একজন মা, তার বোনেরা, তার মেয়েরা এবং তাদের ছোট বাচ্চারা।

ps.e: The oldest and most experienced female, called the matriarch, leads the group.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে বয়স্ক ও অভিজ্ঞ নারী হাতি, যাকে মাট্রিয়ার্ক বলা হয়, দলটিকে নেতৃত্ব দেয়।

ps.e: She decides where to go, when to rest and when to run.
ps.b: সে ঠিক করে কোথায় যেতে হবে, কখন বিশ্রাম নিতে হবে এবং কখন দৌড়াতে হবে।

ps.e: Male elephants leave the family when they are teenagers and then live alone or in small groups.
ps.b: পুরুষ হাতিরা কিশোর বয়সে পরিবার ছেড়ে যায় এবং তারপর একা বা ছোট দলে থাকে।

ps.e: Why does the matriarch's age matter?
ps.b: মাট্রিয়ার্কের বয়স কেন গুরুত্বপূর্ণ?

ps.e: In Amboseli National Park in Kenya, researchers played recordings of calls from elephants of other families.
ps.b: কেনিয়ার আম্বোসেলি জাতীয় উদ্যানে গবেষকরা অন্য পরিবারের হাতিদের ডাকের রেকর্ডিং বাজিয়ে শোনান।

ps.e: Families led by older matriarchs were better at telling friends from strangers.
ps.b: বয়স্ক মাট্রিয়ার্কদের নেতৃত্বাধীন পরিবারগুলো বন্ধু ও অপরিচিতদের আলাদা করতে বেশি পারদর্শী ছিল।

ps.e: When the caller was an unknown elephant, these families moved closer together, as if preparing to defend themselves.
ps.b: ডাকদাতা অচেনা হাতি হলে এই পরিবারগুলো আরও কাছাকাছি সরে আসত, যেন নিজেদের রক্ষার প্রস্তুতি নিচ্ছে।

ps.e: Memory also helps in hard times.
ps.b: কঠিন সময়ে স্মৃতিও সাহায্য করে।

ps.e: In Tanzania, a severe drought in 1993 killed many young elephants.
ps.b: তানজানিয়ায় ১৯৯৩ সালের এক তীব্র খরায় অনেক হাতির বাচ্চা মারা যায়।

ps.e: Families that were led by older matriarchs, who had lived through an earlier drought, lost fewer calves.
ps.b: বয়স্ক মাট্রিয়ার্কদের নেতৃত্বাধীন পরিবারগুলো, যারা আগের একটি খরা পার করে এসেছিল, কম বাচ্চা হারিয়েছিল।

ps.e: Scientists think these experienced females may have remembered where to find food and water when everything nearby had dried up.
ps.b: বিজ্ঞানীরা মনে করেন, এই অভিজ্ঞ নারী হাতিদের হয়তো মনে ছিল কোথায় খাবার ও পানি পাওয়া যাবে, যখন আশপাশের সবকিছু শুকিয়ে গিয়েছিল।

ps.e: Sadly, this knowledge is at risk.
ps.b: দুঃখের বিষয়, এই জ্ঞান এখন ঝুঁকির মুখে।

ps.e: Hunters who kill elephants for their ivory often choose the largest animals, because they carry the biggest tusks, and these can include the oldest females.
ps.b: যারা হাতির দাঁতের জন্য হাতি হত্যা করে, তারা প্রায়ই সবচেয়ে বড় প্রাণীগুলো বেছে নেয়, কারণ সেগুলোর দাঁত সবচেয়ে বড় হয়, আর এদের মধ্যে সবচেয়ে বয়স্ক নারী হাতিরাও থাকতে পারে।

ps.e: When an old matriarch is killed, her family loses its leader and, with her, a lifetime of knowledge.
ps.b: একটি বয়স্ক মাট্রিয়ার্ক মারা গেলে তার পরিবার হারায় তার নেতাকে, আর তার সঙ্গে হারায় সারা জীবনের জ্ঞান।

ps.e: So the next time you see an elephant standing quietly, remember that silence may not be silence at all.
ps.b: তাই পরের বার যখন আপনি একটি হাতিকে চুপচাপ দাঁড়িয়ে থাকতে দেখবেন, মনে রাখবেন, নীরবতা হয়তো আসলে নীরবতা নয়।

ps.e: Elephants are talking, listening and remembering, and we are only beginning to understand the conversation.
ps.b: হাতিরা কথা বলছে, শুনছে এবং মনে রাখছে, আর আমরা কেবল সেই কথোপকথন বুঝতে শুরু করেছি।

cmp/6.title: The Tree Behind Every Chocolate Bar
cmp/6.src: International Cocoa Organization; World Cocoa Foundation; Fairtrade Foundation; Natural History Museum, London
p: Chocolate feels like a simple pleasure. You unwrap it, you taste it, and it is gone. But every piece begins as a seed inside a fruit on a tree that is hard to grow, and the story of that tree reaches from small farms near the equator to shops all over the world.

The cacao tree, whose scientific name means "food of the gods", is a fussy plant. It grows well only in a narrow band of land about twenty degrees north and south of the equator. It needs warm weather, plenty of rain and the shade of taller trees. Its flowers and fruits grow straight out of the trunk and thick branches. Each fruit, called a pod, is about the size of a rugby ball and holds roughly thirty to fifty seeds inside a white, sweet pulp.

Those seeds are not yet chocolate. Farmers cut open the pods and place the seeds and pulp in heaps or boxes for several days. During this time the mixture ferments, which means that tiny living things change it chemically. The seeds then turn brown and begin to lose their bitter taste. After that they are dried in the sun, packed into sacks and sent away to factories, where they are roasted, crushed and mixed with other ingredients.

People have enjoyed cacao for a very long time. The Maya and the Aztecs in Central America drank it as a bitter, frothy drink, often with chilli, and they sometimes used the seeds as money. When cacao reached Europe in the sixteenth century, people added sugar to it, and later inventors found ways to make solid bars. A drink for rulers slowly became a treat for everyone.

Today, more than half of the world's cocoa comes from two countries in West Africa, Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. Most of it is grown by millions of small farmers, many of whom work on plots of just a few hectares. These farmers depend on a crop that they rarely eat themselves. Their income rises and falls with the world price, which can change a lot from one year to the next.

Life for these farmers is not easy. Cocoa trees can be damaged by disease and by insects, and older trees produce fewer pods. Changes in rainfall and rising temperatures make the growing conditions less reliable. In recent years bad harvests have pushed the price of cocoa to very high levels, but high prices do not always mean higher earnings, because a farmer with a poor harvest has less to sell.

Many groups are now working to help. Some teach farmers how to look after their trees, plant new ones and grow other crops between the cocoa trees. Others try to make sure that farmers receive a fairer share of the money that customers pay. Customers can also play a part by choosing chocolate that is certified as responsibly produced, although such labels are not a perfect solution.

The next time you pick up a bar of chocolate, you might think about how far it has travelled. Behind that small piece is a delicate tree, a long process of fermenting and drying, and a farmer waiting to see what the next harvest will bring.

q.q: What is the main idea of the passage?

o: A. Chocolate is more popular today than it was in the past, and many people eat it every single day
B. Cacao can be grown easily anywhere in the world, so farmers face no real difficulties

q.q: The Maya and the Aztecs sometimes used cacao seeds as money.
q.e: Paragraph 4 says they sometimes used the seeds as money.

q.q: What does paragraph 5 say about most cocoa farmers in West Africa?

o: A. They live in big cities far from the farms
B. They are small farmers who depend on a crop they rarely eat

D. They keep all of the profit from the chocolate that is sold in the shops

q.q: According to paragraph 6, why do high cocoa prices not always mean higher earnings?
q.e: Paragraph 6 explains that a poor harvest means less to sell, even when the price is high.
o: A. Customers buy less when prices rise
B. Farmers must pay taxes on the price that they receive

o: A. Several groups are trying to help farmers, but no solution is perfect

o: A. People should remember the work and uncertainty behind a chocolate bar
B. Chocolate will soon disappear from the shops because the trees are all dead

D. Cocoa farmers are always unhappy with their work and want to leave their farms

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
q.e: The passage covers the tree, the process, the history, the farmers and the efforts to help them.
o: A. Chocolate was invented in Europe in the sixteenth century and then spread to farms in Africa, where the trees were first planted
B. Chocolate is expensive only because it is made in large factories that use a lot of power

cmp/7.title: The Doctor Who Told Doctors to Wash Their Hands
p: Washing your hands with soap seems like the most ordinary thing in the world. Yet less than two hundred years ago, many doctors never did it between patients. The man who first showed how important it is was a young Hungarian doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis, and his story is also a story about how hard it can be to change people's minds.

In 1846, Semmelweis began working in the maternity ward of the Vienna General Hospital. The hospital had two clinics for women who were about to give birth. In the first clinic, doctors and medical students looked after the mothers. In the second, midwives did the work. The two clinics were very similar, but the results were not. Many more women died in the first clinic of a disease called childbed fever, which caused a high temperature and often led to death within days.

At the time, no one knew what caused the disease. Semmelweis was troubled by the difference between the clinics. He knew that some women were so afraid of the first clinic that they gave birth in the street instead. He studied every possible explanation. Was it the weather, the crowding, or the way the women lay in bed? None of these seemed to explain the difference.

Then, in 1847, a friend and colleague of Semmelweis died after a student accidentally cut him with a knife during a post-mortem examination. The friend's illness looked just like childbed fever. Semmelweis realised something important. The doctors and students in the first clinic often came straight from the post-mortem room, where they had touched dead bodies. The midwives in the second clinic did not. Perhaps the doctors were carrying something harmful on their hands.

Semmelweis ordered everyone in the first clinic to wash their hands in a strong chlorine solution before touching a patient. The results were striking. In April 1847 about eighteen out of every hundred mothers in the first clinic had died. By June the figure had fallen to about two out of every hundred, close to the level in the second clinic.

Surprisingly, many doctors rejected his idea. Some were offended by the suggestion that they were causing the deaths. Others said that his results did not fit the medical theories of the day. Semmelweis could not explain exactly why washing worked, because the germs that cause disease had not yet been discovered. He also argued angrily with his critics, which did not help his cause.

Semmelweis died in 1865, before his ideas were accepted. Only a few years later, the work of scientists such as Louis Pasteur and Joseph Lister showed that tiny living things, called germs, really do cause infections. Doctors then understood why washing and cleaning were so important.

Today, hand washing is one of the simplest and most effective ways to prevent infections. Hospitals around the world teach it to every member of staff. The story of Semmelweis reminds us that a good idea needs more than evidence. It also needs people who are willing to listen.

cmp/8.title: How the Moon Moves the Sea
p: If you spend a day at the seaside, you may notice something strange. In the morning you can walk far out over wet sand. By afternoon the water has crept up the beach and covered the place where you were standing. A few hours later it moves back again. The sea is breathing in and out, and the reason lies far away in space.

The movement of the sea is called the tide, and it is caused mainly by the Moon. Every object in space pulls on every other object with a force called gravity. The Moon is much smaller than the Earth, but it is close enough to pull on our planet, and the oceans, which can move freely, respond more than the solid ground does.

The Moon pulls the water on the side of the Earth that faces it, and this water rises into a bulge. Strangely, there is also a second bulge on the opposite side of the Earth. This happens because the Moon's pull is weaker on the far side, and so the water there is left behind slightly. As the Earth turns, each coast moves through both bulges every day. This is why most places have two high tides and two low tides in a little more than twenty-four hours.

The Sun also has an effect. It is much bigger than the Moon, but it is also much further away, so its pull on the oceans is smaller. Twice a month, at the new moon and the full moon, the Sun, the Moon and the Earth line up. Their pulls work together and produce especially high and low tides, called spring tides. A week later, when the Sun and the Moon pull from different directions, the tides are weaker. These are called neap tides.

The size of the tide is not the same everywhere. It depends on the shape of the coast and the sea floor. In some places, such as parts of the Mediterranean Sea, the difference between high and low tide is only a few centimetres. In others, the sea can rise and fall dramatically. In the Bay of Fundy in Canada, the water can rise and fall by around sixteen metres, which is about as tall as a five-storey building.

People have always needed to understand the tides. Sailors check them to know when it is safe to enter a harbour. Fishermen and farmers who gather shellfish plan their work around the low tide. Walkers who cross wet sand to reach an island must know when the sea will return, because a rising tide can cut off the path very quickly.

Tides are also a source of energy. When the sea rises, it can push water through a machine called a turbine, and when it falls, it can do the same in the opposite direction. The turbine produces electricity. Because the Moon will keep moving around the Earth for millions of years, tides are completely predictable, which makes them very useful for planning.

Next time you visit the sea, remember that the water you are watching is responding to a distant object in the sky. Each rise and fall is part of a pattern that has been repeating since long before there were people to watch it.

cmp/9.sub: Why leaves change colour in autumn
cmp/9.title: The Secret Colours Inside a Green Leaf
cmp/9.src: USDA Forest Service; Royal Horticultural Society; Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University
p: In many parts of the world, autumn brings a change that people travel long distances to see. Forests that were green all summer turn yellow, orange, red and brown. It can seem as if the trees are painting themselves for a party. But the real reason for the colours is more interesting, and it begins with something very ordinary: the green of the leaf.

Leaves are green because of a chemical called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll captures the energy in sunlight, and the leaf uses this energy to make sugar from water and air. This process is called photosynthesis, and it is the way that trees feed themselves. All through spring and summer, the tree keeps making fresh chlorophyll, so the leaf stays green.

The other colours are present all along, but they are hidden. Leaves contain yellow and orange chemicals called carotenoids. These are the same chemicals that give carrots and bananas their colours. In summer there is so much chlorophyll in the leaf that the green completely covers them.

In autumn, the days become shorter and the weather cooler. The tree senses that winter is coming. It stops making chlorophyll, and the chlorophyll that is already in the leaves slowly breaks down. As the green fades, the yellow and orange that were always there are finally revealed.

Red and purple leaves have a different story. These colours come from chemicals called anthocyanins, which many trees make only in autumn. Sugar becomes trapped in the leaf, and the tree turns some of it into this red colour. Scientists are still discussing why trees do this. Some think the red may protect the leaf while the tree takes back useful materials from it.

The weather affects how bright the colours are. The best displays usually come after a dry, sunny autumn with cool but not freezing nights. Sunshine helps the leaf make plenty of sugar, and cool nights keep that sugar in the leaf. A very wet or very warm autumn tends to give duller colours. Brown leaves, on the other hand, are often just dead leaves from which every other colour has gone.

Finally, the leaves fall. At the base of each leaf stalk, the tree builds a thin layer of cells that gradually seals the connection. When this layer is complete, the leaf drops, and the tree is left with a protected scar where it was attached. By dropping its leaves, the tree saves water and energy during the winter, when there is too little sunlight to make food.
So the next time you walk through an autumn forest, you will know what you are looking at. Some of the colours are new, but many have been there all summer, waiting quietly under the green.

ps.e: This process is called photosynthesis, and it is the way that trees feed themselves.
ps.b: এই প্রক্রিয়াকে বলা হয় সালোকসংশ্লেষণ, আর এভাবেই গাছ নিজের খাবার জোগায়।

ps.e: All through spring and summer, the tree keeps making fresh chlorophyll, so the leaf stays green.
ps.b: বসন্ত ও গ্রীষ্মজুড়ে গাছ নতুন ক্লোরোফিল তৈরি করতেই থাকে, তাই পাতা সবুজ থাকে।

ps.e: The other colours are present all along, but they are hidden.
ps.b: অন্য রংগুলো সবসময়ই উপস্থিত থাকে, কিন্তু লুকানো থাকে।

ps.e: Leaves contain yellow and orange chemicals called carotenoids.
ps.b: পাতায় ক্যারোটিনয়েড নামের হলুদ ও কমলা রাসায়নিক পদার্থ থাকে।

ps.e: These are the same chemicals that give carrots and bananas their colours.
ps.b: এগুলো সেই একই রাসায়নিক যা গাজর ও কলাকে তাদের রং দেয়।

ps.e: In summer there is so much chlorophyll in the leaf that the green completely covers them.
ps.b: গ্রীষ্মে পাতায় ক্লোরোফিল এত বেশি থাকে যে সবুজ রং সেগুলোকে পুরোপুরি ঢেকে রাখে।

ps.e: In autumn, the days become shorter and the weather cooler.
ps.b: হেমন্তে দিন ছোট হয়ে আসে এবং আবহাওয়া ঠান্ডা হয়।

ps.e: The tree senses that winter is coming.
ps.b: গাছ টের পায় শীত আসছে।

ps.e: It stops making chlorophyll, and the chlorophyll that is already in the leaves slowly breaks down.
ps.b: সে ক্লোরোফিল তৈরি করা বন্ধ করে দেয়, আর পাতায় আগে থেকে থাকা ক্লোরোফিল ধীরে ধীরে ভেঙে যায়।

ps.e: As the green fades, the yellow and orange that were always there are finally revealed.
ps.b: সবুজ ফিকে হয়ে এলে সবসময় থাকা হলুদ ও কমলা রং শেষ পর্যন্ত প্রকাশ পায়।

ps.e: Red and purple leaves have a different story.
ps.b: লাল ও বেগুনি পাতার গল্প আলাদা।

ps.e: These colours come from chemicals called anthocyanins, which many trees make only in autumn.
ps.b: এই রংগুলো আসে অ্যান্থোসায়ানিন নামের রাসায়নিক থেকে, যা অনেক গাছ কেবল হেমন্তেই তৈরি করে।

ps.e: Sugar becomes trapped in the leaf, and the tree turns some of it into this red colour.
ps.b: পাতায় চিনি আটকা পড়ে, আর গাছ তার কিছুটা এই লাল রঙে পরিণত করে।

ps.e: Scientists are still discussing why trees do this.
ps.b: গাছ কেন এমন করে, তা নিয়ে বিজ্ঞানীরা এখনও আলোচনা করছেন।

ps.e: Some think the red may protect the leaf while the tree takes back useful materials from it.
ps.b: কেউ কেউ মনে করেন, গাছ যখন পাতা থেকে দরকারি উপাদান ফিরিয়ে নেয় তখন লাল রং পাতাটিকে রক্ষা করতে পারে।

ps.e: The weather affects how bright the colours are.
ps.b: আবহাওয়া রঙের উজ্জ্বলতাকে প্রভাবিত করে।

ps.e: The best displays usually come after a dry, sunny autumn with cool but not freezing nights.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে সুন্দর দৃশ্য সাধারণত আসে শুকনো, রৌদ্রোজ্জ্বল হেমন্তের পর, যখন রাতগুলো ঠান্ডা কিন্তু হিমশীতল নয়।

ps.e: Sunshine helps the leaf make plenty of sugar, and cool nights keep that sugar in the leaf.
ps.b: রোদ পাতাকে প্রচুর চিনি তৈরি করতে সাহায্য করে, আর ঠান্ডা রাত সেই চিনি পাতায় ধরে রাখে।

ps.e: A very wet or very warm autumn tends to give duller colours.
ps.b: খুব ভেজা বা খুব উষ্ণ হেমন্তে রং তুলনামূলক ফ্যাকাশে হয়।

ps.e: Brown leaves, on the other hand, are often just dead leaves from which every other colour has gone.
ps.b: অন্যদিকে, বাদামি পাতা প্রায়ই কেবল মরা পাতা, যা থেকে অন্য সব রং চলে গেছে।

ps.e: Finally, the leaves fall.
ps.b: অবশেষে পাতা ঝরে যায়।

ps.e: At the base of each leaf stalk, the tree builds a thin layer of cells that gradually seals the connection.
ps.b: প্রতিটি পাতার বোঁটার গোড়ায় গাছ কোষের একটি পাতলা স্তর তৈরি করে, যা ধীরে ধীরে সংযোগটি বন্ধ করে দেয়।

ps.e: When this layer is complete, the leaf drops, and the tree is left with a protected scar where it was attached.
ps.b: এই স্তর সম্পূর্ণ হলে পাতা ঝরে পড়ে, আর যেখানে সেটি যুক্ত ছিল সেখানে গাছের গায়ে একটি সুরক্ষিত দাগ থেকে যায়।

ps.e: By dropping its leaves, the tree saves water and energy during the winter, when there is too little sunlight to make food.
ps.b: পাতা ঝরিয়ে গাছ শীতকালে পানি ও শক্তি বাঁচায়, যখন খাবার তৈরির মতো যথেষ্ট সূর্যের আলো থাকে না।

ps.e: So the next time you walk through an autumn forest, you will know what you are looking at.
ps.b: তাই পরের বার হেমন্তের বনে হাঁটলে আপনি জানবেন আপনি কী দেখছেন।

ps.e: Some of the colours are new, but many have been there all summer, waiting quietly under the green.
ps.b: কিছু রং নতুন, কিন্তু অনেক রং গোটা গ্রীষ্ম ধরে সবুজের নিচে চুপচাপ অপেক্ষা করছিল।

cmp/10.title: The City Built on Water Fights the Sea
cmp/10.src: UNESCO World Heritage Centre; Consorzio Venezia Nuova
p: Venice is a city where the streets are made of water. Instead of cars and buses, people travel by boat. More than a thousand years ago, settlers built homes on a group of small islands in a shallow sea called a lagoon, because it was a hard place for enemies to reach. Today the city is loved by visitors from all over the world. But the sea that protected it is now its greatest danger.

To build on soft mud, the first builders pushed thousands of wooden poles deep into the ground. They laid stone on top of the poles and built their houses on the stone. Wood that stays underwater does not rot quickly, so many of these foundations are still strong after centuries. It was a clever way of building, and it allowed Venice to become one of the richest cities in Europe.

Venice floods regularly. The flooding is called acqua alta, which means high water in Italian. It usually happens in autumn and winter, when strong winds push sea water up the Adriatic Sea and into the lagoon. For many years the floods were small, and residents simply put on boots and walked on raised wooden paths.

However, the floods are getting worse. There are two main reasons. First, the sea level is rising because of climate change. Second, the land under Venice is slowly sinking. For much of the twentieth century, water was pumped from the ground below the city, which made the soil sink. Pumping has now stopped, but the damage has remained.

In November 2019, Venice suffered its worst flood in more than fifty years. The water reached about 1.87 metres above the normal sea level, and most of the city was covered. Shops, homes and churches were damaged, and people had to leave their houses. Salt water is especially harmful, because it eats into brick and stone.

To protect the city, engineers built a system of movable gates called MOSE. There are seventy-eight gates, placed across the three openings where the sea enters the lagoon. Normally the gates lie on the bottom of the sea. When a high tide is expected, air is pumped into them and they rise up, closing the lagoon off from the sea. The gates were first used successfully in October 2020.

The project has not been popular with everyone. It cost much more than planned and was finished many years late. Some scientists also worry about its effect on the lagoon, because closing the gates stops the water from circulating. And, as the sea continues to rise, the gates will need to be used more and more often.

The people of Venice have another worry. The number of residents in the old city has fallen to around fifty thousand, because living there is expensive and difficult. Many homes have been turned into holiday flats. A city that was built to be lived in is at risk of becoming a museum, and the fight to save it is a fight for the people who still call it home.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
q.e: The passage covers the building of Venice, flooding, the MOSE gates and the problems of the city.
o: A. How Venice was built and how it is trying to protect itself from the sea
B. How the Adriatic Sea was formed millions of years ago
C. The history of Italian boats and the sailors who built them for the city
D. Why Venice has no cars and uses only boats for travel

q.q: Venice was built in a lagoon because it was difficult for enemies to reach.
q.e: Paragraph 1 says the lagoon was a hard place for enemies to reach.

q.e: Paragraph 2 says they pushed thousands of wooden poles into the ground.
o: A. They used iron plates to hold up the buildings
B. They covered the mud with a thick layer of sand
C. They pushed wooden poles deep into the ground
D. They waited for the mud to dry in the sun

q.q: Wood that stays underwater rots quickly.
q.e: Paragraph 2 says wood that stays underwater does not rot quickly.

q.q: The flooding in Venice is called acqua alta, which means high ____ in Italian.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says acqua alta means high water.

q.q: Why does the land under Venice sink, according to paragraph 4?

o: A. Too many visitors walking around the city
B. Water was pumped from the ground beneath the city
C. Earthquakes that happen every year in the area
D. Heavy buses driving over the bridges every day

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 4?

o: A. Floods are becoming worse because the sea is rising and the land is sinking
B. Floods in Venice are getting smaller and less frequent, because the sea is falling
C. Venice will soon be completely dry, because the lagoon is slowly becoming land
D. Climate change has stopped and the sea is falling, so the city is safe again

q.q: The 2019 flood reached about 1.87 metres above normal sea level.
How do the MOSE gates work?
q.e: Paragraph 6 explains that air is pumped into the gates and they rise.
o: A. They are lowered from the bridges when the water rises in the lagoon
B. They are opened and closed by hand each morning
C. They float on the surface of the sea all the time
D. They lie on the sea bottom and rise when air is pumped into them

q.e: Paragraph 7 says it was finished many years late.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 7?
q.e: Paragraph 7 lists criticisms of the project.
o: A. MOSE will never be used again after its first test, because it did not work well
B. MOSE is a type of boat that is used by the city to carry tourists across the lagoon
C. MOSE has been criticised for its cost, its possible effects and its increasing use
D. Everyone loves MOSE and wants more gates like it, because it has cost very little

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
q.e: The passage covers the history, the flood problem, the gates and the worry about residents.
o: A. Venice is a city with no problems, and it is growing safely, with more residents each year than before, and fewer floods.
B. Venice, built on wooden foundations, is flooding more often and is trying to save itself with gates and by keeping its residents
C. Venice floods only because of its many bridges, which hold back the water in the canals and streets
D. Venice has too many boats, which cause floods when their waves push water over the walls

q.e: The passage does not mention this.

ps.b: যে কাঠ পানির নিচে থাকে তা দ্রুত পচে না, তাই এই ভিতগুলোর অনেকটাই কয়েক শতাব্দী পরও মজবুত আছে।

ps.e: However, the floods are getting worse.

ps.e: There are two main reasons.
ps.b: এর দুটি প্রধান কারণ আছে।

ps.e: First, the sea level is rising because of climate change.

ps.b: ২০১৯ সালের নভেম্বরে ভেনিস পঞ্চাশ বছরেরও বেশি সময়ের মধ্যে সবচেয়ে খারাপ বন্যার মুখে পড়ে।

ps.e: There are seventy-eight gates, placed across the three openings where the sea enters the lagoon.
ps.b: মোট আটাত্তরটি ফটক আছে, যেগুলো বসানো হয়েছে সেই তিনটি মুখে, যেখান দিয়ে সমুদ্র উপহ্রদে ঢোকে।

ps.e: Normally the gates lie on the bottom of the sea.

cmp/11.title: How Paper Travelled Around the World
p: Look around the room you are in. There may be a notebook, a book, a box or a banknote. Paper is so common that we hardly notice it. Yet for most of history, people had to write on much less convenient materials, and the invention of paper changed how knowledge could be saved and shared.

Before paper, writing was done on many different surfaces. In Mesopotamia, people pressed marks into wet clay. In ancient Egypt, they used papyrus, made from a water plant. In Europe, books were written on parchment, which is made from animal skin. These materials worked, but each had a problem. Clay was heavy, papyrus grew only in certain places, and parchment was extremely expensive, because one book could need the skins of many animals.

Paper was developed in China. Traditional accounts say that an official named Cai Lun presented a method of making paper to the emperor in the year 105. Archaeologists have found even older pieces of paper, so Cai Lun probably improved an existing process. He is still remembered because his method used cheap materials, such as old rags, tree bark and fishing nets.

The method was simple but clever. The materials were soaked and beaten until they formed a soft mass of tiny fibres in water. A worker lifted a flat screen through the mixture, so that a thin layer of fibres was left on top. When this layer was pressed and dried, it became a sheet of paper. It was light, smooth and cheap.

For several centuries, the Chinese kept the secret of papermaking within their country. Then the knowledge began to travel west along the Silk Road, the great network of trade routes that joined East and West. By the eighth century, there were paper workshops in Samarkand, in Central Asia, and soon afterwards in Baghdad, where there was a great demand for books.

From the Islamic world, papermaking reached Europe. Mills were built in Spain in the twelfth century and later in Italy and other countries. For a long time, paper in Europe was made from rags, and there was a constant search for old cloth. Then in the fifteenth century, the printing press, which was invented in Germany, made books cheaper than ever, and the demand for paper grew quickly.

In the nineteenth century, a major change took place. Papermakers learned to make paper from wood pulp instead of rags, and machines could produce long rolls of it. Newspapers, school books and letters became cheap enough for ordinary families. More people learned to read, and ideas travelled faster.

Today we use computers and phones, but paper has not disappeared. The world still makes huge amounts of it, and recycling has become important. A material first made from old rags and fishing nets continues to be part of our daily lives, almost two thousand years after Cai Lun.

cmp/12.sub: Emperor penguins in the Antarctic winter
cmp/12.title: The Birds That Choose the Coldest Winter
cmp/12.src: British Antarctic Survey; Australian Antarctic Division; Fretwell et al.
p: Most animals do their best to avoid the cold. Emperor penguins do the opposite. They are the only birds that spend the whole Antarctic winter on the ice, where the temperature can fall far below minus forty degrees Celsius and the wind can blow at the speed of a train. And that is exactly the time of year when they choose to raise their young.

The story begins in autumn, when thousands of emperor penguins walk many kilometres inland from the sea to the breeding place, which is called a colony. Each pair of penguins meets and, in May or June, the female lays a single egg. Then something unusual happens. She passes the egg carefully to her partner, and she walks back to the sea to feed, because laying the egg has used up much of her strength.

The male now takes over. He balances the egg on top of his feet and covers it with a warm flap of skin, called a brood pouch, so that it never touches the ice. If the egg touched the ice, it would freeze within minutes. For about two months, through the worst weather on Earth, the male stands almost without moving, and during all this time he does not eat.

To survive, the males work together. They gather into a huddle, standing close to each other with their bodies touching. Penguins on the windy outer edge slowly move to the inside, while those in the middle take their turn on the outside. In this way no penguin has to suffer the worst cold for long. The huddle can make the temperature in the middle surprisingly warm.

By the time the chick hatches, the male has lost a large part of his body weight. At this moment the females return from the sea, with their stomachs full of food. A female recognises her partner by his call, and she feeds the chick. Now it is the male's turn to go and eat, and for the next few months the parents take turns to look after their chick.

When the chick has grown enough to keep warm, both parents spend more time at the sea, and the chicks gather in groups. They remain on the sea ice until their waterproof feathers grow, which happens in the summer, when the ice starts to break up. The timing is very important. If the ice breaks too soon, the chicks may fall into the water before their feathers are ready.

This is exactly what worries scientists. Emperor penguins depend on stable sea ice. In 2022, satellite pictures showed that in one region of Antarctica the ice broke up early, and almost all of the chicks in several colonies were probably lost. As the world becomes warmer, the sea ice may become less reliable, and emperor penguin numbers could fall.

The emperor penguin is a creature of great patience and teamwork. Its way of life shows how animals can adapt to the hardest conditions on Earth, and it reminds us that even the toughest species can be harmed when the world around them changes.
