ps.e: A single chlorine atom, they said, could destroy thousands of ozone molecules.
ps.b: তাঁরা বললেন, একটিমাত্র ক্লোরিন পরমাণু হাজার হাজার ওজোন অণু ধ্বংস করতে পারে।

ps.e: Their idea was controversial at the time, and some industries doubted it.
ps.b: তাঁদের ধারণাটি তখন বিতর্কিত ছিল, আর কিছু শিল্প এতে সন্দেহ প্রকাশ করেছিল।

ps.e: Then, in 1985, a team from the British Antarctic Survey reported something startling.
ps.b: তারপর ১৯৮৫ সালে ব্রিটিশ অ্যান্টার্কটিক সার্ভের একটি দল চমকে দেওয়ার মতো কিছু জানাল।

ps.e: Measurements over Antarctica showed that, each spring, the amount of ozone had fallen sharply, creating what the press called an "ozone hole".
ps.b: অ্যান্টার্কটিকার ওপরের পরিমাপে দেখা গেল, প্রতি বসন্তে ওজোনের পরিমাণ তীব্রভাবে কমে যায়, যা তৈরি করছিল সেই জিনিস যাকে সংবাদমাধ্যম বলল "ওজোন গর্ত"।

ps.e: The results were so unexpected that the scientists checked their instruments repeatedly.
ps.b: ফলাফল এতটাই অপ্রত্যাশিত ছিল যে বিজ্ঞানীরা বারবার তাঁদের যন্ত্র পরীক্ষা করলেন।

ps.e: Satellite data from NASA soon confirmed that the problem was real and that it was getting worse.
ps.b: নাসার স্যাটেলাইট তথ্য শীঘ্রই নিশ্চিত করল যে সমস্যাটি বাস্তব এবং ক্রমশ খারাপ হচ্ছে।

ps.e: What happened next was remarkable.
ps.b: এরপর যা ঘটল তা ছিল অসাধারণ।

ps.e: In 1987, governments agreed on a treaty called the Montreal Protocol, in which countries promised to reduce and then stop producing the chemicals that damage the ozone layer.
ps.b: ১৯৮৭ সালে সরকারগুলো মন্ট্রিয়ল প্রটোকল নামের একটি চুক্তিতে একমত হলো, যাতে দেশগুলো ওজোন স্তরের ক্ষতিকারক রাসায়নিক উৎপাদন কমাতে এবং পরে বন্ধ করতে প্রতিশ্রুতি দেয়।

ps.e: It was agreed even though some scientific details were still uncertain, because the possible risk was so serious.
ps.b: কিছু বৈজ্ঞানিক খুঁটিনাটি তখনও অনিশ্চিত থাকা সত্ত্বেও এটি সম্মত হয়েছিল, কারণ সম্ভাব্য ঝুঁকি ছিল অত্যন্ত গুরুতর।

ps.e: The treaty also included a flexible system: richer countries had to act first, and poorer countries were given more time and financial help.
ps.b: চুক্তিতে একটি নমনীয় ব্যবস্থাও ছিল: ধনী দেশগুলোকে আগে ব্যবস্থা নিতে হবে, আর গরিব দেশগুলোকে দেওয়া হলো বেশি সময় ও আর্থিক সহায়তা।

ps.e: The Montreal Protocol has since been accepted by every country in the world, making it the first United Nations treaty to be signed by all members.
ps.b: মন্ট্রিয়ল প্রটোকল তখন থেকে বিশ্বের প্রতিটি দেশ গ্রহণ করেছে, ফলে এটি জাতিসংঘের প্রথম চুক্তি যাতে সব সদস্য স্বাক্ষর করেছে।

ps.e: Its rules have been tightened several times, and today around ninety-nine percent of the substances that it controls have been phased out.
ps.b: এর নিয়মগুলো কয়েকবার কঠোর করা হয়েছে, আর আজ এটি যেসব পদার্থ নিয়ন্ত্রণ করে তার প্রায় নিরানব্বই শতাংশ ধীরে ধীরে বন্ধ করা হয়েছে।

ps.e: Industry also found alternatives, which proved that the change was possible without ruining the economy.
ps.b: শিল্পও বিকল্প খুঁজে পেয়েছে, যা প্রমাণ করেছে যে অর্থনীতি ধ্বংস না করেও পরিবর্তন সম্ভব।

ps.e: The results are now visible.
ps.b: ফলাফল এখন দৃশ্যমান।

ps.e: A 2022 scientific assessment concluded that the ozone layer is recovering.
ps.b: ২০২২ সালের একটি বৈজ্ঞানিক মূল্যায়ন সিদ্ধান্তে এসেছে যে ওজোন স্তর সেরে উঠছে।

ps.e: If current policies continue, the ozone over most of the world is expected to return to its 1980 level by about 2040, over the Arctic by about 2045 and over Antarctica by about 2066.
ps.b: বর্তমান নীতি চলতে থাকলে বিশ্বের বেশিরভাগ জায়গার ওজোন প্রায় ২০৪০ সালের মধ্যে, আর্কটিকের ওপরে প্রায় ২০৪৫ সালের মধ্যে এবং অ্যান্টার্কটিকার ওপরে প্রায় ২০৬৬ সালের মধ্যে ১৯৮০ সালের স্তরে ফিরে আসার আশা করা হচ্ছে।

ps.e: The Antarctic hole still appears every year, and its size varies from one year to another, but the long-term trend is encouraging.
ps.b: অ্যান্টার্কটিকার গর্ত এখনও প্রতি বছর দেখা দেয়, আর এর আকার বছর থেকে বছরে বদলায়, কিন্তু দীর্ঘমেয়াদি প্রবণতা আশাব্যঞ্জক।

ps.e: The story is not without warnings.
ps.b: গল্পটি সতর্কবার্তা ছাড়া নয়।

ps.e: In 2018, scientists noticed that the amount of one banned chemical in the air was not falling as fast as expected, which suggested that someone was secretly producing it.
ps.b: ২০১৮ সালে বিজ্ঞানীরা লক্ষ করলেন, একটি নিষিদ্ধ রাসায়নিকের পরিমাণ বাতাসে প্রত্যাশামতো দ্রুত কমছে না, যা ইঙ্গিত দিচ্ছিল কেউ গোপনে এটি তৈরি করছে।

ps.e: Investigators traced much of the pollution to factories in eastern China, and the emissions then declined.
ps.b: তদন্তকারীরা দূষণের বড় অংশের উৎস পূর্ব চীনের কিছু কারখানায় খুঁজে পান, আর এরপর নির্গমন কমে যায়।

ps.e: The incident showed that agreements need to be monitored and enforced.
ps.b: ঘটনাটি দেখাল যে চুক্তি পর্যবেক্ষণ ও বলবৎ করা দরকার।

ps.e: The ozone success is often used as an example of what global cooperation can achieve.
ps.b: ওজোনের সাফল্যকে প্রায়ই বৈশ্বিক সহযোগিতা কী অর্জন করতে পারে তার উদাহরণ হিসেবে ব্যবহার করা হয়।

ps.e: Scientists provided evidence, governments acted before every detail was certain, and industries adapted.
ps.b: বিজ্ঞানীরা প্রমাণ দিলেন, সরকারগুলো প্রতিটি খুঁটিনাটি নিশ্চিত হওয়ার আগেই ব্যবস্থা নিল, আর শিল্পগুলো খাপ খাইয়ে নিল।

ps.e: The same approach is harder to apply to climate change, which touches every part of the economy, but the ozone story proves that the world can agree to act when it chooses to.
ps.b: একই পদ্ধতি জলবায়ু পরিবর্তনে প্রয়োগ করা কঠিনতর, কারণ তা অর্থনীতির প্রতিটি অংশ ছুঁয়ে যায়, কিন্তু ওজোনের গল্প প্রমাণ করে যে বিশ্ব যখন চায় তখন ব্যবস্থা নিতে একমত হতে পারে।

cmp/64.title: The Medicine That Contains No Medicine
cmp/64.src: Hróbjartsson and Gøtzsche; Kaptchuk et al.; Waber et al.; Levine, Gordon and Fields; Beecher
p: In 1955, an American anaesthetist named Henry Beecher published a short paper with a dramatic title: "The Powerful Placebo". Reviewing fifteen studies, he claimed that roughly one-third of patients improved after being given a dummy treatment, such as a sugar pill, which contained nothing capable of curing them. The figure of thirty-five percent entered textbooks, and for decades it was repeated as proof that the mind could heal the body. It was an attractive claim, but a closer look has shown that it was misleading.

The difficulty lies in what patients actually do when they are enrolled in a study. Many illnesses improve by themselves with time; a headache fades, a cold passes. Others rise and fall, so that people who join a trial at a moment when their symptoms are at their worst will probably feel better later, whatever is done to them. When the patients in a trial improve, therefore, it is tempting to credit the placebo, but part of the improvement would have occurred anyway. Only a comparison with a group that receives no treatment at all can separate the genuine placebo effect from natural recovery.

When researchers carried out such comparisons, the picture became more modest. A large review of more than two hundred trials concluded that placebos had no important effect on objective outcomes, such as blood pressure measurements or the size of a tumour. For subjective outcomes, however, notably pain and nausea, there did appear to be a small but real benefit. In other words, a placebo seems unable to shrink a cancer, but it may make a person feel better.

That distinction matters, and so does the mechanism behind it. Pain is not simply a signal that travels from an injury to the brain; it is shaped by what the brain expects. In a classic experiment in the 1970s, patients who had had a tooth removed were given a placebo, and some of them reported less pain. When the researchers then gave them a drug that blocks the body's natural painkillers, known as endorphins, the benefit disappeared. This suggested that the expectation of relief had triggered real chemical changes in the brain, rather than merely persuading people that they felt better.

Expectation can be shaped by surprisingly small details. In one experiment, volunteers were given an identical pill and told that it was a new painkiller, but half were told that it cost two dollars and fifty cents per dose, while the others were told that the price had been reduced to ten cents. The volunteers who believed that they had the expensive pill reported significantly more relief. Colour, brand names and even the manner of a doctor have been shown to influence the effect in similar ways.

The reverse is equally striking. If patients are warned about side effects, some of them develop those symptoms even when they are taking an inert tablet, a phenomenon called the nocebo effect. In some trials, people in the placebo group have stopped taking the pills because of unpleasant side effects that no active ingredient could have caused. The mind, it seems, can produce harm as well as comfort, which complicates the idea that positive thinking is always beneficial.

The most surprising findings concern honesty. It has long been assumed that a placebo works only if the patient believes that it is a real drug. Yet in a 2010 trial of patients with irritable bowel syndrome, one group was given pills that were clearly labelled "placebo", with an explanation that such pills had been shown to help through mind-body processes. These patients reported more relief than a group who received no pills. The study was small and the result needs to be repeated, but it suggests that deception may not be necessary.

This would be welcome news for doctors, who face a genuine ethical dilemma. Prescribing a placebo while pretending that it is a genuine drug violates the trust on which medicine depends. Yet the evidence shows that the context of treatment, including the attention of the doctor and the expectation that a treatment will help, has measurable effects. Some researchers argue that the lesson is not that placebos should be prescribed, but that clinicians should recognise the part that care and communication play in every treatment.

The placebo, then, is neither the miracle that Beecher portrayed nor the empty trick that sceptics sometimes suggest. It is a reminder that human beings are not machines that respond only to chemicals, and that a good trial must be designed carefully if it is to distinguish what a treatment does from what a patient simply expects it to do.

q.q: What is the main purpose of the passage?
q.e: The passage re-examines the claims and explains mechanisms, limits and ethical questions.
o: A. To argue that doctors should lie to patients whenever it might help them
B. To examine what research really shows about the placebo effect and how it works
C. To prove that placebos can cure serious diseases such as cancer in most patients
D. To describe the career of Henry Beecher and the experiments that he carried out

q.q: Beecher's paper claimed that about one-third of patients improved after a dummy treatment.
q.e: Paragraph 1 says roughly one-third improved, a figure of thirty-five percent.

q.q: According to paragraph 2, why is it misleading to credit all improvement in a trial to the placebo?
q.e: Paragraph 2 explains that illnesses improve by themselves or fluctuate.
o: A. Patients cannot tell the difference between the placebo and real medicine
B. Researchers recorded the results badly, and so the data cannot be trusted
C. Some patients would have improved anyway through natural recovery
D. Placebos are expensive, so patients' improvement cannot be paid for

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 2?
q.e: Paragraph 2 argues that only a no-treatment comparison can separate placebo effects from natural recovery.
o: A. Trials should not include control groups, since these make the results harder to read
B. Illnesses never improve without treatment, so every recovery is caused by the placebo
C. Patients join trials when they are well, so trials show no useful differences at all
D. Natural recovery makes it hard to know how much of an improvement is caused by the placebo

q.q: What did the large review in paragraph 3 find about objective outcomes?
q.e: Paragraph 3 says there was no important effect on objective outcomes.
o: A. Placebos had no important effect on them
B. Placebos greatly reduced tumour size
C. Placebos only worked on children
D. Placebos lowered blood pressure in all patients

q.q: Placebos appear to have a small benefit for pain and nausea.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says there seemed to be a small but real benefit for pain and nausea.

q.q: What happened when the patients in the dental experiment were given a drug that blocks endorphins?
o: A. The patients felt no pain
B. The patients refused the drug and left
C. The benefit of the placebo disappeared
D. The placebo became stronger

q.q: What did the dental experiment suggest?
q.e: Paragraph 4 says the expectation had triggered real chemical changes.
o: A. The placebo contained a hidden drug, which is why the patients felt better
B. Endorphins cause pain, and the placebo made the patients produce more of them
C. The expectation of relief can cause real chemical changes in the brain
D. Patients were lying about their pain, because they wanted to please the dentist

q.q: In the pricing experiment, volunteers who believed they had the expensive pill reported significantly more ____.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says they reported significantly more relief.

q.q: The writer states that the colour of a pill has no effect on its results.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says colour has been shown to influence the effect.

q.q: In paragraph 6, the word "inert" most nearly means:
q.e: An inert tablet has no active ingredient.
o: A. bright and attractive in colour
B. without any active effect
C. harmful to the patient's health
D. extremely costly to make

q.q: In paragraph 6, "The mind, it seems, can produce harm as well as comfort." What does this mean?
q.e: The sentence refers to the nocebo effect, where expectation of harm causes symptoms.
o: A. Thinking positively always helps, whatever illness the patient has
B. The mind is not important in illness, since only the body matters
C. Comfort and harm are identical, so a patient cannot tell them apart
D. Expectations can cause unpleasant symptoms as well as relief

q.q: In the irritable bowel syndrome trial, the patients were deceived about the pills.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says the pills were clearly labelled as placebos.

q.q: Why does the writer say the 2010 irritable bowel syndrome result should be treated with caution?
q.e: Paragraph 7 says the study was small and the result needs to be repeated.
o: A. The pills were dangerous
B. The result was published in a newspaper
C. The patients were all doctors
D. The study was small and needs to be repeated

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 8?
q.e: Paragraph 8 describes the dilemma and the suggestion that care and communication matter.
o: A. Doctors should always prescribe placebos, since honesty about them harms the patient
B. Doctors face an ethical problem because the context of care matters but deception damages trust
C. Patients never need attention from their doctors, because the medicine does all the work
D. The ethical problem has been solved, and doctors may now use deception without any risk

q.q: Which of the following best describes the writer's overall attitude to the placebo effect?
q.e: The writer rejects both the miracle story and the empty-trick view.
o: A. Balanced and sceptical of exaggeration, but impressed by what it shows about the mind
B. Dismissive of the whole idea, which the writer regards as a mistake from beginning to end
C. Enthusiastic and uncritical, accepting every claim made about the power of the mind
D. Angry at the medical profession for hiding the truth from its patients for many years

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
q.e: The passage covers the original claim, the correction, the mechanism and the ethical issues.
o: A. The placebo effect is real but smaller and narrower than once claimed, and it raises important questions about expectation, honesty and care
B. Doctors should always prescribe sugar pills, because patients prefer them to real medicine
C. Placebos can cure any illness, and the effect is larger than that of most of the medicines that doctors use, according to the writer.
D. Placebos have been proven to be useless, and doctors should stop using them in every hospital at once

q.q: Placebo pills are more effective when they are blue than when they are white.
q.e: The passage does not mention this.

ps.e: In 1955, an American anaesthetist named Henry Beecher published a short paper with a dramatic title: "The Powerful Placebo".
ps.b: ১৯৫৫ সালে হেনরি বিচার নামের একজন আমেরিকান অজ্ঞানবিদ চিকিৎসক নাটকীয় শিরোনামে একটি ছোট প্রবন্ধ প্রকাশ করেন: "শক্তিশালী প্লাসিবো"।

ps.e: Reviewing fifteen studies, he claimed that roughly one-third of patients improved after being given a dummy treatment, such as a sugar pill, which contained nothing capable of curing them.
ps.b: পনেরোটি গবেষণা পর্যালোচনা করে তিনি দাবি করেন, নকল চিকিৎসা, যেমন চিনির বড়ি, দেওয়ার পর প্রায় এক-তৃতীয়াংশ রোগী সুস্থ বোধ করেছেন, যেখানে সেই বড়িতে এমন কিছু ছিল না যা তাদের সারিয়ে তুলতে পারে।

ps.e: The figure of thirty-five percent entered textbooks, and for decades it was repeated as proof that the mind could heal the body.
ps.b: পঁয়ত্রিশ শতাংশের এই সংখ্যাটি পাঠ্যবইয়ে ঢুকে যায়, আর কয়েক দশক ধরে এটি মন শরীরকে সারাতে পারে তার প্রমাণ হিসেবে আওড়ানো হয়েছে।

ps.e: It was an attractive claim, but a closer look has shown that it was misleading.
ps.b: দাবিটি আকর্ষণীয় ছিল, কিন্তু আরও খুঁটিয়ে দেখলে তা বিভ্রান্তিকর বলে প্রমাণিত হয়েছে।

ps.e: The difficulty lies in what patients actually do when they are enrolled in a study.
ps.b: জটিলতা রয়েছে এই বিষয়ে যে রোগীরা কোনো গবেষণায় অন্তর্ভুক্ত হলে আসলে কী করেন।

ps.e: Many illnesses improve by themselves with time; a headache fades, a cold passes.
ps.b: অনেক অসুখ সময়ের সঙ্গে নিজে থেকেই ভালো হয়ে যায়; মাথাব্যথা কমে যায়, সর্দি চলে যায়।

ps.e: Others rise and fall, so that people who join a trial at a moment when their symptoms are at their worst will probably feel better later, whatever is done to them.
ps.b: অন্যগুলো ওঠানামা করে, ফলে যারা এমন সময় কোনো গবেষণায় যোগ দেন যখন তাদের উপসর্গ সবচেয়ে খারাপ, তাদের সম্ভবত পরে ভালো লাগবে, তাদের ওপর যা-ই করা হোক না কেন।

ps.e: When the patients in a trial improve, therefore, it is tempting to credit the placebo, but part of the improvement would have occurred anyway.
ps.b: তাই কোনো গবেষণায় রোগীরা সুস্থ হলে কৃতিত্ব প্লাসিবোকে দিতে ইচ্ছা করে, কিন্তু উন্নতির একটি অংশ এমনিতেই ঘটত।

ps.e: Only a comparison with a group that receives no treatment at all can separate the genuine placebo effect from natural recovery.
ps.b: শুধু এমন একটি দলের সঙ্গে তুলনা, যারা কোনো চিকিৎসাই পায় না, প্রকৃত প্লাসিবো প্রভাবকে স্বাভাবিক সেরে ওঠা থেকে আলাদা করতে পারে।

ps.e: When researchers carried out such comparisons, the picture became more modest.
ps.b: গবেষকরা এমন তুলনা করার পর ছবিটি আরও সীমিত হয়ে গেল।

ps.e: A large review of more than two hundred trials concluded that placebos had no important effect on objective outcomes, such as blood pressure measurements or the size of a tumour.
ps.b: দুই শতাধিক গবেষণার একটি বড় পর্যালোচনা সিদ্ধান্তে এল যে বস্তুনিষ্ঠ ফলাফলে, যেমন রক্তচাপ মাপা বা টিউমারের আকার, প্লাসিবোর গুরুত্বপূর্ণ কোনো প্রভাব নেই।

ps.e: For subjective outcomes, however, notably pain and nausea, there did appear to be a small but real benefit.
ps.b: তবে ব্যক্তিগত অনুভূতিভিত্তিক ফলাফলে, বিশেষত ব্যথা ও বমি বমি ভাবে, একটি ছোট কিন্তু বাস্তব উপকার দেখা গেল।

ps.e: In other words, a placebo seems unable to shrink a cancer, but it may make a person feel better.
ps.b: অন্য কথায়, প্লাসিবো ক্যানসার ছোট করতে পারে না বলে মনে হয়, কিন্তু একজন মানুষকে ভালো বোধ করাতে পারে।

ps.e: That distinction matters, and so does the mechanism behind it.
ps.b: এই পার্থক্য গুরুত্বপূর্ণ, আর এর পেছনের কার্যপদ্ধতিও।

ps.e: Pain is not simply a signal that travels from an injury to the brain; it is shaped by what the brain expects.
ps.b: ব্যথা কেবল আঘাত থেকে মস্তিষ্কে যাওয়া একটি সংকেত নয়; মস্তিষ্ক কী আশা করে তা দিয়েও এটি প্রভাবিত হয়।

ps.e: In a classic experiment in the 1970s, patients who had had a tooth removed were given a placebo, and some of them reported less pain.
ps.b: ১৯৭০-এর দশকের একটি ক্লাসিক পরীক্ষায় দাঁত তোলা রোগীদের প্লাসিবো দেওয়া হলো, আর তাদের কেউ কেউ কম ব্যথার কথা জানাল।

ps.e: When the researchers then gave them a drug that blocks the body's natural painkillers, known as endorphins, the benefit disappeared.
ps.b: গবেষকরা যখন তাদের শরীরের প্রাকৃতিক ব্যথানাশক, যাকে এন্ডোর্ফিন বলে, তা আটকে দেয় এমন একটি ওষুধ দিলেন, তখন উপকারটি উধাও হয়ে গেল।

ps.e: This suggested that the expectation of relief had triggered real chemical changes in the brain, rather than merely persuading people that they felt better.
ps.b: এ থেকে ধারণা মিলল, স্বস্তির প্রত্যাশা মস্তিষ্কে বাস্তব রাসায়নিক পরিবর্তন ঘটিয়েছিল, কেবল মানুষকে ভালো বোধ করার ধারণা দেয়নি।

ps.e: Expectation can be shaped by surprisingly small details.
ps.b: প্রত্যাশা বিস্ময়করভাবে ছোট খুঁটিনাটি দিয়ে প্রভাবিত হতে পারে।

ps.e: In one experiment, volunteers were given an identical pill and told that it was a new painkiller, but half were told that it cost two dollars and fifty cents per dose, while the others were told that the price had been reduced to ten cents.
ps.b: একটি পরীক্ষায় স্বেচ্ছাসেবকদের অভিন্ন একটি বড়ি দেওয়া হলো এবং বলা হলো এটি নতুন ব্যথানাশক, কিন্তু অর্ধেককে বলা হলো প্রতি ডোজের দাম আড়াই ডলার, আর বাকিদের বলা হলো দাম কমিয়ে দশ সেন্ট করা হয়েছে।

ps.e: The volunteers who believed that they had the expensive pill reported significantly more relief.
ps.b: যারা বিশ্বাস করেছিল তাদের কাছে দামি বড়ি আছে, তারা উল্লেখযোগ্যভাবে বেশি স্বস্তির কথা জানাল।

ps.e: Colour, brand names and even the manner of a doctor have been shown to influence the effect in similar ways.
ps.b: রং, ব্র্যান্ডের নাম, এমনকি চিকিৎসকের আচরণও একই রকম উপায়ে প্রভাব ফেলে বলে দেখা গেছে।

ps.e: The reverse is equally striking.
ps.b: উল্টো ব্যাপারটিও সমানভাবে চোখে পড়ার মতো।

ps.e: If patients are warned about side effects, some of them develop those symptoms even when they are taking an inert tablet, a phenomenon called the nocebo effect.
ps.b: রোগীদের পার্শ্বপ্রতিক্রিয়া সম্পর্কে সতর্ক করা হলে কিছু রোগী নিষ্ক্রিয় বড়ি খেলেও সেই উপসর্গ দেখা দেয়, যে ঘটনাকে বলা হয় নোসিবো প্রভাব।

ps.e: In some trials, people in the placebo group have stopped taking the pills because of unpleasant side effects that no active ingredient could have caused.
ps.b: কিছু গবেষণায় প্লাসিবো দলের লোকেরা অপ্রীতিকর পার্শ্বপ্রতিক্রিয়ার কারণে বড়ি খাওয়া বন্ধ করে দিয়েছে, যা কোনো সক্রিয় উপাদানের পক্ষে ঘটানো সম্ভব ছিল না।

ps.e: The mind, it seems, can produce harm as well as comfort, which complicates the idea that positive thinking is always beneficial.
ps.b: মনে হয় মন যেমন স্বস্তি তৈরি করতে পারে, তেমনি ক্ষতিও, যা ইতিবাচক চিন্তা সবসময় উপকারী এই ধারণাকে জটিল করে তোলে।

ps.e: The most surprising findings concern honesty.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে অবাক করা ফলাফলগুলো সততা নিয়ে।

ps.e: It has long been assumed that a placebo works only if the patient believes that it is a real drug.
ps.b: দীর্ঘদিন ধরে মনে করা হতো যে প্লাসিবো কাজ করে কেবল তখনই, যখন রোগী বিশ্বাস করেন এটি আসল ওষুধ।

ps.e: Yet in a 2010 trial of patients with irritable bowel syndrome, one group was given pills that were clearly labelled "placebo", with an explanation that such pills had been shown to help through mind-body processes.
ps.b: কিন্তু পেটের অসুখ আইবিএস-এ আক্রান্ত রোগীদের ২০১০ সালের এক গবেষণায় একটি দলকে এমন বড়ি দেওয়া হয়েছিল যাতে স্পষ্ট লেখা ছিল "প্লাসিবো", সঙ্গে ব্যাখ্যা ছিল যে এমন বড়ি মন-শরীর প্রক্রিয়ার মাধ্যমে সাহায্য করে বলে দেখা গেছে।

ps.e: These patients reported more relief than a group who received no pills.
ps.b: এই রোগীরা এমন একটি দলের চেয়ে বেশি স্বস্তির কথা জানাল যারা কোনো বড়িই পায়নি।

ps.e: The study was small and the result needs to be repeated, but it suggests that deception may not be necessary.
ps.b: গবেষণাটি ছোট ছিল এবং ফলাফলটি আবার যাচাই করা দরকার, কিন্তু এটি ইঙ্গিত দেয় যে প্রতারণা হয়তো প্রয়োজন নেই।

ps.e: This would be welcome news for doctors, who face a genuine ethical dilemma.
ps.b: এটি চিকিৎসকদের জন্য স্বাগত খবর হবে, যাঁরা সত্যিকারের নৈতিক উভয়সংকটের মুখে পড়েন।

ps.e: Prescribing a placebo while pretending that it is a genuine drug violates the trust on which medicine depends.
ps.b: প্লাসিবোকে আসল ওষুধ বলে ভান করে দেওয়া সেই আস্থাকে লঙ্ঘন করে, যার ওপর চিকিৎসা নির্ভর করে।

ps.e: Yet the evidence shows that the context of treatment, including the attention of the doctor and the expectation that a treatment will help, has measurable effects.
ps.b: তবু প্রমাণ দেখায়, চিকিৎসার প্রেক্ষাপট, যার মধ্যে আছে চিকিৎসকের মনোযোগ ও চিকিৎসা সাহায্য করবে এমন প্রত্যাশা, পরিমাপযোগ্য প্রভাব ফেলে।

ps.e: Some researchers argue that the lesson is not that placebos should be prescribed, but that clinicians should recognise the part that care and communication play in every treatment.
ps.b: কিছু গবেষক যুক্তি দেন, শিক্ষাটি এই নয় যে প্লাসিবো দেওয়া উচিত, বরং চিকিৎসকদের স্বীকার করা উচিত প্রতিটি চিকিৎসায় যত্ন ও যোগাযোগের ভূমিকা কতটা।

ps.e: The placebo, then, is neither the miracle that Beecher portrayed nor the empty trick that sceptics sometimes suggest.
ps.b: তাহলে প্লাসিবো না বিচারের চিত্রিত সেই অলৌকিক জিনিস, না সংশয়বাদীদের মাঝে মাঝে ইঙ্গিত করা ফাঁকা কৌশল।

ps.e: It is a reminder that human beings are not machines that respond only to chemicals, and that a good trial must be designed carefully if it is to distinguish what a treatment does from what a patient simply expects it to do.
ps.b: এটি একটি স্মারক যে মানুষ কেবল রাসায়নিকে সাড়া দেওয়া যন্ত্র নয়, আর একটি ভালো গবেষণা সাবধানে নকশা করা উচিত, যদি চিকিৎসা আসলে কী করে এবং রোগী কেবল কী আশা করে তা আলাদা করতে হয়।

cmp/65.title: Paying for the Road Space You Use
cmp/65.src: Transport for London; Eliasson; Land Transport Authority, Singapore; Metropolitan Transportation Authority, New York; Vickrey
p: Anyone who has sat in a traffic jam has probably wondered why roads seem to be full at some times and almost empty at others. Economists answer that the problem lies in the price. Road space in a busy city is a scarce resource, yet drivers are usually allowed to use it free of charge, so everyone has an incentive to use it at the same popular moments. The result is the familiar crawl, in which each driver wastes time and also slows down everybody else.

The idea that drivers should pay for the congestion they cause is older than most people realise. In 1963, the economist William Vickrey, who later won a Nobel Prize, argued that charging for road use, with prices that rise when roads are busy, would reduce delays more effectively than building new roads. His reasoning was simple: each additional car on a crowded road imposes a cost on all the others, but the driver pays nothing for that cost. A charge would make drivers take account of the damage that they do.

For decades, the idea remained largely theoretical, because politicians feared that it would be unpopular. Singapore was the first to act, introducing a licence to enter its central area in 1975, and later replacing it with an electronic system that charges according to the time and the road. London followed in 2003, when drivers entering the centre of the city were asked to pay a daily fee. Within the first year, traffic in the zone fell noticeably, and journey times improved.

The London experience, however, also illustrates the limits of the policy. Over the following years, the early gains were partly cancelled out. Road space had been given to buses, cyclists and pedestrians, which reduced the capacity for cars, and the growth of taxi-style app services and delivery vans put new vehicles on the road. Critics concluded that charging had not solved congestion permanently, while supporters replied that without the charge the situation would have been much worse.

The most instructive case is Stockholm. In 2006, the city introduced a charge as a seven-month trial, and traffic fell by about a fifth. At the start, a majority of residents opposed the scheme. After seeing the quieter streets and cleaner air, however, many changed their minds, and in a referendum held after the trial, a narrow majority voted to make the charge permanent. The Stockholm experience has since become a standard example of a policy that gains support only after people have experienced it.

Why are such schemes so controversial? One objection concerns fairness. Critics argue that a flat charge hurts poorer drivers more than richer ones, who may hardly notice the cost. Supporters respond that in most big cities the richest residents are the least likely to commute by car, and that the revenue can be used to improve buses and trains, which low-income residents rely on. Whether this happens depends on how the money is actually spent, and that is a matter of political choice and not economic law.

There are also practical worries. Shops fear that customers will stay away, and residents just outside the zone worry about traffic that is diverted onto their streets. Evidence from the cities that have tried charging is mixed on these points: in general, retail activity does not seem to have collapsed, but the experience varies from one place to another, and careful design of the boundary and of exemptions is essential.

New York, the largest American city, introduced its own scheme in January 2025, charging most drivers who enter the southern part of Manhattan. The plan survived years of political and legal battles, and its outcome is being watched closely around the world. Early results are only a first indication, but they will probably be used by both sides of the argument.

What congestion pricing demonstrates, above all, is that a technical solution is never only technical. A charge can reduce traffic only if it is high enough to change behaviour, yet it will survive only if it is seen as fair and if the public can see where the money goes. The most successful schemes have paired a clear economic logic with visible improvements, and they have given residents time to see for themselves that the change was worth it.

q.q: What is the main purpose of the passage?
q.e: The passage explains the economic idea and reviews experiences in several cities.
o: A. To examine the logic, history and difficulties of charging drivers to enter busy city centres
B. To argue that all cars should be banned, because they are the main cause of city problems
C. To explain how taxi apps work and how they have changed the way people travel
D. To describe how Singapore built its roads and why they are the best in the world

q.q: According to paragraph 1, why are roads crowded at some times?
q.e: Paragraph 1 says that free use gives everyone an incentive to use roads at the same moments.
o: A. Cars break down more at peak times, and the broken cars block the other drivers
B. Drivers pay nothing to use them, so everyone wants the popular times
C. Drivers dislike public transport, so they choose the busiest hours for their journeys
D. Roads are always too narrow, so they become crowded whatever the time of day

q.q: William Vickrey argued that building more roads would be more effective than charging drivers.
q.e: Paragraph 2 says he argued that charging would reduce delays more effectively than building roads.

q.q: In paragraph 2, "A charge would make drivers take account of the damage that they do." What does this mean?
q.e: The sentence says charging makes drivers consider the cost they impose on others.
o: A. Drivers would be punished for owning a car, whether or not they used it
B. Drivers would have to repair roads that they had damaged in the past
C. Drivers would have to consider the cost they cause to others
D. Drivers would stop using cars completely, and the roads would be empty

q.q: Which city was the first to introduce a scheme, according to paragraph 3?
q.e: Paragraph 3 says Singapore was first, in 1975.
o: A. New York
B. Stockholm
C. London
D. Singapore

q.q: London introduced its charge in 1975.
Why were the early gains in London partly cancelled out?
o: A. The weather changed, and fewer people wanted to walk or travel by bicycle in the city
B. Road space was given to buses, cyclists and pedestrians, and app services and delivery vans grew
C. The charge was abolished soon afterwards, and traffic returned to the level it was before
D. The population fell, so there were fewer shops and offices in the centre of the city

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 4?
q.e: Paragraph 4 describes the partial loss of gains and the dispute between critics and supporters.
o: A. London's scheme brought gains, but its long-term effect is disputed
B. London's scheme increased traffic, and the charge was later reduced to zero
C. London's scheme failed completely, and the traffic became worse than before
D. London's scheme has no critics, and everyone agrees about its long-term effect

q.q: In Stockholm, the charge was introduced as a seven-month ____.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says it was a seven-month trial.

q.q: In Stockholm, most residents supported the scheme before the trial began.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says a majority opposed it at the start.

q.q: What can we infer from the Stockholm experience?
q.e: Paragraph 5 says that the policy gained support after people experienced it.
o: A. Referendums are unnecessary, since governments always know what voters want
B. Congestion charges are always popular, even before anybody has tried them
C. Residents never change their minds, however much evidence they are shown
D. People may accept a policy more readily after they have seen its benefits

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 6?
q.e: Paragraph 6 explains the fairness objection and the reply that depends on spending choices.
o: A. The main objection is fairness, and the answer depends on how the revenue is used
B. The charge is fair in all cases, so nobody has ever raised an objection to it
C. Poor drivers never pay the charge, because they are excused by the government
D. Revenue cannot be spent on public transport, and so it only helps the government

q.q: In paragraph 6, the word "revenue" most nearly means:
q.e: Revenue is income, here the money collected from the charge.
o: A. letters of complaint
B. queues of waiting vehicles
C. signs beside the road
D. money that is collected

q.q: How do supporters respond to the objection that charges hurt poorer drivers?
o: A. They say poor people never drive, so the charge cannot harm anyone who has little money, and the rich will pay all of it.
B. They say the charge should be removed, because the government should find other income
C. They say the richest residents are the least likely to drive and that revenue can improve public transport
D. They say the charge is very small, so it makes no difference to the choices of drivers

q.q: The writer states that retail activity collapsed in every city that tried charging.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says retail activity does not seem to have collapsed in general.

q.q: What is the writer's attitude towards congestion pricing?
q.e: The writer presents both the benefits and the difficulties.
o: A. Uninterested in it, and unwilling to give any view of its advantages or its costs
B. Strongly against it, and certain that it can never work in any city
C. Balanced: acknowledges its potential but also its political and practical difficulties
D. Completely in favour without reservation, and sure that every objection is wrong

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
q.e: The passage covers the logic, the examples, the objections and the conditions for success.
o: A. Congestion pricing works only in Asia, where drivers are used to paying for the roads
B. Congestion pricing can reduce traffic and has worked in several cities, but its success depends on fairness, good design and public acceptance
C. Congestion pricing has been abandoned everywhere, because it failed to reduce the traffic and made drivers angry
D. Congestion pricing is unnecessary, because roads are never crowded except in a few very large cities of the world, and then only on a few days.

q.q: Electric vehicles are exempt from the charge in every city that uses it.
q.e: The passage does not mention this.

ps.e: Anyone who has sat in a traffic jam has probably wondered why roads seem to be full at some times and almost empty at others.
ps.b: যে কেউ যানজটে বসে থেকেছেন তিনি সম্ভবত ভেবেছেন, কেন রাস্তা কিছু সময় ভরা থাকে আর অন্য সময় প্রায় ফাঁকা।

ps.e: Economists answer that the problem lies in the price.
ps.b: অর্থনীতিবিদরা উত্তর দেন, সমস্যাটি দামের মধ্যে।

ps.e: Road space in a busy city is a scarce resource, yet drivers are usually allowed to use it free of charge, so everyone has an incentive to use it at the same popular moments.
ps.b: ব্যস্ত শহরে রাস্তার জায়গা একটি দুষ্প্রাপ্য সম্পদ, তবু চালকদের সাধারণত বিনামূল্যে তা ব্যবহার করতে দেওয়া হয়, ফলে সবার একই জনপ্রিয় সময়ে তা ব্যবহার করার প্রণোদনা থাকে।

ps.e: The result is the familiar crawl, in which each driver wastes time and also slows down everybody else.
ps.b: ফল হলো পরিচিত সেই ধীরগতি, যেখানে প্রতিটি চালক নিজের সময় নষ্ট করে এবং একই সঙ্গে বাকি সবাইকে ধীর করে দেয়।

ps.e: The idea that drivers should pay for the congestion they cause is older than most people realise.
ps.b: চালকদের তাদের সৃষ্ট যানজটের জন্য মূল্য দেওয়া উচিত, এই ধারণা বেশিরভাগ মানুষ যতটা ভাবে তার চেয়ে পুরোনো।

ps.e: In 1963, the economist William Vickrey, who later won a Nobel Prize, argued that charging for road use, with prices that rise when roads are busy, would reduce delays more effectively than building new roads.
ps.b: ১৯৬৩ সালে অর্থনীতিবিদ উইলিয়াম ভিকরি, যিনি পরে নোবেল পুরস্কার জিতেছিলেন, যুক্তি দিয়েছিলেন যে রাস্তা ব্যবহারে মূল্য ধার্য করলে, রাস্তা ব্যস্ত থাকলে যা বাড়বে, তা নতুন রাস্তা বানানোর চেয়ে আরও কার্যকরভাবে বিলম্ব কমাবে।

ps.e: His reasoning was simple: each additional car on a crowded road imposes a cost on all the others, but the driver pays nothing for that cost.
ps.b: তাঁর যুক্তি ছিল সহজ: ভিড়ের রাস্তায় প্রতিটি বাড়তি গাড়ি বাকি সবার ওপর খরচ চাপিয়ে দেয়, কিন্তু চালক সেই খরচের জন্য কিছু দেয় না।

ps.e: A charge would make drivers take account of the damage that they do.
ps.b: একটি ফি চালকদের তাদের সৃষ্ট ক্ষতি বিবেচনায় নিতে বাধ্য করবে।

ps.e: For decades, the idea remained largely theoretical, because politicians feared that it would be unpopular.
ps.b: কয়েক দশক ধরে ধারণাটি মূলত তাত্ত্বিকই থেকে গিয়েছিল, কারণ রাজনীতিবিদরা ভয় পেতেন এটি অজনপ্রিয় হবে।

ps.e: Singapore was the first to act, introducing a licence to enter its central area in 1975, and later replacing it with an electronic system that charges according to the time and the road.
ps.b: সিঙ্গাপুর প্রথম পদক্ষেপ নেয়, ১৯৭৫ সালে তার কেন্দ্রীয় এলাকায় ঢোকার জন্য একটি অনুমতিপত্র চালু করে, আর পরে এটি বদলে সময় ও রাস্তা অনুযায়ী মূল্য ধার্য করা একটি ইলেকট্রনিক ব্যবস্থা আনে।

ps.e: London followed in 2003, when drivers entering the centre of the city were asked to pay a daily fee.
ps.b: ২০০৩ সালে লন্ডন তা অনুসরণ করে, যখন শহরের কেন্দ্রে ঢোকা চালকদের দৈনিক ফি দিতে বলা হয়।

ps.e: Within the first year, traffic in the zone fell noticeably, and journey times improved.
ps.b: প্রথম বছরের মধ্যে এলাকাটিতে যানবাহন লক্ষণীয়ভাবে কমে এবং যাত্রার সময় উন্নত হয়।

ps.e: The London experience, however, also illustrates the limits of the policy.
ps.b: তবে লন্ডনের অভিজ্ঞতা এই নীতির সীমাবদ্ধতাও তুলে ধরে।

ps.e: Over the following years, the early gains were partly cancelled out.
ps.b: পরবর্তী বছরগুলোতে প্রাথমিক সুফলগুলো আংশিক বাতিল হয়ে যায়।

ps.e: Road space had been given to buses, cyclists and pedestrians, which reduced the capacity for cars, and the growth of taxi-style app services and delivery vans put new vehicles on the road.
ps.b: রাস্তার জায়গা বাস, সাইকেল আরোহী ও পথচারীদের দেওয়া হয়েছিল, যা গাড়ির ধারণক্ষমতা কমিয়ে দেয়, আর ট্যাক্সির মতো অ্যাপ সেবা ও ডেলিভারি ভ্যানের বৃদ্ধি রাস্তায় নতুন যানবাহন নামিয়ে আনে।

ps.e: Critics concluded that charging had not solved congestion permanently, while supporters replied that without the charge the situation would have been much worse.
ps.b: সমালোচকরা সিদ্ধান্তে এলেন, ফি স্থায়ীভাবে যানজট সমাধান করেনি, আর সমর্থকরা জবাব দিলেন, ফি না থাকলে পরিস্থিতি আরও অনেক খারাপ হতো।

ps.e: The most instructive case is Stockholm.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে শিক্ষণীয় দৃষ্টান্ত স্টকহোম।

ps.e: In 2006, the city introduced a charge as a seven-month trial, and traffic fell by about a fifth.
ps.b: ২০০৬ সালে শহরটি সাত মাসের একটি পরীক্ষা হিসেবে ফি চালু করে, আর যানবাহন প্রায় এক-পঞ্চমাংশ কমে যায়।

ps.e: At the start, a majority of residents opposed the scheme.
ps.b: শুরুতে বেশিরভাগ বাসিন্দা প্রকল্পের বিরোধিতা করেছিলেন।

ps.e: After seeing the quieter streets and cleaner air, however, many changed their minds, and in a referendum held after the trial, a narrow majority voted to make the charge permanent.
ps.b: তবে শান্ত রাস্তা ও পরিষ্কার বাতাস দেখে অনেকে মত বদলান, আর পরীক্ষার পর অনুষ্ঠিত গণভোটে অল্প ব্যবধানের সংখ্যাগরিষ্ঠতা ফিটি স্থায়ী করতে ভোট দেয়।

ps.e: The Stockholm experience has since become a standard example of a policy that gains support only after people have experienced it.
ps.b: স্টকহোমের অভিজ্ঞতা তখন থেকে এমন একটি নীতির আদর্শ উদাহরণ, যা সমর্থন পায় মানুষ তা অনুভব করার পরেই।

ps.e: Why are such schemes so controversial?
ps.b: এমন প্রকল্প এত বিতর্কিত কেন?

ps.e: One objection concerns fairness.
ps.b: একটি আপত্তি ন্যায্যতা নিয়ে।

ps.e: Critics argue that a flat charge hurts poorer drivers more than richer ones, who may hardly notice the cost.
ps.b: সমালোচকরা বলেন, সমান হারের ফি গরিব চালকদের বেশি আঘাত করে, যেখানে ধনীরা খরচটা হয়তো খেয়ালই করবেন না।

ps.e: Supporters respond that in most big cities the richest residents are the least likely to commute by car, and that the revenue can be used to improve buses and trains, which low-income residents rely on.
ps.b: সমর্থকরা জবাব দেন, বেশিরভাগ বড় শহরে সবচেয়ে ধনী বাসিন্দারাই গাড়িতে যাতায়াত করার সম্ভাবনা সবচেয়ে কম, এবং আদায় করা অর্থ দিয়ে বাস ও ট্রেনের উন্নতি করা যায়, যার ওপর নিম্ন আয়ের বাসিন্দারা নির্ভর করেন।

ps.e: Whether this happens depends on how the money is actually spent, and that is a matter of political choice and not economic law.
ps.b: এটি ঘটবে কিনা তা নির্ভর করে অর্থ আসলে কীভাবে খরচ হয় তার ওপর, আর সেটি রাজনৈতিক সিদ্ধান্তের বিষয়, অর্থনৈতিক আইনের নয়।

ps.e: There are also practical worries.
ps.b: কিছু ব্যবহারিক দুশ্চিন্তাও আছে।

ps.e: Shops fear that customers will stay away, and residents just outside the zone worry about traffic that is diverted onto their streets.
ps.b: দোকানদাররা ভয় পান যে ক্রেতারা আসবেন না, আর এলাকার ঠিক বাইরের বাসিন্দারা চিন্তিত যে যানবাহন তাঁদের রাস্তায় সরে আসবে।

ps.e: Evidence from the cities that have tried charging is mixed on these points: in general, retail activity does not seem to have collapsed, but the experience varies from one place to another, and careful design of the boundary and of exemptions is essential.
ps.b: যেসব শহর ফি চালু করেছে তাদের প্রমাণ এসব বিষয়ে মিশ্র: সাধারণভাবে খুচরা ব্যবসা ভেঙে পড়েছে বলে মনে হয় না, কিন্তু অভিজ্ঞতা জায়গাভেদে ভিন্ন, আর সীমানা ও অব্যাহতির সতর্ক নকশা অপরিহার্য।

ps.e: New York, the largest American city, introduced its own scheme in January 2025, charging most drivers who enter the southern part of Manhattan.
ps.b: যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের সবচেয়ে বড় শহর নিউইয়র্ক ২০২৫ সালের জানুয়ারিতে নিজস্ব প্রকল্প চালু করে, ম্যানহাটানের দক্ষিণ অংশে ঢোকা বেশিরভাগ চালকের কাছ থেকে ফি নিয়ে।

ps.e: The plan survived years of political and legal battles, and its outcome is being watched closely around the world.
ps.b: পরিকল্পনাটি বছরের পর বছর রাজনৈতিক ও আইনি লড়াইয়ের মধ্য দিয়ে টিকে গেছে, আর এর ফলাফল বিশ্বজুড়ে ঘনিষ্ঠভাবে পর্যবেক্ষণ করা হচ্ছে।

ps.e: Early results are only a first indication, but they will probably be used by both sides of the argument.
ps.b: প্রাথমিক ফলাফল কেবল প্রথম ইঙ্গিত, কিন্তু সম্ভবত তর্কের উভয় পক্ষই তা কাজে লাগাবে।

ps.e: What congestion pricing demonstrates, above all, is that a technical solution is never only technical.
ps.b: যানজট মূল্য নির্ধারণ সবকিছুর ওপরে যা দেখায় তা হলো, একটি কারিগরি সমাধান কখনও কেবল কারিগরি নয়।

ps.e: A charge can reduce traffic only if it is high enough to change behaviour, yet it will survive only if it is seen as fair and if the public can see where the money goes.
ps.b: একটি ফি যানবাহন কমাতে পারে কেবল তখনই, যখন তা আচরণ বদলানোর মতো যথেষ্ট বেশি, আর তা টিকবে কেবল তখনই, যখন এটি ন্যায্য মনে হবে এবং জনগণ দেখতে পাবে অর্থ কোথায় যাচ্ছে।

ps.e: The most successful schemes have paired a clear economic logic with visible improvements, and they have given residents time to see for themselves that the change was worth it.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে সফল প্রকল্পগুলো স্পষ্ট অর্থনৈতিক যুক্তিকে দৃশ্যমান উন্নতির সঙ্গে জুড়েছে, এবং বাসিন্দাদের সময় দিয়েছে নিজে দেখার, যে পরিবর্তনটি সার্থক ছিল।

cmp/66.sub: Tulip mania in the Dutch Republic
cmp/66.title: The Tulip Bubble That May Never Have Burst
cmp/66.src: Goldgar; Garber; Mackay; Rijksmuseum; Dutch National Archives
p: Few stories about money are retold as often as that of the Dutch tulip craze. In the 1630s, we are told, the people of the Netherlands lost their heads over flowers. Ordinary families sold their houses to buy a single bulb, a sailor who mistook a precious bulb for an onion was thrown into prison, and when the market collapsed in February 1637, thousands were ruined. The tale has been used for almost two centuries as a warning about what happens when greed overcomes common sense. The trouble is that much of it may not be true.

The background, at least, is solid. The Dutch Republic in the early seventeenth century was one of the wealthiest societies in Europe, with a booming trade, a growing middle class and a passion for gardens and collecting. Tulips, which had arrived from the Ottoman Empire in the previous century, were a fashionable luxury. The most admired varieties had petals streaked with flame-like patterns. These patterns were unpredictable, because, as scientists discovered much later, they were caused by a virus that weakened the bulb and made it slow to multiply. Rare bulbs were, therefore, genuinely scarce.

Prices for the finest bulbs did rise to extraordinary heights. A single bulb of the famous variety Semper Augustus was reported to have been sold for thousands of guilders, at a time when a skilled craftsman might earn a few hundred in a year. In the winter of 1636 and 1637, the trade became feverish, and bulbs were bought and sold not only in the summer, when they could be dug up, but also in the winter, while they were still in the ground. Buyers signed contracts promising to pay a certain price when the bulbs were delivered months later, in effect a primitive form of futures trading.

Then, in early February 1637, at an auction in the city of Haarlem, buyers failed to appear in the usual numbers, and prices fell. This much is not in doubt. What happened next is where the story begins to dissolve. According to the popular version, which was fixed in the public imagination by the Scottish writer Charles Mackay in 1841, the collapse caused a financial catastrophe across the country. Mackay, however, wrote more than two hundred years after the events, and he drew largely on pamphlets written by moralists who wished to condemn the greed of the age.

Modern historians who have returned to the archives have found strikingly little evidence of the disaster. The cultural historian Anne Goldgar searched through notarial records, court documents and the papers of merchants, and could find hardly a single case of a person who had been ruined by tulips. The market, she concluded, was relatively small, involving mostly merchants and craftsmen who could afford to gamble. Many of the contracts were never fulfilled at all, and the authorities eventually encouraged an arrangement in which buyers could cancel their contracts by paying only a small fraction of the agreed price.

Some economists have gone further and asked whether the high prices were actually irrational. They point out that tulips were a new and desirable commodity, that the supply of the rarest bulbs was limited, and that a rare bulb could be multiplied into new, valuable ones. Even the fall in prices, they suggest, may have been less dramatic than it seems, because the prices that were quoted at the peak were for contracts, not for bulbs that anyone had actually paid for. This argument, too, has its critics, who note that the prices of ordinary bulbs rose as well, and that a fall of more than ninety percent in a few weeks seems extreme.

What, then, can we conclude? It would be unwise to say that nothing happened. There was clearly a speculative surge, and some people lost money and reputation. But the evidence does not support the image of a whole society driven into madness and poverty. It is more accurate to describe a small, excited market that rose quickly and collapsed quickly, causing less harm than the legend suggests.

Why, then, has the legend lasted so long? Perhaps because it is useful. Every time a new market boom has ended in a crash, commentators have reached for the tulips as a symbol, and the story offers a simple moral that people find comforting: that greed is punished. The truth about speculation, in which intelligent people sometimes make plausible bets that turn out to be wrong, is harder to tell, and harder to learn from.

The tulip episode thus teaches two lessons. The first concerns markets, which can rise and fall far more quickly than the value of the underlying goods. The second concerns history itself: that a good story, repeated by authors who care more about its moral than about the facts, can be believed for centuries without anyone having checked.

q.q: What is the main purpose of the passage?
q.e: The passage compares the popular tale with the evidence and explains why the legend survives.
o: A. To describe how to grow tulips and why the Dutch loved them so much
B. To prove that the tulip craze never happened, since no records of it exist
C. To question the popular version of the tulip craze and explain why it has lasted
D. To explain how the Dutch Republic became rich through trade with Asia

q.q: According to the popular story, a sailor who mistook a bulb for an onion was imprisoned.
q.e: Paragraph 1 mentions this part of the popular tale.

q.q: According to paragraph 2, why were the most admired tulip varieties genuinely scarce?
o: A. They were grown only in the Ottoman Empire, and the Dutch had to import every bulb
B. The Dutch government banned them, which made the surviving bulbs very expensive
C. They grew only in winter, so there were very few of them to buy each year
D. The patterns were caused by a virus that weakened the bulb and slowed its multiplication

q.q: The patterns on the most admired tulips were easy to predict.
q.e: Paragraph 2 says the patterns were unpredictable.

q.q: In paragraph 3, "in effect a primitive form of futures trading". What does this mean?
q.e: Contracts promised payment at a fixed price on future delivery, as in futures trading.
o: A. The contracts were an early kind of agreement to buy something at a set price in the future
B. The contracts were forbidden by law, so traders had to make them in secret
C. The Dutch traders invented the stock market, which they used to buy and sell tulips every day
D. The bulbs were delivered immediately, so no agreement about the future was needed

q.q: In early February 1637, at an auction in the city of ____, buyers failed to appear in the usual numbers.
q.e: Paragraph 4 names the city of Haarlem.

q.q: Why does the writer question Mackay's account in paragraph 4?
o: A. He invented the word "guilder", and so misunderstood the prices of the bulbs
B. He was Dutch, and so he had a reason to defend the reputation of his country
C. He did not know about tulips, and had never seen one in his life
D. He wrote more than two hundred years later, using pamphlets by moralists

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 5?
q.e: Paragraph 5 reports Goldgar's findings from the archives.
o: A. Archives prove that thousands were ruined, and the records confirm the old story
B. Archival research has found little evidence that people were ruined by tulips
C. The market was huge and involved all classes, from nobles to the poorest workers
D. Courts ordered buyers to pay in full, so every person who had lost money was repaid

q.q: Anne Goldgar found many cases of people who were ruined by tulips.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says she could find hardly a single case.

q.q: What did the authorities encourage, according to paragraph 5?
o: A. A ban on the sale of bulbs, so that nobody could make or lose money from them again
B. A tax on flowers, which was meant to pay for the damage caused to buyers
C. The destruction of all contracts by court order, with no payment to either side
D. An arrangement in which buyers could cancel contracts by paying a small fraction of the price

q.q: What does the writer suggest about the economists' argument in paragraph 6?
q.e: The writer notes the argument and says it, too, has its critics.
o: A. It is thought-provoking but disputed
B. It has been proved, and the question is now closed
C. It is certainly correct, and nobody disputes it
D. It is nonsense, and the writer rejects all of it

q.q: In paragraph 7, the word "speculative" most nearly means:
q.e: A speculative surge is driven by betting on future price rises.
o: A. related to gardens and the growing of flowers
B. very old, and dating from a much earlier time
C. based on risky guesses about future prices
D. completely safe, and with no chance of any loss

q.q: The writer states that nothing at all happened in the Netherlands in 1637.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says it would be unwise to say that nothing happened.

q.q: Why, according to paragraph 8, has the legend lasted so long?
q.e: Paragraph 8 says that the story is useful as a simple moral.
o: A. It is supported by court records, which prove that many people were ruined
B. It describes a recent event, which many readers remember very well
C. It offers a comforting and simple moral that greed is punished
D. It was written by an official, and so people believed it was true

q.q: Which of the following best describes the writer's attitude to the popular tulip story?
q.e: The writer questions the legend, but recognises that a speculative surge took place.
o: A. Humorous and careless
B. Sceptical but fair
C. Hostile to all historians
D. Fully convinced of its truth

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
q.e: The passage compares the legend with the evidence and explains its persistence.
o: A. The tulip crash ruined the whole Netherlands, and the country took many years to recover from it, according to the old story
B. The famous tulip crash was real but probably much smaller than the legend suggests, and the story lasted because it is a convenient moral
C. Tulips were never valuable, and the stories about their very high prices were invented by later writers
D. The legend has been proved correct by new evidence found in the archives of several Dutch towns

q.q: The most expensive tulip bulb ever sold was bought by a merchant from Amsterdam.
q.e: The passage does not mention this.

ps.e: Few stories about money are retold as often as that of the Dutch tulip craze.
ps.b: অর্থ নিয়ে খুব কম গল্পই ডাচ টিউলিপ-মাতামাতির মতো এত বেশি বলা হয়।

ps.e: In the 1630s, we are told, the people of the Netherlands lost their heads over flowers.
ps.b: আমাদের বলা হয়, ১৬৩০-এর দশকে নেদারল্যান্ডসের মানুষ ফুলের জন্য মাথা হারিয়েছিল।

ps.e: Ordinary families sold their houses to buy a single bulb, a sailor who mistook a precious bulb for an onion was thrown into prison, and when the market collapsed in February 1637, thousands were ruined.
ps.b: সাধারণ পরিবার একটিমাত্র কন্দ কিনতে নিজেদের ঘর বিক্রি করেছিল, একজন নাবিক একটি দামি কন্দকে পেঁয়াজ ভেবে ভুল করায় তাকে কারাগারে ঢোকানো হয়েছিল, আর ১৬৩৭ সালের ফেব্রুয়ারিতে বাজার ভেঙে পড়লে হাজার হাজার মানুষ সর্বস্বান্ত হয়েছিল।

ps.e: The tale has been used for almost two centuries as a warning about what happens when greed overcomes common sense.
ps.b: গল্পটি প্রায় দুই শতাব্দী ধরে সতর্কবার্তা হিসেবে ব্যবহৃত হয়েছে, যখন লোভ সাধারণ বুদ্ধিকে ছাপিয়ে যায় তখন কী ঘটে তার উদাহরণ হিসেবে।

ps.e: The trouble is that much of it may not be true.
ps.b: সমস্যা হলো, এর অনেকটাই হয়তো সত্য নয়।

ps.e: The background, at least, is solid.
ps.b: পটভূমিটি অন্তত নির্ভরযোগ্য।

ps.e: The Dutch Republic in the early seventeenth century was one of the wealthiest societies in Europe, with a booming trade, a growing middle class and a passion for gardens and collecting.
ps.b: সপ্তদশ শতাব্দীর গোড়ার ডাচ প্রজাতন্ত্র ছিল ইউরোপের অন্যতম ধনী সমাজ, রমরমা বাণিজ্য, ক্রমবর্ধমান মধ্যবিত্ত শ্রেণি এবং বাগান ও সংগ্রহের প্রতি আবেগ নিয়ে।

ps.e: Tulips, which had arrived from the Ottoman Empire in the previous century, were a fashionable luxury.
ps.b: টিউলিপ, যা আগের শতাব্দীতে অটোমান সাম্রাজ্য থেকে এসেছিল, ছিল একটি ফ্যাশনদুরস্ত বিলাসদ্রব্য।

ps.e: The most admired varieties had petals streaked with flame-like patterns.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে প্রশংসিত জাতগুলোর পাপড়িতে শিখার মতো ডোরা থাকত।

ps.e: These patterns were unpredictable, because, as scientists discovered much later, they were caused by a virus that weakened the bulb and made it slow to multiply.
ps.b: এই নকশাগুলো ছিল অনির্দেশ্য, কারণ, বিজ্ঞানীরা অনেক পরে আবিষ্কার করেন, এগুলো সৃষ্টি হতো একটি ভাইরাসের কারণে, যা কন্দকে দুর্বল করত এবং এর বংশবৃদ্ধি ধীর করে দিত।

ps.e: Rare bulbs were, therefore, genuinely scarce.
ps.b: তাই বিরল কন্দ সত্যিই দুষ্প্রাপ্য ছিল।

ps.e: Prices for the finest bulbs did rise to extraordinary heights.
ps.b: সেরা কন্দের দাম সত্যিই অসাধারণ উচ্চতায় উঠেছিল।

ps.e: A single bulb of the famous variety Semper Augustus was reported to have been sold for thousands of guilders, at a time when a skilled craftsman might earn a few hundred in a year.
ps.b: সেম্পার অগাস্টাস নামের বিখ্যাত জাতের একটি কন্দ কয়েক হাজার গিল্ডারে বিক্রি হয়েছিল বলে জানা যায়, যখন একজন দক্ষ কারিগর বছরে কয়েক শ গিল্ডার আয় করতে পারতেন।

ps.e: In the winter of 1636 and 1637, the trade became feverish, and bulbs were bought and sold not only in the summer, when they could be dug up, but also in the winter, while they were still in the ground.
ps.b: ১৬৩৬ ও ১৬৩৭ সালের শীতে লেনদেন উত্তেজনাপূর্ণ হয়ে ওঠে, আর কন্দ কেনাবেচা হতো কেবল গ্রীষ্মে নয়, যখন সেগুলো তোলা যেত, বরং শীতেও, যখন সেগুলো মাটির ভেতরেই ছিল।

ps.e: Buyers signed contracts promising to pay a certain price when the bulbs were delivered months later, in effect a primitive form of futures trading.
ps.b: ক্রেতারা এমন চুক্তি সই করতেন, যাতে কয়েক মাস পরে কন্দ হস্তান্তরের সময় একটি নির্দিষ্ট দাম দেওয়ার প্রতিশ্রুতি থাকত, বাস্তবে যা ছিল ভবিষ্যৎ লেনদেনের একটি আদিম রূপ।

ps.e: Then, in early February 1637, at an auction in the city of Haarlem, buyers failed to appear in the usual numbers, and prices fell.
ps.b: তারপর ১৬৩৭ সালের ফেব্রুয়ারির শুরুতে হার্লেম শহরের একটি নিলামে ক্রেতারা সচরাচর সংখ্যায় হাজির হলেন না, আর দাম পড়ে গেল।

ps.e: This much is not in doubt.
ps.b: এটুকু নিয়ে কোনো সন্দেহ নেই।

ps.e: What happened next is where the story begins to dissolve.
ps.b: এরপর যা ঘটল সেখান থেকেই গল্পটি মিলিয়ে যেতে শুরু করে।

ps.e: According to the popular version, which was fixed in the public imagination by the Scottish writer Charles Mackay in 1841, the collapse caused a financial catastrophe across the country.
ps.b: জনপ্রিয় বর্ণনা অনুযায়ী, যা ১৮৪১ সালে স্কটিশ লেখক চার্লস ম্যাকে জনমনে গেঁথে দেন, ভেঙে পড়ার ফলে গোটা দেশে আর্থিক মহাবিপর্যয় ঘটেছিল।

ps.e: Mackay, however, wrote more than two hundred years after the events, and he drew largely on pamphlets written by moralists who wished to condemn the greed of the age.
ps.b: তবে ম্যাকে ঘটনাগুলোর দুই শতাধিক বছর পরে লিখেছিলেন, এবং তিনি মূলত নীতিবাদীদের লেখা পুস্তিকার ওপর নির্ভর করেছিলেন, যারা সেই যুগের লোভের নিন্দা করতে চেয়েছিলেন।

ps.e: Modern historians who have returned to the archives have found strikingly little evidence of the disaster.
ps.b: আধুনিক ইতিহাসবিদরা মহাফেজখানায় ফিরে গিয়ে বিপর্যয়ের প্রমাণ পেয়েছেন চমকে দেওয়ার মতো কম।

ps.e: The cultural historian Anne Goldgar searched through notarial records, court documents and the papers of merchants, and could find hardly a single case of a person who had been ruined by tulips.
ps.b: সাংস্কৃতিক ইতিহাসবিদ অ্যান গোল্ডগার নোটারি নথি, আদালতের কাগজ ও বণিকদের দলিল ঘেঁটে এমন একটিও ঘটনা খুঁজে পাননি যেখানে কেউ টিউলিপের কারণে সর্বস্বান্ত হয়েছিলেন।

ps.e: The market, she concluded, was relatively small, involving mostly merchants and craftsmen who could afford to gamble.
ps.b: তিনি সিদ্ধান্তে এলেন, বাজারটি তুলনামূলকভাবে ছোট ছিল, যাতে মূলত বণিক ও কারিগররা জড়িত ছিলেন, যাঁরা জুয়া খেলার সামর্থ্য রাখতেন।

ps.e: Many of the contracts were never fulfilled at all, and the authorities eventually encouraged an arrangement in which buyers could cancel their contracts by paying only a small fraction of the agreed price.
ps.b: অনেক চুক্তি কখনও পূর্ণই হয়নি, আর কর্তৃপক্ষ শেষ পর্যন্ত এমন একটি ব্যবস্থাকে উৎসাহ দেয়, যাতে ক্রেতারা সম্মত দামের একটি ছোট ভগ্নাংশ দিয়েই চুক্তি বাতিল করতে পারতেন।

ps.e: Some economists have gone further and asked whether the high prices were actually irrational.
ps.b: কিছু অর্থনীতিবিদ আরও এগিয়ে গিয়ে প্রশ্ন তুলেছেন, উঁচু দামগুলো সত্যিই অযৌক্তিক ছিল কি না।

ps.e: They point out that tulips were a new and desirable commodity, that the supply of the rarest bulbs was limited, and that a rare bulb could be multiplied into new, valuable ones.
ps.b: তাঁরা উল্লেখ করেন, টিউলিপ ছিল একটি নতুন ও আকর্ষণীয় পণ্য, সবচেয়ে বিরল কন্দের সরবরাহ ছিল সীমিত, আর একটি বিরল কন্দ থেকে নতুন, মূল্যবান কন্দ বংশবিস্তার করা যেত।

ps.e: Even the fall in prices, they suggest, may have been less dramatic than it seems, because the prices that were quoted at the peak were for contracts, not for bulbs that anyone had actually paid for.
ps.b: এমনকি দামের পতনও, তাঁদের মতে, মনে হওয়ার চেয়ে কম নাটকীয় হতে পারে, কারণ চূড়ায় যে দামগুলো উদ্ধৃত হয়েছিল তা ছিল চুক্তির, এমন কন্দের নয় যার জন্য কেউ আসলে টাকা দিয়েছে।

ps.e: This argument, too, has its critics, who note that the prices of ordinary bulbs rose as well, and that a fall of more than ninety percent in a few weeks seems extreme.
ps.b: এই যুক্তিরও সমালোচক আছেন, যাঁরা উল্লেখ করেন যে সাধারণ কন্দের দামও বেড়েছিল, এবং কয়েক সপ্তাহে নব্বই শতাংশের বেশি পতন চরম বলে মনে হয়।

ps.e: What, then, can we conclude?
ps.b: তাহলে আমরা কী সিদ্ধান্তে আসতে পারি?

ps.e: It would be unwise to say that nothing happened.
ps.b: কিছুই ঘটেনি বলা বুদ্ধিমানের হবে না।

ps.e: There was clearly a speculative surge, and some people lost money and reputation.
ps.b: স্পষ্টতই একটি ফাটকাবাজির উত্থান ছিল, আর কিছু মানুষ টাকা ও সুনাম হারিয়েছিল।

ps.e: But the evidence does not support the image of a whole society driven into madness and poverty.
ps.b: কিন্তু প্রমাণ এমন চিত্র সমর্থন করে না যে একটি গোটা সমাজ উন্মাদনা ও দারিদ্র্যে ঠেলে দেওয়া হয়েছিল।

ps.e: It is more accurate to describe a small, excited market that rose quickly and collapsed quickly, causing less harm than the legend suggests.
ps.b: এটি বর্ণনা করা আরও নির্ভুল হবে একটি ছোট, উত্তেজিত বাজার হিসেবে, যা দ্রুত উঠেছিল আর দ্রুত ভেঙে পড়েছিল, কিংবদন্তির ইঙ্গিতের চেয়ে কম ক্ষতি করে।

ps.e: Why, then, has the legend lasted so long?
ps.b: তাহলে কিংবদন্তিটি এত দীর্ঘ সময় টিকে আছে কেন?

ps.e: Perhaps because it is useful.
ps.b: সম্ভবত কারণ এটি কাজের।

ps.e: Every time a new market boom has ended in a crash, commentators have reached for the tulips as a symbol, and the story offers a simple moral that people find comforting: that greed is punished.
ps.b: যতবার কোনো নতুন বাজার-উত্থান ধসে শেষ হয়েছে, ভাষ্যকাররা প্রতীক হিসেবে টিউলিপের কাছে ফিরে গেছেন, আর গল্পটি একটি সহজ নীতিশিক্ষা দেয় যা মানুষ আরামদায়ক মনে করে: যে লোভের শাস্তি হয়।

ps.e: The truth about speculation, in which intelligent people sometimes make plausible bets that turn out to be wrong, is harder to tell, and harder to learn from.
ps.b: ফাটকাবাজির আসল সত্য, যেখানে বুদ্ধিমান মানুষ কখনও কখনও বিশ্বাসযোগ্য বাজি ধরেন যা ভুল প্রমাণিত হয়, তা বলা আরও কঠিন, আর তা থেকে শেখাও কঠিনতর।

ps.e: The tulip episode thus teaches two lessons.
ps.b: টিউলিপের ঘটনা তাই দুটি শিক্ষা দেয়।

ps.e: The first concerns markets, which can rise and fall far more quickly than the value of the underlying goods.
ps.b: প্রথমটি বাজার নিয়ে, যা অন্তর্নিহিত পণ্যের মূল্যের চেয়ে অনেক দ্রুত ওঠানামা করতে পারে।

ps.e: The second concerns history itself: that a good story, repeated by authors who care more about its moral than about the facts, can be believed for centuries without anyone having checked.
ps.b: দ্বিতীয়টি ইতিহাস নিয়ে: একটি ভালো গল্প, যা এমন লেখকরা বারবার বলেন যাঁরা তথ্যের চেয়ে নীতিশিক্ষা নিয়ে বেশি ভাবেন, কেউ যাচাই না করেই কয়েক শতাব্দী ধরে বিশ্বাস করা যেতে পারে।

cmp/67.sub: Wolves in Yellowstone and trophic cascades
cmp/67.title: The Wolves That Supposedly Changed the Rivers
cmp/67.src: US National Park Service; Ripple and Beschta; Marshall, Hobbs and Cooper; Smith, Peterson and Houston
p: A short film widely shared on the internet tells a beautiful story. When wolves returned to Yellowstone National Park in the 1990s, it says, they did far more than reduce the numbers of deer. They changed the behaviour of the animals around them, which allowed trees to grow back, which brought back beavers and birds, which in turn altered the course of the rivers. It is a thrilling idea, that a single predator can reshape a landscape, and it contains a good deal of truth. But as scientists have studied Yellowstone more closely, they have found that the full story is less tidy than the film suggests.

The background is well established. Wolves were hunted until they had been eliminated from Yellowstone by the 1920s, because they were regarded as a threat to livestock and to the elk and deer that people liked to hunt. In their absence, the elk population grew large, and many ecologists worried that the animals were eating too much of the young willow and aspen trees along the streams. After a long debate, the authorities decided to bring wolves back. In 1995 and 1996, thirty-one wolves were captured in Canada and released in the park.

The wolves thrived, and the number of elk in the main part of the park fell dramatically in the following years. Ecologists call the chain of effects that follows when a top predator changes an ecosystem a trophic cascade, and the idea is one of the most influential in modern ecology. Researchers proposed that the wolves had triggered one in Yellowstone in two ways: first by killing elk, and second by frightening them, so that elk avoided open valleys where they could be easily caught, a theory known as the "landscape of fear".

Some of the evidence supported this idea. In places, willows and aspens that had been heavily browsed for decades began to grow taller, and the number of beaver colonies increased, since beavers rely on willows for food and dams. Scientists who emphasised the role of wolves argued that the ecosystem was moving back towards a more natural state.

Other researchers, however, were more cautious. The elk population had been declining for reasons that had nothing to do with wolves, they pointed out: hunting outside the park, harsh winters, and the arrival of other predators such as bears and cougars all played a part. Drought and a warming climate also affect how much water is available to young trees, and so how well they grow. In one study, researchers measured the water levels and the growth of willows and concluded that the changes in vegetation could be explained to a large extent by climate and by differences in the quantity of water, rather than by the wolves.

The claim about rivers has attracted the sharpest criticism. It is true that a stronger growth of willows can help to stabilise stream banks and that beaver dams change the way water flows. However, careful measurements have found that the effects on the actual shape of channels are modest and vary from stream to stream. The notion that wolves had "changed the course" of rivers was, according to some hydrologists, a dramatic exaggeration of a small effect.

The debate is not simply about who is right. It reflects a genuine difficulty in studying ecosystems. Yellowstone is a single large place, and there is only one of it; scientists cannot rerun the experiment with and without wolves under identical conditions. Many factors changed at once, so separating their effects requires many years of data and sophisticated statistics. Different groups, looking at different locations and using different methods, naturally reach different conclusions.

This does not make the wolves unimportant. Most researchers agree that the return of the wolves has had substantial effects: it has changed where and how the elk feed, provided food for scavengers such as ravens and bears, and made Yellowstone a much more complete ecosystem. Where they differ is the size of the effects, and the extent to which the park's recovery can be credited to a single species.

The lesson of Yellowstone is therefore twofold. First, large predators matter, and removing them can have consequences that nobody predicted. Second, the most appealing stories in science are not always the most accurate. An ecosystem is a web of countless connections, and a clean chain of cause and effect, however satisfying, is often a simplification of something far more complicated.

q.q: What is the main purpose of the passage?
q.e: The passage presents the popular story and then the more cautious scientific view.
o: A. To describe how to hunt elk and why the hunters of Yellowstone needed wolves
B. To prove that wolves are harmful to national parks, and that they should be removed
C. To explain why rivers change course and how this affects animals and plants
D. To compare the popular story of Yellowstone's wolves with what scientists have found

q.q: The popular film claims that wolves changed the course of rivers.
q.e: Paragraph 1 says the film claims that wolves altered the course of the rivers.

q.q: Why had wolves been eliminated from Yellowstone by the 1920s?
o: A. They had been protected by law, so hunters could not shoot them any more
B. They had died of disease, which spread quickly through the packs in the early years
C. They had moved to Canada, where there were more elk and fewer people
D. They were regarded as a threat to livestock and to animals that people liked to hunt

q.q: Thirty-one wolves were released in Yellowstone in 1995 and 1996.
q.e: Paragraph 2 says thirty-one wolves were captured in Canada and released.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 3?
q.e: Paragraph 3 describes the fall in elk and the cascade hypothesis.
o: A. Wolves avoided elk, and so the elk could eat the young trees without any fear
B. Ecologists rejected the idea of trophic cascades, and said the wolves had no effect at all
C. The wolves thrived, elk numbers fell, and researchers proposed that a trophic cascade had followed
D. Elk numbers rose after the wolves came, and the willows grew back more slowly than before

q.q: In paragraph 3, the "landscape of fear" refers to the idea that:
q.e: The paragraph explains that elk avoided open valleys.
o: A. trees are afraid of fire, and so they grow only in wet places
B. visitors are frightened of wolves, and so they stay near the main roads
C. elk avoid places where wolves can easily catch them
D. wolves are afraid of people, and so they avoid the roads in the park

q.q: Beavers rely on willows for food and for building ____.
q.e: Paragraph 4 says beavers rely on willows for food and dams.

q.q: According to paragraph 4, the number of beaver colonies increased.
q.e: Paragraph 4 says the number of beaver colonies increased.

q.q: According to paragraph 5, why were some researchers cautious about crediting the wolves?
q.e: Paragraph 5 lists hunting, winters, other predators, drought and climate.
o: A. The willows had been planted by people, and not by the wolves or by nature
B. The wolves were not seen again after 1996, so there was no evidence about their effects
C. The elk had migrated to Canada, so the number in the park was falling
D. Elk numbers had been falling for other reasons too, and climate affected tree growth

q.q: What did one study of willows conclude?
o: A. The beavers had eaten the willows, and this had caused all the changes in the valley
B. Wolves were the only cause of change, and nothing else had affected the willows
C. Changes in vegetation could largely be explained by climate and water, not wolves
D. The willows were dying, and the wolves had been unable to save them

q.q: What does the writer suggest about the claim that wolves changed the course of rivers?
q.e: Paragraph 6 reports that effects on channels are modest, so the claim is an exaggeration.
o: A. It was invented by hydrologists
B. It exaggerates a small effect
C. It is the main finding of all researchers
D. It has been proved by careful measurements

q.q: In paragraph 6, the word "modest" most nearly means:
o: A. expensive
B. small
C. dangerous
D. hidden

q.q: The writer states that scientists can easily repeat the Yellowstone experiment without wolves.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says scientists cannot rerun the experiment under identical conditions.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 7?
q.e: Paragraph 7 explains the difficulty of studying a single ecosystem.
o: A. It is difficult to separate the effects of many factors in a single large ecosystem
B. Statistics are not used in ecology, so the effects cannot be measured at all
C. Scientists have enough data to settle the debate, and the answer is now clear
D. Yellowstone is a small park, so the effects of the wolves are easy to see

q.q: Which of the following best describes the writer's attitude to the popular wolf story?
q.e: The writer admires the idea but points out its oversimplification.
o: A. Appreciative of its appeal, but critical of its tidiness
B. Indifferent to the subject, and unwilling to say what the evidence shows
C. Totally dismissive, and unwilling to accept any part of the story
D. Completely approving, and sure that the story is entirely correct

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
q.e: The passage presents real effects, the debate and the lesson about simple stories.
o: A. Scientists agree about every effect of the wolves, so the debate in the park is now over
B. Wolves have had real effects in Yellowstone, but the dramatic popular story oversimplifies a complex ecosystem
C. Wolves changed the rivers completely, and scientists have proved every part of the popular story
D. Wolves have had no effect in Yellowstone, and the story about them is an invention of the media

q.e: The passage does not mention this.

ps.b: ইয়েলোস্টোনের শিক্ষা তাই দ্বিমুখী।

ps.b: প্রথমত, বড় শিকারি প্রাণী গুরুত্বপূর্ণ, আর তাদের সরিয়ে দিলে এমন পরিণতি হতে পারে যা কেউ আগে ভাবেনি।

cmp/68.sub: Easter Island (Rapa Nui) and the collapse debate
cmp/68.title: Did the People of Easter Island Destroy Themselves?
cmp/68.src: Diamond; Hunt and Lipo; Moreno-Mayar et al.; UNESCO World Heritage Centre; Peiser
p: On a small triangle of land in the South Pacific, more than three thousand kilometres from the nearest continent, stand almost a thousand enormous stone figures. The island is known to the world as Easter Island, but its people call it Rapa Nui. The statues, called moai, are up to ten metres high and weigh many tonnes. For centuries, visitors have asked the same question: how could a small and isolated society carve and move such monuments? And, even more strikingly, what happened to it?

For many readers, the best-known answer comes from the geographer Jared Diamond. In his popular book Collapse, he described Easter Island as a warning to the whole planet. According to his account, Polynesian settlers arrived around the year 800 and found a forested island. As their population grew, they cut down the trees for farmland, for canoes and for rollers to move the statues. Eventually the forest disappeared, the soil weakened, and food became scarce. Society fell into warfare and hunger, and the population collapsed. The islanders, in this view, committed "ecocide": they destroyed the environment on which their survival depended.

It is a powerful and tidy story, and it has been told in countless documentaries and classrooms. But in recent years it has been challenged by researchers who have looked again at the evidence, and the challenges come from several directions.

The first concerns the date of arrival. More careful radiocarbon dating has suggested that people did not reach the island until about the year 1200, several centuries later than Diamond assumed. If the settlers arrived later, the story of a society that thrived for a thousand years and then ruined itself needs to be shortened considerably, and the timeline for the deforestation and the statues becomes much tighter.

The second challenge concerns the cause of the lost forest. The settlers brought with them the Polynesian rat, a stowaway on their canoes, and archaeologists have found palm nuts with the marks of rat teeth. Rats breed extremely fast, and they eat seeds; a few of them, in an island with no natural enemies, could have multiplied into millions. Some researchers argue that the rats may have been at least as important as the people in preventing young palm trees from growing, so the forest may have been lost less through human greed than through an accidental invasion.

The third challenge concerns the size and fate of the population. Diamond suggested that the population had risen to as many as fifteen thousand before it crashed, but archaeologists who have studied the number of houses and the island's farmland now estimate that the peak was probably only a few thousand. Genetic studies of the modern islanders also failed to find signs of a sudden population collapse before the first Europeans arrived. In this alternative account, the islanders were not self-destroyers but skilled farmers who adapted to a difficult environment by using stones to protect crops from the wind and sun.

What then caused the dramatic fall in population that the records clearly show? The critics point to the arrival of Europeans. The first recorded visit was by a Dutch ship on Easter Sunday in 1722, which gave the island its English name. Over the following century, contacts with foreign ships brought diseases to which the islanders had no resistance. Worse followed in the 1860s, when slave raiders from Peru kidnapped about a third of the population, among them many of the community's leaders. By 1877, only 111 islanders were left.

This does not mean that the earlier story is entirely wrong. Almost all researchers accept that the island's trees did largely disappear, and that the islanders had to adapt to a poorer environment. Where the disagreement lies is in the interpretation: whether the society collapsed because of its own mistakes, or whether it endured for centuries by clever adaptation and was destroyed by outside forces. The question is not purely academic, because the version that we believe determines the lesson that we draw, and it also affects how the Rapa Nui people are portrayed.

It is striking that the claim of a self-inflicted collapse became so well known while an alternative version, which gives the islanders more credit, remained in the background. Perhaps a story in which humans foolishly ruin their world is simply more appealing as a warning than a story in which a society survives for centuries and is then overwhelmed. Whichever version proves closer to the truth, the island reminds us that the past is often more complicated than the lessons that we try to draw from it.

o: A. They carried diseases to the trees

q.e: To endure is to last or survive over a long time.
o: A. survived for a long time
B. travelled across a wide sea
C. argued about a hard question
D. vanished after a short time

q.q: The writer states that all researchers agree that the islanders destroyed their own society.
q.e: Paragraph 8 says the disagreement is about interpretation.

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
