ps.b: এই বিকল্প বর্ণনায় দ্বীপবাসীরা আত্মধ্বংসকারী নয়, বরং দক্ষ কৃষক, যারা ফসলকে বাতাস ও রোদ থেকে বাঁচাতে পাথর ব্যবহার করে একটি কঠিন পরিবেশের সঙ্গে খাপ খাইয়ে নিয়েছিল।

ps.e: What then caused the dramatic fall in population that the records clearly show?
ps.b: তাহলে জনসংখ্যার নাটকীয় পতনের কারণ কী, যা নথিপত্রে স্পষ্ট দেখা যায়?

ps.e: The critics point to the arrival of Europeans.
ps.b: সমালোচকরা ইউরোপীয়দের আগমনের দিকে ইঙ্গিত করেন।

ps.e: The first recorded visit was by a Dutch ship on Easter Sunday in 1722, which gave the island its English name.
ps.b: প্রথম নথিভুক্ত পরিদর্শন ছিল ১৭২২ সালের ইস্টার সানডেতে একটি ডাচ জাহাজের, যা দ্বীপটিকে তার ইংরেজি নাম দিয়েছিল।

ps.e: Over the following century, contacts with foreign ships brought diseases to which the islanders had no resistance.
ps.b: পরবর্তী শতাব্দীতে বিদেশি জাহাজের সংস্পর্শ এমন রোগ নিয়ে এল যার বিরুদ্ধে দ্বীপবাসীদের কোনো প্রতিরোধ ক্ষমতা ছিল না।

ps.e: Worse followed in the 1860s, when slave raiders from Peru kidnapped about a third of the population, among them many of the community's leaders.
ps.b: আরও খারাপ কিছু ঘটল ১৮৬০-এর দশকে, যখন পেরুর দাস-হানাদাররা জনসংখ্যার প্রায় এক-তৃতীয়াংশকে অপহরণ করল, যাদের মধ্যে ছিলেন সম্প্রদায়ের অনেক নেতাও।

ps.e: By 1877, only 111 islanders were left.
ps.b: ১৮৭৭ সালের মধ্যে মাত্র ১১১ জন দ্বীপবাসী অবশিষ্ট ছিলেন।

ps.e: This does not mean that the earlier story is entirely wrong.
ps.b: এর মানে এই নয় যে আগের গল্পটি পুরোপুরি ভুল।

ps.e: Almost all researchers accept that the island's trees did largely disappear, and that the islanders had to adapt to a poorer environment.
ps.b: প্রায় সব গবেষকই মানেন যে দ্বীপের গাছ বহুলাংশে সত্যিই অদৃশ্য হয়েছিল, এবং দ্বীপবাসীদের একটি দরিদ্রতর পরিবেশের সঙ্গে খাপ খাইয়ে নিতে হয়েছিল।

ps.e: Where the disagreement lies is in the interpretation: whether the society collapsed because of its own mistakes, or whether it endured for centuries by clever adaptation and was destroyed by outside forces.
ps.b: মতভেদ রয়েছে ব্যাখ্যায়: সমাজটি কি নিজের ভুলের কারণে ধসে পড়েছিল, নাকি চতুর অভিযোজনের মাধ্যমে শতাব্দীর পর শতাব্দী টিকে ছিল এবং বাইরের শক্তি তাকে ধ্বংস করেছে।

ps.e: The question is not purely academic, because the version that we believe determines the lesson that we draw, and it also affects how the Rapa Nui people are portrayed.
ps.b: প্রশ্নটি নিছক তাত্ত্বিক নয়, কারণ আমরা যে সংস্করণ বিশ্বাস করি তা নির্ধারণ করে আমরা কোন শিক্ষা নেব, আর এটি রাপা নুই জনগণকে কীভাবে চিত্রিত করা হয় তাকেও প্রভাবিত করে।

ps.e: It is striking that the claim of a self-inflicted collapse became so well known while an alternative version, which gives the islanders more credit, remained in the background.
ps.b: এটি লক্ষণীয় যে আত্মঘাতী ধসের দাবিটি এত বিখ্যাত হয়ে উঠল, অথচ এমন একটি বিকল্প সংস্করণ, যা দ্বীপবাসীদের বেশি কৃতিত্ব দেয়, পটভূমিতেই থেকে গেল।

ps.e: Perhaps a story in which humans foolishly ruin their world is simply more appealing as a warning than a story in which a society survives for centuries and is then overwhelmed.
ps.b: হয়তো মানুষ নির্বোধের মতো নিজেদের পৃথিবী ধ্বংস করে এমন একটি গল্প সতর্কবার্তা হিসেবে বেশি আকর্ষণীয়, এমন গল্পের চেয়ে যেখানে একটি সমাজ শতাব্দীর পর শতাব্দী টিকে থেকে তারপর পরাভূত হয়।

ps.e: Whichever version proves closer to the truth, the island reminds us that the past is often more complicated than the lessons that we try to draw from it.
ps.b: কোন সংস্করণ সত্যের কাছাকাছি প্রমাণিত হোক না কেন, দ্বীপটি আমাদের মনে করিয়ে দেয় যে অতীত প্রায়ই আমাদের টানা শিক্ষাগুলোর চেয়ে অনেক বেশি জটিল।

cmp/69.title: When the Experiment Is Repeated
cmp/69.src: Open Science Collaboration; Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn; Begley and Ellis; Ranehill et al.; Center for Open Science
p: Science is often described as a self-correcting activity: a researcher announces a finding, others repeat the work, and mistakes are eventually weeded out. In the early 2010s, a group of psychologists decided to test whether this was really happening. The answer, when it arrived, shocked many in the field and led to a period that is now called the replication crisis. It is a story that matters not only to psychologists but to anyone who reads about the latest scientific discovery.

The most famous test was a project completed in 2015. A large team of researchers, working together as the Open Science Collaboration, selected one hundred studies that had been published in three leading psychology journals in 2008. They then carried out new versions of each experiment, usually with larger numbers of participants and with the help of the original authors. The result was sobering. In the original papers, ninety-seven of the studies had reported a statistically significant result. When they were repeated, only about thirty-six did, and the size of the effects was, on average, roughly half of what had first been reported.

The finding did not stand alone. A few years earlier, a pharmaceutical company had tried to repeat fifty-three important studies in cancer research and managed to confirm the results of only six. Cases of outright fraud, such as that of a well-known Dutch psychologist who was found to have invented data for dozens of papers, drew public attention. But it soon became clear that deliberate fraud was not the main cause of the problem. The explanation lay in the ordinary incentives of the scientific profession.

One cause is publication bias. Journals prefer exciting, positive results, and researchers know that a paper reporting that nothing happened is far harder to publish. Studies that fail are therefore quietly left in a drawer, a phenomenon known as the file-drawer problem, and the published literature gives a distorted impression of how reliable a result really is. A reader sees the successes but not the many failed attempts that remained invisible.

A second cause is flexibility in analysis. A researcher who collects data has many choices to make: which participants to exclude, which measurements to combine, when to stop collecting. Each choice is defensible, but together they give a researcher many chances to find something that looks significant. In a well-known demonstration in 2011, three researchers showed that by exploiting such freedom, they could "prove" that listening to a particular song made people younger. The point was not that anybody believed it, but that the usual standards of evidence could be met by an absurd claim. Sometimes called "p-hacking", the practice is usually not dishonest; it is the result of wishing to find something.

A third cause is simply that many studies were too small. A study with few participants has a low chance of detecting a real effect, and when it does produce a significant result, that result is more likely to be a fluke or an exaggeration. Many famous findings in psychology, such as the claim that standing in a "power pose" changes hormone levels and confidence, were based on small samples, and did not hold up when larger groups were tested.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that psychology is worthless or that science has failed. Many effects have been confirmed repeatedly, and the discovery of the problem was itself an act of science correcting itself. Moreover, a failed replication does not always prove that the original was wrong. The new study may have used a different population, a different setting or a slightly different procedure, and the effect may depend on those conditions. Establishing which of these explanations is right is slow and often uncertain.

The reaction in the field has been constructive. Researchers now increasingly register their plans in advance, stating what they intend to measure and how they will analyse it, so that they cannot adjust the analysis after seeing the results. Some journals accept papers on the strength of the question and the method, before the data are collected, which removes the temptation to prefer positive findings. Larger samples, open sharing of data and collaborations between laboratories have become more common.

For the general reader, the lesson is not to distrust all science, but to treat single studies with caution. A striking result from one small experiment, reported in a headline, deserves less confidence than a finding that has been repeated by different teams in different places. In this sense, the replication crisis has made science more honest about its own limits, and ultimately more reliable.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 4?

o: A. All studies are published, so the record is complete and gives a fair picture of the evidence

q.q: What does the term "file-drawer problem" refer to?
q.e: Paragraph 4 explains that failed studies are quietly left in a drawer.
o: A. The sharing of too much data with others
B. Failed studies being left unpublished
C. Important documents lost by mistake
D. Fraud in the laboratory by researchers

q.q: According to paragraph 5, why can researchers using flexible analysis find results that look significant?

o: A. They never make choices, so every result they find is a true one
B. They use too much data, which makes the answers hard to read

q.q: The 2011 demonstration was intended to show that listening to a song really makes people younger.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says the point was to show that an absurd claim could meet normal standards of evidence.

q.q: In paragraph 6, the word "fluke" most nearly means:
q.e: A fluke is something that happens by chance.
o: A. a result due to chance
B. a famous researcher in the field
C. a large sample
D. a deliberate trick

q.q: The writer states that the power pose study was based on a large sample.
q.e: Paragraph 6 says such findings were based on small samples.

q.q: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 7?
q.e: Paragraph 7 says the problem should not lead to the conclusion that science has failed.
o: A. Psychology should be closed, since its results cannot be trusted by anyone
B. Failed replications do not prove that science has failed or that the original result was wrong
C. All replications succeeded, and so the original studies were shown to be correct in every case
D. Original studies are always right, so a failed replication must be a mistake

q.q: Which of the following best describes the writer's attitude to the replication crisis?
q.e: The writer treats it as a real problem and highlights the positive response.
o: A. Humorous, and amused by the mistakes that researchers have made
B. Serious but constructive, seeing it as an opportunity for science to improve
C. Despairing, and convinced that science can no longer find any reliable result
D. Hostile to scientists, whom the writer blames for the whole problem

q.q: Which of the following is the best summary of the whole passage?
q.e: The passage covers the evidence, the causes, the cautions and the reforms.
o: A. The replication crisis revealed that many findings do not hold up, due to ordinary pressures in research, and reforms are making science more reliable
B. Science cannot be trusted at all, since most findings in every field have been shown to be false
C. Psychology has been proved wrong in every study that has been repeated, and the whole subject should now be rejected by all scientists.

q.e: The passage does not mention this.

ps.b: একটি কারণ প্রকাশনার পক্ষপাত।

ps.e: Journals prefer exciting, positive results, and researchers know that a paper reporting that nothing happened is far harder to publish.
ps.b: সাময়িকীগুলো উত্তেজনাপূর্ণ, ইতিবাচক ফল পছন্দ করে, আর গবেষকরা জানেন যে "কিছুই ঘটেনি" জানানো প্রবন্ধ প্রকাশ করা অনেক কঠিন।

ps.e: Studies that fail are therefore quietly left in a drawer, a phenomenon known as the file-drawer problem, and the published literature gives a distorted impression of how reliable a result really is.
ps.b: তাই যেসব গবেষণা ব্যর্থ হয় সেগুলো নিঃশব্দে ড্রয়ারে পড়ে থাকে, যে ঘটনাকে বলা হয় ফাইল-ড্রয়ার সমস্যা, আর প্রকাশিত সাহিত্য একটি ফলাফল আসলে কতটা নির্ভরযোগ্য সে সম্পর্কে বিকৃত ধারণা দেয়।

ps.e: A reader sees the successes but not the many failed attempts that remained invisible.
ps.b: পাঠক সাফল্যগুলো দেখেন, কিন্তু অসংখ্য ব্যর্থ প্রচেষ্টা, যা অদৃশ্য থেকে গেছে, দেখেন না।

ps.e: A second cause is flexibility in analysis.
ps.b: দ্বিতীয় কারণ বিশ্লেষণের নমনীয়তা।

ps.e: A researcher who collects data has many choices to make: which participants to exclude, which measurements to combine, when to stop collecting.
ps.b: তথ্য সংগ্রহকারী একজন গবেষককে অনেক সিদ্ধান্ত নিতে হয়: কোন অংশগ্রহণকারীদের বাদ দেবেন, কোন পরিমাপ একত্র করবেন, কখন তথ্য সংগ্রহ বন্ধ করবেন।

ps.e: Each choice is defensible, but together they give a researcher many chances to find something that looks significant.
ps.b: প্রতিটি সিদ্ধান্ত সমর্থনযোগ্য, কিন্তু সব মিলিয়ে তা একজন গবেষককে এমন কিছু খুঁজে পাওয়ার অনেক সুযোগ দেয় যা উল্লেখযোগ্য দেখায়।

ps.e: In a well-known demonstration in 2011, three researchers showed that by exploiting such freedom, they could "prove" that listening to a particular song made people younger.
ps.b: ২০১১ সালের একটি সুপরিচিত প্রদর্শনীতে তিনজন গবেষক দেখালেন, এমন স্বাধীনতাকে কাজে লাগিয়ে তাঁরা "প্রমাণ" করতে পারেন যে একটি বিশেষ গান শুনলে মানুষ বয়সে ছোট হয়ে যায়।

ps.e: The point was not that anybody believed it, but that the usual standards of evidence could be met by an absurd claim.
ps.b: বিষয়টি এই ছিল না যে কেউ তা বিশ্বাস করেছে, বরং এই যে প্রমাণের সাধারণ মানদণ্ড একটি অযৌক্তিক দাবিও পূরণ করতে পারে।

ps.e: Sometimes called "p-hacking", the practice is usually not dishonest; it is the result of wishing to find something.
ps.b: কখনও কখনও "পি-হ্যাকিং" নামে পরিচিত এই চর্চা সাধারণত অসৎ নয়; এটি কিছু খুঁজে পাওয়ার ইচ্ছার ফল।

ps.e: A third cause is simply that many studies were too small.
ps.b: তৃতীয় কারণ হলো, অনেক গবেষণা ছিল নিছকই খুব ছোট।

ps.e: A study with few participants has a low chance of detecting a real effect, and when it does produce a significant result, that result is more likely to be a fluke or an exaggeration.
ps.b: কম অংশগ্রহণকারীর গবেষণায় প্রকৃত প্রভাব শনাক্ত হওয়ার সম্ভাবনা কম, আর যখন তা উল্লেখযোগ্য ফল দেয়, সেই ফল আকস্মিক ঘটনা বা অতিরঞ্জন হওয়ার সম্ভাবনা বেশি।

ps.e: Many famous findings in psychology, such as the claim that standing in a "power pose" changes hormone levels and confidence, were based on small samples, and did not hold up when larger groups were tested.
ps.b: মনোবিজ্ঞানের অনেক বিখ্যাত আবিষ্কার, যেমন "পাওয়ার পোজে" দাঁড়ালে হরমোনের মাত্রা ও আত্মবিশ্বাস বদলে যায় এই দাবি, ছিল ছোট নমুনার ওপর ভিত্তি করে, এবং বড় দলে পরীক্ষা করলে তা টেকেনি।

ps.e: It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that psychology is worthless or that science has failed.
ps.b: তবে এই সিদ্ধান্তে আসা ভুল হবে যে মনোবিজ্ঞান মূল্যহীন বা বিজ্ঞান ব্যর্থ হয়েছে।

ps.e: Many effects have been confirmed repeatedly, and the discovery of the problem was itself an act of science correcting itself.
ps.b: অনেক প্রভাব বারবার নিশ্চিত হয়েছে, আর সমস্যাটি আবিষ্কার করাই ছিল বিজ্ঞানের নিজেকে শুধরে নেওয়ার একটি কাজ।

ps.e: Moreover, a failed replication does not always prove that the original was wrong.
ps.b: তাছাড়া, একটি ব্যর্থ পুনরাবৃত্তি সবসময় প্রমাণ করে না যে মূল গবেষণাটি ভুল ছিল।

ps.e: The new study may have used a different population, a different setting or a slightly different procedure, and the effect may depend on those conditions.
ps.b: নতুন গবেষণায় হয়তো ভিন্ন জনগোষ্ঠী, ভিন্ন পরিবেশ বা কিছুটা ভিন্ন পদ্ধতি ব্যবহার হয়েছে, আর প্রভাবটি সেই শর্তের ওপর নির্ভর করতে পারে।

ps.e: Establishing which of these explanations is right is slow and often uncertain.
ps.b: এর কোন ব্যাখ্যা সঠিক তা প্রতিষ্ঠা করা ধীর এবং প্রায়ই অনিশ্চিত।

ps.e: The reaction in the field has been constructive.
ps.b: এই ক্ষেত্রের প্রতিক্রিয়া গঠনমূলক হয়েছে।

ps.e: Researchers now increasingly register their plans in advance, stating what they intend to measure and how they will analyse it, so that they cannot adjust the analysis after seeing the results.
ps.b: গবেষকরা এখন ক্রমশ আগেই নিজেদের পরিকল্পনা নিবন্ধন করেন, কী মাপবেন এবং কীভাবে বিশ্লেষণ করবেন তা উল্লেখ করে, যাতে ফল দেখার পর বিশ্লেষণ বদলাতে না পারেন।

ps.e: Some journals accept papers on the strength of the question and the method, before the data are collected, which removes the temptation to prefer positive findings.
ps.b: কিছু সাময়িকী তথ্য সংগ্রহের আগেই প্রশ্ন ও পদ্ধতির জোরে প্রবন্ধ গ্রহণ করে, যা ইতিবাচক ফলকে বেশি পছন্দ করার প্রলোভন দূর করে।

ps.e: Larger samples, open sharing of data and collaborations between laboratories have become more common.
ps.b: বড় নমুনা, খোলাভাবে তথ্য ভাগ করা এবং গবেষণাগারগুলোর মধ্যে সহযোগিতা আরও সাধারণ হয়ে উঠেছে।

ps.e: For the general reader, the lesson is not to distrust all science, but to treat single studies with caution.
ps.b: সাধারণ পাঠকের জন্য শিক্ষাটি সব বিজ্ঞানকে অবিশ্বাস করা নয়, বরং একক গবেষণাকে সতর্কতার সঙ্গে নেওয়া।

ps.e: A striking result from one small experiment, reported in a headline, deserves less confidence than a finding that has been repeated by different teams in different places.
ps.b: একটি ছোট পরীক্ষা থেকে আসা চমকপ্রদ ফল, যা শিরোনামে প্রচারিত, বিভিন্ন জায়গায় বিভিন্ন দল বারবার যাচাই করা আবিষ্কারের চেয়ে কম আস্থার যোগ্য।

ps.e: In this sense, the replication crisis has made science more honest about its own limits, and ultimately more reliable.
ps.b: এই অর্থে পুনরাবৃত্তি-সংকট বিজ্ঞানকে নিজের সীমাবদ্ধতা সম্পর্কে আরও সৎ করেছে, এবং শেষ পর্যন্ত আরও নির্ভরযোগ্য।

cmp/13.title: The Engineers With Eight Legs
cmp/13.src: Natural History Museum, London; Smithsonian National Zoo; Royal Society of Chemistry
p: Many people feel uncomfortable when they see a spider, but spiders are among the most skilful builders in the animal world. Without tools, plans or teachers, a spider can produce a net so fine that it is almost invisible and yet strong enough to catch a flying insect at full speed. The secret of this ability is silk.

Spider silk is a protein made inside the spider's body. It is stored as a liquid, and when the spider needs it, the liquid is pulled out through tiny tubes at the end of the body called spinnerets. As it leaves the body, the liquid becomes a solid thread. A single spider can make several different kinds of silk, each for a different job. Some threads are sticky, some are dry, and some are very stretchy.

The best-known use of silk is the web. The round web of the garden spider, called an orb web, is built in a careful order. First the spider makes a frame and a few straight lines that run to the centre like the spokes of a wheel. Then it adds a spiral of sticky thread. When an insect flies into the web, it sticks, and the shaking of the thread tells the spider where its meal is. Many spiders repair or replace their web every day.

However, not all spiders build webs to catch food. Wolf spiders chase their prey across the ground, and jumping spiders leap on it from a distance. Even these hunters use silk. They leave a thread behind them as a safety line, so that they can climb back if they fall, and they use silk to wrap their eggs. A female spider often makes a soft case of silk, called an egg sac, and guards it until the baby spiders are ready to come out.

Baby spiders have a clever way of travelling. Some climb to the top of a plant, lift their bodies into the air and release a long thread of silk. The wind catches the thread and carries them away, sometimes for many kilometres. This is called ballooning. Charles Darwin noticed hundreds of tiny spiders landing on his ship when it was far from the coast, and the observation helped him to understand how animals can reach distant islands.

Scientists are very interested in spider silk because of its special properties. Weight for weight, some kinds of silk are as strong as steel, and yet they can stretch a long way without breaking. Researchers hope to use silk-like materials for very fine stitches for operations, for light but strong clothing and even for protection against bullets. A material that comes from a harmless animal, rather than from oil, would also be better for the environment.

There is one big problem. Spiders cannot be kept together on a farm in the way that silkworms are, because they tend to attack and eat each other. For this reason, researchers have tried to copy the silk instead. They have placed the spider's silk genes inside other living things, such as bacteria, and used these to produce the protein in a laboratory. The results are promising, but making silk that is as good as the real thing is still difficult.

Spiders also help people in a quieter way. Because they eat enormous numbers of insects, including flies and mosquitoes, they help to control pests in gardens, farms and homes. Most spiders are harmless to humans, and only a few kinds have a bite that is dangerous. So the next time you see a spider in the corner of a room, remember that it is a clever engineer and a free pest controller.

ps.e: Spider silk is a protein made inside the spider's body.

ps.b: কোনো পোকা জালে উড়ে এসে পড়লে তা আটকে যায়, আর সুতার কাঁপুনি মাকড়সাকে জানিয়ে দেয় তার খাবার কোথায়।

ps.e: Many spiders repair or replace their web every day.
ps.b: অনেক মাকড়সা প্রতিদিন তাদের জাল মেরামত বা বদলে নেয়।

ps.e: However, not all spiders build webs to catch food.
ps.b: তবে সব মাকড়সা খাবার ধরতে জাল বোনে না।

ps.e: Wolf spiders chase their prey across the ground, and jumping spiders leap on it from a distance.
ps.b: নেকড়ে মাকড়সা মাটিতে শিকারের পিছু ধাওয়া করে, আর লাফানো মাকড়সা দূর থেকে লাফিয়ে তার ওপর পড়ে।

ps.e: Even these hunters use silk.
ps.b: এই শিকারিরাও সুতা ব্যবহার করে।

ps.e: They leave a thread behind them as a safety line, so that they can climb back if they fall, and they use silk to wrap their eggs.
ps.b: তারা পেছনে একটি সুতা রেখে যায় নিরাপত্তা-রেখা হিসেবে, যাতে পড়ে গেলে উঠে আসতে পারে, আর ডিম মুড়তেও সুতা ব্যবহার করে।

ps.e: A female spider often makes a soft case of silk, called an egg sac, and guards it until the baby spiders are ready to come out.
ps.b: স্ত্রী মাকড়সা প্রায়ই সুতার একটি নরম খোল বানায়, যাকে বলা হয় ডিমের থলি, এবং বাচ্চারা বেরোনোর জন্য প্রস্তুত না হওয়া পর্যন্ত তা পাহারা দেয়।

ps.e: Baby spiders have a clever way of travelling.
ps.b: মাকড়সার বাচ্চাদের ভ্রমণের একটি চতুর উপায় আছে।

ps.e: Some climb to the top of a plant, lift their bodies into the air and release a long thread of silk.
ps.b: কেউ কেউ গাছের মাথায় উঠে শরীর বাতাসে তুলে ধরে এবং একটি লম্বা সুতা ছেড়ে দেয়।

ps.e: The wind catches the thread and carries them away, sometimes for many kilometres.
ps.b: বাতাস সুতাটি ধরে ফেলে তাদের উড়িয়ে নিয়ে যায়, কখনও বহু কিলোমিটার।

ps.e: This is called ballooning.
ps.b: একে বলা হয় বেলুনিং।

ps.e: Charles Darwin noticed hundreds of tiny spiders landing on his ship when it was far from the coast, and the observation helped him to understand how animals can reach distant islands.
ps.b: চার্লস ডারউইন লক্ষ করেছিলেন, উপকূল থেকে অনেক দূরে তাঁর জাহাজে শত শত ক্ষুদ্র মাকড়সা এসে নামছে, আর এই পর্যবেক্ষণ তাঁকে বুঝতে সাহায্য করেছিল প্রাণীরা কীভাবে দূরবর্তী দ্বীপে পৌঁছাতে পারে।

ps.e: Scientists are very interested in spider silk because of its special properties.
ps.b: বিজ্ঞানীরা মাকড়সার সুতা নিয়ে খুব আগ্রহী এর বিশেষ বৈশিষ্ট্যের কারণে।

ps.e: Weight for weight, some kinds of silk are as strong as steel, and yet they can stretch a long way without breaking.
ps.b: ওজনের হিসাবে, কিছু ধরনের সুতা ইস্পাতের মতোই শক্ত, অথচ না ছিঁড়ে অনেকটা টানা যায়।

ps.e: Researchers hope to use silk-like materials for very fine stitches for operations, for light but strong clothing and even for protection against bullets.
ps.b: গবেষকরা আশা করছেন, অস্ত্রোপচারের জন্য অতি সূক্ষ্ম সেলাই, হালকা অথচ শক্ত পোশাক, এমনকি গুলি থেকে সুরক্ষার জন্য সুতার মতো উপাদান ব্যবহার করবেন।

ps.e: A material that comes from a harmless animal, rather than from oil, would also be better for the environment.
ps.b: তেলের বদলে নিরীহ প্রাণী থেকে পাওয়া উপাদান পরিবেশের জন্যও ভালো হতো।

ps.e: There is one big problem.
ps.b: একটি বড় সমস্যা আছে।

ps.e: Spiders cannot be kept together on a farm in the way that silkworms are, because they tend to attack and eat each other.
ps.b: রেশম পোকার মতো মাকড়সাদের খামারে একসঙ্গে রাখা যায় না, কারণ তারা একে অপরকে আক্রমণ করে খেয়ে ফেলে।

ps.e: For this reason, researchers have tried to copy the silk instead.
ps.b: এ কারণে গবেষকরা বরং সুতাটি নকল করার চেষ্টা করেছেন।

ps.e: They have placed the spider's silk genes inside other living things, such as bacteria, and used these to produce the protein in a laboratory.
ps.b: তাঁরা মাকড়সার সুতার জিন অন্য জীবের ভেতরে, যেমন ব্যাকটেরিয়ায়, বসিয়ে গবেষণাগারে প্রোটিনটি তৈরি করেছেন।

ps.e: The results are promising, but making silk that is as good as the real thing is still difficult.
ps.b: ফল আশাব্যঞ্জক, কিন্তু আসলটির মতো ভালো সুতা তৈরি করা এখনও কঠিন।

ps.e: Spiders also help people in a quieter way.
ps.b: মাকড়সারা মানুষকে আরও নীরবভাবে সাহায্য করে।

ps.e: Because they eat enormous numbers of insects, including flies and mosquitoes, they help to control pests in gardens, farms and homes.
ps.b: যেহেতু তারা মাছি ও মশাসহ বিপুল সংখ্যক পোকা খায়, তারা বাগান, খামার ও ঘরে ক্ষতিকর পোকা নিয়ন্ত্রণে সাহায্য করে।

ps.e: Most spiders are harmless to humans, and only a few kinds have a bite that is dangerous.
ps.b: বেশিরভাগ মাকড়সা মানুষের জন্য ক্ষতিহীন, আর কেবল কয়েক ধরনের মাকড়সার কামড় বিপজ্জনক।

ps.e: So the next time you see a spider in the corner of a room, remember that it is a clever engineer and a free pest controller.
ps.b: তাই পরের বার ঘরের কোণে একটি মাকড়সা দেখলে মনে রাখবেন, সে একজন চতুর প্রকৌশলী এবং বিনামূল্যের পোকা-দমনকারী।

cmp/14.title: One Plant, Many Teas
cmp/14.src: Tea Association; International Tea Committee; British Museum; Science Museum Group; Bangladesh Tea Board
p: After water, tea is probably the most popular drink in the world. Every day, people in almost every country boil water, pour it over dry leaves and wait a few minutes. The habit is so ordinary that few of us stop to ask where it came from. Yet the story of tea crosses continents, and it has changed the history of trade, farming and even politics.

According to a Chinese legend, tea was discovered by accident about five thousand years ago. The emperor Shennong was boiling water under a tree when a few leaves blew into the pot. He tasted the drink and found it pleasant. We cannot be sure that this really happened, but we do know that people in China were drinking tea long ago, first as a medicine and later as a daily pleasure.

It surprises many people to learn that black tea, green tea, white tea and oolong tea all come from the same plant. The plant is a bush called Camellia sinensis. The difference between the types lies in how the leaves are treated after they are picked. For green tea, the leaves are heated quickly to stop them from changing colour. For black tea, the leaves are rolled and left in the air, so that they turn dark and develop a stronger flavour. Drinks made from flowers, herbs or fruit, such as mint or chamomile tea, are often called teas, but they do not come from this plant.

Tea slowly travelled out of China. Buddhist monks carried it to Japan, where it became part of a famous ceremony. In the seventeenth century, Dutch and Portuguese traders brought it to Europe by ship. At first it was very expensive and was drunk only by the rich, but as the quantities grew, the price fell, and by the eighteenth century tea had become the national drink of Britain.

Tea also played a part in a famous protest. In 1773, American settlers were angry about a British tax on tea. A group of them boarded ships in Boston harbour and threw hundreds of boxes of tea into the water. The event, known as the Boston Tea Party, is remembered as one of the steps towards the American Revolution.

For a long time, China was almost the only country that sold tea to the world, and this made foreign traders uncomfortable. In the nineteenth century, the British began to grow tea in their own territories. They discovered that a wild type of tea plant grew in Assam in north-east India, and they opened large tea gardens there. Tea growing soon spread to Sri Lanka, then called Ceylon, and to the hills of Sylhet, in what is now Bangladesh, where the green slopes of Srimangal are famous today.

Today, tea is grown in many countries, with China and India producing the largest amounts. Kenya and Sri Lanka are also important producers. Millions of people work on tea farms, and most of the picking is still done by hand, because a machine cannot easily choose the youngest leaves. This work is hard, and the workers often earn very little, so many groups are trying to make tea farming fairer.

The humble cup of tea is therefore much more than a drink. It carries the history of empires, the work of farmers and a custom that many people share. Whether you add milk, sugar, lemon or nothing at all, you are taking part in a story that is thousands of years old.

ps.b: তাদের একটি দল বোস্টন বন্দরে জাহাজে উঠে শত শত বাক্স চা পানিতে ছুড়ে ফেলল।

ps.e: The event, known as the Boston Tea Party, is remembered as one of the steps towards the American Revolution.
ps.b: বোস্টন টি পার্টি নামে পরিচিত এই ঘটনা আমেরিকান বিপ্লবের দিকে যাওয়ার একটি ধাপ হিসেবে স্মরণ করা হয়।

ps.e: For a long time, China was almost the only country that sold tea to the world, and this made foreign traders uncomfortable.
ps.b: দীর্ঘদিন চীন ছিল প্রায় একমাত্র দেশ যে বিশ্বকে চা বিক্রি করত, আর এতে বিদেশি ব্যবসায়ীরা অস্বস্তিতে ছিলেন।

ps.e: In the nineteenth century, the British began to grow tea in their own territories.
ps.b: উনবিংশ শতাব্দীতে ব্রিটিশরা নিজেদের অধীন অঞ্চলে চা চাষ শুরু করল।

ps.e: They discovered that a wild type of tea plant grew in Assam in north-east India, and they opened large tea gardens there.
ps.b: তারা আবিষ্কার করল উত্তর-পূর্ব ভারতের আসামে একটি বুনো ধরনের চা গাছ জন্মায়, আর সেখানে বড় চা বাগান খুলল।

ps.e: Tea growing soon spread to Sri Lanka, then called Ceylon, and to the hills of Sylhet, in what is now Bangladesh, where the green slopes of Srimangal are famous today.
ps.b: চা চাষ শিগগিরই ছড়াল শ্রীলঙ্কায়, তখনকার সিলনে, এবং বর্তমান বাংলাদেশের সিলেটের পাহাড়ে, যেখানে শ্রীমঙ্গলের সবুজ ঢাল আজ বিখ্যাত।

ps.e: Today, tea is grown in many countries, with China and India producing the largest amounts.
ps.b: আজ চা অনেক দেশে চাষ হয়, চীন ও ভারত সবচেয়ে বেশি উৎপাদন করে।

ps.e: Kenya and Sri Lanka are also important producers.
ps.b: কেনিয়া ও শ্রীলঙ্কাও গুরুত্বপূর্ণ উৎপাদক।

ps.e: Millions of people work on tea farms, and most of the picking is still done by hand, because a machine cannot easily choose the youngest leaves.
ps.b: লক্ষ লক্ষ মানুষ চা-খামারে কাজ করেন, আর বেশিরভাগ পাতা তোলা এখনও হাতে হয়, কারণ যন্ত্র সহজে সবচেয়ে কচি পাতা বাছতে পারে না।

ps.e: This work is hard, and the workers often earn very little, so many groups are trying to make tea farming fairer.
ps.b: এই কাজ কঠিন, আর শ্রমিকরা প্রায়ই খুব কম আয় করেন, তাই অনেক সংগঠন চা-চাষকে আরও ন্যায্য করার চেষ্টা করছে।

ps.e: The humble cup of tea is therefore much more than a drink.
ps.b: তাই সাধারণ এক কাপ চা একটি পানীয়ের চেয়ে অনেক বেশি কিছু।

ps.e: It carries the history of empires, the work of farmers and a custom that many people share.
ps.b: এটি বহন করে সাম্রাজ্যের ইতিহাস, কৃষকদের শ্রম এবং এমন একটি রীতি যা অনেক মানুষ ভাগ করে নেয়।

ps.e: Whether you add milk, sugar, lemon or nothing at all, you are taking part in a story that is thousands of years old.
ps.b: আপনি দুধ, চিনি, লেবু বা কিছুই না মেশান, আপনি হাজার হাজার বছরের পুরোনো একটি গল্পের অংশ হচ্ছেন।

cmp/15.title: Why the Ground Shakes
cmp/15.src: United States Geological Survey; Japan Meteorological Agency; British Geological Survey
p: For most of the time, the ground beneath our feet seems solid and still. But every day, somewhere on Earth, it shakes. Most of these tremors are too small to feel. A few are powerful enough to shake buildings, crack roads and change the lives of millions of people. To understand why this happens, we need to look at the way our planet is built.

The outer layer of the Earth, called the crust, is not one solid piece. It is broken into huge slabs called tectonic plates, which fit together like the pieces of a puzzle. The plates float slowly on the hot, soft rock beneath them. They move very slowly, usually only a few centimetres a year, which is about the speed at which a fingernail grows. Over millions of years, however, this movement is enough to push up mountains and open oceans.

The places where plates meet are called faults. At a fault, the plates do not slide past each other smoothly. Their edges are rough, and they get stuck. The plates keep trying to move, so the pressure builds up, much as it does when you bend a ruler. After years or even centuries, the rock suddenly breaks, and the plates jump forward. The sudden release of energy sends waves through the ground in all directions. This is an earthquake.

The point underground where the rock breaks is called the focus, and the place on the surface directly above it is called the epicentre. The waves are strongest near the epicentre and become weaker with distance. Scientists record them with an instrument called a seismograph, which draws a line that stays flat when the ground is still and jumps up and down when it shakes.

The size of an earthquake is described by a number called its magnitude. The scale is not simple. Each step up on the scale means that the shaking in the ground is about ten times larger, and that the earthquake releases about thirty-two times more energy. An earthquake of magnitude seven is therefore enormously more powerful than one of magnitude five. Earthquakes below magnitude three are rarely felt, while those above magnitude seven can cause serious destruction.

Most earthquakes occur along the edges of the plates. The best-known region is the Ring of Fire, which runs around the edge of the Pacific Ocean and includes Japan, Chile and parts of the United States. South Asia, including Bangladesh, also lies near the meeting place of several plates, and a large earthquake in the region is considered possible in the future.

Can earthquakes be predicted? Despite many attempts, scientists cannot say exactly when or where the next big earthquake will happen. They can say which regions are most at risk, and they can estimate the chance of a large earthquake over many years, but not the day. For this reason, the best protection is preparation.

Preparation begins with buildings. Most of the people who die in earthquakes are killed by collapsing buildings, not by the shaking itself. In countries such as Japan, new buildings must follow strict rules, and some are built on special bases that move gently with the ground. Japan also has a warning system that detects the first, weaker waves and sends an alert seconds before the strong waves arrive. Those few seconds are enough to stop trains and give people time to take cover.

What should you do if the ground begins to shake? Experts give simple advice: drop to the ground, take cover under a strong table and hold on until the shaking stops. Stay away from windows and heavy objects that could fall. Earthquakes cannot be stopped, but knowledge and preparation can save many lives.

ps.e: After years or even centuries, the rock suddenly breaks, and the plates jump forward.
ps.b: কয়েক বছর বা এমনকি কয়েক শতাব্দী পর পাথর হঠাৎ ভেঙে যায়, আর পাতগুলো লাফিয়ে এগিয়ে যায়।

ps.e: The sudden release of energy sends waves through the ground in all directions.
ps.b: শক্তির এই আকস্মিক নির্গমন মাটির ভেতর দিয়ে সব দিকে তরঙ্গ পাঠায়।

ps.e: This is an earthquake.
ps.b: এটিই ভূমিকম্প।

ps.e: The point underground where the rock breaks is called the focus, and the place on the surface directly above it is called the epicentre.
ps.b: ভূগর্ভের যে বিন্দুতে পাথর ভাঙে তাকে বলা হয় কেন্দ্র, আর তার ঠিক ওপরে ভূপৃষ্ঠের স্থানটিকে বলা হয় উপকেন্দ্র।

ps.e: The waves are strongest near the epicentre and become weaker with distance.
ps.b: তরঙ্গগুলো উপকেন্দ্রের কাছে সবচেয়ে শক্তিশালী এবং দূরত্বের সঙ্গে দুর্বল হয়ে আসে।

ps.e: Scientists record them with an instrument called a seismograph, which draws a line that stays flat when the ground is still and jumps up and down when it shakes.
ps.b: বিজ্ঞানীরা এগুলো রেকর্ড করেন সিসমোগ্রাফ নামের যন্ত্র দিয়ে, যা এমন একটি রেখা আঁকে যা মাটি স্থির থাকলে সোজা থাকে আর কাঁপলে ওপরে-নিচে লাফায়।

ps.e: The size of an earthquake is described by a number called its magnitude.
ps.b: ভূমিকম্পের আকার বোঝানো হয় মাত্রা নামের একটি সংখ্যা দিয়ে।

ps.e: The scale is not simple.
ps.b: স্কেলটি সরল নয়।

ps.e: Each step up on the scale means that the shaking in the ground is about ten times larger, and that the earthquake releases about thirty-two times more energy.
ps.b: স্কেলে প্রতিটি ধাপ ওপরে ওঠার অর্থ মাটিতে কম্পন প্রায় দশগুণ বড়, আর ভূমিকম্প প্রায় বত্রিশগুণ বেশি শক্তি ছাড়ে।

ps.e: An earthquake of magnitude seven is therefore enormously more powerful than one of magnitude five.
ps.b: তাই মাত্রা সাতের ভূমিকম্প মাত্রা পাঁচের চেয়ে বিপুলভাবে বেশি শক্তিশালী।

ps.e: Earthquakes below magnitude three are rarely felt, while those above magnitude seven can cause serious destruction.
ps.b: মাত্রা তিনের নিচের ভূমিকম্প খুব কমই অনুভূত হয়, আর সাতের ওপরেরগুলো গুরুতর ধ্বংস ঘটাতে পারে।

ps.e: Most earthquakes occur along the edges of the plates.
ps.b: বেশিরভাগ ভূমিকম্প ঘটে পাতগুলোর কিনারা বরাবর।

ps.e: The best-known region is the Ring of Fire, which runs around the edge of the Pacific Ocean and includes Japan, Chile and parts of the United States.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে পরিচিত অঞ্চল হলো রিং অফ ফায়ার, যা প্রশান্ত মহাসাগরের কিনারা ঘিরে আছে এবং জাপান, চিলি ও যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের কিছু অংশ এর অন্তর্ভুক্ত।

ps.e: South Asia, including Bangladesh, also lies near the meeting place of several plates, and a large earthquake in the region is considered possible in the future.
ps.b: বাংলাদেশসহ দক্ষিণ এশিয়াও কয়েকটি পাতের মিলনস্থলের কাছে অবস্থিত, আর এই অঞ্চলে ভবিষ্যতে একটি বড় ভূমিকম্প সম্ভব বলে মনে করা হয়।

ps.e: Can earthquakes be predicted?
ps.b: ভূমিকম্প কি আগে থেকে বলা যায়?

ps.e: Despite many attempts, scientists cannot say exactly when or where the next big earthquake will happen.
ps.b: বহু চেষ্টা সত্ত্বেও বিজ্ঞানীরা ঠিক কখন বা কোথায় পরবর্তী বড় ভূমিকম্প হবে তা বলতে পারেন না।

ps.e: They can say which regions are most at risk, and they can estimate the chance of a large earthquake over many years, but not the day.
ps.b: কোন অঞ্চল সবচেয়ে ঝুঁকিতে তা তাঁরা বলতে পারেন, এবং বহু বছরের মধ্যে একটি বড় ভূমিকম্পের সম্ভাবনা অনুমান করতে পারেন, কিন্তু দিন বলতে পারেন না।

ps.e: For this reason, the best protection is preparation.
ps.b: এ কারণে সর্বোত্তম সুরক্ষা হলো প্রস্তুতি।

ps.e: Preparation begins with buildings.
ps.b: প্রস্তুতি শুরু হয় ভবন দিয়ে।

ps.e: Most of the people who die in earthquakes are killed by collapsing buildings, not by the shaking itself.
ps.b: ভূমিকম্পে যারা মারা যায় তাদের বেশিরভাগই মারা যায় ধসে পড়া ভবনে, কম্পনে নয়।

ps.e: In countries such as Japan, new buildings must follow strict rules, and some are built on special bases that move gently with the ground.
ps.b: জাপানের মতো দেশে নতুন ভবনকে কড়া নিয়ম মানতে হয়, আর কিছু ভবন বিশেষ ভিত্তির ওপর বানানো হয় যা মাটির সঙ্গে আলতোভাবে নড়ে।

ps.e: Japan also has a warning system that detects the first, weaker waves and sends an alert seconds before the strong waves arrive.
ps.b: জাপানে একটি সতর্কতা ব্যবস্থাও আছে, যা প্রথম, দুর্বল তরঙ্গ শনাক্ত করে এবং শক্তিশালী তরঙ্গ আসার কয়েক সেকেন্ড আগে সতর্কবার্তা পাঠায়।

ps.e: Those few seconds are enough to stop trains and give people time to take cover.
ps.b: এই কয়েক সেকেন্ডই ট্রেন থামাতে এবং মানুষকে আশ্রয় নেওয়ার সময় দিতে যথেষ্ট।

ps.e: What should you do if the ground begins to shake?
ps.b: মাটি কাঁপতে শুরু করলে কী করা উচিত?

ps.e: Experts give simple advice: drop to the ground, take cover under a strong table and hold on until the shaking stops.
ps.b: বিশেষজ্ঞরা সহজ পরামর্শ দেন: মাটিতে বসে পড়ুন, শক্ত টেবিলের নিচে আশ্রয় নিন এবং কাঁপুনি থামা পর্যন্ত আঁকড়ে থাকুন।

ps.e: Stay away from windows and heavy objects that could fall.
ps.b: জানালা এবং পড়ে যেতে পারে এমন ভারী জিনিস থেকে দূরে থাকুন।

ps.e: Earthquakes cannot be stopped, but knowledge and preparation can save many lives.
ps.b: ভূমিকম্প থামানো যায় না, কিন্তু জ্ঞান ও প্রস্তুতি অনেক প্রাণ বাঁচাতে পারে।

cmp/16.title: The Wall That Was Never Just One Wall
cmp/16.src: UNESCO World Heritage Centre; State Administration of Cultural Heritage of China; British Museum; National Geographic Society
p: Most people imagine the Great Wall of China as a single, long wall that winds across the mountains. This picture is not completely wrong, but it is not the whole truth either. The Great Wall is really a collection of many walls, towers and fortresses that were built over a period of more than two thousand years by different rulers.

The story begins in the third century before the common era. At that time, China was divided into several kingdoms, and each one built walls to protect itself from its neighbours and from the nomadic peoples of the north. When the first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, brought the country together in 221 BCE, he ordered that many of these earlier walls be joined and extended. Little of his wall remains today, because it was mostly made of packed earth, which slowly washes away in the rain.

Later dynasties repaired and added to the wall, but the parts that most visitors see were built much more recently. They date from the Ming dynasty, between the fourteenth and the seventeenth centuries. The Ming builders used bricks and stone, and they made the wall higher and stronger, with watchtowers and gates at regular distances. In 2012, a Chinese survey that measured all the known walls of all the dynasties concluded that their total length was more than twenty-one thousand kilometres.

The wall had several purposes. Its first job was defence: soldiers on top could watch for enemies and fight from a height. But it also controlled movement. Merchants and travellers who wished to cross the border had to pass through the gates, where officials could check them and collect taxes. The wall was an important part of life along the Silk Road, the trade route that joined China with the lands to the west.

The towers also carried messages. When a guard saw enemy soldiers, he lit a fire on top of a tower. At night, the flames were visible for a long way, and by day, the guards sent up smoke. The next tower repeated the signal, and so the news could travel along the wall much faster than a rider on a horse.

Building the wall was dreadful work. Soldiers, farmers and prisoners were forced to carry stone and earth, often in remote places with cold winters and little food. Many workers died, and over the centuries the wall acquired a sad reputation as a place of suffering. Chinese stories and poems about the wall often speak about the families who waited for men who never returned.

Did the wall succeed? The answer depends on the period. Sometimes it was effective, and sometimes it was not. A wall is only as strong as the soldiers who guard it, and an army that is determined can often find a gap or a gate that can be opened. In 1644, the Manchu army entered China not by breaking the wall, but through a gate that was opened for them in the middle of a war between Chinese forces.

A popular story says that the Great Wall can be seen from space with the naked eye. This is a myth. The wall is long but narrow, and astronauts have said that it is very difficult to pick out from orbit. Today the wall is a World Heritage Site, and millions of people walk along it each year. The greatest threats now are not armies but weather, plants and the feet of tourists.

cmp/17.title: The Animals That Sleep With Half a Brain
cmp/17.src: Marine Mammal Center; Scripps Institution of Oceanography; Mukhametov; Dolphin Communication Project
p: Every night, most of us lie down, close our eyes and fall into a deep sleep. The whole brain rests, and for a few hours we are unaware of the world around us. For a dolphin, this would be impossible. A dolphin lives in the sea, where danger can appear from any direction, and it has another problem that no land animal has: it must remember to breathe.

Dolphins are mammals, not fish. They do not take oxygen from the water through gills. Instead, they have lungs and breathe air through a hole at the top of their heads, called a blowhole. A dolphin must swim to the surface every few minutes to take a breath. Unlike a person, who breathes automatically even when asleep, a dolphin controls each breath consciously. If it fell into a deep sleep, it would simply stop breathing and drown.

Nature has solved this problem in an unusual way. When a dolphin sleeps, only one half of its brain goes to sleep at a time. The other half stays awake and keeps working. Scientists call this unihemispheric sleep, which means sleep with one half of the brain. After a few hours, the two halves swap roles, so that each one gets the rest it needs.

The sleeping dolphin does not look like a sleeping person. It usually swims slowly near the surface, often in a gentle circle. One eye is closed, and the other remains open. Scientists have noticed that the eye that stays open is connected to the half of the brain that is awake. The dolphin keeps watching for enemies such as sharks, and it can also keep an eye on the other members of its group.

This ability to sleep with half a brain is useful in other ways too. A dolphin that is resting can still rise to the surface for air, avoid collisions with other animals and stay close to its family. Dolphins live in groups called pods, and sleeping dolphins often swim side by side in a tight formation. In this way, the whole pod rests while still being protected.

The most surprising evidence comes from mothers and newborn calves. Researchers who watched dolphin families found that, for the first weeks after birth, the mother and her baby hardly sleep at all. They stay active day and night. This is probably because a newborn calf must be kept close to its mother and protected from predators, and it needs to learn to breathe at the right moment. Surprisingly, neither of them seems to suffer from the lack of rest, and after some weeks their sleep returns to normal.

Dolphins are not the only animals that sleep in this way. Some birds can keep one eye open and one side of the brain awake while resting in a group, especially the birds at the edge of the group, who are most exposed to danger. Whales and seals also show similar habits. Each of these animals has found its own solution to the same problem: how to rest without becoming a target.

Studying how dolphins sleep helps scientists to understand more about sleep itself. We still do not fully understand why animals need sleep, and the dolphin shows us that the brain can rest in more than one way. It is a remarkable reminder that nature does not follow a single rule, and that the creatures around us have solved the challenges of life in ways that we are only beginning to understand.

cmp/18.title: The Number That Means Nothing
cmp/18.src: Oxford University; Bodleian Libraries; Encyclopaedia Britannica; MacTutor History of Mathematics archive
p: Imagine trying to do arithmetic without the number zero. How would you write the number one hundred and five? You would need to show that there are no tens, and without a symbol for "nothing", this is surprisingly hard. Zero seems so simple that we take it for granted, yet it took humans thousands of years to invent it. Today, it is one of the most important ideas in mathematics.

The first step was not a number but a gap. About four thousand years ago, the Babylonians wrote numbers using a system based on sixty. At first, they left an empty space when a place had no value, but spaces were easy to miss. Later they began to use a special mark to show that a place was empty. This mark helped, but they did not use it as a number that could be added or multiplied. It was a placeholder only.

Other peoples came to similar ideas independently. The Maya of Central America used a shell-shaped symbol for zero in their calendars. The ancient Greeks, who were brilliant mathematicians, never developed a zero. They thought mainly about shapes, and the idea of a number for "nothing" seemed strange to them. The Romans also had no zero. Look at a clock face with Roman numerals, and you will find no symbol for it.

The breakthrough came in India. Indian mathematicians began to use a dot or a small circle to show an empty place, and they gradually realised that it could be treated as a number in its own right. A very old Indian manuscript, called the Bakhshali manuscript, contains hundreds of dots that are used in this way. In 2017, scientists at the University of Oxford tested the birch bark on which it was written and found that parts of it are about 1,700 years old, which makes it the oldest known use of a zero symbol.

In the year 628, the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote down clear rules for zero. He explained that adding zero to a number leaves the number unchanged, and that a number multiplied by zero gives zero. He also tried to explain what happens when we divide by zero, but this puzzle was not solved properly for many centuries. His work was the first time that zero was treated as a true number.

The idea then travelled west. Scholars in the Islamic world, working in cities such as Baghdad, learned the Indian numerals and wrote books about them. One of them, al-Khwarizmi, wrote an influential book on calculation using the new system, and the word "algorithm" comes from the Latin form of his name. Through trade, the numbers, including the zero, reached North Africa and Spain.

In the year 1202, an Italian merchant named Fibonacci, who had learned the system while living in North Africa, published a book that introduced the Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe. At first, many Europeans were suspicious. Some governments even banned the numerals, because they thought that a zero could be used to cheat in business. In time, however, the new system proved so much easier than Roman numerals that it spread across the continent.

Zero matters because it makes the place-value system work. In the number 305, the zero tells us that there are no tens. Without it, 305 and 35 would look the same. Zero also allows us to write very large and very small numbers, and it is essential in modern science, banking and technology. Computers, for example, store all their information as long lists of zeros and ones.

The next time you write a number such as 100, think about the long journey that the humble zero has made. It began as a gap in a Babylonian table, became a dot in an Indian manuscript and travelled across continents before reaching us. It reminds us that even the simplest ideas can take generations of human effort.
