cmp/85.title: Globalisation and Inequality: Who Gained?
cmp/85.src: Milanovic; World Bank; Autor, Dorn and Hanson; Our World in Data
p: Few words in public debate are used with as much passion and as little precision as "globalisation". In economic terms, it refers to the growing integration of the world's economies through trade, investment, the movement of people and the spread of technology and ideas. Its supporters credit it with lifting hundreds of millions of people out of poverty, while its opponents blame it for the loss of jobs and for widening the gap between rich and poor. The truth, as so often, depends on whom one is looking at.

The case in favour begins with a simple argument made by the early economist David Ricardo: if each country concentrates on what it produces relatively well and trades for the rest, total output rises and everyone can, in principle, be better off. The evidence of the past forty years lends this support. Since 1990, the proportion of the world's population living in extreme poverty has fallen from nearly forty per cent to under ten per cent, and much of that decline took place in China and India, countries that opened up to trade and foreign investment.

Yet averages can conceal as much as they reveal. The economist Branko Milanovic has plotted what is known as the "elephant curve", which shows the growth in real income of people at each level of the global income distribution between 1988 and 2008. The curve rises steeply for the poor and the middle classes of Asia, flattens for the lower middle classes of the wealthy countries and then rises sharply again for the richest one per cent. The shape resembles an elephant, with the lower middle class of the rich world at the narrow dip of the trunk.

This pattern helps to explain the anger of many workers in industrial regions of Europe and North America. A well-known study of the "China shock" estimated that competition from Chinese imports eliminated about two million American jobs between 1999 and 2011. Importantly, the study found that the displaced workers did not simply move on to new employment; many remained jobless or took lower-paid positions, and the damage was concentrated in particular towns whose economies depended on a single industry.

Globalisation has also affected inequality within countries differently from inequality between them. As poor nations have caught up with rich ones, the gap between countries has narrowed. But within many countries, including China, India and the United States, the gap between the richest and the rest has widened. The reasons are debated; trade is one, but technological change, which rewards educated workers and those who own capital, is probably at least as important, and the two are hard to separate.

Economists also point out that the benefits and costs of trade are distributed unevenly. Consumers gain from cheaper goods, and exporting firms from larger markets, but these gains are spread thinly across millions of people, while the losses are concentrated on a few. In principle, the winners could compensate the losers and still be better off. In practice, support for retraining and regional development has often been weak and slow, which may explain why the political reaction against trade has been so strong.

Recent events have strengthened these doubts. The financial crisis of 2008 showed how a shock in one country could spread quickly through connected banking systems. The pandemic and the war in Ukraine exposed the risk of depending on distant suppliers for medicines, microchips and energy. As a result, many governments now speak of "resilience" and of bringing production closer to home, although economists warn that withdrawing from trade could make everyone poorer.

The debate, then, is less about whether globalisation produces gains, since the evidence is strong that it does, than about how those gains are shared and who bears the cost of change. Most economists would argue that the problem lies not in open trade itself but in the failure to cushion those it harms, through education, unemployment support and investment in struggling regions. Whether governments are willing to do so, and to pay for it, is likely to determine whether openness remains politically sustainable.

q.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
q.e: The passage weighs gains and costs.
o: A. Globalisation has made everyone equally rich, and so no action is needed to share the gains or to manage any costs
B. Globalisation has produced large gains but unevenly shared ones, and the challenge is how to share them and manage the costs
C. Globalisation has ended all trade between countries, and caused a world crisis that has lasted for decades
D. Globalisation has harmed every country, and nobody has gained from more trade between nations in the last fifty years

o: A. The growth of a single country at the cost of all the others, through war and trade
B. The closing of borders, so that each country can protect its own workers and its own industries from foreign trade
C. The growing integration of the world's economies through trade, investment, movement of people and spread of ideas
D. The end of technology, as machines are replaced by traditional methods of making things by hand

o: A. If each country concentrates on what it produces relatively well and trades, total output rises

q.q: What did the study of the "China shock" estimate?
o: A. Competition from Chinese imports eliminated about two million American jobs between 1999 and 2011
B. American workers moved easily to new jobs, and nobody lost any income

o: A. It has disappeared
B. It has doubled
C. It has widened
D. It has narrowed

q.q: According to paragraph 5, which factor, besides trade, probably affects inequality within countries?
o: A. Population growth only
B. The weather
C. Language
D. Technological change

q.q: Why has the political reaction against trade been so strong, according to paragraph 6?
o: A. Consumers dislike cheap goods, and so they vote against any party that supports trade, even when prices fall
B. Exporters lost money, and they have asked the governments to end the trade
C. The losses are concentrated on a few while the gains are spread thinly, and support for the losers has been weak
D. Trade laws are too simple, so most voters cannot understand how they work

q.q: What risk did the pandemic and the war in Ukraine expose?
o: A. Having too many local factories, which then made more goods than were needed
B. Rising wages, which forced companies to move their factories to other countries
C. Too much unemployment benefit, which made people unwilling to work in industry
D. Depending on distant suppliers for medicines, microchips and energy

q.q: Economists warn that withdrawing from trade could make everyone poorer.
What does the writer suggest in the last paragraph?
o: A. Education has no role, since workers cannot learn the skills they now need
B. Governments should do nothing, since the market will repair the harm itself, given a little more time
C. The problem lies in the failure to cushion those harmed rather than in open trade itself
D. Open trade should be abolished, because it has harmed so many families

ps.b: "চায়না শক" নিয়ে একটি সুপরিচিত গবেষণা অনুমান করে যে চীনা আমদানির প্রতিযোগিতা ১৯৯৯ থেকে ২০১১ সালের মধ্যে প্রায় বিশ লক্ষ আমেরিকান চাকরি শেষ করে দিয়েছে।

ps.e: Importantly, the study found that the displaced workers did not simply move on to new employment; many remained jobless or took lower-paid positions, and the damage was concentrated in particular towns whose economies depended on a single industry.
ps.b: গুরুত্বপূর্ণভাবে, গবেষণাটি দেখে যে স্থানচ্যুত শ্রমিকরা কেবল নতুন কাজে চলে যাননি; অনেকে বেকার থেকে গেছেন বা কম বেতনের পদ নিয়েছেন, এবং ক্ষতি কেন্দ্রীভূত হয়েছে এমন নির্দিষ্ট শহরে যাদের অর্থনীতি একটিমাত্র শিল্পের ওপর নির্ভরশীল ছিল।

ps.e: Globalisation has also affected inequality within countries differently from inequality between them.
ps.b: বিশ্বায়ন দেশগুলোর মধ্যকার বৈষম্য ও দেশের ভেতরের বৈষম্যকে ভিন্নভাবে প্রভাবিত করেছে।

ps.e: As poor nations have caught up with rich ones, the gap between countries has narrowed.
ps.b: দরিদ্র দেশগুলো ধনীদের নাগাল ধরার সঙ্গে সঙ্গে দেশগুলোর মধ্যকার ব্যবধান কমেছে।

ps.e: But within many countries, including China, India and the United States, the gap between the richest and the rest has widened.
ps.b: কিন্তু চীন, ভারত ও যুক্তরাষ্ট্রসহ অনেক দেশের ভেতরে সবচেয়ে ধনী ও বাকিদের মধ্যকার ব্যবধান বেড়েছে।

ps.e: The reasons are debated; trade is one, but technological change, which rewards educated workers and those who own capital, is probably at least as important, and the two are hard to separate.
ps.b: কারণগুলো নিয়ে বিতর্ক আছে; বাণিজ্য একটি, কিন্তু প্রযুক্তিগত পরিবর্তন, যা শিক্ষিত শ্রমিক ও মূলধনের মালিকদের পুরস্কৃত করে, সম্ভবত অন্তত সমান গুরুত্বপূর্ণ, এবং দুটিকে আলাদা করা কঠিন।

ps.e: Economists also point out that the benefits and costs of trade are distributed unevenly.
ps.b: অর্থনীতিবিদরা এও উল্লেখ করেন যে বাণিজ্যের লাভ ও ক্ষতি অসমভাবে বণ্টিত হয়।

ps.e: Consumers gain from cheaper goods, and exporting firms from larger markets, but these gains are spread thinly across millions of people, while the losses are concentrated on a few.
ps.b: ভোক্তারা সস্তা পণ্যে এবং রপ্তানিকারক প্রতিষ্ঠান বড় বাজারে লাভ করে, কিন্তু এই লাভ কোটি কোটি মানুষের মধ্যে পাতলাভাবে ছড়ায়, আর ক্ষতি কেন্দ্রীভূত হয় অল্প কয়েকজনের ওপর।

ps.e: In principle, the winners could compensate the losers and still be better off.
ps.b: নীতিগতভাবে বিজয়ীরা পরাজিতদের ক্ষতিপূরণ দিয়েও ভালো থাকতে পারত।

ps.e: In practice, support for retraining and regional development has often been weak and slow, which may explain why the political reaction against trade has been so strong.
ps.b: বাস্তবে পুনঃপ্রশিক্ষণ ও আঞ্চলিক উন্নয়নে সহায়তা প্রায়ই দুর্বল ও ধীর হয়েছে, যা ব্যাখ্যা করতে পারে বাণিজ্যের বিরুদ্ধে রাজনৈতিক প্রতিক্রিয়া কেন এত শক্তিশালী।

ps.e: Recent events have strengthened these doubts.
ps.b: সাম্প্রতিক ঘটনা এই সন্দেহ আরও জোরালো করেছে।

ps.e: The financial crisis of 2008 showed how a shock in one country could spread quickly through connected banking systems.
ps.b: ২০০৮ সালের আর্থিক সংকট দেখিয়েছে এক দেশের আঘাত কীভাবে সংযুক্ত ব্যাংক ব্যবস্থার মাধ্যমে দ্রুত ছড়িয়ে পড়তে পারে।

ps.e: The pandemic and the war in Ukraine exposed the risk of depending on distant suppliers for medicines, microchips and energy.
ps.b: অতিমারি ও ইউক্রেনের যুদ্ধ ওষুধ, মাইক্রোচিপ ও জ্বালানির জন্য দূরের সরবরাহকারীদের ওপর নির্ভরতার ঝুঁকি উন্মোচিত করেছে।

ps.e: As a result, many governments now speak of "resilience" and of bringing production closer to home, although economists warn that withdrawing from trade could make everyone poorer.
ps.b: ফলে অনেক সরকার এখন "সহনশীলতা" এবং উৎপাদন ঘরের কাছে আনার কথা বলে, যদিও অর্থনীতিবিদরা সতর্ক করেন যে বাণিজ্য থেকে সরে আসা সবাইকে আরও দরিদ্র করতে পারে।

ps.e: The debate, then, is less about whether globalisation produces gains, since the evidence is strong that it does, than about how those gains are shared and who bears the cost of change.
ps.b: তাই বিতর্কটি বিশ্বায়ন লাভ আনে কি না তা নিয়ে কম, কারণ প্রমাণ জোরালো যে আনে, বরং সেই লাভ কীভাবে ভাগ হয় এবং পরিবর্তনের মূল্য কে বহন করে তা নিয়ে।

ps.e: Most economists would argue that the problem lies not in open trade itself but in the failure to cushion those it harms, through education, unemployment support and investment in struggling regions.
ps.b: অধিকাংশ অর্থনীতিবিদ যুক্তি দেবেন যে সমস্যা মুক্ত বাণিজ্যে নয়, বরং যাঁরা ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত হন তাঁদের শিক্ষা, বেকারত্ব সহায়তা ও দুর্দশাগ্রস্ত অঞ্চলে বিনিয়োগের মাধ্যমে রক্ষা করতে ব্যর্থতায়।

ps.e: Whether governments are willing to do so, and to pay for it, is likely to determine whether openness remains politically sustainable.
ps.b: সরকারগুলো তা করতে এবং তার খরচ দিতে ইচ্ছুক কি না তা-ই সম্ভবত ঠিক করবে উন্মুক্ততা রাজনৈতিকভাবে টেকসই থাকবে কি না।

cmp/86.title: Do We Really Choose? Neuroscience and Free Will
cmp/86.src: Libet et al.; Soon et al.; Schurger, Sitt and Dehaene; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
p: Every day, we act on the feeling that we are in charge of what we do. We believe that we could have taken a different road to work, ordered a different meal or said something other than what we said. This sense of freedom underlies our moral and legal systems, since we praise and blame people only on the assumption that they could have acted otherwise. Yet over the past half century, findings from neuroscience have been presented as a challenge to that assumption, and the debate they provoked is far from settled.

The best-known experiment was carried out in the early 1980s by the American physiologist Benjamin Libet. Volunteers were asked to flex a finger or wrist whenever they felt the urge, and to note the position of a rapidly moving dot on a clock face at the moment they became aware of deciding to move. Electrodes on the scalp recorded a slow build-up of electrical activity in the brain, called the readiness potential. To Libet's surprise, this activity began several hundred milliseconds before the volunteers reported being aware of a decision.

Many commentators drew a dramatic conclusion: if the brain begins preparing an action before we are conscious of choosing it, then conscious choice cannot be the cause. Consciousness, on this view, merely announces what the brain has already decided, like a press secretary who reports on a policy rather than making it. Later studies using brain scans seemed to strengthen the case. In one, researchers could predict, with accuracy a little above chance, which of two buttons a person would press several seconds before the person said they had decided.

These experiments have been criticised on several grounds. First, the task was peculiar: participants were told to act on a whim, which is quite different from weighing up reasons about a career or a marriage. Second, the timing of conscious awareness is difficult to measure, since it depends on a person's own report. Third, and most importantly, a 2012 reinterpretation proposed that the readiness potential is not a hidden decision at all. Because the brain's activity fluctuates randomly, they argued, a movement is simply more likely when the fluctuation happens to cross a threshold, and the slow build-up appears only when many trials are averaged.

Even if the experiments were flawless, philosophers argue, it would not follow that free will is an illusion, because the answer depends on what is meant by the term. Libertarians hold that a free act must not be fully determined by earlier events, so that the agent could genuinely have done otherwise. Hard determinists agree with this definition but believe that every event, including every brain process, is caused by earlier events, so that no one is free. Both groups therefore treat free will as incompatible with determinism.

A third position, called compatibilism, rejects this incompatibility. Compatibilists, who include many contemporary philosophers, argue that freedom does not require escaping the laws of nature. To act freely, they say, is to act on one's own reasons and desires, without coercion or compulsion, and with the ability to respond to reasons. A person who gives money to charity because she cares about others is free in the sense that matters, even if her caring has causes in her upbringing and her brain. On this view, a brain-based explanation of a decision does not make the decision any less one's own.

The question has practical weight. Some researchers argue that if people believe that free will is an illusion, they may take less responsibility for their conduct; in one often-cited study, participants who had been persuaded that free will does not exist were more willing to cheat on a test. Others have been unable to replicate the effect. In law, courts already recognise that serious mental illness, or a brain tumour affecting behaviour, may reduce responsibility, and some neuroscientists urge that punishment should focus on deterrence and protection of society rather than on retribution.

The honest summary is that neuroscience has not disproved free will, but it has made some simple pictures of it harder to defend. It suggests that much of what we do is prepared by processes of which we are unaware, and that the feeling of deciding is an imperfect guide to the causes of action. Whether this threatens human freedom depends largely on how freedom is defined. If it means being an uncaused cause, it is probably unattainable; if it means thinking carefully and acting on one's own reasons, it is something that most of us possess, in greater or lesser degree.

q.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
q.e: The passage weighs the evidence and the definitions.
o: A. Philosophers have stopped discussing free will, since the question is now settled
B. Neuroscience has proved that free will is an illusion, and so no person can be held responsible for any act that they do.
C. Neuroscience has proved that free will is certain, and so the debate among philosophers is over for ever
D. Neuroscience has challenged simple views of free will but has not settled the question, which depends on how free will is defined

q.q: What assumption underlies our moral and legal systems, according to paragraph 1?
o: A. That all actions are accidents of nature
B. That people could have acted otherwise
C. That laws never change
D. That brains cannot be studied

q.q: What were volunteers in Libet's experiment asked to do?
o: A. Flex a finger or wrist when they felt the urge and note the position of a dot on a clock
B. Solve a puzzle while the electrodes on their heads measured the time taken
C. Count backwards from a hundred, and tell the scientist when they felt tired or bored
D. Choose a career from a list, and explain the reason for their choice

q.q: In Libet's experiment, brain activity began after the volunteers reported being aware of a decision.
q.e: Paragraph 2 says it began several hundred milliseconds before.

q.q: The slow build-up of electrical activity in the brain is called the ____ potential.
What comparison is made for consciousness in paragraph 3?
o: A. A teacher of a class, who plans every lesson in advance
B. A captain steering a ship, who decides where it will go
C. A press secretary who reports a policy rather than making it
D. A judge in a court, who gives the final decision in a case

q.q: What could researchers predict in the later brain-scan study?
o: A. Which of two buttons a person would press, several seconds before the person said they had decided
B. What the person would eat for lunch, several hours before the meal
C. The person's job, from a short test that was given to them at the start of the experiment
D. The person's age, from the pattern of the brain's activity, several minutes before the test

q.q: What is the first criticism of these experiments in paragraph 4?
o: A. The volunteers were too old to give a fair result about the brain
B. The clock was too slow, so the timing of the urge was wrong
C. The task was peculiar, since participants acted on a whim
D. The scalp electrodes were too heavy, and so they changed the readings

q.q: What did the 2012 reinterpretation propose?
o: A. The readiness potential proves free will, because it appears before any movement and is controlled by the person who moves.
B. The experiment must be repeated by children, whose brains work in a simpler way than those of adults
C. The brain is not active before a movement, and so nothing is decided early by the brain at all
D. The readiness potential is not a hidden decision; the brain's random fluctuation crossing a threshold makes a movement more likely

q.q: What do libertarians hold about a free act?
o: A. It must be forced
B. It must not be fully determined by earlier events
C. It must be legal
D. It must be determined by earlier events and by nothing else

q.q: Hard determinists believe that no one is free because every event is caused by earlier events.
According to compatibilists, what does it mean to act freely?
o: A. To act without any cause at all, so that nothing in the past matters
B. To act without thinking, since thought only gets in the way of freedom
C. To act on one's own reasons and desires, without coercion or compulsion
D. To act against the law, so as to show that one is not controlled

q.q: What happened in the study mentioned in paragraph 7?
o: A. Participants became more honest, because they felt that they had to take care
B. Participants persuaded that free will does not exist were more willing to cheat
C. Participants lost their memory of the test, and could not answer the questions
D. Participants refused to take part, since they did not wish to give up free will

q.q: The writer says the effect in that study has been confirmed by every later attempt.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says others have been unable to replicate it.

q.q: What does the writer conclude in the last paragraph?
o: A. Neuroscience has not disproved free will, but it has made some simple pictures of it harder to defend
B. The brain makes no decisions, since all actions are caused by the body
C. Free will is simple and obvious, and no experiment can ever change that
D. Free will has been disproved, and so we should stop blaming people for their acts, in every court and school

q.q: Libet was awarded a Nobel Prize for his work on free will.
q.e: The passage does not mention this.

ps.b: পরবর্তী গবেষণায় মস্তিষ্ক স্ক্যান ব্যবহার করে যুক্তি আরও জোরালো মনে হয়।

ps.e: In one, researchers could predict, with accuracy a little above chance, which of two buttons a person would press several seconds before the person said they had decided.
ps.b: একটিতে গবেষকরা কোন দুটি বোতামের কোনটি একজন চাপবেন তা সম্ভাবনার চেয়ে সামান্য বেশি নির্ভুলতায় অনুমান করতে পারেন, ব্যক্তি সিদ্ধান্ত নিয়েছেন বলার কয়েক সেকেন্ড আগে।

ps.e: These experiments have been criticised on several grounds.
ps.b: এই পরীক্ষাগুলো কয়েকটি কারণে সমালোচিত হয়েছে।

ps.e: First, the task was peculiar: participants were told to act on a whim, which is quite different from weighing up reasons about a career or a marriage.
ps.b: প্রথমত, কাজটি ছিল অদ্ভুত: অংশগ্রহণকারীদের খেয়ালবশে কাজ করতে বলা হয়েছিল, যা কর্মজীবন বা বিয়ের কারণ ওজন করার থেকে সম্পূর্ণ আলাদা।

ps.e: Second, the timing of conscious awareness is difficult to measure, since it depends on a person's own report.
ps.b: দ্বিতীয়ত, সচেতন অবগতির সময় মাপা কঠিন, কারণ এটি ব্যক্তির নিজের বিবরণের ওপর নির্ভর করে।

ps.e: Third, and most importantly, a 2012 reinterpretation proposed that the readiness potential is not a hidden decision at all.
ps.b: তৃতীয়ত, এবং সবচেয়ে গুরুত্বপূর্ণ, ২০১২ সালের একটি পুনর্ব্যাখ্যা প্রস্তাব করে যে প্রস্তুতি বিভব মোটেই কোনো লুকানো সিদ্ধান্ত নয়।

ps.e: Because the brain's activity fluctuates randomly, they argued, a movement is simply more likely when the fluctuation happens to cross a threshold, and the slow build-up appears only when many trials are averaged.
ps.b: তাঁরা যুক্তি দেন, মস্তিষ্কের সক্রিয়তা এলোমেলোভাবে ওঠানামা করে বলে ওঠানামা কোনো সীমা পার হলে একটি নড়াচড়ার সম্ভাবনা কেবল বাড়ে, এবং ধীর বৃদ্ধিটি তখনই দেখা যায় যখন অনেক চেষ্টার গড় করা হয়।

ps.e: Even if the experiments were flawless, philosophers argue, it would not follow that free will is an illusion, because the answer depends on what is meant by the term.
ps.b: পরীক্ষাগুলো নিখুঁত হলেও দার্শনিকরা যুক্তি দেন যে তা থেকে এটি প্রমাণিত হয় না যে স্বাধীন ইচ্ছা একটি মায়া, কারণ উত্তরটি নির্ভর করে শব্দটি দিয়ে কী বোঝানো হচ্ছে তার ওপর।

ps.e: Libertarians hold that a free act must not be fully determined by earlier events, so that the agent could genuinely have done otherwise.
ps.b: স্বাধীনতাবাদীরা মনে করেন একটি স্বাধীন কাজ অবশ্যই পূর্ববর্তী ঘটনাবলি দ্বারা সম্পূর্ণ নির্ধারিত হবে না, যাতে কর্তা সত্যিই অন্যভাবে করতে পারত।

ps.e: Hard determinists agree with this definition but believe that every event, including every brain process, is caused by earlier events, so that no one is free.
ps.b: কঠোর নিয়তিবাদীরা এই সংজ্ঞায় একমত, কিন্তু বিশ্বাস করেন মস্তিষ্কের প্রতিটি প্রক্রিয়াসহ প্রতিটি ঘটনা পূর্ববর্তী ঘটনার ফল, তাই কেউ স্বাধীন নয়।

ps.e: Both groups therefore treat free will as incompatible with determinism.
ps.b: তাই দুই দলই স্বাধীন ইচ্ছাকে নিয়তিবাদের সঙ্গে অসঙ্গত বলে গণ্য করে।

ps.e: A third position, called compatibilism, rejects this incompatibility.
ps.b: তৃতীয় অবস্থানটি, যাকে সঙ্গতিবাদ বলে, এই অসঙ্গতি প্রত্যাখ্যান করে।

ps.e: Compatibilists, who include many contemporary philosophers, argue that freedom does not require escaping the laws of nature.
ps.b: সঙ্গতিবাদীরা, যাঁদের মধ্যে অনেক সমসাময়িক দার্শনিক আছেন, যুক্তি দেন স্বাধীনতার জন্য প্রকৃতির নিয়ম এড়ানো দরকার হয় না।

ps.e: To act freely, they say, is to act on one's own reasons and desires, without coercion or compulsion, and with the ability to respond to reasons.
ps.b: তাঁদের মতে, স্বাধীনভাবে কাজ করা মানে নিজের কারণ ও ইচ্ছা অনুযায়ী কাজ করা, জবরদস্তি বা বাধ্যবাধকতা ছাড়া এবং কারণের প্রতি সাড়া দেওয়ার সামর্থ্য নিয়ে।

ps.e: A person who gives money to charity because she cares about others is free in the sense that matters, even if her caring has causes in her upbringing and her brain.
ps.b: যে নারী অন্যদের প্রতি যত্নের কারণে দান করেন, তাঁর যত্নের কারণ তাঁর লালনপালন ও মস্তিষ্কে থাকলেও তিনি সেই অর্থে স্বাধীন যা গুরুত্বপূর্ণ।

ps.e: On this view, a brain-based explanation of a decision does not make the decision any less one's own.
ps.b: এই দৃষ্টিতে একটি সিদ্ধান্তের মস্তিষ্কভিত্তিক ব্যাখ্যা সিদ্ধান্তটিকে কম নিজের করে তোলে না।

ps.e: The question has practical weight.
ps.b: প্রশ্নটির ব্যবহারিক গুরুত্ব আছে।

ps.e: Some researchers argue that if people believe that free will is an illusion, they may take less responsibility for their conduct; in one often-cited study, participants who had been persuaded that free will does not exist were more willing to cheat on a test.
ps.b: কিছু গবেষক যুক্তি দেন মানুষ স্বাধীন ইচ্ছাকে মায়া বলে বিশ্বাস করলে নিজের আচরণের দায় কম নিতে পারে; প্রায়ই উদ্ধৃত একটি গবেষণায় যাঁদের বোঝানো হয়েছিল স্বাধীন ইচ্ছা নেই তাঁরা পরীক্ষায় নকল করতে বেশি ইচ্ছুক ছিলেন।

ps.e: Others have been unable to replicate the effect.
ps.b: অন্যরা এই প্রভাব পুনরাবৃত্তি করতে পারেননি।

ps.e: In law, courts already recognise that serious mental illness, or a brain tumour affecting behaviour, may reduce responsibility, and some neuroscientists urge that punishment should focus on deterrence and protection of society rather than on retribution.
ps.b: আইনে আদালত ইতিমধ্যে স্বীকার করে যে গুরুতর মানসিক অসুস্থতা বা আচরণে প্রভাব ফেলা মস্তিষ্কের টিউমার দায় কমাতে পারে, এবং কিছু স্নায়ুবিজ্ঞানী জোর দেন শাস্তিতে প্রতিশোধের বদলে নিবৃত্তকরণ ও সমাজ রক্ষায় মনোযোগ থাকা উচিত।

ps.e: The honest summary is that neuroscience has not disproved free will, but it has made some simple pictures of it harder to defend.
ps.b: সৎ সারসংক্ষেপ হলো স্নায়ুবিজ্ঞান স্বাধীন ইচ্ছা অপ্রমাণ করেনি, কিন্তু এর কিছু সরল চিত্র রক্ষা করা কঠিন করেছে।

ps.e: It suggests that much of what we do is prepared by processes of which we are unaware, and that the feeling of deciding is an imperfect guide to the causes of action.
ps.b: এটি ইঙ্গিত দেয় আমরা যা করি তার বেশিরভাগ এমন প্রক্রিয়ায় প্রস্তুত হয় যার সম্পর্কে আমরা অজ্ঞ, এবং সিদ্ধান্ত নেওয়ার অনুভূতি কাজের কারণের একটি অপূর্ণ নির্দেশক।

ps.e: Whether this threatens human freedom depends largely on how freedom is defined.
ps.b: এটি মানুষের স্বাধীনতার জন্য হুমকি কি না তা মূলত নির্ভর করে স্বাধীনতার সংজ্ঞার ওপর।

ps.e: If it means being an uncaused cause, it is probably unattainable; if it means thinking carefully and acting on one's own reasons, it is something that most of us possess, in greater or lesser degree.
ps.b: এর মানে যদি হয় কারণহীন কারণ হওয়া, তবে তা সম্ভবত অর্জন অসম্ভব; আর যদি হয় সাবধানে ভাবা ও নিজের কারণ অনুযায়ী কাজ করা, তবে তা এমন কিছু যা আমাদের অধিকাংশের কম-বেশি আছে।

cmp/87.title: Public or Private? Who Should Explore Space
cmp/87.src: NASA; NASA Office of Inspector General; Jonathan McDowell
p: For the first half-century of the space age, the exploration of space was almost entirely the business of governments. The Soviet Union and the United States competed to reach orbit and then the Moon, and the cost, enormous by any standard, was met by taxpayers. In the past two decades, however, private companies have taken over a growing share of the work. They launch satellites, carry cargo and astronauts to the International Space Station and, increasingly, propose to take paying customers to orbit and beyond. This shift has raised a question that was once of interest only to specialists: who should be in charge of exploring space?

The argument for the private sector begins with cost. In the 1970s, the Space Shuttle was designed to make access to orbit routine and cheap, but each flight ended up costing about a billion dollars. Private firms, which have to answer to investors and customers, have devised ways to reduce the price. The most striking has been the development of rockets whose first stage returns to Earth and lands upright, so that it can fly again. Since the first successful landing in 2015, the cost of sending a kilogram into orbit has fallen by a large factor.

Governments have supported this change deliberately. In 2006, NASA began to buy cargo deliveries to the International Space Station from commercial suppliers, rather than owning and running the vehicles itself. A few years later, it did the same for crews. Under such "fixed-price" contracts, the company bears the risk of cost overruns, and NASA pays for results instead of effort. The agency estimates that this method has saved it a considerable amount compared with its traditional contracts, in which the government covered whatever the work cost.

Supporters also argue that private companies are more willing to take risks and to learn from failure. A government agency, answerable to politicians and the public, cannot easily accept the loss of a costly rocket, and a single accident may endanger an entire programme. A company can build prototypes, watch them explode and improve the next one, an approach that is faster and, in the long run, may be safer. Competition among companies can also drive innovation in the way that a single agency cannot.

Nevertheless, there are good reasons for caution. Private firms exist to make a profit, and profit is not always compatible with science. The most valuable discoveries, such as the first detailed images of distant galaxies or the exploration of the outer planets, produce knowledge that is shared by all but cannot be sold. Left to the market, there might be little investment in such work. Governments, which can take a long view and are not required to show a return, have traditionally funded it, and many believe that they should continue to do so.

There are also concerns about dependence. If a government relies on one company for access to space, it may have little bargaining power when prices rise or when the company's priorities change. The involvement of a handful of very wealthy individuals raises further questions, since decisions of public importance, such as the use of satellite networks in a war, may be taken by a private owner who is not accountable to voters. Critics argue that a public service should not be exposed to the whims of a few people.

Legal questions remain unresolved. Under the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, no nation may claim the Moon or any other celestial body, and states are responsible for the activities of their private companies. But the treaty says nothing clear about whether a company may own the resources, such as water ice or minerals, that it extracts. Several countries have passed laws that allow their companies to keep what they mine, and others argue that this violates the principle that space is the common heritage of humankind.

Most experts therefore envisage partnership rather than a contest. Governments are likely to remain responsible for deep-space science, for the setting of safety rules and for the protection of a shared environment, including the growing problem of debris in orbit. Companies, meanwhile, can take on routine activities such as launches and satellite services, and reduce their cost. The challenge will be to ensure that the benefits of a more open space economy are shared widely, and that the rules keep pace with the ambitions of those who are eager to profit from it.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
q.e: The passage compares public and private roles.
o: A. How rockets are built, and which materials are used in their engines
B. Why astronauts need training, and how long it takes them to learn
C. The growing role of private companies in space and the debate about who should lead exploration
D. The history of the Moon landings only, and the people who took part in them, from the first flight to the last

q.q: For the first half-century of the space age, exploration was almost entirely carried out by governments.
Which of these do private companies do now, according to paragraph 1?
o: A. Control the weather, by using satellites that are owned by the companies
B. Run the United Nations, which now depends on companies to make its decisions
C. Build the Moon, which was made by engineers in the last ten years
D. Launch satellites and carry cargo and astronauts to the International Space Station

q.q: How much did each Space Shuttle flight end up costing?
o: A. About a thousand dollars
B. Nothing
C. About a billion dollars
D. About a million dollars

q.q: What is the most striking cost-cutting development mentioned?
o: A. Rockets that never land, but are left to fall into the sea
B. Rockets without fuel, which are pushed upwards by the wind
C. Rockets made of paper, which are light and burn up when they return
D. Rockets whose first stage lands upright so it can fly again

q.q: Since the first successful landing in 2015, the cost of sending a kilogram into orbit has fallen by a large ____.
q.e: Paragraph 2 says by a large factor.

q.q: What does NASA pay for under fixed-price contracts?
o: A. Results instead of effort
B. Effort instead of results
C. Nothing at all
D. Whatever the work costs

q.q: Why can a company accept the loss of a rocket more easily than a government agency?
o: A. Companies are not allowed to test, so they must accept any failure
B. A government agency is answerable to politicians and the public
C. Government rockets are cheaper, so an agency can afford to lose them
D. Companies never lose rockets, because their engineers are more careful

q.q: What approach to development can a company follow, according to paragraph 4?
o: A. Build only one rocket, and use all the money to make it perfect
B. Build prototypes, watch them explode and improve the next one
C. Copy foreign designs, which have already been proved to work well
D. Avoid all tests, so that no failure is seen by the public

q.q: Why might the market invest little in some of the most valuable discoveries?
o: A. They are illegal, and so a company cannot own the results
B. The knowledge is shared by all but cannot be sold
C. They are too cheap, so no company can make a profit from them
D. They need no equipment, so the market does not wish to pay for them

q.q: The writer says governments are required to show a return on their space spending.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says governments are not required to show a return.

q.q: What is the concern about depending on one company?
o: A. The government may have little bargaining power when prices rise or priorities change
B. The company may become too small, and so be unable to build large rockets for the government
C. The company may work too slowly, and so miss the dates it promised
D. The company may stop paying taxes, and so reduce the money for schools

q.q: What does the Outer Space Treaty of 1967 say?
o: A. No nation may claim the Moon or any other celestial body
B. Rockets must be reused, so that less waste is left in space
C. Only the United States may fly in space, since it paid for the treaty
D. Companies may own planets, if they are the first to land upon them

q.q: The treaty clearly states whether a company may own the resources it extracts.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says it says nothing clear about this.

q.q: What do most experts envisage, according to the last paragraph?
o: A. A ban on private launches, so that only national agencies may fly
B. Companies controlling all space law, with governments as their customers
C. Governments leaving space completely, so that companies may do all the work
D. Partnership between governments and companies rather than a contest

q.q: Private companies have already landed a vehicle on the surface of Mars.
q.e: The passage does not mention this.

ps.e: The Soviet Union and the United States competed to reach orbit and then the Moon, and the cost, enormous by any standard, was met by taxpayers.
ps.b: সোভিয়েত ইউনিয়ন ও যুক্তরাষ্ট্র কক্ষপথে এবং পরে চাঁদে পৌঁছাতে প্রতিযোগিতা করে, এবং যেকোনো মানদণ্ডে বিপুল সেই খরচ বহন করেছেন করদাতারা।

ps.e: In the past two decades, however, private companies have taken over a growing share of the work.
ps.b: গত দুই দশকে অবশ্য বেসরকারি কোম্পানিগুলো কাজের ক্রমবর্ধমান অংশ নিয়ে নিয়েছে।

ps.e: They launch satellites, carry cargo and astronauts to the International Space Station and, increasingly, propose to take paying customers to orbit and beyond.
ps.b: তারা উপগ্রহ উৎক্ষেপণ করে, আন্তর্জাতিক মহাকাশ স্টেশনে মালামাল ও নভোচারী পৌঁছে দেয়, এবং ক্রমশ অর্থ দেওয়া গ্রাহকদের কক্ষপথে ও তার বাইরে নেওয়ার প্রস্তাব দেয়।

ps.e: This shift has raised a question that was once of interest only to specialists: who should be in charge of exploring space?

ps.e: The argument for the private sector begins with cost.
ps.b: বেসরকারি খাতের পক্ষে যুক্তি শুরু হয় খরচ দিয়ে।

ps.e: In the 1970s, the Space Shuttle was designed to make access to orbit routine and cheap, but each flight ended up costing about a billion dollars.
ps.b: ১৯৭০-এর দশকে স্পেস শাটল ডিজাইন করা হয়েছিল কক্ষপথে পৌঁছানো নিয়মিত ও সস্তা করতে, কিন্তু প্রতিটি উড্ডয়নে শেষ পর্যন্ত খরচ হতো প্রায় এক বিলিয়ন ডলার।

ps.e: Private firms, which have to answer to investors and customers, have devised ways to reduce the price.
ps.b: বিনিয়োগকারী ও গ্রাহকদের কাছে জবাবদিহি করতে হয় এমন বেসরকারি প্রতিষ্ঠান দাম কমানোর উপায় বের করেছে।

ps.e: The most striking has been the development of rockets whose first stage returns to Earth and lands upright, so that it can fly again.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে চোখে পড়ার মতো হলো এমন রকেটের উন্নয়ন যার প্রথম ধাপ পৃথিবীতে ফিরে সোজা হয়ে নামে, যাতে তা আবার উড়তে পারে।

ps.e: Since the first successful landing in 2015, the cost of sending a kilogram into orbit has fallen by a large factor.
ps.b: ২০১৫ সালে প্রথম সফল অবতরণের পর থেকে প্রতি কিলোগ্রাম কক্ষপথে পাঠানোর খরচ বিপুল গুণে কমেছে।

ps.e: Governments have supported this change deliberately.
ps.b: সরকারগুলো ইচ্ছাকৃতভাবে এই পরিবর্তনকে সমর্থন করেছে।

ps.e: In 2006, NASA began to buy cargo deliveries to the International Space Station from commercial suppliers, rather than owning and running the vehicles itself.
ps.b: ২০০৬ সালে নাসা নিজে যান মালিকানায় রেখে চালানোর বদলে বাণিজ্যিক সরবরাহকারীদের কাছ থেকে আন্তর্জাতিক মহাকাশ স্টেশনে মালামাল পাঠানো কিনতে শুরু করে।

ps.e: A few years later, it did the same for crews.
ps.b: কয়েক বছর পর তারা নভোচারীদের জন্যও তা-ই করে।

ps.e: Under such "fixed-price" contracts, the company bears the risk of cost overruns, and NASA pays for results instead of effort.
ps.b: এমন "নির্দিষ্ট মূল্যের" চুক্তিতে কোম্পানি খরচ বেড়ে যাওয়ার ঝুঁকি বহন করে, এবং নাসা প্রচেষ্টার বদলে ফলের জন্য অর্থ দেয়।

ps.e: The agency estimates that this method has saved it a considerable amount compared with its traditional contracts, in which the government covered whatever the work cost.
ps.b: সংস্থাটির অনুমান, কাজে যা-ই খরচ হোক সরকার তা বহন করত এমন প্রচলিত চুক্তির তুলনায় এই পদ্ধতিতে তাদের যথেষ্ট সাশ্রয় হয়েছে।

ps.e: Supporters also argue that private companies are more willing to take risks and to learn from failure.
ps.b: সমর্থকরা এও যুক্তি দেন যে বেসরকারি কোম্পানি ঝুঁকি নিতে এবং ব্যর্থতা থেকে শিখতে বেশি ইচ্ছুক।

ps.e: A government agency, answerable to politicians and the public, cannot easily accept the loss of a costly rocket, and a single accident may endanger an entire programme.
ps.b: রাজনীতিক ও জনগণের কাছে জবাবদিহি করতে হয় এমন একটি সরকারি সংস্থা সহজে একটি দামি রকেট হারানো মেনে নিতে পারে না, এবং একটিমাত্র দুর্ঘটনা পুরো কর্মসূচিকে বিপন্ন করতে পারে।

ps.e: A company can build prototypes, watch them explode and improve the next one, an approach that is faster and, in the long run, may be safer.
ps.b: একটি কোম্পানি প্রোটোটাইপ বানাতে, সেগুলোকে বিস্ফোরিত হতে দেখতে এবং পরেরটি উন্নত করতে পারে, যে পদ্ধতি দ্রুততর এবং দীর্ঘমেয়াদে হয়তো নিরাপদতরও।

ps.e: Competition among companies can also drive innovation in the way that a single agency cannot.
ps.b: কোম্পানিগুলোর মধ্যকার প্রতিযোগিতাও এমনভাবে উদ্ভাবন চালাতে পারে যা একটিমাত্র সংস্থা পারে না।

ps.e: Nevertheless, there are good reasons for caution.
ps.b: তবু সতর্কতার ভালো কারণ আছে।

ps.e: Private firms exist to make a profit, and profit is not always compatible with science.
ps.b: বেসরকারি প্রতিষ্ঠান থাকে মুনাফার জন্য, এবং মুনাফা সবসময় বিজ্ঞানের সঙ্গে সঙ্গতিপূর্ণ নয়।

ps.e: The most valuable discoveries, such as the first detailed images of distant galaxies or the exploration of the outer planets, produce knowledge that is shared by all but cannot be sold.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে মূল্যবান আবিষ্কারগুলো, যেমন দূরের ছায়াপথের প্রথম বিস্তারিত ছবি বা বাইরের গ্রহগুলোর অন্বেষণ, এমন জ্ঞান দেয় যা সবাই ভাগ করে নেয় কিন্তু বিক্রি করা যায় না।

ps.e: Left to the market, there might be little investment in such work.
ps.b: বাজারের হাতে ছেড়ে দিলে এমন কাজে হয়তো সামান্যই বিনিয়োগ হতো।

ps.e: Governments, which can take a long view and are not required to show a return, have traditionally funded it, and many believe that they should continue to do so.
ps.b: সরকার, যারা দীর্ঘমেয়াদি দৃষ্টি রাখতে পারে এবং যাদের লাভ দেখাতে হয় না, ঐতিহ্যগতভাবে এতে অর্থ দিয়েছে, এবং অনেকের বিশ্বাস তাদের তা চালিয়ে যাওয়া উচিত।

ps.e: There are also concerns about dependence.
ps.b: নির্ভরতা নিয়েও উদ্বেগ আছে।

ps.e: If a government relies on one company for access to space, it may have little bargaining power when prices rise or when the company's priorities change.
ps.b: একটিমাত্র কোম্পানির ওপর মহাকাশে প্রবেশের জন্য নির্ভর করলে দাম বাড়লে বা কোম্পানির অগ্রাধিকার বদলালে সরকারের দর কষাকষির ক্ষমতা সামান্যই থাকতে পারে।

ps.e: The involvement of a handful of very wealthy individuals raises further questions, since decisions of public importance, such as the use of satellite networks in a war, may be taken by a private owner who is not accountable to voters.
ps.b: গুটিকয়েক অতি ধনী ব্যক্তির সম্পৃক্ততা আরও প্রশ্ন তোলে, কারণ যুদ্ধে উপগ্রহ নেটওয়ার্ক ব্যবহারের মতো জনগুরুত্বের সিদ্ধান্ত এমন একজন বেসরকারি মালিক নিতে পারেন যিনি ভোটারদের কাছে জবাবদিহি করেন না।

ps.e: Critics argue that a public service should not be exposed to the whims of a few people.
ps.b: সমালোচকরা যুক্তি দেন কিছু মানুষের খেয়ালের ওপর একটি জনসেবাকে ছেড়ে দেওয়া উচিত নয়।

ps.e: Legal questions remain unresolved.
ps.b: আইনি প্রশ্ন অমীমাংসিত রয়ে গেছে।

ps.e: Under the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, no nation may claim the Moon or any other celestial body, and states are responsible for the activities of their private companies.
ps.b: ১৯৬৭ সালের মহাকাশ চুক্তি অনুযায়ী কোনো জাতি চাঁদ বা অন্য কোনো মহাজাগতিক বস্তু দাবি করতে পারে না, এবং রাষ্ট্রগুলো নিজেদের বেসরকারি কোম্পানির কার্যকলাপের জন্য দায়ী।

ps.e: But the treaty says nothing clear about whether a company may own the resources, such as water ice or minerals, that it extracts.
ps.b: কিন্তু একটি কোম্পানি জলবরফ বা খনিজের মতো যে সম্পদ উত্তোলন করে তার মালিক হতে পারে কি না সে বিষয়ে চুক্তিতে স্পষ্ট কিছু বলা নেই।

ps.e: Several countries have passed laws that allow their companies to keep what they mine, and others argue that this violates the principle that space is the common heritage of humankind.
ps.b: কয়েকটি দেশ আইন করেছে যে তাদের কোম্পানি যা খনন করবে তা রাখতে পারবে, এবং অন্যরা যুক্তি দেয় এতে মহাকাশ মানবজাতির যৌথ উত্তরাধিকার, এই নীতি লঙ্ঘিত হয়।

ps.e: Most experts therefore envisage partnership rather than a contest.
ps.b: তাই অধিকাংশ বিশেষজ্ঞ প্রতিযোগিতার বদলে অংশীদারিত্বের কথা ভাবেন।

ps.e: Governments are likely to remain responsible for deep-space science, for the setting of safety rules and for the protection of a shared environment, including the growing problem of debris in orbit.
ps.b: সরকারগুলো সম্ভবত গভীর মহাকাশ বিজ্ঞান, নিরাপত্তা নিয়ম নির্ধারণ এবং কক্ষপথে বাড়তে থাকা আবর্জনার সমস্যাসহ একটি ভাগ করা পরিবেশের সুরক্ষার দায়িত্বে থাকবে।

ps.e: Companies, meanwhile, can take on routine activities such as launches and satellite services, and reduce their cost.
ps.b: এদিকে কোম্পানিগুলো উৎক্ষেপণ ও উপগ্রহ সেবার মতো নিয়মিত কাজ নিয়ে তার খরচ কমাতে পারে।

ps.e: The challenge will be to ensure that the benefits of a more open space economy are shared widely, and that the rules keep pace with the ambitions of those who are eager to profit from it.
ps.b: চ্যালেঞ্জ হবে নিশ্চিত করা যে আরও উন্মুক্ত মহাকাশ অর্থনীতির সুবিধা ব্যাপকভাবে ভাগ হয়, এবং নিয়ম সেই সব মানুষের উচ্চাকাঙ্ক্ষার সঙ্গে তাল মেলায় যারা তা থেকে মুনাফা করতে আগ্রহী।

cmp/44.title: Antarctica: A Continent Devoted to Science
cmp/44.src: Antarctic Treaty Secretariat; British Antarctic Survey; National Science Foundation
p: Antarctica is the coldest, windiest and driest continent on Earth. Almost the whole of it is covered by a vast sheet of ice, in places more than four kilometres thick. Nobody has ever lived there permanently, and it has no cities, no governments and no native population. Yet, at any time of year, thousands of people are working there, and almost all of them are scientists or the staff who support them.

The reason for this unusual situation is a treaty. In 1959, twelve countries signed the Antarctic Treaty, and it came into force two years later. The agreement states that the continent may be used for peaceful purposes only. Military bases and weapons tests are banned, and no country may claim the land as its own. Since then, many more countries have joined, and the treaty is often described as a rare example of successful international cooperation.

For researchers, Antarctica is a natural laboratory. Because the air is so clean and so dry, astronomers can observe distant stars with very little interference. Geologists study rocks that are hundreds of millions of years old, and some of the meteorites that have fallen from space are easy to find against the white background. The continent is also far from industrial pollution, so it is an ideal place to measure the condition of the atmosphere.

The ice itself is perhaps the most valuable resource of all. Each year, snow falls and is slowly compressed into new layers, trapping tiny bubbles of air. By drilling deep into the ice and removing long cylinders, called ice cores, scientists can read this record like the pages of a book. The deepest cores contain air that is around eight hundred thousand years old, and they show how the climate and the level of greenhouse gases have changed over time.

Life in such a harsh place is not easy. During the winter, the sun does not rise for months, and temperatures at inland stations can fall below minus sixty degrees Celsius. Staff must be carefully selected and given medical checks, because rescue in an emergency may be impossible for weeks. Supplies are brought by ship and aircraft during the short summer, and everything, including rubbish, must be managed with great care.

The animals that live on the coast are adapted to the cold. Penguins, seals and seabirds feed in the rich waters of the Southern Ocean, where a small shrimp-like creature called krill is the basis of the food chain. Some scientists are worried that warming seas and commercial fishing for krill could threaten this balance. The research carried out in Antarctica therefore helps governments to decide how much fishing should be allowed.

There are also concerns about the ice. If the great ice sheets were to melt, the level of the oceans would rise by many metres, and coastal cities around the world would be at risk. Satellites and field teams now measure the thickness and movement of the ice every year. Although the picture is complicated, with some regions losing ice and others gaining a little, the overall trend is one of loss.

The treaty has recently been tested by growing interest in the continent's resources and by tourism, which attracts tens of thousands of visitors each season. Even so, its supporters argue that the arrangement has survived because every country benefits from sharing knowledge. Antarctica shows that nations can agree to put science before ownership, a lesson that may become more valuable as other shared regions, such as the oceans and space, come under pressure.

q.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
q.e: The passage describes the treaty and the science carried out there.
o: A. Antarctica is a continent used for peaceful scientific research under an international treaty
B. Penguins are the only animals in the world's oceans
C. Tourists should be banned from all cold places in the world
D. Antarctica should be divided between rich countries that can afford to explore it

q.q: Antarctica has a permanent native population.
q.e: Paragraph 1 says nobody has ever lived there permanently.

q.q: In paragraph 1, how thick is the ice in places?
o: A. More than four kilometres
B. Less than a kilometre
C. Exactly one kilometre in thickness
D. About four metres

q.q: What does the Antarctic Treaty say about the continent?
o: A. It can be used for mining
B. It may be used for peaceful purposes only
C. It is open for military training in some places
D. It belongs to twelve countries

q.q: According to paragraph 2, the Antarctic Treaty came into force in ____ years after it was signed.
q.e: Paragraph 2 says it came into force two years later.

q.q: Why can astronomers observe stars well from Antarctica?
o: A. There are many telescopes already
B. The air is very clean and dry
C. The days are very long
D. The sky is always dark

q.q: Why are meteorites easy to find in Antarctica?
o: A. They are very large, and can be seen from the air
B. They are always buried deep under the ice
C. They glow in the dark
D. They stand out against the white background

q.q: What are ice cores?
o: A. Machines that make snow for the stations in winter
B. Frozen fish that are kept for scientists to study
C. Maps of the continent
D. Long cylinders of ice removed by drilling

q.q: The deepest ice cores contain air about eight hundred thousand years old.
Why must staff be carefully selected for winter work?
o: A. Rescue in an emergency may be impossible for weeks
B. The stations are very large, and need many workers
C. There is too much food, and it must be eaten quickly
D. The sun shines all night

q.q: What is the basis of the food chain in the Southern Ocean?
o: A. Penguins
B. Seabirds
C. Seals
D. Krill

q.q: Why do some scientists worry about krill?
o: A. Krill are too large for the penguins to eat
B. Penguins have stopped eating krill, and have moved away
C. Warming seas and commercial fishing could threaten the balance
D. Krill are poisonous

q.q: The writer says all regions of Antarctica are losing ice.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says some regions lose ice and others gain a little.

q.q: According to paragraph 7, why is it important to measure the ice?
o: A. It is needed for building
B. If the ice sheets melted, sea levels would rise and coastal cities would be at risk
C. It makes the continent warmer, and so it is a danger to workers and to visitors there
D. Tourists want to see it, and the ice is a popular attraction

q.q: What does the writer suggest in the last paragraph?
o: A. Only space needs protection
B. The treaty has completely failed, and countries now fight over Antarctica
C. Antarctica shows that nations can put science before ownership
D. Tourists will end the treaty, since they are more powerful than scientists

q.q: The Antarctic Treaty has been signed by more than fifty countries.
q.e: The passage does not mention this.

ps.e: Antarctica is the coldest, windiest and driest continent on Earth.
ps.b: অ্যান্টার্কটিকা পৃথিবীর সবচেয়ে ঠান্ডা, সবচেয়ে ঝোড়ো ও সবচেয়ে শুষ্ক মহাদেশ।

ps.e: Almost the whole of it is covered by a vast sheet of ice, in places more than four kilometres thick.
ps.b: এর প্রায় পুরোটাই এক বিশাল বরফের চাদরে ঢাকা, কোথাও কোথাও যার পুরুত্ব চার কিলোমিটারের বেশি।

ps.e: Nobody has ever lived there permanently, and it has no cities, no governments and no native population.
ps.b: সেখানে কেউ কখনও স্থায়ীভাবে বাস করেনি, এবং সেখানে কোনো শহর, সরকার বা আদিবাসী জনগোষ্ঠী নেই।

ps.e: Yet, at any time of year, thousands of people are working there, and almost all of them are scientists or the staff who support them.
ps.b: তবু বছরের যেকোনো সময়ে হাজার হাজার মানুষ সেখানে কাজ করেন, এবং তাঁদের প্রায় সবাই বিজ্ঞানী বা তাঁদের সহায়তাকারী কর্মী।

ps.e: The reason for this unusual situation is a treaty.
ps.b: এই অস্বাভাবিক পরিস্থিতির কারণ একটি চুক্তি।

ps.e: In 1959, twelve countries signed the Antarctic Treaty, and it came into force two years later.
ps.b: ১৯৫৯ সালে বারোটি দেশ অ্যান্টার্কটিক চুক্তিতে স্বাক্ষর করে, এবং দুই বছর পর তা কার্যকর হয়।

ps.e: The agreement states that the continent may be used for peaceful purposes only.
ps.b: চুক্তিতে বলা আছে মহাদেশটি শুধু শান্তিপূর্ণ উদ্দেশ্যে ব্যবহার করা যাবে।

ps.e: Military bases and weapons tests are banned, and no country may claim the land as its own.
ps.b: সামরিক ঘাঁটি ও অস্ত্র পরীক্ষা নিষিদ্ধ, এবং কোনো দেশ ভূমিটিকে নিজের বলে দাবি করতে পারে না।

ps.e: Since then, many more countries have joined, and the treaty is often described as a rare example of successful international cooperation.
ps.b: তখন থেকে আরও অনেক দেশ যোগ দিয়েছে, এবং চুক্তিটিকে প্রায়ই আন্তর্জাতিক সহযোগিতার এক বিরল সফল উদাহরণ বলা হয়।

ps.e: For researchers, Antarctica is a natural laboratory.
ps.b: গবেষকদের কাছে অ্যান্টার্কটিকা এক প্রাকৃতিক গবেষণাগার।

ps.e: Because the air is so clean and so dry, astronomers can observe distant stars with very little interference.
ps.b: বাতাস এত পরিষ্কার ও শুষ্ক হওয়ায় জ্যোতির্বিজ্ঞানীরা খুব সামান্য বাধা নিয়ে দূরের তারা পর্যবেক্ষণ করতে পারেন।

ps.e: Geologists study rocks that are hundreds of millions of years old, and some of the meteorites that have fallen from space are easy to find against the white background.
ps.b: ভূতত্ত্ববিদরা কয়েকশো মিলিয়ন বছরের পুরোনো পাথর নিয়ে গবেষণা করেন, এবং মহাকাশ থেকে পড়া কিছু উল্কাপিণ্ড সাদা পটভূমিতে সহজে খুঁজে পাওয়া যায়।

ps.e: The continent is also far from industrial pollution, so it is an ideal place to measure the condition of the atmosphere.
ps.b: মহাদেশটি শিল্পদূষণ থেকেও দূরে, তাই বায়ুমণ্ডলের অবস্থা মাপার জন্য এটি আদর্শ জায়গা।

ps.e: The ice itself is perhaps the most valuable resource of all.
ps.b: বরফ নিজেই হয়তো সবচেয়ে মূল্যবান সম্পদ।

ps.e: Each year, snow falls and is slowly compressed into new layers, trapping tiny bubbles of air.
ps.b: প্রতি বছর তুষার পড়ে এবং ধীরে ধীরে চাপা পড়ে নতুন স্তর হয়ে যায়, আর ক্ষুদ্র বাতাসের বুদবুদ আটকে রাখে।

ps.e: By drilling deep into the ice and removing long cylinders, called ice cores, scientists can read this record like the pages of a book.
ps.b: গভীরে খুঁড়ে লম্বা চোঙাকৃতি বরফের নমুনা, যাকে আইস কোর বলে, তুলে আনলে বিজ্ঞানীরা বইয়ের পাতার মতো এই নথি পড়তে পারেন।

ps.e: The deepest cores contain air that is around eight hundred thousand years old, and they show how the climate and the level of greenhouse gases have changed over time.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে গভীর কোরগুলোতে প্রায় আট লক্ষ বছরের পুরোনো বাতাস আছে, এবং সেগুলো দেখায় সময়ের সাথে জলবায়ু ও গ্রিনহাউস গ্যাসের মাত্রা কীভাবে বদলেছে।

ps.e: Life in such a harsh place is not easy.
ps.b: এমন কঠোর জায়গায় জীবন সহজ নয়।

ps.e: During the winter, the sun does not rise for months, and temperatures at inland stations can fall below minus sixty degrees Celsius.
ps.b: শীতকালে মাসের পর মাস সূর্য ওঠে না, এবং ভেতরের দিকের কেন্দ্রগুলোতে তাপমাত্রা মাইনাস ষাট ডিগ্রি সেলসিয়াসের নিচে নামতে পারে।

ps.e: Staff must be carefully selected and given medical checks, because rescue in an emergency may be impossible for weeks.
ps.b: কর্মীদের সাবধানে বাছাই করতে হয় এবং চিকিৎসা পরীক্ষা করাতে হয়, কারণ জরুরি অবস্থায় কয়েক সপ্তাহ ধরে উদ্ধার সম্ভব নাও হতে পারে।

ps.e: Supplies are brought by ship and aircraft during the short summer, and everything, including rubbish, must be managed with great care.
ps.b: ছোট গ্রীষ্মকালে জাহাজ ও বিমানে সরবরাহ আনা হয়, এবং আবর্জনাসহ সবকিছু অত্যন্ত যত্নের সঙ্গে সামলাতে হয়।

ps.e: The animals that live on the coast are adapted to the cold.
ps.b: উপকূলের প্রাণীরা ঠান্ডার সঙ্গে খাপ খাইয়ে নিয়েছে।

ps.e: Penguins, seals and seabirds feed in the rich waters of the Southern Ocean, where a small shrimp-like creature called krill is the basis of the food chain.
ps.b: পেঙ্গুইন, সিলমাছ ও সামুদ্রিক পাখিরা দক্ষিণ মহাসাগরের সমৃদ্ধ জলে খাবার খায়, যেখানে ক্রিল নামের চিংড়ির মতো একটি ক্ষুদ্র প্রাণী খাদ্যশৃঙ্খলের ভিত্তি।

ps.e: Some scientists are worried that warming seas and commercial fishing for krill could threaten this balance.
ps.b: কিছু বিজ্ঞানী উদ্বিগ্ন যে উষ্ণ হয়ে ওঠা সমুদ্র এবং ক্রিলের বাণিজ্যিক মাছ ধরা এই ভারসাম্যের জন্য হুমকি হতে পারে।

ps.e: The research carried out in Antarctica therefore helps governments to decide how much fishing should be allowed.
ps.b: তাই অ্যান্টার্কটিকায় চালানো গবেষণা সরকারগুলোকে কতটুকু মাছ ধরার অনুমতি দেওয়া উচিত তা ঠিক করতে সাহায্য করে।

ps.e: There are also concerns about the ice.
ps.b: বরফ নিয়েও উদ্বেগ আছে।

ps.e: If the great ice sheets were to melt, the level of the oceans would rise by many metres, and coastal cities around the world would be at risk.
ps.b: বিশাল বরফের চাদর গলে গেলে সাগরের উচ্চতা বহু মিটার বেড়ে যাবে, এবং বিশ্বজুড়ে উপকূলের শহরগুলো ঝুঁকিতে পড়বে।

ps.e: Satellites and field teams now measure the thickness and movement of the ice every year.
ps.b: উপগ্রহ ও মাঠপর্যায়ের দলগুলো এখন প্রতি বছর বরফের পুরুত্ব ও গতি মাপে।

ps.e: Although the picture is complicated, with some regions losing ice and others gaining a little, the overall trend is one of loss.
ps.b: ছবিটি জটিল, কিছু অঞ্চল বরফ হারাচ্ছে আবার কিছু অঞ্চলে সামান্য বাড়ছে, তবু সামগ্রিক প্রবণতা ক্ষয়ের।

ps.e: The treaty has recently been tested by growing interest in the continent's resources and by tourism, which attracts tens of thousands of visitors each season.
ps.b: মহাদেশটির সম্পদের প্রতি বাড়তি আগ্রহ এবং পর্যটনের কারণে চুক্তিটি সম্প্রতি পরীক্ষার মুখে পড়েছে, প্রতি মৌসুমে যা কয়েক দশ হাজার দর্শনার্থীকে টানে।

ps.e: Even so, its supporters argue that the arrangement has survived because every country benefits from sharing knowledge.
ps.b: তবু এর সমর্থকরা যুক্তি দেন যে ব্যবস্থাটি টিকে আছে কারণ জ্ঞান ভাগ করে নিলে প্রত্যেক দেশই লাভবান হয়।

ps.e: Antarctica shows that nations can agree to put science before ownership, a lesson that may become more valuable as other shared regions, such as the oceans and space, come under pressure.
ps.b: অ্যান্টার্কটিকা দেখায় যে জাতিগুলো মালিকানার আগে বিজ্ঞানকে স্থান দিতে সম্মত হতে পারে, এমন একটি শিক্ষা যা সমুদ্র ও মহাকাশের মতো অন্যান্য ভাগ করা অঞ্চল চাপের মুখে পড়লে আরও মূল্যবান হতে পারে।

cmp/45.title: Green Spaces and the Mind
cmp/45.src: World Health Organization Regional Office for Europe; Bratman et al.; White et al.
p: More than half of the world's people now live in cities, and the proportion is expected to keep rising. Cities offer jobs, schools and hospitals, but they also bring noise, crowding and pollution. Researchers have become increasingly interested in a simple question: does contact with nature in the city make people feel better, or is it only a pleasant extra?

A well-known experiment was carried out by a team at Stanford University. Volunteers walked for ninety minutes, some through a park with trees and grass and others along a busy road. Afterwards, those who had walked in the park reported fewer repetitive negative thoughts, and scans showed lower activity in a part of the brain linked to worry. The group that walked beside the traffic showed no such change.

Other studies have looked at large numbers of people over a long period. A study in the United Kingdom, which involved almost twenty thousand participants, found that those who spent at least two hours a week in natural settings were more likely to report good health and a high level of wellbeing. The benefit appeared whether the time was taken in one long visit or several short ones, and it was seen in men and women, young and old.

Several explanations have been offered. Green spaces encourage exercise, which is known to protect against depression and anxiety. They also provide places to meet neighbours, and social contact reduces loneliness. Trees filter dust from the air and cool the streets in summer, and a quiet place away from traffic gives the nervous system a chance to recover. Some scientists add that the gentle, varied patterns of nature hold our attention without tiring it.

However, the evidence is not entirely straightforward. People who are already healthy or wealthy may be more likely to visit parks, which could make the benefits look larger than they are. Moreover, most studies show a connection rather than proof of cause. For this reason, the most convincing research compares the same people before and after a new park has been built or an empty plot has been turned into a garden.

Such projects have produced encouraging results. In one American city, volunteers cleaned up vacant, rubbish-filled plots and planted grass and trees. Residents of the neighbourhoods concerned later reported feeling less depressed, and the number of reported crimes with guns fell. The cost per plot was small, which suggests that modest changes can be effective.

There is also a question of fairness. Parks and tree-lined streets are not evenly shared: poorer districts often have fewer of them, which means that those who may benefit most have the least access. Some city governments now map the amount of green space in each area and set targets for improving it. Others encourage schools, rooftops and balconies to be planted with greenery.

None of this means that a park can replace medical treatment for a serious mental illness. Nevertheless, planners and doctors increasingly accept that the design of a city affects the health of its citizens. A few trees and a place to sit may seem a small matter, but, taken across millions of people, they may reduce a great deal of unnecessary suffering.

o: A. Contact with nature in cities appears to improve people's mental wellbeing

o: A. Replace medical treatment for serious mental illness
