ps.b: অনেক মানুষ এর চেয়ে অনেক বেশি শব্দের মধ্যে বাস করেন।

ps.e: The European Environment Agency estimated that around one in five Europeans is exposed to levels of traffic noise that are harmful to health.
ps.b: ইউরোপীয় পরিবেশ সংস্থার অনুমান, প্রতি পাঁচজন ইউরোপীয়ের একজন স্বাস্থ্যের জন্য ক্ষতিকর মাত্রার যানবাহনের শব্দের সংস্পর্শে আছেন।

ps.e: In large cities in other parts of the world, the figures are often worse, with horns, construction, loudspeakers and aircraft combining to produce a constant background roar.
ps.b: বিশ্বের অন্যান্য অঞ্চলের বড় শহরগুলোতে পরিসংখ্যান প্রায়ই আরও খারাপ, যেখানে হর্ন, নির্মাণকাজ, লাউডস্পিকার ও বিমান মিলে একটি অবিরাম পটভূমি গর্জন তৈরি করে।

ps.e: The best-known effect of loud noise is damage to hearing.
ps.b: জোরালো শব্দের সবচেয়ে পরিচিত প্রভাব শ্রবণশক্তির ক্ষতি।

ps.e: Exposure to very loud sounds, whether from a machine or headphones, can destroy the sensitive cells in the inner ear, and once these are lost, they do not grow back.
ps.b: যন্ত্র বা হেডফোন থেকে খুব জোরালো শব্দের সংস্পর্শ অন্তঃকর্ণের সংবেদনশীল কোষ নষ্ট করতে পারে, এবং একবার এগুলো হারিয়ে গেলে আর গজায় না।

ps.e: However, hearing loss usually needs sound above about 85 decibels over a long period.
ps.b: তবে শ্রবণশক্তি হারাতে সাধারণত দীর্ঘ সময় প্রায় ৮৫ ডেসিবেলের ওপরে শব্দ লাগে।

ps.e: The more widespread concern about everyday noise is that it affects the body in a different way.
ps.b: দৈনন্দিন শব্দ নিয়ে আরও ব্যাপক উদ্বেগ হলো এটি শরীরকে অন্যভাবে প্রভাবিত করে।

ps.e: When we hear a sudden or loud sound, the body reacts as if there were a threat.
ps.b: আমরা হঠাৎ বা জোরালো শব্দ শুনলে শরীর এমনভাবে সাড়া দেয় যেন কোনো হুমকি আছে।

ps.e: The heart beats faster, blood pressure rises and the body releases stress hormones.
ps.b: হৃদয় দ্রুত স্পন্দিত হয়, রক্তচাপ বাড়ে এবং শরীর স্ট্রেস হরমোন নির্গত করে।

ps.e: This reaction is useful if a car is coming towards us, but if it happens repeatedly over many years, it may contribute to high blood pressure, heart disease and stroke.
ps.b: একটি গাড়ি আমাদের দিকে এলে এই সাড়া কাজের, কিন্তু বহু বছর ধরে বারবার ঘটলে এটি উচ্চ রক্তচাপ, হৃদরোগ ও স্ট্রোকে ভূমিকা রাখতে পারে।

ps.e: Studies of people living near airports and busy roads have found higher rates of such problems.
ps.b: বিমানবন্দর ও ব্যস্ত সড়কের কাছে বসবাসকারী মানুষদের গবেষণায় এমন সমস্যার উচ্চতর হার পাওয়া গেছে।

ps.e: Sleep is especially vulnerable.
ps.b: ঘুম বিশেষভাবে ঝুঁকিপ্রবণ।

ps.e: Even if a person does not wake up completely, noise at night can cause brief changes in the brain and heart.
ps.b: কেউ পুরোপুরি জেগে না উঠলেও রাতের শব্দ মস্তিষ্ক ও হৃদয়ে সংক্ষিপ্ত পরিবর্তন ঘটাতে পারে।

ps.e: Poor sleep, in turn, is associated with tiredness, difficulty in concentrating and a higher risk of other illnesses.
ps.b: খারাপ ঘুমের ফলে ক্লান্তি, মনোযোগ দিতে অসুবিধা এবং অন্যান্য রোগের উচ্চতর ঝুঁকি দেখা যায়।

ps.e: The WHO has estimated that, in Western Europe alone, the loss of healthy life years caused by traffic noise is counted in the hundreds of thousands each year.
ps.b: বিশ্ব স্বাস্থ্য সংস্থা অনুমান করেছে যে কেবল পশ্চিম ইউরোপেই যানবাহনের শব্দে সুস্থ জীবনবর্ষের ক্ষতি প্রতি বছর কয়েক লক্ষে গোনা হয়।

ps.e: Children may be particularly affected.
ps.b: শিশুরা বিশেষভাবে প্রভাবিত হতে পারে।

ps.e: Several studies have found that pupils in schools under aircraft flight paths or beside busy roads performed worse on reading tests than those in quieter schools, and when a noisy airport was closed and a new one opened elsewhere, the reading scores of children near the old airport improved while those near the new one fell.
ps.b: কয়েকটি গবেষণায় দেখা গেছে বিমানের উড্ডয়নপথের নিচের বা ব্যস্ত সড়কের পাশের স্কুলের শিক্ষার্থীরা শান্ত স্কুলের শিক্ষার্থীদের চেয়ে পড়ার পরীক্ষায় খারাপ করেছে, এবং একটি কোলাহলপূর্ণ বিমানবন্দর বন্ধ হয়ে অন্যত্র নতুন একটি খুললে পুরোনো বিমানবন্দরের কাছের শিশুদের পড়ার নম্বর বেড়েছে আর নতুনটির কাছের শিশুদের কমেছে।

ps.e: Researchers caution, however, that other factors such as poverty and air pollution may also play a part.
ps.b: গবেষকরা অবশ্য সতর্ক করেন যে দারিদ্র্য ও বায়ুদূষণের মতো অন্য কারণও ভূমিকা রাখতে পারে।

ps.e: The solutions are mostly practical.
ps.b: সমাধানগুলো বেশিরভাগই ব্যবহারিক।

ps.e: Road surfaces that reduce tyre noise, electric vehicles, lower speed limits, barriers beside motorways and the better design of flight paths can all make a difference.
ps.b: টায়ারের শব্দ কমানো সড়কের পৃষ্ঠ, বৈদ্যুতিক গাড়ি, কম গতিসীমা, মোটরওয়ের পাশে দেয়াল এবং বিমানের উড্ডয়নপথের উন্নততর নকশা সবই পার্থক্য আনতে পারে।

ps.e: At home, thicker windows, soft furnishings and trees can lessen the sound that enters.
ps.b: বাড়িতে মোটা জানালা, নরম আসবাব ও গাছ ভেতরে ঢোকা শব্দ কমাতে পারে।

ps.e: Cities can also protect "quiet areas" such as parks.
ps.b: শহরগুলো পার্কের মতো "শান্ত এলাকা"ও সুরক্ষিত রাখতে পারে।

ps.e: Although noise may seem a small problem compared with others, it can be reduced at reasonable cost, and the result is a healthier and calmer place to live.
ps.b: শব্দ অন্যান্য সমস্যার তুলনায় ছোট মনে হলেও যুক্তিসংগত খরচে তা কমানো যায়, এবং ফলাফল বাস করার জন্য একটি সুস্থ ও শান্ত জায়গা।

cmp/51.title: Do We Still Need Libraries?
cmp/51.src: International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions; American Library Association; Pew Research Center; UNESCO
p: For many people, the word "library" brings to mind a quiet room with long shelves of books and a person stamping dates on cards. In an age when a phone can bring up almost any fact in seconds, and millions of books can be read on a screen, it is fair to ask whether libraries have a future. Some local councils have decided that they do not, and have closed branches to save money. Yet, in many countries, libraries are busier and more varied than ever.

The idea of a library is very old. The great library of Alexandria, founded in Egypt more than two thousand years ago, aimed to collect all the knowledge of the known world. In the Islamic world, centres such as the House of Wisdom in Baghdad gathered scholars who translated and copied books from many languages. Public lending libraries, open to ordinary citizens, became common in Europe and North America in the nineteenth century, and were often seen as a way to educate workers and to improve society.

Today, the book is only a part of what a library offers. Many libraries lend e-books and audiobooks, provide free computers and Wi-Fi, and run classes on subjects such as languages, job skills and computer use. Children attend story-time and homework clubs. Some libraries even lend tools, seeds, musical instruments or equipment for 3D printing. The common idea is that the library gives people access to things that they could not easily afford alone.

This role is especially important for those without a home internet connection. Surveys in the United States have found that a significant number of people use library computers to look for work, apply for benefits or complete school assignments. In a society where more and more services are online, the library helps to reduce what is called the "digital divide", the gap between those who have technology and the skills to use it, and those who do not.

Libraries also provide something that is hard to measure: a shared public space. Unlike a cafe or a shopping centre, a library does not expect people to buy anything. Students can study there, older people can meet others and newcomers to a country can find help in learning the language. Researchers who study communities have described libraries as "social infrastructure", places that encourage people of different backgrounds to meet and to build trust.

Librarians, too, have a role that has changed. In a world full of information, the difficulty is no longer finding it but judging whether it is true. Librarians teach people how to search, how to check a source and how to recognise false or misleading claims. This skill, sometimes called information literacy, may be more useful than the ability to find a single book on a shelf.

Nevertheless, libraries face real difficulties. Budgets have been cut in many places, and opening hours reduced. Publishers charge libraries higher prices for e-books than ordinary readers pay, and place limits on how often they can be lent. Critics also point out that many people, especially the young, rarely visit, and ask whether the money would be better spent on other services.

Supporters reply that a library is good value, because for each pound or dollar spent, it brings benefits to many people, including some of the poorest. They argue that cutting libraries would be a false economy: a small saving today could result in a loss of skills, learning and community life that is much harder to rebuild. The most successful libraries, it seems, are those that listen to their communities and change with them, while keeping their central promise: knowledge free to all.

q.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
q.e: The passage argues libraries remain useful.
o: A. Libraries still serve important purposes in the digital age, though they face difficulties
B. Libraries are no longer needed, since computers can give any book
C. Libraries were invented in Europe
D. Books are better than computers, so libraries should keep only books and close all the other services

q.q: Why have some local councils closed library branches?
o: A. Because libraries are too noisy
B. Because nobody reads
C. To save money
D. Because books are banned

q.q: What was the aim of the library of Alexandria?
o: A. To collect all the knowledge of the known world
B. To teach children
C. To sell books to scholars from many countries
D. To lend tools and seeds to the farmers of Egypt

q.q: Public lending libraries became common in Europe and North America in the nineteenth century.
Which of these do some libraries lend, according to paragraph 3?
o: A. Houses and rooms for visitors from other countries
B. Tools, seeds, musical instruments or equipment for 3D printing
C. Cars and bicycles for people who cannot afford to buy them
D. Food

q.q: A library gives people access to things that they could not easily ____ alone.
What do some people in the United States use library computers for?
o: A. To print money for the local council
B. To watch films only
C. To look for work, apply for benefits or complete school assignments
D. To play games only, since most people have no work and no interest in learning

q.q: What is the "digital divide"?
o: A. A tax on the internet that is paid by people who use a library
B. A broken computer that has to be repaired at the library before anyone can use it
C. A kind of library card that works only on the internet and not in the building
D. The gap between those who have technology and the skills to use it, and those who do not

q.q: What is special about a library compared with a cafe or shopping centre?
o: A. It is bigger than a cafe, and is open all night
B. It sells coffee and food to the readers at low prices
C. It is open all night
D. It does not expect people to buy anything

q.q: What do researchers call libraries in paragraph 5?
o: A. Book stores
B. Quiet shops
C. Social infrastructure
D. Digital warehouses and stores

q.q: Why may information literacy be useful, according to paragraph 6?
o: A. The difficulty is no longer finding information but judging whether it is true
B. Computers cannot search
C. Books are too heavy for people to carry from shelf to shelf, so they prefer a small screen
D. Nobody has time to read, so short sources are needed

q.q: Publishers charge libraries lower prices for e-books than ordinary readers pay.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says they charge higher prices.

q.q: What criticism is mentioned in paragraph 7?
o: A. Librarians are rude to people who ask for help
B. Libraries have too many computers
C. Libraries are too cheap to be taken seriously by councils
D. Many people, especially the young, rarely visit

q.q: Why do supporters say that cutting libraries would be a "false economy"?
o: A. Libraries are never used by young people, so closing them would harm nobody
B. A small saving today could cause a loss of skills, learning and community life that is hard to rebuild
C. Books are free in shops, so libraries are not needed and can safely be closed
D. Libraries make a large profit, which would be lost if the council closed them, and the council would then have less money.

q.q: What do the most successful libraries do, according to the writer?
o: A. Close their doors in the evening and open only on weekdays, to save the cost of staff
B. Listen to their communities and change with them while keeping their central promise
C. Sell their books in order to pay for new computers and for new rooms
D. Stop lending e-books, since nobody wishes to read them on a screen

q.q: The oldest library in the world is found in Iraq.
q.e: The passage does not mention this.

ps.e: For many people, the word "library" brings to mind a quiet room with long shelves of books and a person stamping dates on cards.
ps.b: অনেকের কাছে "লাইব্রেরি" শব্দটি মনে আনে লম্বা বইয়ের তাকওয়ালা একটি শান্ত ঘর এবং কার্ডে তারিখের ছাপ দেওয়া একজন মানুষ।

ps.e: In an age when a phone can bring up almost any fact in seconds, and millions of books can be read on a screen, it is fair to ask whether libraries have a future.
ps.b: যে যুগে একটি ফোন কয়েক সেকেন্ডে প্রায় যেকোনো তথ্য এনে দেয় এবং লক্ষ লক্ষ বই পর্দায় পড়া যায়, সেখানে লাইব্রেরির ভবিষ্যৎ আছে কি না তা জিজ্ঞেস করা ন্যায্য।

ps.e: Some local councils have decided that they do not, and have closed branches to save money.
ps.b: কিছু স্থানীয় পরিষদ ঠিক করেছে নেই, এবং অর্থ বাঁচাতে শাখা বন্ধ করেছে।

ps.e: Yet, in many countries, libraries are busier and more varied than ever.
ps.b: তবু অনেক দেশে লাইব্রেরি আগের চেয়ে বেশি ব্যস্ত ও বৈচিত্র্যময়।

ps.e: The idea of a library is very old.
ps.b: লাইব্রেরির ধারণা অনেক পুরোনো।

ps.e: The great library of Alexandria, founded in Egypt more than two thousand years ago, aimed to collect all the knowledge of the known world.
ps.b: মিশরে দুই হাজার বছরেরও বেশি আগে প্রতিষ্ঠিত আলেকজান্দ্রিয়ার মহান লাইব্রেরি পরিচিত বিশ্বের সব জ্ঞান সংগ্রহ করতে চেয়েছিল।

ps.e: In the Islamic world, centres such as the House of Wisdom in Baghdad gathered scholars who translated and copied books from many languages.
ps.b: ইসলামি বিশ্বে বাগদাদের বায়তুল হিকমার মতো কেন্দ্র এমন পণ্ডিতদের একত্র করেছিল যাঁরা বহু ভাষা থেকে বই অনুবাদ ও অনুলিপি করতেন।

ps.e: Public lending libraries, open to ordinary citizens, became common in Europe and North America in the nineteenth century, and were often seen as a way to educate workers and to improve society.
ps.b: সাধারণ নাগরিকদের জন্য উন্মুক্ত গণ ধার-লাইব্রেরি ঊনবিংশ শতাব্দীতে ইউরোপ ও উত্তর আমেরিকায় সাধারণ হয়ে ওঠে, এবং প্রায়ই শ্রমিকদের শিক্ষিত করা ও সমাজ উন্নত করার উপায় হিসেবে দেখা হতো।

ps.e: Today, the book is only a part of what a library offers.
ps.b: আজ বই লাইব্রেরির পরিষেবার একটি অংশ মাত্র।

ps.e: Many libraries lend e-books and audiobooks, provide free computers and Wi-Fi, and run classes on subjects such as languages, job skills and computer use.
ps.b: অনেক লাইব্রেরি ই-বুক ও অডিওবই ধার দেয়, বিনামূল্যে কম্পিউটার ও ওয়াই-ফাই দেয়, এবং ভাষা, কর্মদক্ষতা ও কম্পিউটার ব্যবহারের মতো বিষয়ে ক্লাস চালায়।

ps.e: Children attend story-time and homework clubs.
ps.b: শিশুরা গল্প শোনার আসর ও হোমওয়ার্ক ক্লাবে যোগ দেয়।

ps.e: Some libraries even lend tools, seeds, musical instruments or equipment for 3D printing.
ps.b: কিছু লাইব্রেরি এমনকি যন্ত্রপাতি, বীজ, বাদ্যযন্ত্র বা থ্রিডি প্রিন্টিংয়ের সরঞ্জাম ধার দেয়।

ps.e: The common idea is that the library gives people access to things that they could not easily afford alone.
ps.b: সাধারণ ধারণা হলো লাইব্রেরি মানুষকে এমন জিনিসের নাগাল দেয় যা তারা একা সহজে কিনতে পারত না।

ps.e: This role is especially important for those without a home internet connection.
ps.b: বাড়িতে ইন্টারনেট নেই এমনদের জন্য এই ভূমিকা বিশেষভাবে গুরুত্বপূর্ণ।

ps.e: Surveys in the United States have found that a significant number of people use library computers to look for work, apply for benefits or complete school assignments.
ps.b: যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের জরিপে দেখা গেছে উল্লেখযোগ্য সংখ্যক মানুষ কাজ খুঁজতে, ভাতার জন্য আবেদন করতে বা স্কুলের কাজ শেষ করতে লাইব্রেরির কম্পিউটার ব্যবহার করে।

ps.e: In a society where more and more services are online, the library helps to reduce what is called the "digital divide", the gap between those who have technology and the skills to use it, and those who do not.
ps.b: যে সমাজে ক্রমশ বেশি পরিষেবা অনলাইনে, সেখানে লাইব্রেরি তথাকথিত "ডিজিটাল বৈষম্য" কমাতে সাহায্য করে, অর্থাৎ যাদের প্রযুক্তি ও তা ব্যবহারের দক্ষতা আছে এবং যাদের নেই তাদের মধ্যকার ব্যবধান।

ps.e: Libraries also provide something that is hard to measure: a shared public space.
ps.b: লাইব্রেরি এমন কিছুও দেয় যা মাপা কঠিন: একটি ভাগ করা জনপরিসর।

ps.e: Unlike a cafe or a shopping centre, a library does not expect people to buy anything.
ps.b: ক্যাফে বা শপিং সেন্টারের মতো নয়, লাইব্রেরি কাউকে কিছু কিনতে বলে না।

ps.e: Students can study there, older people can meet others and newcomers to a country can find help in learning the language.
ps.b: শিক্ষার্থীরা সেখানে পড়তে পারে, বয়স্করা অন্যদের সঙ্গে দেখা করতে পারেন এবং কোনো দেশে নতুন আসা মানুষ ভাষা শিখতে সাহায্য পেতে পারেন।

ps.e: Researchers who study communities have described libraries as "social infrastructure", places that encourage people of different backgrounds to meet and to build trust.
ps.b: সম্প্রদায় নিয়ে গবেষকরা লাইব্রেরিকে "সামাজিক অবকাঠামো" বলেছেন, এমন জায়গা যা বিভিন্ন পটভূমির মানুষকে দেখা করতে ও বিশ্বাস গড়তে উৎসাহ দেয়।

ps.e: Librarians, too, have a role that has changed.
ps.b: গ্রন্থাগারিকদের ভূমিকাও বদলেছে।

ps.e: In a world full of information, the difficulty is no longer finding it but judging whether it is true.
ps.b: তথ্যে ভরা বিশ্বে এখন সমস্যা তা খুঁজে পাওয়া নয়, বরং তা সত্য কি না যাচাই করা।

ps.e: Librarians teach people how to search, how to check a source and how to recognise false or misleading claims.
ps.b: গ্রন্থাগারিকরা মানুষকে শেখান কীভাবে খুঁজতে হয়, কীভাবে উৎস পরীক্ষা করতে হয় এবং কীভাবে ভুল বা বিভ্রান্তিকর দাবি চিনতে হয়।

ps.e: This skill, sometimes called information literacy, may be more useful than the ability to find a single book on a shelf.
ps.b: এই দক্ষতা, যাকে কখনও কখনও তথ্য সাক্ষরতা বলা হয়, তাকের ওপর একটি বই খুঁজে পাওয়ার সামর্থ্যের চেয়ে বেশি কাজের হতে পারে।

ps.e: Nevertheless, libraries face real difficulties.
ps.b: তবু লাইব্রেরি বাস্তব অসুবিধার মুখে।

ps.e: Budgets have been cut in many places, and opening hours reduced.
ps.b: অনেক জায়গায় বাজেট কাটা হয়েছে এবং খোলার সময় কমানো হয়েছে।

ps.e: Publishers charge libraries higher prices for e-books than ordinary readers pay, and place limits on how often they can be lent.
ps.b: প্রকাশকরা সাধারণ পাঠকদের চেয়ে লাইব্রেরির কাছ থেকে ই-বুকের বেশি দাম নেয়, এবং কতবার ধার দেওয়া যাবে তার সীমা বেঁধে দেয়।

ps.e: Critics also point out that many people, especially the young, rarely visit, and ask whether the money would be better spent on other services.
ps.b: সমালোচকরাও উল্লেখ করেন যে অনেক মানুষ, বিশেষ করে তরুণরা, কমই যায়, এবং প্রশ্ন করেন অর্থ অন্য পরিষেবায় ব্যয় করা ভালো হতো কি না।

ps.e: Supporters reply that a library is good value, because for each pound or dollar spent, it brings benefits to many people, including some of the poorest.
ps.b: সমর্থকরা জবাব দেন যে লাইব্রেরি ভালো মূল্যের, কারণ প্রতিটি পাউন্ড বা ডলার ব্যয়ে এটি অনেক মানুষকে, এমনকি সবচেয়ে দরিদ্রদেরও, উপকার দেয়।

ps.e: They argue that cutting libraries would be a false economy: a small saving today could result in a loss of skills, learning and community life that is much harder to rebuild.
ps.b: তাঁদের যুক্তি, লাইব্রেরি কাটা হবে একটি ভুল সাশ্রয়: আজকের সামান্য সঞ্চয় দক্ষতা, শেখা ও সম্প্রদায়জীবনের এমন ক্ষতি ঘটাতে পারে যা পুনর্গঠন করা অনেক কঠিন।

ps.e: The most successful libraries, it seems, are those that listen to their communities and change with them, while keeping their central promise: knowledge free to all.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে সফল লাইব্রেরিগুলো, মনে হয়, সেগুলোই যারা নিজেদের সম্প্রদায়ের কথা শোনে এবং তাদের সঙ্গে বদলায়, আর নিজেদের কেন্দ্রীয় প্রতিশ্রুতি ধরে রাখে: সবার জন্য বিনামূল্যে জ্ঞান।

cmp/52.title: Planting Trees: Easier Said Than Done
cmp/52.src: African Union; UN Convention to Combat Desertification; Holl and Brancalion; Food and Agriculture Organization
p: Planting trees is one of the most popular ideas for helping the planet. Trees take in carbon dioxide from the air as they grow, they provide homes for animals, and they protect soil and water. Governments, companies and ordinary people have all announced plans to plant millions, and even billions, of trees. Yet experts warn that planting trees is much harder than it sounds, and that the results are not always as good as the headlines suggest.

The scale of forest loss explains the enthusiasm. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization, the world has lost around 420 million hectares of forest since 1990, an area larger than the European Union. Most of the loss has occurred in the tropics, where forests are cleared for farming, cattle and timber. Since forests store a great deal of carbon, their destruction is a major source of the gases that warm the climate.

One well-known project is the Great Green Wall in Africa. Launched in 2007, it aimed to plant a belt of trees about 8,000 kilometres long across the Sahel, the dry region south of the Sahara desert, in order to hold back the advance of the desert. In its early years, many of the saplings that were planted died because of drought, poor soil or lack of care, and progress was far slower than planned. The target, to restore 100 million hectares by 2030, is unlikely to be met.

Nevertheless, the project has taught important lessons. In some places, farmers have achieved better results through a method called farmer-managed natural regeneration, in which they protect and encourage young trees that are already sprouting from old roots in their fields, rather than planting new ones. In Niger, this approach has helped to restore millions of hectares of farmland, at a very low cost, and has increased crop yields and the supply of firewood.

The first lesson, then, is that survival matters more than the number of trees planted. A tree that is planted and then dies absorbs no carbon at all. Ecologists stress that the right trees must be planted in the right place. A forest of a single fast-growing species, for example, supports far less wildlife and is more vulnerable to disease and fire than a natural forest with many different species.

The second lesson is that local people must benefit. If villagers lose access to land that they have used for grazing or farming, they may have little reason to protect the new trees, and conflicts may arise over ownership. Successful schemes tend to give communities a stake in the forest, through income from fruit, timber or tourism. Without this, planting may be a short-lived effort, abandoned when outside funding ends.

A third concern is that tree planting can be used as an excuse. Some companies pay for trees to be planted to "offset" their pollution, so that they can continue to burn fuel without making any change. But a young tree takes decades to absorb the amount of carbon that a car or aeroplane emits in a short time, and it may be cut down or burnt before then. Scientists agree that cutting emissions is essential, and that tree planting can supplement this, not replace it.

Experts therefore make a simple recommendation: protect the forests that already exist, because an old forest holds far more carbon and wildlife than a new plantation, and allow damaged land to recover naturally where possible. Planting should be reserved for places where nature cannot restore itself, and should be backed by long-term care and the support of local communities. A tree is a good start, but it is the forest that matters.

q.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
q.e: The passage explains the difficulties and lessons of planting trees.
o: A. Only governments should plant trees, because companies and villagers cannot be trusted
B. Planting trees is useless, since the trees soon die and release all of their carbon again
C. Trees grow without any help from people, and need no care once the seeds have been planted, so nobody should manage them.
D. Planting trees is useful but must be done carefully, with the right trees, local support and long-term care

q.q: Which of these is NOT given as a benefit of trees in paragraph 1?
o: A. They protect soil and water
B. They take in carbon dioxide
C. They make rain fall more often
D. They provide homes for animals

q.q: How much forest has the world lost since 1990, according to the FAO?
o: A. Around 4 hectares
B. Around 4,000 hectares in all
C. None
D. Around 420 million hectares

q.q: Why are forests cleared in the tropics?
o: A. For farming, cattle and timber
B. For making deserts, which are then sold to companies
C. For building airports and new roads between towns
D. For hunting only

q.q: The Great Green Wall was launched in the year ____.
What was the aim of the Great Green Wall?
o: A. To dig a canal that would bring water from the sea
B. To plant a belt of trees across the Sahel to hold back the desert
C. To build a stone wall across the Sahel to stop travellers
D. To plant a garden in a city

q.q: Why did many early saplings die?
o: A. Because of snow that fell on the young trees in winter
B. Because of drought, poor soil or lack of care
C. Because of floods that washed the young trees away
D. Because of insects only

q.q: What is farmer-managed natural regeneration?
o: A. Cutting all the old trees so that new ones can grow
B. Protecting and encouraging young trees that sprout from old roots in fields
C. Planting only imported trees in neat rows across the fields, with fences to protect them
D. Building fences

q.q: In Niger, farmer-managed natural regeneration has been very costly.
q.e: Paragraph 4 says it was done at a very low cost.

q.q: What is the first lesson, according to paragraph 5?
o: A. Fast-growing trees are best, because they absorb carbon sooner
B. Fruit trees are bad
C. Survival matters more than the number of trees planted
D. Planting more trees is always better, however they are planted

q.q: Why is a forest of a single fast-growing species a problem?
o: A. It supports less wildlife and is more vulnerable to disease and fire
B. It cannot absorb any carbon from the air, so it does not help the climate
C. It grows too slowly to provide any shade or wood for local people
D. It uses no water, so the soil around it becomes too dry for other plants

q.q: What do successful schemes give to communities?
o: A. A stake in the forest through income from fruit, timber or tourism
B. A reduction in taxes if they plant a certain number of trees
C. Free cars
D. New houses built beside the forest by the government

q.q: The writer says tree planting can fully replace the cutting of emissions.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says it can supplement cutting emissions, not replace it.

q.q: Why is the "offset" argument weak, according to paragraph 7?
o: A. Companies never pay for trees, so the idea is only a promise that is made to the public
B. Trees cannot absorb carbon, so planting does not help the climate in any way, even after many years of growth.
C. A young tree takes decades to absorb the carbon that a car or aeroplane emits quickly, and may be cut or burnt first
D. Cars use no fuel, and aeroplanes release very little carbon into the air

q.q: What do experts recommend in paragraph 8?
o: A. Cut old forests in order to plant new and faster-growing ones in neat rows
B. Plant trees everywhere, whatever the soil and the climate, and never stop to check
C. Stop caring about forests, and leave the land to farmers and builders
D. Protect existing forests and allow damaged land to recover naturally where possible

q.q: China has planted more trees than any other country in the last ten years.
q.e: The passage does not mention this.

ps.e: Most of the loss has occurred in the tropics, where forests are cleared for farming, cattle and timber.

ps.b: ২০৩০ সালের মধ্যে ১০ কোটি হেক্টর পুনরুদ্ধারের লক্ষ্য পূরণ হওয়ার সম্ভাবনা কম।

ps.e: Nevertheless, the project has taught important lessons.
ps.b: তবু প্রকল্পটি গুরুত্বপূর্ণ শিক্ষা দিয়েছে।

ps.e: In some places, farmers have achieved better results through a method called farmer-managed natural regeneration, in which they protect and encourage young trees that are already sprouting from old roots in their fields, rather than planting new ones.
ps.b: কিছু জায়গায় কৃষকরা কৃষক-পরিচালিত প্রাকৃতিক পুনর্জন্ম নামের একটি পদ্ধতিতে ভালো ফল পেয়েছেন, যাতে তাঁরা নতুন গাছ লাগানোর বদলে নিজেদের ক্ষেতে পুরোনো শিকড় থেকে গজানো তরুণ গাছ রক্ষা ও লালন করেন।

ps.e: In Niger, this approach has helped to restore millions of hectares of farmland, at a very low cost, and has increased crop yields and the supply of firewood.
ps.b: নাইজারে এই পদ্ধতি অত্যন্ত কম খরচে লক্ষ লক্ষ হেক্টর কৃষিজমি পুনরুদ্ধারে সাহায্য করেছে এবং ফসলের ফলন ও জ্বালানি কাঠের জোগান বাড়িয়েছে।

ps.e: The first lesson, then, is that survival matters more than the number of trees planted.
ps.b: তাহলে প্রথম শিক্ষা হলো লাগানো গাছের সংখ্যার চেয়ে টিকে থাকা বেশি গুরুত্বপূর্ণ।

ps.e: A tree that is planted and then dies absorbs no carbon at all.
ps.b: যে গাছ লাগিয়ে মরে যায় তা একদমই কার্বন শোষণ করে না।

ps.e: Ecologists stress that the right trees must be planted in the right place.
ps.b: বাস্তুবিদরা জোর দেন যে সঠিক জায়গায় সঠিক গাছ লাগাতে হবে।

ps.e: A forest of a single fast-growing species, for example, supports far less wildlife and is more vulnerable to disease and fire than a natural forest with many different species.
ps.b: উদাহরণস্বরূপ, একটিমাত্র দ্রুত বাড়া প্রজাতির বন অনেক বিভিন্ন প্রজাতির প্রাকৃতিক বনের চেয়ে অনেক কম বন্যপ্রাণী ধারণ করে এবং রোগ ও আগুনের প্রতি বেশি ঝুঁকিপ্রবণ।

ps.e: The second lesson is that local people must benefit.
ps.b: দ্বিতীয় শিক্ষা হলো স্থানীয় মানুষকে উপকৃত হতে হবে।

ps.e: If villagers lose access to land that they have used for grazing or farming, they may have little reason to protect the new trees, and conflicts may arise over ownership.
ps.b: গ্রামবাসীরা যে জমি পশুচারণ বা চাষে ব্যবহার করত তার নাগাল হারালে নতুন গাছ রক্ষা করার কারণ তাদের কমই থাকে, এবং মালিকানা নিয়ে সংঘাত হতে পারে।

ps.e: Successful schemes tend to give communities a stake in the forest, through income from fruit, timber or tourism.
ps.b: সফল প্রকল্পগুলো ফল, কাঠ বা পর্যটনের আয়ের মাধ্যমে সম্প্রদায়কে বনে অংশীদারিত্ব দেয়।

ps.e: Without this, planting may be a short-lived effort, abandoned when outside funding ends.
ps.b: এটি ছাড়া গাছ লাগানো ক্ষণস্থায়ী প্রচেষ্টা হতে পারে, বাইরের অর্থায়ন শেষ হলে যা পরিত্যক্ত হয়।

ps.e: A third concern is that tree planting can be used as an excuse.
ps.b: তৃতীয় উদ্বেগ হলো গাছ লাগানো অজুহাত হিসেবে ব্যবহৃত হতে পারে।

ps.e: Some companies pay for trees to be planted to "offset" their pollution, so that they can continue to burn fuel without making any change.
ps.b: কিছু কোম্পানি তাদের দূষণের "ক্ষতিপূরণ" করতে গাছ লাগানোর অর্থ দেয়, যাতে তারা কোনো পরিবর্তন না করেই জ্বালানি পোড়াতে পারে।

ps.e: But a young tree takes decades to absorb the amount of carbon that a car or aeroplane emits in a short time, and it may be cut down or burnt before then.
ps.b: কিন্তু একটি গাছ একটি গাড়ি বা বিমান অল্প সময়ে যে পরিমাণ কার্বন ছাড়ে তা শোষণ করতে দশকের পর দশক নেয়, এবং তার আগেই তা কাটা বা পুড়ে যেতে পারে।

ps.e: Scientists agree that cutting emissions is essential, and that tree planting can supplement this, not replace it.
ps.b: বিজ্ঞানীরা একমত যে নির্গমন কমানো অপরিহার্য, এবং গাছ লাগানো তার পরিপূরক হতে পারে, বিকল্প নয়।

ps.e: Experts therefore make a simple recommendation: protect the forests that already exist, because an old forest holds far more carbon and wildlife than a new plantation, and allow damaged land to recover naturally where possible.
ps.b: তাই বিশেষজ্ঞরা একটি সহজ সুপারিশ করেন: যেসব বন আছে সেগুলো রক্ষা করুন, কারণ পুরোনো বন নতুন আবাদি বনের চেয়ে অনেক বেশি কার্বন ও বন্যপ্রাণী ধারণ করে, এবং সম্ভব হলে ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত জমিকে প্রাকৃতিকভাবে সেরে উঠতে দিন।

ps.e: Planting should be reserved for places where nature cannot restore itself, and should be backed by long-term care and the support of local communities.
ps.b: গাছ লাগানো সেসব জায়গার জন্য রাখা উচিত যেখানে প্রকৃতি নিজে পুনরুদ্ধার করতে পারে না, এবং তাতে দীর্ঘমেয়াদি যত্ন ও স্থানীয় সম্প্রদায়ের সমর্থন থাকা উচিত।

ps.e: A tree is a good start, but it is the forest that matters.
ps.b: একটি গাছ ভালো শুরু, কিন্তু যা গুরুত্বপূর্ণ তা বন।

cmp/53.title: Why Do We Laugh?
cmp/53.src: Provine; Panksepp and Burgdorf; Dunbar et al.; Scott et al.
p: Everyone laughs, in every culture and in every language, yet few of us stop to ask why. Laughter seems to be a response to something funny, but the scientist Robert Provine, who spent years listening to people in shopping centres and on city streets, reached a surprising conclusion. Most of the laughter that he recorded followed remarks that were not funny at all, such as "I'll see you later" or "It was nice meeting you". Laughter, it seems, has less to do with jokes than with relationships.

This finding is supported by other research. People are about thirty times more likely to laugh when they are with others than when they are alone. Babies begin to laugh at about three or four months of age, long before they can speak or understand a joke, and they usually laugh in response to a smile, a tickle or a game with a parent. Laughter, in other words, is an ancient form of communication that comes before language.

There is evidence that it is even older than humans. The neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp found that young rats, when tickled, make high-pitched sounds that are too high for people to hear without special equipment, and that they seem to enjoy being tickled, chasing the researcher's hand and returning for more. Chimpanzees and other apes also produce a panting sound during play. Many scientists therefore think that laughter began as a signal that "this is only play", which prevented a playful fight from turning into a real one.

For humans, laughter appears to strengthen social bonds. The psychologist Robin Dunbar and his colleagues found that after watching a comedy together, people were able to tolerate pain for longer than after watching a serious film. The researchers suggest that laughing causes the brain to release endorphins, natural chemicals that reduce pain and produce a feeling of well-being. Sharing such feelings may help to explain why friends who laugh together often feel close.

Laughter is also contagious. Hearing others laugh can make us laugh, even when we do not know what is funny, which is why recorded laughter is used in television comedies. Brain scans show that the sound of laughter activates the parts of the brain that prepare the face muscles for smiling. It appears that we automatically copy the emotions of those around us, and this helps groups of people to feel connected.

Of course, humour does also play a part, and psychologists have long tried to explain what makes something funny. One theory suggests that we laugh to feel superior, as when we see someone slip on a banana skin. Another says that laughter releases tension, as with jokes about embarrassing subjects. The most widely accepted view, however, is the incongruity theory: we laugh when something surprising breaks our expectations, but proves harmless.

Not all laughter is friendly. People can laugh to mock, to exclude or to hide embarrassment, and researchers distinguish between genuine laughter, which is involuntary, and polite or forced laughter, which is controlled. Studies suggest that listeners can often tell the difference, because genuine laughs are higher in pitch, less regular and more difficult to fake. A group laughing at one of its members may strengthen the group, but at that person's cost.

The most useful lesson from the research may be that laughter is a social skill, not simply a reaction. It signals friendship, relieves tension and invites others to join in. Some doctors have even tried laughter therapy in hospitals and care homes, although the evidence that it improves health directly is limited. What seems clear is that a life with plenty of shared laughter is one in which people feel more connected to each other.

ps.e: Laughter is also contagious.
ps.b: হাসি সংক্রামকও।

ps.e: Hearing others laugh can make us laugh, even when we do not know what is funny, which is why recorded laughter is used in television comedies.
ps.b: অন্যদের হাসতে শুনলে আমরাও হাসতে পারি, এমনকি কী মজার তা না জানলেও, এ কারণেই টেলিভিশনের কমেডিতে রেকর্ড করা হাসি ব্যবহৃত হয়।

ps.e: Brain scans show that the sound of laughter activates the parts of the brain that prepare the face muscles for smiling.
ps.b: মস্তিষ্ক স্ক্যানে দেখা যায় হাসির শব্দ মস্তিষ্কের সেই অংশগুলোকে সক্রিয় করে যা মুখের পেশিকে হাসির জন্য প্রস্তুত করে।

ps.e: It appears that we automatically copy the emotions of those around us, and this helps groups of people to feel connected.
ps.b: মনে হয় আমরা স্বয়ংক্রিয়ভাবে চারপাশের মানুষের আবেগ অনুকরণ করি, এবং এটি মানুষের দলকে সংযুক্ত বোধ করতে সাহায্য করে।

ps.e: Of course, humour does also play a part, and psychologists have long tried to explain what makes something funny.
ps.b: অবশ্যই কৌতুকও ভূমিকা রাখে, এবং মনোবিজ্ঞানীরা দীর্ঘদিন ধরে ব্যাখ্যা করতে চেয়েছেন কী কিছুকে মজার করে।

ps.e: One theory suggests that we laugh to feel superior, as when we see someone slip on a banana skin.
ps.b: একটি তত্ত্ব বলে আমরা শ্রেষ্ঠ বোধ করতে হাসি, যেমন কাউকে কলার খোসায় পিছলে পড়তে দেখলে।

ps.e: Another says that laughter releases tension, as with jokes about embarrassing subjects.
ps.b: আরেকটি বলে হাসি উত্তেজনা মুক্ত করে, যেমন বিব্রতকর বিষয় নিয়ে কৌতুকে।

ps.e: The most widely accepted view, however, is the incongruity theory: we laugh when something surprising breaks our expectations, but proves harmless.
ps.b: তবে সবচেয়ে ব্যাপকভাবে গৃহীত মত হলো অসংগতি তত্ত্ব: আমরা হাসি যখন বিস্ময়কর কিছু আমাদের প্রত্যাশা ভেঙে দেয় কিন্তু নিরীহ প্রমাণিত হয়।

ps.e: Not all laughter is friendly.
ps.b: সব হাসি বন্ধুত্বপূর্ণ নয়।

ps.e: People can laugh to mock, to exclude or to hide embarrassment, and researchers distinguish between genuine laughter, which is involuntary, and polite or forced laughter, which is controlled.
ps.b: মানুষ উপহাস করতে, বাদ দিতে বা বিব্রতবোধ লুকাতে হাসতে পারে, এবং গবেষকরা আসল হাসি, যা অনিচ্ছাকৃত, ও ভদ্রতার বা জোর করা হাসি, যা নিয়ন্ত্রিত, তার মধ্যে পার্থক্য করেন।

ps.e: Studies suggest that listeners can often tell the difference, because genuine laughs are higher in pitch, less regular and more difficult to fake.
ps.b: গবেষণা ইঙ্গিত দেয় শ্রোতারা প্রায়ই তফাত বুঝতে পারে, কারণ আসল হাসি সুরে উঁচু, কম নিয়মিত এবং নকল করা কঠিন।

ps.e: A group laughing at one of its members may strengthen the group, but at that person's cost.
ps.b: একটি দল তার একজন সদস্যকে নিয়ে হাসলে দলটি শক্তিশালী হতে পারে, কিন্তু সেই ব্যক্তির মূল্যে।

ps.e: The most useful lesson from the research may be that laughter is a social skill, not simply a reaction.
ps.b: গবেষণার সবচেয়ে কাজের শিক্ষা সম্ভবত এই যে হাসি কেবল প্রতিক্রিয়া নয়, একটি সামাজিক দক্ষতা।

ps.e: It signals friendship, relieves tension and invites others to join in.
ps.b: এটি বন্ধুত্বের ইঙ্গিত দেয়, উত্তেজনা কমায় এবং অন্যদের যোগ দিতে আমন্ত্রণ জানায়।

ps.e: Some doctors have even tried laughter therapy in hospitals and care homes, although the evidence that it improves health directly is limited.
ps.b: কিছু ডাক্তার এমনকি হাসপাতাল ও যত্নকেন্দ্রে হাসির থেরাপি চেষ্টা করেছেন, যদিও এটি সরাসরি স্বাস্থ্য ভালো করে এমন প্রমাণ সীমিত।

ps.e: What seems clear is that a life with plenty of shared laughter is one in which people feel more connected to each other.
ps.b: যা স্পষ্ট মনে হয় তা হলো প্রচুর ভাগ করা হাসিভরা জীবন এমন একটি জীবন যেখানে মানুষ একে অপরের সঙ্গে বেশি সংযুক্ত বোধ করে।

cmp/101.title: Reading the Clock in Carbon
cmp/101.src: Libby (Nobel lecture, 1960); Reimer et al., IntCal20 (2020); Spalding et al. (2005); Suess (1960s) and bristlecone pine studies
p: In the late 1940s the chemist Willard Libby proposed that every living thing carries within it a clock, one that begins to run at the moment of death. The idea rested on a modest observation about the upper atmosphere, where cosmic rays strike nitrogen and release neutrons, which in turn convert a small fraction of nitrogen atoms into a radioactive isotope of carbon known as carbon-14. This isotope combines with oxygen, disperses through the air as carbon dioxide and is absorbed by plants during photosynthesis, and from plants it passes to the animals that eat them. For as long as an organism lives, it continually exchanges carbon with its surroundings, so the proportion of carbon-14 in its tissues remains close to that of the atmosphere.

Death interrupts this exchange. Thereafter, no fresh carbon-14 enters the tissue, while the atoms already present decay at a steady and predictable rate, so that roughly half have disappeared after 5,730 years. By measuring what fraction remains in a fragment of wood, bone or charcoal, Libby reasoned, one could calculate how long ago the organism had died. The method earned him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960, and archaeologists welcomed it as a means of escaping the dependence on written records and stylistic guesswork that had long constrained their discipline. For the first time, a hearth in a cave on one continent could be compared directly, in time, with a burial mound on another.

Yet Libby's scheme rested on an assumption that he himself acknowledged to be provisional: that the concentration of carbon-14 in the atmosphere had remained constant through the millennia. Early tests on objects of known age, such as timbers from Egyptian tombs, seemed to bear this out, and the discrepancies that appeared were commonly attributed to experimental error. It was only when researchers compared radiocarbon measurements with an independent chronology, the annual growth rings of trees, that the difficulty became undeniable. Bristlecone pines in the White Mountains of California, some of which are several thousand years old, allowed scientists to count rings back through time and then to analyse the carbon in each one. The results showed that radiocarbon ages systematically underestimated true ages, in the case of material around ten thousand years old by well over a thousand years.

The explanation lay in the fact that the production of carbon-14 is anything but steady. It rises and falls with the intensity of cosmic radiation reaching the Earth, which is modulated by the strength of the planet's magnetic field and by fluctuations in solar activity; it is further complicated by the movement of carbon between the atmosphere, the oceans and living matter, a process that can sequester carbon for centuries before releasing it again. A raw radiocarbon measurement, therefore, does not yield a calendar date at all, but rather a figure expressed in "radiocarbon years", which must be translated into calendar years by reference to a calibration curve.

Constructing such curves has become a collaborative undertaking of remarkable ambition. Tree rings provide the most reliable record for the last several millennia, but beyond them researchers have turned to corals, to mineral deposits in caves and to the layered sediments of lakes, notably Lake Suigetsu in Japan, whose annual layers preserve fragments of leaves that can be dated both by counting and by measurement. Successive versions of the international calibration curve, which now extends back some fifty-five thousand years, incorporate these records, and each revision narrows the uncertainty or, occasionally, shifts a published date by several decades. Because of the curve's irregular shape, a single measurement may correspond to more than one range of calendar years, and results are therefore reported as probabilities rather than as single dates.

Technical advances have been equally consequential. For three decades, laboratories counted the faint radioactive emissions of each sample, a method that demanded relatively large quantities of material and long counting times. From the late 1970s, accelerator mass spectrometry made it possible to count the carbon-14 atoms themselves, so that a sample weighing a few milligrams, such as a single seed or a scrap of parchment, could be dated. The gain in sensitivity was not without cost, however, since the older a sample is, the less carbon-14 survives in it: after fifty thousand years only about 0.2 percent of the original quantity remains, and even a trace of modern contamination, from handling, glue or microscopic roots, can make a very ancient specimen appear thousands of years younger than it is.

Human activity has introduced further distortions, some of them troublesome and others unexpectedly useful. The burning of fossil fuels, which contain no carbon-14, has diluted the proportion of the isotope in the atmosphere, so that objects from the industrial era can seem older than they are. Conversely, the atmospheric testing of nuclear weapons in the 1950s and early 1960s almost doubled the concentration of carbon-14 in the northern hemisphere, until a treaty signed in 1963 largely ended such tests and allowed the level to decline again. This "bomb pulse" has been exploited by forensic scientists, who can estimate the year of birth of a person from the carbon in tooth enamel, which forms in childhood, and it has even been applied to check the claimed vintage of wines.

Radiocarbon dating thus illustrates how a scientific technique matures, not by being proved right once and for all, but by being tested repeatedly against independent evidence. Libby's original assumption was mistaken in detail yet fertile in consequence: the very discrepancies that seemed to threaten the method became the means by which it was refined, and the curve built to correct it has since become a record of the planet's changing magnetic and solar history in its own right. Contemporary researchers regard a radiocarbon date not as a verdict but as a statement of probability, whose reliability depends as much on the care with which a sample was chosen and cleaned as on the sophistication of the instruments. The technique remains indispensable, but it is most valuable in the hands of those who understand its limits.

q.q: Which statement best summarises the passage as a whole?
q.e: The passage follows the method from Libby's idea, through its flaw, to its correction and present use.
o: A. Radiocarbon dating rested on a flawed early assumption, but testing against independent evidence turned it into a refined method whose results are expressed as probabilities.
B. Libby's original method proved so accurate that later corrections changed almost nothing about the dates it gave.
C. Tree rings have shown that radiocarbon dating cannot be trusted for any sample older than ten thousand years.
D. Nuclear weapons tests made radiocarbon dating useless for every sample from the twentieth century onwards.

q.q: According to paragraph 1, why does the proportion of carbon-14 in a living organism stay close to that of the atmosphere?
q.e: Paragraph 1: the organism keeps exchanging carbon, so the proportion stays close to the atmosphere's.
o: A. Because the organism continually exchanges carbon with its surroundings.
B. Because plants and animals produce carbon-14 inside their own cells.
C. Because cosmic rays strike living tissue directly and replace the carbon.
D. Because carbon-14 does not decay at all while an organism is alive.

q.q: What does paragraph 2 suggest about the effect of radiocarbon dating on archaeology?
q.e: The last sentence of paragraph 2 compares a cave hearth on one continent with a burial mound on another.
o: A. It was rejected by most archaeologists until the Nobel Prize was awarded.
B. It allowed sites far apart to be placed on a common timescale without relying on written records or stylistic judgement.
C. It showed that written records from the ancient world had been unreliable for centuries.
D. It made the comparison of artistic styles the most trusted way of dating objects.

q.q: In paragraph 3, the discrepancies "were commonly attributed to experimental error". What does this mean?
q.e: 'Attributed to' means 'explained as being caused by'.
o: A. The experiments were deliberately carried out in the wrong way.
B. Libby blamed other scientists for the mistakes in his own work.
C. The differences showed that the tests had never been repeated.
D. Most people assumed that the differences were caused by mistakes in measurement.

q.q: According to paragraph 4, why can a raw radiocarbon measurement not be read directly as a calendar date?
q.e: Paragraph 4 says production 'rises and falls' with cosmic radiation, magnetism and solar activity.
o: A. Because calendar years were counted differently in different centuries.
B. Because the oceans absorb all of the carbon-14 that reaches the atmosphere.
C. Because the rate at which carbon-14 is produced has varied over time.
D. Because carbon-14 decays at a rate that changes with the temperature of the soil.

q.q: In paragraph 6, the word "consequential" is closest in meaning to
q.e: 'Equally consequential' means the advances had results as important as the earlier ones.
o: A. important in its results.
B. limited in its use.
C. expensive to apply.
D. unexpected by scientists.

q.q: Why might a very old sample appear younger than it really is?
q.e: Paragraph 6: after fifty thousand years only about 0.2 percent remains, so even a trace of contamination matters.
o: A. A tiny amount of modern carbon can outweigh the very small quantity of original carbon-14 left.
B. Accelerator mass spectrometry shortens the apparent age of every large sample.
C. Old samples gradually take in more carbon-14 from the soil as the centuries pass.
D. Fossil fuels add carbon-14 to the sample while it is being studied.

q.q: What is the writer's view of Libby's original assumption in the final paragraph?
q.e: The writer calls it 'mistaken in detail yet fertile in consequence'.
o: A. It was entirely correct and has never needed any change.
B. It is now of interest only to historians of science.
C. It was mistaken in detail, but it led to useful improvements in the method.
D. It was careless, and the method should have been abandoned.

q.q: Libby estimated the time of death by measuring how much carbon-14 remained in a sample.
Radiocarbon ages of the bristlecone pine rings were found to be too old.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says radiocarbon ages systematically underestimated true ages, so they were too young.

q.q: Accelerator mass spectrometry is cheaper to run than counting radioactive emissions.
The burning of fossil fuels has made modern objects look younger than they really are.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says they can seem older.

q.q: The results of radiocarbon dating are reported as ____ rather than as single dates.
Accelerator mass spectrometry made it possible to date a sample weighing only a few ____.
The "bomb pulse" was caused by the atmospheric testing of ____ in the 1950s and early 1960s.

ps.e: In the late 1940s the chemist Willard Libby proposed that every living thing carries within it a clock, one that begins to run at the moment of death.
ps.b: ১৯৪০-এর দশকের শেষ দিকে রসায়নবিদ উইলার্ড লিবি প্রস্তাব করেন যে প্রতিটি জীবিত প্রাণীর ভেতরে একটি ঘড়ি আছে, যা মৃত্যুর মুহূর্ত থেকে চলতে শুরু করে।

ps.e: The idea rested on a modest observation about the upper atmosphere, where cosmic rays strike nitrogen and release neutrons, which in turn convert a small fraction of nitrogen atoms into a radioactive isotope of carbon known as carbon-14.
ps.b: ধারণাটির ভিত্তি ছিল ঊর্ধ্ব বায়ুমণ্ডল নিয়ে একটি সামান্য পর্যবেক্ষণ: সেখানে মহাজাগতিক রশ্মি নাইট্রোজেনকে আঘাত করে নিউট্রন মুক্ত করে, আর সেই নিউট্রন নাইট্রোজেনের অল্প কিছু পরমাণুকে কার্বন-১৪ নামে কার্বনের একটি তেজস্ক্রিয় আইসোটোপে পরিণত করে।

ps.e: This isotope combines with oxygen, disperses through the air as carbon dioxide and is absorbed by plants during photosynthesis, and from plants it passes to the animals that eat them.
ps.b: এই আইসোটোপ অক্সিজেনের সঙ্গে মিশে কার্বন ডাই-অক্সাইড হিসেবে বাতাসে ছড়িয়ে পড়ে এবং সালোকসংশ্লেষণের সময় উদ্ভিদ তা শোষণ করে, আর উদ্ভিদ থেকে তা যায় সেই প্রাণীদের দেহে যারা উদ্ভিদ খায়।

ps.e: For as long as an organism lives, it continually exchanges carbon with its surroundings, so the proportion of carbon-14 in its tissues remains close to that of the atmosphere.
ps.b: একটি জীব যতক্ষণ বেঁচে থাকে, ততক্ষণ সে তার পরিবেশের সঙ্গে ক্রমাগত কার্বন বিনিময় করে, তাই তার দেহকলায় কার্বন-১৪-এর অনুপাত বায়ুমণ্ডলের অনুপাতের কাছাকাছি থাকে।

ps.e: Death interrupts this exchange.
ps.b: মৃত্যু এই বিনিময় থামিয়ে দেয়।

ps.e: Thereafter, no fresh carbon-14 enters the tissue, while the atoms already present decay at a steady and predictable rate, so that roughly half have disappeared after 5,730 years.
ps.b: এরপর কলায় আর নতুন কার্বন-১৪ ঢোকে না, অথচ যে পরমাণুগুলো আগে থেকেই আছে সেগুলো এক স্থির ও অনুমানযোগ্য হারে ক্ষয় হতে থাকে, ফলে প্রায় ৫,৭৩০ বছরে অর্ধেক পরমাণু শেষ হয়ে যায়।

ps.e: By measuring what fraction remains in a fragment of wood, bone or charcoal, Libby reasoned, one could calculate how long ago the organism had died.
ps.b: লিবির যুক্তি ছিল, কাঠ, হাড় বা কাঠকয়লার একটি টুকরোয় কার্বন-১৪-এর কতটুকু অংশ বাকি আছে তা মেপে হিসাব করা যায় জীবটি কত আগে মারা গেছে।

ps.e: The method earned him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960, and archaeologists welcomed it as a means of escaping the dependence on written records and stylistic guesswork that had long constrained their discipline.
ps.b: এই পদ্ধতির জন্য তিনি ১৯৬০ সালে রসায়নে নোবেল পুরস্কার পান, আর প্রত্নতাত্ত্বিকেরা একে স্বাগত জানান, কারণ এতে লিখিত নথি আর শৈলীগত অনুমানের ওপর নির্ভরতা কাটানো গেল, যা তাঁদের বিষয়টিকে দীর্ঘদিন সীমাবদ্ধ করে রেখেছিল।

ps.e: For the first time, a hearth in a cave on one continent could be compared directly, in time, with a burial mound on another.
ps.b: প্রথমবারের মতো এক মহাদেশের একটি গুহার চুলার সঙ্গে অন্য মহাদেশের একটি সমাধিস্তূপের সময়ের সরাসরি তুলনা করা সম্ভব হলো।

ps.e: Yet Libby's scheme rested on an assumption that he himself acknowledged to be provisional: that the concentration of carbon-14 in the atmosphere had remained constant through the millennia.
ps.b: তবে লিবির পরিকল্পনা এমন এক ধারণার ওপর দাঁড়িয়ে ছিল যাকে তিনি নিজেই সাময়িক বলে স্বীকার করেছিলেন: হাজার হাজার বছর ধরে বায়ুমণ্ডলে কার্বন-১৪-এর ঘনত্ব অপরিবর্তিত ছিল।

ps.e: Early tests on objects of known age, such as timbers from Egyptian tombs, seemed to bear this out, and the discrepancies that appeared were commonly attributed to experimental error.
ps.b: মিসরীয় সমাধির কাঠের কড়িকাঠের মতো জানা বয়সের বস্তুর ওপর প্রথম দিকের পরীক্ষাগুলো এটিকে সমর্থন করছে বলেই মনে হয়েছিল, আর যে গরমিলগুলো দেখা দিয়েছিল সেগুলোকে সাধারণত পরীক্ষার ভুল বলে ধরা হতো।

ps.e: It was only when researchers compared radiocarbon measurements with an independent chronology, the annual growth rings of trees, that the difficulty became undeniable.

cmp/102.topic: Earth Science and the History of Science
cmp/102.title: The Drifting Continents: Why a Correct Idea Waited Fifty Years
cmp/102.src: Wegener (1915); Hess (1962); Vine and Matthews (1963); Tharp and Heezen; Oreskes, The Rejection of Continental Drift
p: When the German meteorologist Alfred Wegener argued in 1912 that the continents had once formed a single landmass and had since drifted apart, he was not the first to notice that the coastlines of South America and Africa seem to fit together like pieces of a puzzle. What distinguished his proposal was the range of evidence he assembled to support it, drawn from geology, palaeontology and climatology, and the confidence with which he claimed that the similarity could not be a coincidence. His book on the subject, first published in German in 1915 and revised several times, set out the case in detail, yet for nearly half a century it was regarded by most geologists as an ingenious but untenable fantasy.

Wegener's evidence was substantial. Fossils of the same freshwater reptile, Mesosaurus, had been found in South America and southern Africa, two regions now separated by thousands of kilometres of salt water, and the remains of a distinctive fern-like plant, Glossopteris, turned up on continents scattered across the southern hemisphere. Rock formations and mountain belts appeared to continue from one side of the Atlantic to the other, as if a single chain had been cut in two. Even more striking were the traces of an ancient ice age, found in regions such as India and Australia that are now warm, and the coal deposits of the polar regions, which implied a luxuriant vegetation where there is now only ice.

His critics did not deny these observations; they questioned the explanation. Many geologists preferred to account for the fossils by supposing that narrow land bridges had once connected the continents before sinking beneath the sea, a hypothesis that required no movement of the continents themselves. More fundamentally, Wegener could not say what force might move continents. He suggested that they ploughed through the oceanic crust, propelled by the Earth's rotation and by tidal forces, but physicists calculated that such forces were far too feeble to shift masses of rock of that size, and that the solid crust of the ocean floor would not yield to them in any case. A theory that described what had happened without a credible account of how it could have happened seemed, to the scientific establishment, to be incomplete in the most damaging way.

It would be a mistake to attribute this rejection simply to conservatism. The standards that Wegener's contemporaries applied were, in important respects, reasonable ones: an extraordinary claim ought to be accompanied by a plausible mechanism, and the mechanism he offered was demonstrably inadequate. His position as an outsider, trained in meteorology rather than geology, may have encouraged some specialists to dismiss him, but the objections of Harold Jeffreys and others rested on genuine physical reasoning. A few researchers, notably the British geologist Arthur Holmes, suggested that slow currents of heat within the Earth's mantle might carry the continents along, yet this idea remained speculative, and Wegener himself died in 1930 during an expedition to Greenland, long before the argument was resolved.

The resolution came from an unexpected direction, as the technology developed for the Second World War was turned to the exploration of the sea floor. Echo-sounding surveys revealed a continuous mountain range running beneath the middle of the Atlantic, with a rift valley along its crest, a feature that Marie Tharp and Bruce Heezen mapped with painstaking care during the 1950s. Meanwhile, studies of the magnetism preserved in ancient rocks suggested that the continents had moved relative to the magnetic poles, a conclusion that was difficult to explain unless the land itself had shifted.

In 1962 the American geologist Harry Hess proposed that new oceanic crust is created at the mid-ocean ridges, where molten rock rises and solidifies, and that the sea floor then spreads outwards on either side, eventually sinking back into the mantle at deep ocean trenches. The hypothesis made a testable prediction. Because the Earth's magnetic field has reversed its direction many times, the rock forming at a ridge should record the field of its time, producing parallel stripes of alternating polarity that mirror one another on either side. When such stripes were identified in 1963, and when deep-sea drilling later showed that the sediments and rocks of the ocean floor grow steadily older with distance from the ridges, none of them older than about two hundred million years, the case for spreading became very difficult to resist.

Within a few years the scattered findings had been combined into the theory of plate tectonics, according to which the Earth's outer shell is divided into rigid plates that move, at a few centimetres a year, over a softer layer beneath. Crucially, the continents are not ploughing through the ocean floor, as Wegener had imagined, but are carried passively on the plates, like cargo on a conveyor belt. The mechanism that had been missing was therefore not a modified version of his own, but a different one altogether, and it explained, in addition, the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes that his theory had never addressed.

The history of continental drift is sometimes told as a parable of the stubbornness of authority, but a more careful reading suggests a subtler lesson. Wegener was right about the central fact and wrong about the cause, and the scientific community was right to demand an explanation while being slow to recognise how much of his evidence would eventually survive. The episode shows that the acceptance of a new idea depends not only on the quality of the evidence but also on the availability of the means to test it, and that a hypothesis may deserve serious attention long before it can be proved.

q.q: What is the main point of the passage?
q.e: The passage balances the strength of the evidence against the weakness of the mechanism.
o: A. Wegener's idea was accepted only when new evidence supplied the mechanism it lacked, and its earlier rejection had reasonable grounds.
B. Wegener's own explanation of how continents move was later confirmed by studies of the ocean floor.
C. Continental drift was proved correct as soon as the magnetism of ancient rocks was measured.

ps.b: কয়েক বছরের মধ্যে ছড়ানো-ছিটানো আবিষ্কারগুলো মিলিয়ে প্লেট টেকটনিক্স তত্ত্ব গড়ে উঠল, যা অনুসারে পৃথিবীর বাইরের খোলস কঠিন প্লেটে বিভক্ত, আর প্লেটগুলো নিচের তুলনামূলক নরম স্তরের ওপর বছরে কয়েক সেন্টিমিটার হারে সরে।

ps.e: Crucially, the continents are not ploughing through the ocean floor, as Wegener had imagined, but are carried passively on the plates, like cargo on a conveyor belt.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে গুরুত্বপূর্ণ কথা, ভেগেনারের কল্পনার মতো মহাদেশগুলো সমুদ্রতলের ভেতর দিয়ে লাঙল চালিয়ে যায় না, বরং কনভেয়র বেল্টের ওপর মালপত্রের মতো প্লেটের ওপর নিষ্ক্রিয়ভাবে বাহিত হয়।

ps.e: The mechanism that had been missing was therefore not a modified version of his own, but a different one altogether, and it explained, in addition, the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes that his theory had never addressed.
ps.b: যে কার্যপদ্ধতিটি অনুপস্থিত ছিল তা তাই তাঁর নিজের পদ্ধতির কোনো সংশোধিত রূপ ছিল না, ছিল সম্পূর্ণ ভিন্ন একটি; আর এটি অতিরিক্ত হিসেবে ভূমিকম্প ও আগ্নেয়গিরির বণ্টনও ব্যাখ্যা করল, যা তাঁর তত্ত্ব কখনও স্পর্শ করেনি।

ps.e: The history of continental drift is sometimes told as a parable of the stubbornness of authority, but a more careful reading suggests a subtler lesson.
ps.b: মহাদেশীয় সঞ্চরণের ইতিহাস কখনও কখনও কর্তৃপক্ষের একগুঁয়েমির উপাখ্যান হিসেবে বলা হয়, কিন্তু আরও সতর্ক পাঠ একটি সূক্ষ্মতর শিক্ষার ইঙ্গিত দেয়।

ps.e: Wegener was right about the central fact and wrong about the cause, and the scientific community was right to demand an explanation while being slow to recognise how much of his evidence would eventually survive.
ps.b: ভেগেনার কেন্দ্রীয় তথ্যে সঠিক ছিলেন কিন্তু কারণে ভুল, আর বৈজ্ঞানিক সম্প্রদায় ব্যাখ্যা দাবি করে সঠিক ছিল, যদিও তাঁর প্রমাণের কতটা শেষ পর্যন্ত টিকে যাবে তা বুঝতে দেরি করেছিল।

ps.e: The episode shows that the acceptance of a new idea depends not only on the quality of the evidence but also on the availability of the means to test it, and that a hypothesis may deserve serious attention long before it can be proved.
ps.b: ঘটনাটি দেখায় যে নতুন ধারণার গ্রহণযোগ্যতা শুধু প্রমাণের মানের ওপর নয়, তা পরীক্ষা করার উপায় পাওয়ার ওপরও নির্ভর করে, আর কোনো অনুমান প্রমাণিত হওয়ার অনেক আগেই গুরুত্ব দিয়ে বিবেচনার যোগ্য হতে পারে।

cmp/103.title: The House of Butterflies: How Lead Was Taken Out of Petrol
cmp/103.src: Patterson (1965); Murozumi, Chow and Patterson (1969); Needleman and others; US EPA phase-out records; UNEP (2021)
p: In December 1921, a young engineer at the General Motors research laboratory in Dayton, Ohio, found that a small quantity of a compound called tetraethyl lead, added to petrol, eliminated the metallic knocking that plagued the high-compression engines of the day. Thomas Midgley Jr. and his employers recognised at once that the discovery would allow cars to become more powerful and more efficient. They also knew that ethanol, which worked almost as well, could not be patented, whereas a new lead compound could, and the company that developed it would therefore enjoy a profitable monopoly. Leaded petrol went on sale in 1923, and within a few years it had become the standard fuel across the United States.

The dangers were evident from the start, at least to those who worked closest to the product. In 1924, several employees at a plant in New Jersey that manufactured the additive died, and many more suffered tremors and hallucinations, so that the building acquired the grim nickname "the house of butterflies". Sales were suspended briefly in some cities, and a panel convened by the federal government in 1925 considered the question. It concluded that there was no evidence that leaded petrol was dangerous when properly handled, though it recommended further study. The industry's response was to fund the research itself, and the physician it selected, Robert Kehoe, argued for decades that the small amounts of lead absorbed from exhaust were within the body's natural tolerance.

That conclusion was challenged, almost by accident, by a geochemist with no interest in petrol at all. In the 1950s Clair Patterson, working at the California Institute of Technology, set out to determine the age of the Earth by measuring the proportions of lead isotopes in meteorites, which are believed to have formed at the same time as the planet. The project succeeded, yielding a figure of roughly 4.5 billion years that has barely changed since. Along the way, however, Patterson was troubled by an obstinate problem: his samples were repeatedly contaminated with lead, and the contamination persisted however carefully he cleaned his equipment, so that he was eventually obliged to construct one of the first laboratories in which the air itself was filtered.

The source of the contamination, he came to suspect, was not his laboratory but the world. If lead was present almost everywhere that he looked, in dust, in seawater and in the glassware he used, then the natural level of the metal in the environment might be far lower than anyone had assumed, and the quantities that people absorbed might be hundreds of times greater than those of their ancestors. To test the idea, he compared lead in the deep ocean with that near the surface, and later analysed layers of ancient ice from Greenland, whose lead content rose steeply only after the introduction of leaded petrol. The pattern was difficult to explain in any other way.

Patterson's findings, published during the 1960s, met determined opposition. Companies that profited from lead questioned his data, and he reportedly found that some of his sources of funding became less secure. Yet the scientific case gradually strengthened, as studies of children in industrial cities associated even modest exposure with reduced attention and lower scores on intelligence tests. Lead is now known to damage the developing nervous system, and there is no level of exposure that researchers regard as entirely harmless. These findings, together with growing concern about the pollution of cities, led the United States to begin phasing out leaded petrol in the 1970s, and its use in road vehicles ended there in 1996.

The effects of the policy were measurable. Between the late 1970s and the early 1990s, the average concentration of lead in the blood of American children fell by roughly four-fifths, a decline closely matched by the decline in the amount of lead sold in fuel. Some researchers have gone further, proposing that the fall in childhood exposure helped to reduce violent crime a generation later, though this claim remains contested, since crime rates were influenced by many other changes and the statistical evidence is open to different interpretations. What is not in dispute is the scale of the original exposure, which affected, on some estimates, the greater part of the population of the industrial world.

The story has a further irony. Midgley, who in his lifetime was celebrated as a brilliant inventor, was also responsible for developing the first chlorofluorocarbons, the refrigerants that were later found to be destroying the ozone layer. Two of the most damaging industrial chemicals of the twentieth century thus came from the same laboratory bench, and both were introduced as solutions to genuine technical problems. Each was adopted widely before its effects on health or the environment had been properly examined, and each was defended, for years, by people with a financial interest in the product.

Leaded petrol disappeared gradually across the world, and the United Nations announced in 2021 that its use in cars had finally ended, nearly a century after it was first sold. The history is often cited as a warning about the difficulty of judging the safety of a technology that is already profitable and widely used. It also shows how a discovery can emerge from work that appears quite unrelated, since the evidence that did most to expose the hazard came not from medicine but from a scientist who wished only to measure the age of the planet.

cmp/104.title: Was Farming a Mistake? Rethinking the Neolithic Revolution
cmp/104.src: Childe (1936); Diamond (1987); Cohen and Armelagos (1984); Fuller and others on domestication; Göbekli Tepe excavation reports
p: For most of the twentieth century, the origin of farming was told as a story of progress. Some ten thousand years ago, according to the familiar account, human beings who had lived by hunting animals and gathering wild plants discovered that seeds could be sown and animals herded, and they abandoned a precarious existence for the security of the field and the village. The archaeologist V. Gordon Childe, who coined the phrase "Neolithic revolution" in the 1930s, regarded the change as the foundation of civilisation, since a reliable food surplus made possible towns, specialised crafts, writing and government. The narrative was appealing, but as evidence accumulated it began to look increasingly doubtful.

One difficulty is that farming did not arise once, in a single place, as an invention that then spread. It emerged independently in at least half a dozen regions: wheat, barley and lentils in the Fertile Crescent of south-west Asia; rice and millet in China; maize in Mexico; potatoes in the Andes; and other crops in New Guinea, in sub-Saharan Africa and in eastern North America. If agriculture were plainly superior to foraging, it is hard to see why it should have appeared so late in the long history of the species, or why so many peoples seem to have adopted it only after the passage of thousands of years in which the necessary plants were available to them.

A second difficulty concerns the pace of change. Careful study of the remains of cereals has shown that the characteristics that distinguish domesticated plants, such as seed heads that do not shatter when ripe and so can be harvested, evolved slowly, probably over a millennium or more. People were therefore cultivating wild plants, and perhaps managing the land around them, long before the crops were genetically transformed. Domestication, on this view, was not a revolution but a prolonged and uneven process in which foraging and farming overlapped, and in which societies could move in either direction.

Why people began to cultivate at all remains disputed. One influential explanation points to climate. At the end of the last ice age, a sudden return of cold and dry conditions, which lasted for more than a thousand years, may have reduced the availability of wild food in the Near East and encouraged communities to cultivate the stands of cereal on which they depended. Other scholars stress population pressure, arguing that groups that had grown more settled and more numerous were forced to extract more food from a limited territory. A third line of argument is social rather than ecological. The remarkable stone enclosures at Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, built by people who apparently did not farm, suggest that large gatherings and shared rituals may have preceded agriculture, and that the need to feed those who assembled could have encouraged the intensive use of grain.

What is clearer is that the first farmers did not necessarily live better than the foragers they replaced. Skeletons from many early agricultural communities show a decline in stature, an increase in dental decay and signs of anaemia and infection, and the contrast with the bones of earlier hunter-gatherers has led some researchers to describe the adoption of farming as a trap. A diet dominated by a few starchy crops is nutritionally narrow; dense settlements are favourable to infectious disease, particularly when people live beside their livestock; and a failed harvest could not be offset by moving elsewhere. The geographer Jared Diamond went so far as to call agriculture "the worst mistake in the history of the human race", a deliberately provocative phrase that nevertheless captured a real puzzle.

The puzzle has a plausible solution, which is that what was bad for individuals could be good for populations. Farming communities were able to feed more people from a given area, and because they were sedentary, women could bear children at shorter intervals than was possible for mobile foragers who had to carry their young. Even if farmers were smaller and less healthy, their numbers grew faster, and they gradually displaced or absorbed their neighbours, much as a modest but steadily growing business may eventually overtake a more prosperous but static one. On this reasoning, farming spread not because it improved the lives of those who adopted it, but because it enabled those who practised it to outnumber others.

The picture that emerges is therefore less flattering to human foresight than the old story, but it is arguably more interesting. Agriculture appears to have developed through many small adjustments, none of which was intended to change the course of history, and its long-term consequences, including cities, states and inequality, followed from decisions that must have seemed sensible at the time. That a transformation of such magnitude can result from a succession of local choices, rather than a single act of vision, is one of the more sobering lessons that prehistory offers.

q.q: Which statement best expresses the main argument of the passage?
q.e: The passage questions the old story and ends with the population explanation.
o: A. Early farmers lived longer and healthier lives than foragers, which is why farming eventually spread.
B. Farming probably spread through a gradual, uneven process in which its ability to support larger populations mattered more than any benefit to individual health.
C. Farming was invented once, in south-west Asia, and was quickly adopted because it was clearly superior to foraging.
D. Climate change at the end of the last ice age is now accepted as the sole cause of farming.

o: A. Farming ended the need for any form of government or law.
B. Farming allowed hunters to travel more widely and trade with distant peoples.
C. Farming made people healthier and so able to live to a great age.
D. A reliable food surplus made towns, specialised crafts, writing and government possible.

q.q: What difficulty for the traditional story is raised in paragraph 2?
q.e: The paragraph points to independent origins and the long delay.
o: A. Farming appears to have been invented by only one people, who then travelled the world.
B. The crops listed could not have been grown without modern tools.
C. There is no evidence that wheat and barley were ever grown in the Fertile Crescent.
D. If farming was plainly better, it is hard to see why it appeared so late and in so many separate places.

q.q: What does "societies could move in either direction" mean in paragraph 3?
q.e: The sentence describes the overlap between foraging and farming.
o: A. Societies could choose between planting seeds and herding animals.
B. A society might add farming to its way of life, or might return to foraging.
C. Societies could travel in two different directions across the land.
D. Societies could grow in size or become smaller as the climate changed.

q.q: What does the evidence from Göbekli Tepe suggest, according to paragraph 4?
o: A. Large gatherings and shared rituals may have come before agriculture.
B. Climate change forced the builders to abandon the site.
C. Farming began in Turkey before it began anywhere else.
D. The builders of the enclosures lived mainly on cultivated grain.

q.q: In paragraph 5, the word "provocative" is closest in meaning to
o: A. difficult for most readers to understand.
B. borrowed from earlier writers.
C. based on very recent evidence.
D. intended to cause a strong reaction.

q.q: According to paragraph 6, why did farming communities outnumber foragers?
q.e: Paragraph 6 explains the advantage in numbers.
o: A. Foragers abandoned their way of life because it was too dangerous.
B. Foragers were less healthy and died younger than farmers did.
C. Settled life let women bear children more often, and farms could feed more people from the same land.
D. Farmers fought and defeated the foragers in organised wars.

q.q: How does the writer regard the new account of the origins of farming?
q.e: Paragraph 7 begins by contrasting the two.
o: A. As a complete explanation that leaves no questions unanswered.
B. As less reliable than the old story, because it relies on skeletons.
C. As less flattering to human foresight than the old story, but more interesting.
D. As proof that early people made no real decisions.

q.q: Farming arose independently in more than one region of the world.
q.e: Paragraph 2 lists at least half a dozen regions.

q.q: The features that mark domesticated cereals evolved within a single generation.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says the change took 'a millennium or more'.

q.q: Göbekli Tepe was abandoned because of a change in the climate.
q.e: The passage does not say why the site was abandoned.

q.q: Skeletons of early farmers show that they were taller than the foragers who came before them.
q.e: Paragraph 5 mentions a decline in stature.

A diet dominated by a few ____ crops is nutritionally narrow.
