cmp/105.title: Reading the Library of Ice
cmp/105.src: Petit and others (1999); EPICA Community Members (2004); Lüthi and others (2008); Dansgaard and others; Yan and others (2019)
p: Every winter, snow falls on the interior of Antarctica and Greenland, and because the temperatures there are so low that little of it ever melts, each year's layer is buried beneath the next. Under the weight of the layers above, the snow is gradually compressed into ice, and in the process small pockets of air are sealed inside it. These bubbles are, in effect, samples of the atmosphere as it was when the snow fell, and since the ice sheets have been accumulating for hundreds of thousands of years, a column drilled through them provides a record of the past that no other source can match. Glaciologists who recover and analyse such cores have been described as reading a library in which each shelf holds a different year.

Dating the record is the first challenge. In the uppermost sections, where the snow falls heavily and the annual layers are thick, the layers can be counted much as the rings of a tree are, aided by seasonal variations in the chemistry of the ice and by spikes of sulphate left by known volcanic eruptions. Deeper down, however, the layers become thinner as the ice is squeezed and begins to flow, so that scientists must rely on computer models of the way the ice has thinned, checked against the volcanic layers and against the timing of changes that are known from other records. The resulting chronologies are not exact, and their uncertainty grows with depth.

The ice itself preserves information about temperature. Water molecules contain two forms of oxygen, one slightly heavier than the other, and the proportion of the heavy form in snowfall depends on the temperature at which the snow formed, because heavier molecules condense more readily in cold air. By measuring this ratio along a core, researchers can reconstruct how conditions at the site varied over time. The record from Vostok station in East Antarctica, extracted in the 1990s, extended back around 420,000 years, and a later core from Dome C, drilled by a European consortium, extended the record to roughly 800,000 years, spanning eight cycles of cold glacial periods and warmer intervals between them.

Even more striking is the evidence from the trapped air. Analysis of the bubbles showed that the concentration of carbon dioxide rose and fell in step with temperature through every one of these cycles, remaining between roughly 170 and 300 parts per million until the industrial era. The present concentration, well above 400 parts per million, lies far outside that range, a comparison that has done much to persuade the public as well as scientists that the current rise is without precedent in the length of the record. The correlation does not by itself demonstrate cause, but it fits well with the physics of the greenhouse effect and with the evidence of independent climate models.

The relationship between the two records is, however, more subtle than the simple pairing suggests. In several analyses of the transitions from glacial to warmer conditions, temperature appears to begin rising some centuries before carbon dioxide does. Sceptics have sometimes cited this lag as evidence that carbon dioxide cannot drive climate. Climate scientists reply that the lag is exactly what would be expected if the initial warming was triggered by slow changes in the Earth's orbit, which altered the distribution of sunlight, and if the carbon dioxide released from the warming oceans then amplified the change. On this reading, the gas was both an effect and a cause, a feedback rather than a trigger, and the ice cores illustrate how a phenomenon may play a part in a sequence without being its first step.

There are also technical complications that careful researchers acknowledge. Air is not sealed in the ice at the surface, but only when the porous snow has been compressed to a depth of fifty to a hundred metres, so the gas in any layer is younger than the ice surrounding it, by as much as several thousand years at the coldest and driest sites. Failing to account for this difference would distort the apparent timing of the two series. Moreover, the properties of the ice itself must be considered, since gases can be altered by chemical reactions or by the slow movement of the ice, and some measurements, such as those of certain trace gases, are more reliable than others.

Despite these limitations, ice cores have become among the most influential sources in the study of climate. They show that abrupt changes of several degrees have occurred in Greenland within a few decades, a finding that undermined the assumption that the climate always changes gradually. The search continues for older ice, with fragments recovered from exposed blue ice in Antarctica dated to more than two million years, and with projects aiming to drill a continuous core reaching back beyond a million. Each extension of the record tests existing theories of how the climate system behaves, and the answers, locked in ice that fell as snow long before our species existed, may help to indicate what lies ahead.

ps.e: These bubbles are, in effect, samples of the atmosphere as it was when the snow fell, and since the ice sheets have been accumulating for hundreds of thousands of years, a column drilled through them provides a record of the past that no other source can match.

ps.e: Glaciologists who recover and analyse such cores have been described as reading a library in which each shelf holds a different year.
ps.b: যে হিমবিজ্ঞানীরা এসব কোর উদ্ধার ও বিশ্লেষণ করেন তাঁদের বলা হয়েছে এমন এক গ্রন্থাগারের পাঠক যেখানে প্রতিটি তাক আলাদা আলাদা বছর ধারণ করে।

ps.e: Dating the record is the first challenge.

ps.e: In the uppermost sections, where the snow falls heavily and the annual layers are thick, the layers can be counted much as the rings of a tree are, aided by seasonal variations in the chemistry of the ice and by spikes of sulphate left by known volcanic eruptions.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে ওপরের অংশে, যেখানে তুষারপাত ভারী এবং বার্ষিক স্তর পুরু, সেখানে গাছের বলয়ের মতোই স্তর গুনে নেওয়া যায়, বরফের রসায়নের ঋতুভিত্তিক তারতম্য এবং জানা আগ্নেয়গিরির অগ্ন্যুৎপাতে জমা হওয়া সালফেটের তীক্ষ্ণ চূড়া এতে সাহায্য করে।

ps.e: Deeper down, however, the layers become thinner as the ice is squeezed and begins to flow, so that scientists must rely on computer models of the way the ice has thinned, checked against the volcanic layers and against the timing of changes that are known from other records.
ps.b: তবে আরও গভীরে বরফ চাপে পড়ে বইতে শুরু করায় স্তরগুলো পাতলা হয়ে যায়, তাই বিজ্ঞানীদের নির্ভর করতে হয় বরফ কীভাবে পাতলা হয়েছে তার কম্পিউটার মডেলের ওপর, যা আগ্নেয়গিরির স্তর এবং অন্যান্য নথি থেকে জানা পরিবর্তনের সময়ের সঙ্গে মিলিয়ে দেখা হয়।

ps.e: The resulting chronologies are not exact, and their uncertainty grows with depth.
ps.b: ফলে পাওয়া কালপঞ্জি নিখুঁত নয়, আর গভীরতার সঙ্গে এর অনিশ্চয়তা বাড়ে।

ps.e: The ice itself preserves information about temperature.
ps.b: বরফ নিজেই তাপমাত্রা সম্পর্কে তথ্য ধরে রাখে।

ps.e: Water molecules contain two forms of oxygen, one slightly heavier than the other, and the proportion of the heavy form in snowfall depends on the temperature at which the snow formed, because heavier molecules condense more readily in cold air.
ps.b: জলের অণুতে অক্সিজেনের দুটি রূপ থাকে, একটি অন্যটির চেয়ে সামান্য ভারী, আর তুষারপাতে ভারী রূপের অনুপাত নির্ভর করে তুষার যে তাপমাত্রায় তৈরি হয়েছিল তার ওপর, কারণ ভারী অণু ঠান্ডা বাতাসে আরও সহজে ঘনীভূত হয়।

ps.e: By measuring this ratio along a core, researchers can reconstruct how conditions at the site varied over time.
ps.b: একটি কোর বরাবর এই অনুপাত মেপে গবেষকেরা স্থানটির পরিস্থিতি সময়ের সঙ্গে কীভাবে বদলেছে তা পুনর্গঠন করতে পারেন।

ps.e: The record from Vostok station in East Antarctica, extracted in the 1990s, extended back around 420,000 years, and a later core from Dome C, drilled by a European consortium, extended the record to roughly 800,000 years, spanning eight cycles of cold glacial periods and warmer intervals between them.
ps.b: পূর্ব অ্যান্টার্কটিকার ভস্টক স্টেশনের ১৯৯০-এর দশকে তোলা নথিটি প্রায় ৪,২০,০০০ বছর পর্যন্ত বিস্তৃত ছিল, আর ইউরোপীয় একটি কনসোর্টিয়ামের খোঁড়া ডোম সি-র পরের কোরটি নথিকে প্রায় ৮,০০,০০০ বছরে প্রসারিত করল, যাতে শীতল হিমযুগ ও তাদের মাঝের উষ্ণ সময়ের আটটি চক্র ধরা পড়েছে।

ps.e: Even more striking is the evidence from the trapped air.
ps.b: আরও বিস্ময়কর হলো আটকে থাকা বাতাস থেকে পাওয়া প্রমাণ।

ps.e: Analysis of the bubbles showed that the concentration of carbon dioxide rose and fell in step with temperature through every one of these cycles, remaining between roughly 170 and 300 parts per million until the industrial era.
ps.b: বুদবুদ বিশ্লেষণে দেখা গেল কার্বন ডাই-অক্সাইডের ঘনত্ব এই প্রতিটি চক্রে তাপমাত্রার সঙ্গে তাল মিলিয়ে বেড়েছে ও কমেছে, এবং শিল্পযুগ পর্যন্ত তা মোটামুটি প্রতি দশ লক্ষে ১৭০ থেকে ৩০০ অংশের মধ্যে ছিল।

ps.e: The present concentration, well above 400 parts per million, lies far outside that range, a comparison that has done much to persuade the public as well as scientists that the current rise is without precedent in the length of the record.
ps.b: বর্তমান ঘনত্ব, প্রতি দশ লক্ষে ৪০০ অংশেরও অনেক ওপরে, সেই পরিসরের বহু বাইরে; এই তুলনা বিজ্ঞানীদের পাশাপাশি জনসাধারণকেও বোঝাতে অনেক সাহায্য করেছে যে বর্তমান বৃদ্ধি নথির দৈর্ঘ্যের মধ্যে নজিরবিহীন।

ps.e: The correlation does not by itself demonstrate cause, but it fits well with the physics of the greenhouse effect and with the evidence of independent climate models.
ps.b: সম্পর্ক নিজে কারণ প্রমাণ করে না, তবে এটি গ্রিনহাউস প্রভাবের পদার্থবিজ্ঞান এবং স্বাধীন জলবায়ু মডেলের প্রমাণের সঙ্গে ভালোভাবে মেলে।

ps.e: The relationship between the two records is, however, more subtle than the simple pairing suggests.
ps.b: দুটি নথির সম্পর্ক অবশ্য সহজ জোড়া মেলানোর চেয়ে আরও সূক্ষ্ম।

ps.e: In several analyses of the transitions from glacial to warmer conditions, temperature appears to begin rising some centuries before carbon dioxide does.
ps.b: হিমযুগ থেকে উষ্ণ অবস্থায় রূপান্তরের কয়েকটি বিশ্লেষণে দেখা যায়, কার্বন ডাই-অক্সাইডের আগেই কয়েক শতাব্দী ধরে তাপমাত্রা বাড়তে শুরু করে।

ps.e: Sceptics have sometimes cited this lag as evidence that carbon dioxide cannot drive climate.
ps.b: সন্দেহবাদীরা মাঝে মাঝে এই ব্যবধানকে প্রমাণ হিসেবে তুলেছেন যে কার্বন ডাই-অক্সাইড জলবায়ু চালাতে পারে না।

ps.e: Climate scientists reply that the lag is exactly what would be expected if the initial warming was triggered by slow changes in the Earth's orbit, which altered the distribution of sunlight, and if the carbon dioxide released from the warming oceans then amplified the change.
ps.b: জলবায়ু বিজ্ঞানীরা জবাব দেন যে ঠিক এমনটাই প্রত্যাশিত, যদি প্রাথমিক উষ্ণায়ন পৃথিবীর কক্ষপথের ধীর পরিবর্তনে ঘটে থাকে, যা সূর্যালোকের বণ্টন বদলে দিয়েছিল, এবং উষ্ণ হতে থাকা সাগর থেকে নির্গত কার্বন ডাই-অক্সাইড পরে পরিবর্তনটিকে বাড়িয়ে তুলে থাকে।

ps.e: On this reading, the gas was both an effect and a cause, a feedback rather than a trigger, and the ice cores illustrate how a phenomenon may play a part in a sequence without being its first step.
ps.b: এই পাঠ অনুযায়ী, গ্যাসটি ছিল একাধারে ফল ও কারণ, একটি প্রতিক্রিয়া চক্র, সূচনা নয়, আর বরফের কোর দেখায় কীভাবে কোনো ঘটনা একটি ধারাবাহিকতার প্রথম ধাপ না হয়েও তাতে ভূমিকা রাখতে পারে।

ps.e: There are also technical complications that careful researchers acknowledge.
ps.b: এমন কিছু কারিগরি জটিলতাও আছে যা সতর্ক গবেষকেরা স্বীকার করেন।

ps.e: Air is not sealed in the ice at the surface, but only when the porous snow has been compressed to a depth of fifty to a hundred metres, so the gas in any layer is younger than the ice surrounding it, by as much as several thousand years at the coldest and driest sites.
ps.b: বাতাস পৃষ্ঠে বরফে সিল হয় না, সিল হয় শুধু তখনই যখন ছিদ্রযুক্ত তুষার পঞ্চাশ থেকে একশো মিটার গভীরতায় সংকুচিত হয়, তাই যেকোনো স্তরের গ্যাস তার চারপাশের বরফের চেয়ে নবীন, সবচেয়ে ঠান্ডা ও শুষ্ক স্থানে কয়েক হাজার বছর পর্যন্ত।

ps.e: Failing to account for this difference would distort the apparent timing of the two series.
ps.b: এই পার্থক্য হিসাবে না ধরলে দুটি ধারার আপাত সময়ের সম্পর্ক বিকৃত হয়ে যেত।

ps.e: Moreover, the properties of the ice itself must be considered, since gases can be altered by chemical reactions or by the slow movement of the ice, and some measurements, such as those of certain trace gases, are more reliable than others.
ps.b: তা ছাড়া বরফের নিজের ধর্ম বিবেচনা করতে হয়, কারণ রাসায়নিক বিক্রিয়া বা বরফের ধীর নড়াচড়ায় গ্যাস বদলে যেতে পারে, এবং কিছু পরিমাপ, যেমন কিছু ক্ষুদ্র মাত্রার গ্যাসের, অন্যগুলোর চেয়ে বেশি নির্ভরযোগ্য।

ps.e: Despite these limitations, ice cores have become among the most influential sources in the study of climate.
ps.b: এসব সীমাবদ্ধতা সত্ত্বেও বরফের কোর জলবায়ু গবেষণায় সবচেয়ে প্রভাবশালী উৎসগুলোর একটি হয়ে উঠেছে।

ps.e: They show that abrupt changes of several degrees have occurred in Greenland within a few decades, a finding that undermined the assumption that the climate always changes gradually.
ps.b: এগুলো দেখায় যে গ্রিনল্যান্ডে কয়েক দশকের মধ্যে কয়েক ডিগ্রির আকস্মিক পরিবর্তন ঘটেছে, এই আবিষ্কার সেই ধারণাকে দুর্বল করেছে যে জলবায়ু সব সময় ধীরে ধীরে বদলায়।

ps.e: The search continues for older ice, with fragments recovered from exposed blue ice in Antarctica dated to more than two million years, and with projects aiming to drill a continuous core reaching back beyond a million.
ps.b: আরও পুরোনো বরফের খোঁজ চলছে, অ্যান্টার্কটিকার উন্মুক্ত নীল বরফ থেকে উদ্ধার হওয়া টুকরো দুই মিলিয়ন বছরেরও বেশি পুরোনো বলে নির্ণীত হয়েছে, আর এমন প্রকল্প আছে যা দশ লক্ষ বছরের ওপরে পৌঁছানো একটানা কোর খোঁড়ার লক্ষ্য রাখে।

ps.e: Each extension of the record tests existing theories of how the climate system behaves, and the answers, locked in ice that fell as snow long before our species existed, may help to indicate what lies ahead.
ps.b: নথির প্রতিটি সম্প্রসারণ জলবায়ু ব্যবস্থা কীভাবে আচরণ করে তার বিদ্যমান তত্ত্বগুলোকে পরীক্ষা করে, আর আমাদের প্রজাতির অস্তিত্বের অনেক আগে তুষার হয়ে পড়া বরফে আটকে থাকা এই উত্তরগুলো হয়তো সামনে কী আছে তার ইঙ্গিত দিতে পারে।

cmp/106.title: How the Brain Learned to Read
cmp/106.src: Dehaene, Reading in the Brain (2009); Seymour, Aro and Erskine (2003); Castles, Rastle and Nation (2018)
p: Reading feels so natural to those who have mastered it that it is easy to overlook how improbable an accomplishment it is. Spoken language is, for human beings, an inheritance: children acquire it without formal instruction, in every society, provided they hear it spoken around them. Writing, by contrast, is a cultural invention of perhaps five thousand years ago, a span far too short for natural selection to have shaped a brain specifically for the purpose. A child learning to read is therefore using a mind that evolved for other tasks, and one of the central questions of cognitive neuroscience is how such a mind accomplishes what it was never designed to do.

The most influential answer comes from the French neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene, who proposes that reading depends on what he calls neuronal recycling. According to this hypothesis, the cultural inventions that humans create are shaped by the constraints of the brain they must fit, and writing systems have evolved to take advantage of circuits that already existed. In particular, scripts around the world are built from simple strokes whose shapes resemble the junctions and edges that the visual system has long been tuned to recognise in natural scenes, such as the places where branches meet or where one object overlaps another. Letters, on this view, have survived because they were easy for the brain to see.

Brain imaging has supported the hypothesis by identifying a small region on the left side of the visual cortex that responds strongly to written words. Located at the base of the brain, this area appears to be involved in the recognition of objects and faces in people who cannot read, but in literate adults it becomes specialised for the shapes of letters and for familiar words. Strikingly, it is activated in broadly similar places in readers of languages as dissimilar as English, Chinese and Hebrew, which suggests that its function does not depend on any particular writing system. It is sometimes called the visual word form area, although some researchers caution that the name implies a degree of specialisation that has yet to be established.

Reading, however, requires more than seeing. A reader must connect the visual form of a word to its sound and its meaning, and this involves a network of regions that include those used for speech. The efficiency of the connections matters, since a fluent reader does not decode each letter in turn but recognises whole words almost instantly. Studies of eye movements show that the gaze does not sweep smoothly along a line but jumps in short movements, pausing for roughly a quarter of a second on one word after another, and that readers absorb information only from a narrow window around the point of fixation. The impression of effortless continuity is, to a considerable degree, an illusion constructed by the brain.

The difficulties experienced by people with dyslexia are therefore best understood as problems of connection. In most cases, the underlying weakness appears to lie in the processing of the sounds of language, which makes it hard to link letters with the speech sounds they represent, and brain scans of dyslexic readers often show reduced activity in the left-hemisphere regions that support this linking. The consequences depend heavily on the writing system. Languages such as Italian and Finnish, in which each letter corresponds closely to a sound, are mastered by most children more quickly than English, whose spelling is notoriously irregular, and the effects of dyslexia are therefore easier to detect in English-speaking communities.

The comparison across languages illustrates a broader principle, namely that the burden of learning to read is shared between the learner and the script. A large study of European children found that those acquiring literacy in languages with transparent spelling achieved accurate decoding within the first year of schooling, whereas English-speaking children required considerably longer, a discrepancy attributable not to their intelligence or to the quality of their teachers but to the inconsistency of the system they were attempting to master. The finding has occasionally been invoked in support of reforming English spelling, a proposal that has repeatedly failed to win acceptance, partly because the irregularities preserve information about the origins and relationships of words.

These findings have implications for teaching, although they should be applied with caution. Reviews of the research generally conclude that children benefit from explicit instruction in the relationships between letters and sounds, since this is the skill on which the rest of reading is built. This does not mean that other aspects of literacy, such as vocabulary and comprehension, can be neglected, nor does it settle every dispute between those who favour different methods. Nevertheless, the evidence offers a firmer foundation than the debates of earlier decades, which were often conducted on the basis of belief and anecdote.

There is, finally, a quieter lesson in the discovery that learning to read changes the brain. Adults who learn to read late in life show measurable differences in the way their visual and language areas respond, compared with those who have never been taught. The achievement of literacy, which seems so ordinary, is therefore a physical transformation as well as an educational one, and the cost of failing to teach it well is correspondingly high. A skill that the brain was never built for turns out to be possible only because the brain is, within limits, unusually adaptable.

ps.b: গবেষণার পর্যালোচনাগুলো সাধারণত এই সিদ্ধান্তে আসে যে অক্ষর ও ধ্বনির সম্পর্ক নিয়ে সুস্পষ্ট নির্দেশনায় শিশুরা উপকৃত হয়, কারণ এই দক্ষতার ওপরই বাকি পড়া দাঁড়ায়।

ps.e: This does not mean that other aspects of literacy, such as vocabulary and comprehension, can be neglected, nor does it settle every dispute between those who favour different methods.

cmp/107.title: The Secret of Roman Concrete
cmp/107.src: Jackson and others (2013); Seymour and others (2023); Vitruvius, On Architecture; Pantheon structural studies
p: Almost two thousand years after it was poured, the dome of the Pantheon in Rome still stands, and it remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Its builders, working in the second century, had no steel bars to hold the structure together and no mechanical means of testing the strength of what they were making. Yet the building has survived earthquakes, floods and centuries of neglect, whereas many modern concrete structures, built with far greater scientific knowledge, begin to deteriorate within a few decades. The contrast has long puzzled engineers and has recently attracted the attention of materials scientists, who have begun to ask what the Romans knew that has since been forgotten.

The basic ingredients are not mysterious. Roman concrete was made by mixing lime with volcanic ash, most famously from the region around Pozzuoli near Naples, and with fragments of brick or stone that served as a coarse filler. The ash is the crucial element, because it reacts chemically with lime and water to form a hard, stable compound, an effect that allowed the mixture to set even beneath the sea. Modern cement, by contrast, is made by heating limestone and clay to extremely high temperatures, a process invented in the nineteenth century and now responsible for several percent of the world's carbon dioxide emissions. If the Roman recipe could be understood and adapted, the potential savings would be considerable.

The first major clue came from the Roman harbours. In the early 2010s, a team led by the geologist Marie Jackson examined cores drilled from breakwaters that had stood in the Mediterranean for two thousand years. They found that seawater had not damaged the concrete but had, in a sense, improved it. As the water seeped slowly through the material, it reacted with the volcanic ash and lime to produce rare crystals, notably a mineral called aluminous tobermorite, which grew within the cracks and pores and bound the structure more firmly together. Modern concrete is designed to resist seawater, not to be strengthened by it, and the discovery suggested a fundamentally different approach.

A second discovery concerned the small white fragments of lime that are found throughout Roman concrete. For many years, these lumps were assumed to be evidence of careless mixing, a sign that the builders had failed to blend the ingredients thoroughly. A group at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology proposed in 2023 that they might instead be a deliberate feature. According to their hypothesis, the Romans mixed quicklime directly with the other ingredients while it was still hot, a process that produces fragments rich in reactive calcium. When a crack later opens in the concrete and water enters it, the calcium dissolves and crystallises again as calcium carbonate, which fills the gap. In laboratory tests, cracked samples made in this way were reported to have healed within a few weeks, while those made by conventional methods did not.

These findings should be treated with some caution. The studies were carried out on a limited number of samples, and the theory that the Romans used hot mixing is a hypothesis about a process for which no complete written description survives. The classical author Vitruvius did record that lime and volcanic ash were used, but he did not set out the details of the technique, and archaeologists have long suspected that practical knowledge passed between builders without being written down. Moreover, a recipe that works in an ancient monument is not necessarily suitable for modern construction, where speed and predictability are required.

There is also a risk of romanticising the past. Not every Roman building has survived, and those that have are, to some extent, the ones that were well made or fortunate in their location. Many structures collapsed or were demolished, and the ones that remain give a biased impression of the quality of ancient work. Reinforced concrete, in turn, was an innovation that allowed engineers to build bridges, tower blocks and dams that the Romans could never have attempted, though its steel interior is also its weakness, since moisture that reaches the metal causes it to corrode and expand, cracking the surrounding material.

Nevertheless, the study of Roman concrete has already had practical consequences. Several research groups and companies are experimenting with mixtures that incorporate volcanic ash or other natural additives, in the hope of producing concrete that lasts longer and requires less energy to make. The ambition is not to reproduce the past exactly but to learn from it, and to design materials whose durability does not depend on constant maintenance. If the effort succeeds, the greatest lesson of the Pantheon may be less about Roman skill than about the value of building things to last.

ps.b: পরীক্ষাগারের পরীক্ষায় এভাবে তৈরি ফাটলযুক্ত নমুনা কয়েক সপ্তাহের মধ্যে সেরে উঠেছে বলে জানানো হয়েছে, যেখানে প্রচলিত পদ্ধতিতে তৈরি নমুনা তা পারেনি।

ps.e: These findings should be treated with some caution.
ps.b: এই ফলাফলগুলো কিছুটা সতর্কতার সঙ্গে দেখা উচিত।

ps.e: The studies were carried out on a limited number of samples, and the theory that the Romans used hot mixing is a hypothesis about a process for which no complete written description survives.
ps.b: গবেষণাগুলো সীমিতসংখ্যক নমুনার ওপর করা হয়েছে, আর রোমানরা গরম মেশানোর পদ্ধতি ব্যবহার করত এই তত্ত্বটি এমন এক প্রক্রিয়া নিয়ে অনুমান যার কোনো সম্পূর্ণ লিখিত বিবরণ টিকে নেই।

ps.e: The classical author Vitruvius did record that lime and volcanic ash were used, but he did not set out the details of the technique, and archaeologists have long suspected that practical knowledge passed between builders without being written down.
ps.b: শাস্ত্রীয় লেখক ভিত্রুভিয়াস লিপিবদ্ধ করেছিলেন যে চুন ও আগ্নেয় ছাই ব্যবহৃত হতো, কিন্তু কৌশলের খুঁটিনাটি লেখেননি, আর প্রত্নতাত্ত্বিকেরা দীর্ঘদিন সন্দেহ করেছেন যে ব্যবহারিক জ্ঞান লিখিত না হয়েই নির্মাতাদের মধ্যে হস্তান্তরিত হতো।

ps.e: Moreover, a recipe that works in an ancient monument is not necessarily suitable for modern construction, where speed and predictability are required.
ps.b: তা ছাড়া প্রাচীন স্মৃতিস্তম্ভে যে রেসিপি কাজ করে তা আধুনিক নির্মাণে অপরিহার্যভাবে উপযুক্ত নয়, যেখানে গতি ও অনুমানযোগ্যতা প্রয়োজন।

ps.e: There is also a risk of romanticising the past.
ps.b: অতীতকে মোহনীয় করে দেখার ঝুঁকিও আছে।

ps.e: Not every Roman building has survived, and those that have are, to some extent, the ones that were well made or fortunate in their location.
ps.b: রোমের প্রতিটি ভবন টিকে নেই, আর যেগুলো টিকে আছে সেগুলো কিছুটা এমন ভবন যা ভালোভাবে তৈরি বা অবস্থানের কারণে ভাগ্যবান।

ps.e: Many structures collapsed or were demolished, and the ones that remain give a biased impression of the quality of ancient work.
ps.b: অনেক কাঠামো ধসে পড়েছে বা ভেঙে ফেলা হয়েছে, আর যেগুলো রয়ে গেছে সেগুলো প্রাচীন কাজের মান সম্পর্কে একটি পক্ষপাতদুষ্ট ধারণা দেয়।

ps.e: Reinforced concrete, in turn, was an innovation that allowed engineers to build bridges, tower blocks and dams that the Romans could never have attempted, though its steel interior is also its weakness, since moisture that reaches the metal causes it to corrode and expand, cracking the surrounding material.
ps.b: শক্তিবর্ধিত কংক্রিট, অন্যদিকে, এমন এক উদ্ভাবন যা প্রকৌশলীদের সেতু, বহুতল ভবন ও বাঁধ বানাতে দিয়েছে যা রোমানরা কখনও চেষ্টাও করতে পারত না, যদিও এর ইস্পাতের ভেতরের অংশই এর দুর্বলতা, কারণ ধাতুতে আর্দ্রতা পৌঁছালে তা মরচে ধরে ফুলে ওঠে এবং চারপাশের উপাদান ফাটিয়ে দেয়।

ps.e: Nevertheless, the study of Roman concrete has already had practical consequences.
ps.b: তবু রোমান কংক্রিট নিয়ে গবেষণার ইতিমধ্যে ব্যবহারিক ফল দেখা গেছে।

ps.e: Several research groups and companies are experimenting with mixtures that incorporate volcanic ash or other natural additives, in the hope of producing concrete that lasts longer and requires less energy to make.
ps.b: বেশ কয়েকটি গবেষণা দল ও কোম্পানি আগ্নেয় ছাই বা অন্যান্য প্রাকৃতিক সংযোজক মিশিয়ে এমন মিশ্রণ নিয়ে পরীক্ষা করছে, আশা করছে যে এমন কংক্রিট তৈরি হবে যা বেশি টেকে এবং বানাতে কম শক্তি লাগে।

ps.e: The ambition is not to reproduce the past exactly but to learn from it, and to design materials whose durability does not depend on constant maintenance.
ps.b: উচ্চাকাঙ্ক্ষা অতীতকে হুবহু নকল করা নয়, বরং তা থেকে শেখা, এবং এমন উপাদান তৈরি করা যার স্থায়িত্ব নিরন্তর রক্ষণাবেক্ষণের ওপর নির্ভর করে না।

ps.e: If the effort succeeds, the greatest lesson of the Pantheon may be less about Roman skill than about the value of building things to last.
ps.b: এই প্রচেষ্টা সফল হলে প্যান্থিয়নের সবচেয়ে বড় শিক্ষা হয়তো রোমান দক্ষতা নিয়ে যতটা নয়, তার চেয়ে বেশি হবে স্থায়ী করে কিছু গড়ার মূল্য নিয়ে।

cmp/108.title: Why English Spelling Is So Strange
cmp/108.src: Caxton and early printing; the Great Vowel Shift (Jespersen; Lass); Johnson (1755); Webster (1828); Oxford English Dictionary
p: Anyone who has acquired English as a second language will, at some point, have wondered why its orthography is so unreliable. The letters in "though", "through" and "tough" imply sounds that bear almost no relation to those actually uttered, and the silent letters in "knight", "debt" and "island" appear to serve no function whatsoever. The explanation lies partly in the history of the language and partly in the contingencies of publishing, and it reveals how a writing system can become fossilised at a particular moment while the speech it represents continues to evolve.

Between roughly 1400 and 1700, the pronunciation of the long vowels in English altered dramatically, in a series of changes that linguists call the Great Vowel Shift. In the time of Chaucer, the word "bite" would have sounded something like "beet", "mouse" something like "moose", and "name" like the first syllable of "nah-muh". Over the following three centuries, the vowels moved upwards in the mouth, and those that could move no higher turned into diphthongs, so that "mouse" and "bite" acquired the sounds they have now. The shift was gradual and uneven, and it did not affect every dialect uniformly. Its causes remain a matter of controversy, although some scholars have conjectured that the migration of speakers into London from disparate regions disrupted established patterns of pronunciation.

The timing was inauspicious for spelling. In 1476, William Caxton established the first printing press in England, and printers began to standardise the way in which words were written. Many of the spellings they adopted mirrored the pronunciation of the late Middle Ages, shortly before the vowels began to alter. By the time the shift had run its course, the written forms had become established, and the printed page recorded sounds that people no longer made. The "e" at the end of "name", which was once pronounced, remains in print as a silent marker of the length of the vowel before it, and the combinations of letters in words such as "knight", where the initial consonant and the "gh" were once sounded, survived the disappearance of the sounds themselves.

Printing was not the only influence. During the sixteenth century, scholars who admired Latin tried to make English words resemble their classical ancestors, sometimes with little justification. The "b" in "debt" was inserted because the Latin word was "debitum", although the word had reached English through French, in which it had no such letter. The "s" in "island", similarly, was introduced under the mistaken impression that the word was related to "isle", from Latin, when in fact the two words have different origins. Such interpolations lent the language an air of erudition, but they exacerbated the discrepancy between spelling and speech.

Attempts to impose order on the confusion have met with mixed success. Samuel Johnson's dictionary of 1755 recorded the usage of his day and did a great deal to establish a single accepted form for most words, though Johnson himself admitted that he could not control the habits of the language. Across the Atlantic, Noah Webster proposed a number of simplifications in the early nineteenth century, some of which, such as "color" and "center", were widely adopted in the United States, while many of his more radical suggestions were not. The result is that two national standards exist, differing in a few hundred words, and that neither is entirely consistent.

It is tempting to conclude that English spelling ought to be reformed, and the proposal has been advanced repeatedly by writers, educators and politicians. Yet the obstacles are formidable. There is no single accent to serve as a model, since the vowels of a speaker from Glasgow differ from those of one from Sydney or Chicago, and a spelling that suited one would be misleading to another. The irregularities also preserve information about the history of words, which helps readers to see the relationship between those that look alike, such as "sign" and "signature". Finally, reform would sever the connection between the existing body of literature and future readers, a price that few societies have been prepared to pay.

What the history of English spelling illustrates, then, is the gradual collision of two processes that proceed at different velocities. Speech changes ceaselessly, in ways that no authority can arrest, whereas writing, once it has been printed and taught, tends to remain static. Every language with a long written tradition faces some version of the problem. English has simply faced it earlier than most, and with more borrowed vocabulary than most, which is why its spelling continues to trouble those who learn it.

q.q: Which statement best sums up the passage?
q.e: The passage explains the causes and then the difficulty of reform.
o: A. English spelling is irregular because printing fixed the written forms before pronunciation had finished changing, other influences added to the gap, and reform is difficult.
B. English spelling was designed to be difficult so that only scholars could use it.
C. English spelling is irregular because the language has no rules and has never been studied.
D. English spelling has been reformed several times, and it is now fully regular in the United States.

q.q: What was the Great Vowel Shift?
o: A. A change in the pronunciation of the long vowels in English between roughly 1400 and 1700.
B. A movement of people into London from different regions of England.
C. A change in the grammar of English caused by the influence of Latin.
D. A change in the spelling of English words made by Caxton's printers.

q.q: Why do many English spellings no longer match the way words are said?
o: A. The vowels changed first, and printers then copied the new sounds.
B. Printing fixed the spellings before the vowel shift had finished, so they record older sounds.
C. Printers deliberately chose spellings that were hard to pronounce.
D. Caxton wrote all words as they were spoken in his own village.

q.q: In paragraph 3, the word "inauspicious" is closest in meaning to
o: A. unpopular.
B. unnecessary.
C. unfavourable.
D. unexpected.

q.q: Why was a "b" added to the word "debt"?
o: A. Printers needed the extra letter to fill a line.
B. Scholars wanted the word to look more like its Latin ancestor, "debitum".
C. The letter came from the French form of the word.
D. The letter was pronounced in medieval English.

q.q: What did Noah Webster do, according to paragraph 5?
o: A. He removed all silent letters from the language.
B. He compiled the first dictionary of the English language.
C. He persuaded Britain to accept the spellings used in America.
D. He proposed simplified spellings, some of which, such as "color", were widely adopted in the United States.

q.q: Which of the following is given as a reason why spelling reform is difficult?
o: A. There are too few dictionaries to explain the changes.
B. There is no single accent that could serve as a model for everyone.
C. Printers refuse to use new spellings.
D. Most people already spell words according to their pronunciation.

q.q: What is the main point of the final paragraph?
q.e: The paragraph sums up the two processes.
o: A. English is the only language with a written tradition.
B. Writing should always be changed whenever speech changes.
C. Speech keeps changing while writing, once fixed, stays still, and English has felt this more than most languages.
D. Spelling has no connection with the history of a language.

q.q: In Chaucer's time, the word "mouse" would have sounded something like "moose".
Scholars agree on what caused the Great Vowel Shift.
q.e: Paragraph 2 says its causes remain a matter of controversy.

q.q: The word "debt" came into English through French.
Johnson's dictionary sold more copies than any earlier dictionary.
In 1476, William ____ established the first printing press in England.
Samuel Johnson's dictionary was published in ____.
Reformers face the problem that there is no single ____ to serve as a model.

ps.b: মুদ্রণই একমাত্র প্রভাব ছিল না।

ps.e: During the sixteenth century, scholars who admired Latin tried to make English words resemble their classical ancestors, sometimes with little justification.
ps.b: ষোড়শ শতাব্দীতে যে পণ্ডিতেরা লাতিনের প্রশংসা করতেন তাঁরা ইংরেজি শব্দকে তাদের শাস্ত্রীয় পূর্বপুরুষের মতো দেখাতে চেষ্টা করেন, কখনও কখনও খুব কম যুক্তিতে।

ps.e: The "b" in "debt" was inserted because the Latin word was "debitum", although the word had reached English through French, in which it had no such letter.
ps.b: ‘debt’-এর ‘b’ বসানো হয়েছিল কারণ লাতিন শব্দটি ছিল ‘debitum’, যদিও শব্দটি ফরাসির মধ্য দিয়ে ইংরেজিতে এসেছিল, যেখানে ওই অক্ষর ছিল না।

ps.e: The "s" in "island", similarly, was introduced under the mistaken impression that the word was related to "isle", from Latin, when in fact the two words have different origins.
ps.b: ‘island’-এর ‘s’-ও একইভাবে ঢোকানো হয়েছিল এই ভুল ধারণায় যে শব্দটি লাতিন থেকে আসা ‘isle’-এর সঙ্গে সম্পর্কিত, অথচ আসলে দুটি শব্দের উৎস আলাদা।

ps.e: Such interpolations lent the language an air of erudition, but they exacerbated the discrepancy between spelling and speech.
ps.b: এমন সংযোজন ভাষাটিকে আরও পাণ্ডিত্যপূর্ণ দেখালেও বানান ও উচ্চারণের ব্যবধান বাড়িয়ে দিল।

ps.e: Attempts to impose order on the confusion have met with mixed success.
ps.b: বিশৃঙ্খলায় শৃঙ্খলা আনার চেষ্টা মিশ্র সাফল্য পেয়েছে।

ps.e: Samuel Johnson's dictionary of 1755 recorded the usage of his day and did a great deal to establish a single accepted form for most words, though Johnson himself admitted that he could not control the habits of the language.
ps.b: স্যামুয়েল জনসনের ১৭৫৫ সালের অভিধান তাঁর সময়ের ব্যবহার লিপিবদ্ধ করেছিল এবং বেশির ভাগ শব্দের জন্য একটি গৃহীত রূপ প্রতিষ্ঠায় অনেক সাহায্য করেছিল, যদিও জনসন নিজে স্বীকার করেছিলেন যে ভাষার অভ্যাস তিনি নিয়ন্ত্রণ করতে পারেন না।

ps.e: Across the Atlantic, Noah Webster proposed a number of simplifications in the early nineteenth century, some of which, such as "color" and "center", were widely adopted in the United States, while many of his more radical suggestions were not.
ps.b: আটলান্টিকের ওপারে নোয়া ওয়েবস্টার উনিশ শতকের গোড়ায় কয়েকটি সরলীকরণ প্রস্তাব করেন, যার কিছু, যেমন ‘color’ ও ‘center’, যুক্তরাষ্ট্রে ব্যাপকভাবে গৃহীত হয়, আর তাঁর আরও আমূল প্রস্তাবের অনেকগুলো গৃহীত হয়নি।

ps.e: The result is that two national standards exist, differing in a few hundred words, and that neither is entirely consistent.
ps.b: ফলে দুটি জাতীয় মান আছে, যা কয়েকশো শব্দে ভিন্ন, আর কোনোটিই পুরোপুরি সংগতিপূর্ণ নয়।

ps.e: It is tempting to conclude that English spelling ought to be reformed, and the proposal has been advanced repeatedly by writers, educators and politicians.
ps.b: ইংরেজি বানান সংস্কার করা উচিত, এমন সিদ্ধান্তে আসা লোভনীয়, আর প্রস্তাবটি লেখক, শিক্ষাবিদ ও রাজনীতিবিদেরা বারবার তুলেছেন।

ps.e: Yet the obstacles are formidable.
ps.b: তবু বাধাগুলো প্রচণ্ড।

ps.e: There is no single accent to serve as a model, since the vowels of a speaker from Glasgow differ from those of one from Sydney or Chicago, and a spelling that suited one would be misleading to another.
ps.b: আদর্শ হিসেবে কোনো একক উচ্চারণ নেই, কারণ গ্লাসগোর বক্তার স্বরধ্বনি সিডনি বা শিকাগোর বক্তার থেকে আলাদা, আর একজনের জন্য উপযুক্ত বানান অন্যজনের কাছে বিভ্রান্তিকর হবে।

ps.e: The irregularities also preserve information about the history of words, which helps readers to see the relationship between those that look alike, such as "sign" and "signature".
ps.b: অনিয়মগুলো শব্দের ইতিহাস সম্পর্কে তথ্যও সংরক্ষণ করে, যা ‘sign’ ও ‘signature’-এর মতো দেখতে একই রকম শব্দগুলোর সম্পর্ক বুঝতে পাঠকদের সাহায্য করে।

ps.e: Finally, reform would sever the connection between the existing body of literature and future readers, a price that few societies have been prepared to pay.
ps.b: সবশেষে, সংস্কার বিদ্যমান সাহিত্য ও ভবিষ্যৎ পাঠকদের মধ্যকার যোগসূত্র কেটে দেবে, এমন মূল্য যা খুব কম সমাজই দিতে প্রস্তুত থেকেছে।

ps.e: What the history of English spelling illustrates, then, is the gradual collision of two processes that proceed at different velocities.
ps.b: ইংরেজি বানানের ইতিহাস তাই যা দেখায় তা হলো ভিন্ন গতিতে চলা দুটি প্রক্রিয়ার ধীর সংঘর্ষ।

ps.e: Speech changes ceaselessly, in ways that no authority can arrest, whereas writing, once it has been printed and taught, tends to remain static.
ps.b: কথ্য ভাষা অবিরাম বদলায়, এমনভাবে যা কোনো কর্তৃপক্ষ থামাতে পারে না, অথচ লিখিত ভাষা একবার ছাপা ও শেখানো হয়ে গেলে স্থির থাকতে চায়।

ps.e: Every language with a long written tradition faces some version of the problem.
ps.b: দীর্ঘ লিখিত ঐতিহ্যের প্রতিটি ভাষাই এই সমস্যার কোনো না কোনো রূপের মুখোমুখি হয়।

ps.e: English has simply faced it earlier than most, and with more borrowed vocabulary than most, which is why its spelling continues to trouble those who learn it.
ps.b: ইংরেজি তার মুখোমুখি হয়েছে অধিকাংশের আগেই, এবং অধিকাংশের চেয়ে বেশি ধার করা শব্দভান্ডার নিয়ে, যে কারণে এর বানান শিক্ষার্থীদের বিব্রত করতে থাকে।

cmp/109.title: From Plague Lists to Statistics: Graunt and Halley
cmp/109.src: Graunt (1662); Halley (1693); Hald, A History of Probability and Statistics; Equitable Life records
p: In the early seventeenth century, the parish clerks of London began to circulate a weekly tabulation of the deaths recorded in the city, together with the ostensible causes of each. The Bills of Mortality, as they were known, were conceived as an early-warning mechanism for plague, since a sudden rise in burials within a particular parish signalled that contagion was advancing. They were printed on single sheets, sold for a penny and consumed chiefly by apprehensive Londoners who wished to judge whether it was prudent to remain in the capital. It occurred to very few of their readers that the sheets might contain information of an altogether different kind.

That insight belonged to John Graunt, a prosperous haberdasher with no formal training in mathematics. From the 1650s onwards, Graunt assembled the bills for several decades and subjected them to a form of scrutiny that no one had previously attempted. In 1662 he published his findings in a slim volume whose conclusions were so original that its author was elected to the Royal Society soon afterwards. Among other results, he observed that slightly more boys than girls were born each year, in a ratio of roughly fourteen to thirteen, and that this proportion remained remarkably stable, which implied that it was governed by something more systematic than chance.

Graunt also remarked that burials in London consistently outnumbered baptisms, a deficit that could be sustained only by a steady influx of migrants from the countryside. He drew on the bills to estimate the capital's population, and he made a first, tentative attempt to calculate the probability that a person of a given age would survive to a later one. His methods were crude and his data deeply unreliable. Causes of death were assigned by "searchers", elderly women who inspected the bodies and reported what they believed they saw, so that a death attributed to "fright" or "grief" probably reflected the searcher's conjecture rather than any medical judgement. Graunt was acutely conscious of such deficiencies and endeavoured to compensate for them, which is part of what distinguishes his work from mere compilation.

The next decisive advance was made by Edmond Halley, the astronomer now remembered chiefly for the comet that bears his name. In the early 1690s he obtained records of births and deaths from the city of Breslau, in what is now Poland, which had been maintained with unusual diligence and which, because the community was comparatively closed, were far less distorted by migration than the London figures. From these he constructed a table indicating how many people of each age could be expected to survive, and he employed it to calculate the equitable price of an annuity, a payment made annually for the remainder of a person's life. The calculation demonstrated that the annuities then being sold by governments were substantially underpriced, since purchasers were likely to outlive the assumptions of those who sold them.

Halley's table did not immediately transform the business of insurance, but it established a principle of lasting consequence. If the lifespans of large populations conformed to a regular pattern, then the unpredictable death of any individual could be regarded as a single event within a predictable whole, and an institution could attach a price to the risk of it. This idea, which now seems self-evident, rested on the discovery that apparently capricious events display regularities once they are counted in sufficient quantity. By 1762, the Equitable Life Assurance Society had begun to apply such reasoning systematically to life insurance, and the profession of the actuary had come into being.

The significance of these early inquiries extends well beyond the financial sphere. Graunt and Halley were among the first to demonstrate that the study of society could be made empirical, founded on enumeration and comparison rather than on speculation or inherited authority. Their work contributed to the emergence of the discipline later known as statistics, and it encouraged governments to gather systematic data about their populations. The lesson was by no means obvious in advance, and its origin is faintly ironic: a document produced to help people escape from an epidemic had furnished the beginnings of a science that now underpins the planning of hospitals, pensions and public health.

q.q: Which statement best sums up the passage?
q.e: The passage traces how the bills led to statistics.
o: A. Graunt and Halley discovered the cause of the plague by studying the Bills of Mortality.
B. Insurance companies in the seventeenth century used Halley's table to cure disease.
C. The Bills of Mortality were accurate records of every cause of death in London.
D. Records made to track the plague were turned by Graunt and Halley into early statistics, which later supported insurance and the study of society.

q.q: According to paragraph 1, what were the Bills of Mortality originally intended to do?
o: A. Warn people when plague was spreading through the parishes.
B. Help the government to collect taxes from each parish.
C. Record the number of births in the city of London.
D. Teach readers how to avoid the disease.

q.q: In paragraph 1, the word "ostensible" is closest in meaning to
q.e: 'Ostensible causes' are those that appear to be the causes.
o: A. apparent.
B. hidden.
C. medical.
D. important.

q.q: What did Graunt's finding about boys and girls suggest to him?
q.e: Paragraph 2 says the ratio was 'remarkably stable'.
o: A. That the number of boys changed greatly from one year to the next.
B. That boys were more likely to die of the plague than girls.
C. That the proportion was governed by something more systematic than chance.
D. That fewer girls were registered because of a mistake by the clerks.

q.q: Why were the causes of death in the bills unreliable?
o: A. They were changed by the government to hide the spread of plague.
B. They were assigned by searchers, who reported what they believed they saw.
C. They were chosen at random by the printers.
D. They were written by doctors who had never examined the bodies.

q.q: Why did Halley use records from Breslau rather than from London?
o: A. Breslau was a comparatively closed community, so migration distorted its figures less.
B. Breslau had suffered less from the plague than London.
C. Breslau had a larger population than London.
D. The records from London had been destroyed by fire.

q.q: What principle did Halley's table establish?
o: A. That the deaths of individuals are unpredictable, but large populations follow patterns that allow risks to be priced.
B. That insurance companies should avoid selling annuities.
C. That governments should print the bills more often.
D. That everyone in a given population will live to the same age.

q.q: What is the "irony" mentioned at the end of the passage?
q.e: The last sentence states the irony.
o: A. Graunt became rich by selling the bills to the Royal Society.
B. A document made to help people flee an epidemic gave rise to a science used in planning public health.
C. The searchers were more accurate than modern doctors.
D. Halley is remembered for his comet rather than for his table.

q.q: The Bills of Mortality were sold for a penny.
Graunt had trained as a mathematician.
q.e: Paragraph 2 says he had no formal training in mathematics.

q.q: Halley visited the city of Breslau himself to collect the records.
q.e: The passage says only that he obtained the records.

q.q: Halley's table immediately transformed the insurance business.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says it did not immediately do so.

cmp/110.title: The Black Death and the Price of Labour
cmp/110.src: Statute of Labourers (1351); Herlihy; Brenner debate; Campbell, The Great Transition; Allen on English wages
p: Between 1347 and 1351, the disease that later generations called the Black Death swept through Europe, killing, by most modern estimates, between a third and a half of its inhabitants. Arriving by ship from the Black Sea and propagating with astonishing rapidity along trade routes and waterways, it overwhelmed the capacity of communities to inter their dead. The human toll was immense, and contemporary accounts, from Italian chroniclers to English monks, convey a pervasive sense of helpless horror. Historians have long been preoccupied with the aftermath, since the epidemic also precipitated an abrupt and profound shift in the equilibrium between population and resources.

The underlying economic logic was straightforward. Before the plague, Europe had been densely populated, and land was scarce while labour was plentiful, which enabled landowners to exact high rents and to pay meagre wages. After it, the position was reversed. Fields lay untended for want of workers, and the survivors found that their labour had acquired an unprecedented premium. Peasants abandoned the estates on which they had been born in pursuit of higher remuneration, and landlords who tried to retain them were undermined by rivals prepared to offer more favourable terms. In England, real wages rose sharply in the decades after the epidemic and remained high for much of the following century.

The authorities did not acquiesce in this transformation. In 1351, the English Parliament passed the Statute of Labourers, which attempted to fix wages at the levels that had prevailed before the plague and to forbid workers from leaving their employers. Similar laws were enacted in France and elsewhere. The measures were enforced in some localities and provoked considerable resentment, but they proved impossible to sustain, since the economic incentives for both parties to evade them were overwhelming. The friction between a ruling class intent on preserving the old order and a labouring population that had acquired novel bargaining power contributed to the unrest that culminated in the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381, although that rising was triggered more directly by a new poll tax.

The longer-term consequences were more intricate, and they varied considerably from one region to another. In much of western Europe, the shortage of labour accelerated the decline of serfdom, the system in which peasants were bound to the land of their lords, and encouraged a shift from cultivation of grain towards sheep farming and other activities that required fewer workers. In many parts of eastern Europe, however, the outcome was almost the opposite. There, landowners were stronger and the towns were weaker, and the lords responded to the loss of labour by tightening their control over the peasantry, so that serfdom became harsher in the following centuries. The same demographic shock thus produced different results according to the social institutions that it encountered.

Historians have invoked this contrast to argue that institutions matter at least as much as demographic figures. It is insufficient to know that a population has declined; one must also ascertain who wields power, how disputes are adjudicated and what entitlements ordinary people possess. Some economists have gone further and suggested that the high wages of western Europe after the plague encouraged the use of labour-saving technology and helped to lay the foundations for later growth. The hypothesis is appealing but contentious, since numerous other factors were operating and the evidence for a direct causal connection is elusive.

A further caveat is warranted. The mortality was not evenly distributed, and the figures on which historians rely are uncertain, because many records were lost and others were compiled for purposes, such as taxation, that give a partial view. Population recovery was slow, and in many regions numbers did not return to the levels of the early fourteenth century for hundreds of years, since the plague returned repeatedly in smaller outbreaks. Whatever advantages accrued to the survivors were purchased at the price of a catastrophe, and it would be misleading to characterise the epidemic as an economic opportunity.

The Black Death nevertheless remains a striking illustration of how a catastrophe can alter the structure of a society. It showed that the distribution of wealth and power was not fixed by nature or tradition, but depended on the balance between the people who worked and the resources that they worked on. When that balance was abruptly disturbed, ordinary workers acquired a leverage that no statute could readily dislodge, and those in authority discovered that the arrangements they had taken for granted were considerably more precarious than they had appeared.

q.q: Which statement best sums up the passage?
q.e: The passage describes the shock, the responses and the cautions.
o: A. The Black Death upset the balance between labour and land, with effects that differed according to local institutions, and its lessons must be drawn with care.
B. The Black Death had few lasting effects, because wage laws restored the old order.
C. The Black Death was an economic opportunity that benefited all survivors equally.
D. The Black Death ended serfdom everywhere in Europe within a single generation.

q.q: According to paragraph 2, why did wages rise after the epidemic?
q.e: Paragraph 2 explains the change in the balance of labour and land.
o: A. Workers became scarce, so landowners had to compete to hire them.
B. The price of land fell and workers were able to buy it.
C. Parliament had ordered an increase in pay to reward the survivors.
D. Landowners voluntarily chose to share their wealth with the survivors.

q.q: In paragraph 3, the phrase "did not acquiesce in" is closest in meaning to
q.e: To 'acquiesce' is to accept something, usually reluctantly.
o: A. did not understand.
B. did not accept without protest.
C. did not hear about.
D. did not benefit from.

q.q: Why were the wage laws impossible to maintain?
o: A. The laws were repealed within a year of being passed.
B. Parliament had no power to enforce laws outside London.
C. The workers who objected were all killed by the plague.
D. Both employers and workers had strong reasons to ignore them.

q.q: According to paragraph 4, how did the outcomes differ between western and eastern Europe?
o: A. Serfdom ended in the east but became harsher in the west.
B. Serfdom declined in much of the west, but in many parts of the east it became harsher.
C. The plague was far more severe in the east than in the west.
D. Wages rose in the east but fell in the west.

q.q: What do historians conclude from the difference between east and west?
o: A. That serfdom was a more efficient system than free labour.
B. That population fell faster in the east than in the west.
C. That social institutions matter at least as much as population numbers.
D. That economists have no interest in the plague.

q.q: What is the writer's view of describing the plague as an economic opportunity?
o: A. It would be misleading, because any advantages were bought at the price of a catastrophe.
B. It is the only way to explain the rise of the English Parliament.
C. It is unimportant, because the figures are too uncertain.
D. It is accurate, because most survivors became wealthy.

q.q: What does the final sentence mean by saying the arrangements were "considerably more precarious than they had appeared"?
o: A. The laws had been written in a careless and hasty way.
B. Those in authority learned that the social order was far less secure than they had assumed.
C. Ordinary workers had arranged the changes in advance.
D. The authorities decided that the old arrangements should be kept.

q.q: The plague reached Europe by ship from the Black Sea.
The Statute of Labourers succeeded in keeping wages at their pre-plague level.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says the measures proved impossible to maintain.

q.q: France was the first country to pass laws controlling wages.
q.e: Paragraph 3 says only that similar laws were passed in France.

ps.b: ফ্রান্স ও অন্যত্র অনুরূপ আইন প্রণীত হয়।

ps.e: The measures were enforced in some localities and provoked considerable resentment, but they proved impossible to sustain, since the economic incentives for both parties to evade them were overwhelming.
ps.b: ব্যবস্থাগুলো কিছু এলাকায় কার্যকর করা হয় এবং যথেষ্ট ক্ষোভ সৃষ্টি করে, কিন্তু সেগুলো টিকিয়ে রাখা অসম্ভব প্রমাণিত হয়, কারণ উভয় পক্ষেরই সেগুলো এড়ানোর অর্থনৈতিক প্রণোদনা ছিল অপ্রতিরোধ্য।

ps.e: The friction between a ruling class intent on preserving the old order and a labouring population that had acquired novel bargaining power contributed to the unrest that culminated in the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381, although that rising was triggered more directly by a new poll tax.
ps.b: পুরোনো ব্যবস্থা রক্ষায় আগ্রহী শাসকশ্রেণি এবং নতুন দরকষাকষির ক্ষমতা অর্জন করা শ্রমজীবী জনগণের মধ্যকার সংঘাত ১৩৮১ সালের ইংরেজ কৃষক বিদ্রোহে চূড়ান্ত অশান্তিতে অবদান রেখেছিল, যদিও সেই অভ্যুত্থান আরও সরাসরি শুরু হয়েছিল একটি নতুন মাথাপিছু করে।

ps.e: The longer-term consequences were more intricate, and they varied considerably from one region to another.
ps.b: দীর্ঘমেয়াদি ফল ছিল আরও জটিল, এবং অঞ্চলভেদে যথেষ্ট ভিন্ন।

ps.e: In much of western Europe, the shortage of labour accelerated the decline of serfdom, the system in which peasants were bound to the land of their lords, and encouraged a shift from cultivation of grain towards sheep farming and other activities that required fewer workers.
ps.b: পশ্চিম ইউরোপের বেশির ভাগে শ্রমের ঘাটতি দাসপ্রথার অবসান ত্বরান্বিত করল, যে ব্যবস্থায় কৃষকেরা তাদের প্রভুদের জমির সঙ্গে বাঁধা ছিল, আর শস্যচাষ থেকে ভেড়াপালন ও কম শ্রমিক লাগে এমন অন্য কাজে সরে যাওয়াকে উৎসাহিত করল।

ps.e: In many parts of eastern Europe, however, the outcome was almost the opposite.
ps.b: পূর্ব ইউরোপের বহু অংশে অবশ্য ফল ছিল প্রায় বিপরীত।

ps.e: There, landowners were stronger and the towns were weaker, and the lords responded to the loss of labour by tightening their control over the peasantry, so that serfdom became harsher in the following centuries.
ps.b: সেখানে জমির মালিকেরা ছিলেন শক্তিশালী আর শহরগুলো দুর্বল, এবং প্রভুরা শ্রমের ঘাটতির জবাবে কৃষকদের ওপর নিয়ন্ত্রণ আরও কঠোর করলেন, ফলে পরবর্তী শতাব্দীগুলোতে ভূমিদাসত্ব আরও নিষ্ঠুর হলো।

ps.e: The same demographic shock thus produced different results according to the social institutions that it encountered.
ps.b: একই জনসংখ্যাগত ধাক্কা তাই সামাজিক প্রতিষ্ঠানের ধরন অনুযায়ী ভিন্ন ফল দিল।

ps.e: Historians have invoked this contrast to argue that institutions matter at least as much as demographic figures.
ps.b: ঐতিহাসিকেরা এই বৈপরীত্যকে যুক্তি হিসেবে তুলেছেন যে সংখ্যার মতোই প্রতিষ্ঠানও অন্তত সমান গুরুত্বপূর্ণ।

ps.e: It is insufficient to know that a population has declined; one must also ascertain who wields power, how disputes are adjudicated and what entitlements ordinary people possess.
ps.b: জনসংখ্যা কমেছে এটুকু জানা যথেষ্ট নয়; কার হাতে ক্ষমতা, বিরোধ কীভাবে নিষ্পত্তি হয় এবং সাধারণ মানুষের কী অধিকার আছে তাও জানতে হয়।

ps.e: Some economists have gone further and suggested that the high wages of western Europe after the plague encouraged the use of labour-saving technology and helped to lay the foundations for later growth.
ps.b: কিছু অর্থনীতিবিদ আরও এগিয়ে বলেছেন যে প্লেগের পর পশ্চিম ইউরোপের উচ্চ মজুরি শ্রম-সাশ্রয়ী প্রযুক্তি ব্যবহারে উৎসাহ দিয়েছিল এবং পরবর্তী প্রবৃদ্ধির ভিত্তি তৈরিতে সাহায্য করেছিল।

ps.e: The hypothesis is appealing but contentious, since numerous other factors were operating and the evidence for a direct causal connection is elusive.
ps.b: অনুমানটি আকর্ষণীয় কিন্তু বিতর্কিত, কারণ আরও অনেক উপাদান কাজ করছিল এবং সরাসরি কার্যকারণ সম্পর্কের প্রমাণ খুঁজে পাওয়া কঠিন।

ps.e: A further caveat is warranted.
ps.b: আরেকটি সতর্কতা প্রয়োজন।

ps.e: The mortality was not evenly distributed, and the figures on which historians rely are uncertain, because many records were lost and others were compiled for purposes, such as taxation, that give a partial view.
ps.b: মৃত্যু সমানভাবে বণ্টিত ছিল না, এবং ঐতিহাসিকেরা যে সংখ্যার ওপর নির্ভর করেন তা অনিশ্চিত, কারণ অনেক নথি হারিয়ে গেছে আর অন্যগুলো কর আদায়ের মতো উদ্দেশ্যে সংকলিত হওয়ায় আংশিক চিত্র দেয়।

ps.e: Population recovery was slow, and in many regions numbers did not return to the levels of the early fourteenth century for hundreds of years, since the plague returned repeatedly in smaller outbreaks.
ps.b: জনসংখ্যার পুনরুদ্ধার ছিল ধীর, আর অনেক অঞ্চলে সংখ্যা চতুর্দশ শতকের গোড়ার স্তরে ফিরতে শত শত বছর লেগেছে, কারণ প্লেগ ছোট ছোট প্রাদুর্ভাবে বারবার ফিরে এসেছিল।

ps.e: Whatever advantages accrued to the survivors were purchased at the price of a catastrophe, and it would be misleading to characterise the epidemic as an economic opportunity.
ps.b: বেঁচে যাওয়া মানুষেরা যে সুবিধা পেয়েছিল তা এক বিপর্যয়ের মূল্যে কেনা, আর মহামারিটিকে অর্থনৈতিক সুযোগ হিসেবে বর্ণনা করা বিভ্রান্তিকর হবে।

ps.e: The Black Death nevertheless remains a striking illustration of how a catastrophe can alter the structure of a society.
ps.b: তবু ব্ল্যাক ডেথ একটি বিপর্যয় কীভাবে সমাজের কাঠামো বদলে দিতে পারে তার একটি চমকপ্রদ দৃষ্টান্ত হয়ে আছে।

ps.e: It showed that the distribution of wealth and power was not fixed by nature or tradition, but depended on the balance between the people who worked and the resources that they worked on.
ps.b: এটি দেখিয়েছিল যে সম্পদ ও ক্ষমতার বণ্টন প্রকৃতি বা ঐতিহ্য দিয়ে বাঁধা নয়, বরং নির্ভর করে যারা কাজ করে তাদের সংখ্যা এবং তারা যে সম্পদের ওপর কাজ করে তার ভারসাম্যের ওপর।

ps.e: When that balance was abruptly disturbed, ordinary workers acquired a leverage that no statute could readily dislodge, and those in authority discovered that the arrangements they had taken for granted were considerably more precarious than they had appeared.
ps.b: সেই ভারসাম্য হঠাৎ বিঘ্নিত হলে সাধারণ শ্রমিকেরা এমন প্রভাব অর্জন করল যা কোনো আইন সহজে সরাতে পারত না, আর যাঁরা কর্তৃত্বে ছিলেন তাঁরা আবিষ্কার করলেন যে তাঁরা যে ব্যবস্থাগুলো স্বতঃসিদ্ধ ধরে নিয়েছিলেন সেগুলো তাঁদের ভাবনার চেয়ে অনেক বেশি ভঙ্গুর।

cmp/111.title: The Scientists Who Guarded the Seeds
cmp/111.src: Vavilov's expedition records; accounts of the siege of Leningrad; Svalbard Global Seed Vault and ICARDA reports; FAO
p: In the autumn of 1941, as German forces closed around Leningrad, the staff of a research institute in the city confronted a dilemma that most of their fellow citizens would have found bewildering. The building held one of the largest collections of seeds and plant specimens in the world, assembled over two decades by the botanist Nikolai Vavilov, and it was crammed with rice, wheat, peas and potatoes. The city was about to enter a siege that would last nearly nine hundred days and kill more than a million of its inhabitants, most of them through hunger. According to the accounts that survive, several of the scientists entrusted with the collection perished of starvation at their desks rather than consume the seeds they had been charged with safeguarding.

Vavilov, who had been born in Moscow in 1887, had spent years leading expeditions to more than sixty countries in search of the wild relatives and traditional varieties of the crops on which people depend. His expeditions led him to postulate that cultivated plants had originated in a limited number of regions, now designated centres of diversity, where the greatest variety of each crop could be found. The idea has since been refined and criticised, but it remains influential, and it lent practical direction to the systematic gathering of seeds. The Leningrad collection, which grew to include several hundred thousand samples, was intended as insurance against the failure of any single variety.

His career ended in conflict with the Soviet state. Vavilov defended the principles of genetics at a time when the agronomist Trofim Lysenko, who enjoyed the support of Stalin, insisted that inherited characteristics could be altered by training plants in new conditions. The claim was mistaken but politically expedient, since it promised rapid improvements in harvests, and those who contradicted it jeopardised their careers and their liberty. Vavilov was arrested in 1940 and sentenced to death, a penalty that was later commuted. He died in a prison in Saratov in 1943, of starvation, while the collection that he had built was still being defended by his former colleagues.

The story of Leningrad is sometimes recounted as a parable of devotion to science, and it merits remembrance as such. It is also a reminder of why such collections exist. The varieties of crops that farmers grow today represent only a fraction of those once cultivated, since modern agriculture privileges a handful of high-yielding types that are amenable to large-scale production. Some estimates suggest that a large proportion of the genetic diversity in crops was lost during the twentieth century, though the figures are uncertain and disputed. The danger is that a pathogen or a shift in climate could devastate a widely planted variety, and the traits that might have afforded protection, such as resistance to a particular fungus, may already have vanished along with the older varieties that possessed them.

Seed banks are the response to this risk. Hundreds of them now exist around the world, storing samples of crops and their wild relatives under cold, dry conditions that keep the seeds alive for decades or longer. Because any individual repository may be damaged by war, mismanagement or natural disaster, a further layer of safeguard has been devised. In 2008, a facility known as the Svalbard Global Seed Vault opened in a mountain on an Arctic island in Norway, where the surrounding rock is naturally frozen. It does not own the seeds that it houses, which remain the property of the institutions that deposited them, but it keeps duplicates in safe custody, and it was designed to accommodate several million samples.

The vault has already been used. In 2015, researchers working for an agricultural institute that had been based in Aleppo, in Syria, withdrew seeds for the first time, because the civil war had made it impossible to maintain the original collection there. The institute used the copies to rebuild its stocks at new sites in other countries, which showed that the principle of duplication could work in practice. The episode amounted to a modest vindication of the reasoning that had once motivated Vavilov's staff, and it demonstrated the purpose of a seed bank more persuasively than any argument could.

Seed banks cannot solve the problems of agriculture on their own. A sample in a freezer preserves a variety but not the knowledge of how to cultivate it, nor the farming communities that engendered it, and the collections themselves are costly to maintain and incompletely documented. Even so, they represent a form of long-term planning that is rare in public life: a commitment to preserve something whose value may be required only in some future emergency that no one can foresee. It is a commitment that, in Leningrad, was kept at a very high price.

o: A. Vavilov's collection shows why seed banks matter, and modern banks protect crop diversity by keeping duplicates, though they cannot solve every problem.
B. Seed banks are no longer needed because modern farms grow enough varieties.

D. Vavilov invented the first seed bank in the world while in prison.

o: A. It proved that genetics was a false science.

o: A. To own and sell the seeds it receives from other countries.

o: A. They are the only way to preserve farming knowledge.
