cmp/128.title: The Mystery of Easter Island
cmp/128.src: Hunt and Lipo, The Statues That Walked (2011); Hunt and Lipo (2012)
p: Easter Island is one of the most isolated inhabited places on the planet, and its remoteness is a large part of its mystery. It lies in the Pacific Ocean, more than three thousand kilometres from the coast of South America, and the nearest inhabited island is more than a thousand kilometres away. Yet when a Dutch expedition arrived there on Easter Sunday in 1722, they were astonished to find hundreds of enormous stone statues standing across the landscape. The people who made them had vanished from the pages of history, and the question of how they achieved it has intrigued visitors ever since.

The statues are called moai, and there are nearly a thousand of them. They were skilfully carved from volcanic rock between about the thirteenth and the seventeenth centuries by the Polynesian settlers who arrived on the island and called it Rapa Nui. Most of the statues represent a human head and torso, and the average height is about four metres, although the tallest one that was ever erected is almost ten metres high. Some weigh more than eighty tonnes.

The most perplexing question is how the carvers managed to move them. Most of the statues were made in a single quarry, and many were transported for several kilometres to platforms along the coast. Old stories told by the islanders claimed that the statues had walked. In 2012, researchers tested a theory that closely matches these legends. They tied ropes around the head of a replica statue, and a team of people rocked it from side to side, so that it moved forward in a series of small steps. The experiment succeeded, which suggests that the old accounts may preserve a memory of a genuine method.

Another famous mystery concerns what happened to the island's society. A popular story, told in many books, holds that the settlers cut down all of the trees in order to move the statues, destroyed their own environment and then died out. Some scientists now consider this account to be an oversimplification, and they have challenged its main conclusions. They point out that rats, which arrived with the first settlers, probably ate the seeds of the palm trees and prevented the forest from recovering. Evidence from excavations suggests that the population was not as large as was once believed, and that the people adapted to the loss of the forest by using stones to protect their crops.

Whatever the true explanation, the island's population fell dramatically after Europeans arrived. Diseases, slave raids and conflict reduced the number of inhabitants to only about a hundred by 1877. Nevertheless, the descendants of the original settlers survived, and today the people of Rapa Nui have kept their language and their traditions alive.

The statues themselves have also found a new role. Many of them have been restored and are protected as part of a national park, which attracts visitors from all over the world. They remain a powerful reminder that a small community, cooperating with limited resources, can accomplish remarkable things, and that the achievements of ancient societies deserve our respect. They also teach us to be careful about accepting a single dramatic story as the whole truth.

q.e: The scientists say the popular story leaves out important facts.
o: A. a new discovery.
B. a very detailed study.
C. an explanation that is too simple.
D. a famous legend.

q.q: What lesson does the writer draw at the end?
o: A. Ancient societies knew very little.
B. Always believe the oldest stories.
C. Visitors should avoid the island.
D. Be careful about accepting a single dramatic story as the whole truth.

q.q: The statues are called moai.
By 1877, the island's population had risen to several thousand.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says only about a hundred.

q.q: Most statues were made in many different quarries around the island.
The statues were carved from ____ rock.
The settlers used stones to protect their ____ after the forest was lost.
The statues are protected as part of a national ____.

ps.e: Easter Island is one of the most isolated inhabited places on the planet, and its remoteness is a large part of its mystery.
ps.b: ইস্টার দ্বীপ পৃথিবীর সবচেয়ে বিচ্ছিন্ন বসতিপূর্ণ জায়গাগুলোর একটি, আর এর দূরত্বই এর রহস্যের বড় একটি অংশ।

ps.e: It lies in the Pacific Ocean, more than three thousand kilometres from the coast of South America, and the nearest inhabited island is more than a thousand kilometres away.
ps.b: এটি প্রশান্ত মহাসাগরে, দক্ষিণ আমেরিকার উপকূল থেকে তিন হাজার কিলোমিটারেরও বেশি দূরে, আর সবচেয়ে কাছের বসতিপূর্ণ দ্বীপ এক হাজার কিলোমিটারেরও বেশি দূরে।

ps.e: Yet when a Dutch expedition arrived there on Easter Sunday in 1722, they were astonished to find hundreds of enormous stone statues standing across the landscape.
ps.b: তবু ১৭২২ সালের ইস্টার রবিবারে একটি ডাচ অভিযাত্রী দল যখন সেখানে পৌঁছাল, তারা অবাক হয়ে দেখল ভূদৃশ্যজুড়ে শত শত বিশাল পাথরের মূর্তি দাঁড়িয়ে আছে।

ps.e: The people who made them had vanished from the pages of history, and the question of how they achieved it has intrigued visitors ever since.
ps.b: যারা এগুলো বানিয়েছিল তারা ইতিহাসের পাতা থেকে হারিয়ে গিয়েছিল, আর কীভাবে তারা এটি করেছিল সেই প্রশ্ন তখন থেকে দর্শনার্থীদের কৌতূহলী করে রেখেছে।

ps.e: The statues are called moai, and there are nearly a thousand of them.
ps.b: মূর্তিগুলোকে বলা হয় মোয়াই, আর এগুলোর সংখ্যা প্রায় এক হাজার।

ps.e: They were skilfully carved from volcanic rock between about the thirteenth and the seventeenth centuries by the Polynesian settlers who arrived on the island and called it Rapa Nui.
ps.b: পলিনেশীয় বসতি স্থাপনকারীরা, যারা দ্বীপে এসে এর নাম দিয়েছিল রাপা নুই, তারা এগুলো দক্ষতার সঙ্গে আগ্নেয় শিলা কেটে ত্রয়োদশ থেকে সপ্তদশ শতাব্দীর মধ্যে তৈরি করেছিল।

ps.e: Most of the statues represent a human head and torso, and the average height is about four metres, although the tallest one that was ever erected is almost ten metres high.
ps.b: বেশিরভাগ মূর্তি একটি মানুষের মাথা ও ধড় প্রকাশ করে, আর গড় উচ্চতা প্রায় চার মিটার, যদিও এ পর্যন্ত খাড়া করা সবচেয়ে উঁচুটি প্রায় দশ মিটার।

ps.e: Some weigh more than eighty tonnes.
ps.b: কিছু মূর্তির ওজন আশি টনেরও বেশি।

ps.e: The most perplexing question is how the carvers managed to move them.
ps.b: সবচেয়ে বিভ্রান্তিকর প্রশ্নটি হলো কারিগরেরা এগুলো সরাতে পারল কীভাবে।

ps.e: Most of the statues were made in a single quarry, and many were transported for several kilometres to platforms along the coast.
ps.b: বেশিরভাগ মূর্তি একটিমাত্র পাথরের খনিতে তৈরি হয়েছিল, আর অনেকগুলো কয়েক কিলোমিটার পথ পেরিয়ে উপকূলের বেদিতে নিয়ে যাওয়া হয়েছিল।

ps.e: Old stories told by the islanders claimed that the statues had walked.
ps.b: দ্বীপবাসীদের বলা পুরোনো গল্পে দাবি করা হতো মূর্তিগুলো হেঁটে গিয়েছিল।

ps.e: In 2012, researchers tested a theory that closely matches these legends.
ps.b: ২০১২ সালে গবেষকেরা এই কিংবদন্তির সঙ্গে কাছাকাছি মিল রাখা একটি তত্ত্ব পরীক্ষা করলেন।

ps.e: They tied ropes around the head of a replica statue, and a team of people rocked it from side to side, so that it moved forward in a series of small steps.
ps.b: তাঁরা একটি নকল মূর্তির মাথার চারপাশে দড়ি বাঁধলেন, আর একদল মানুষ সেটিকে পাশ থেকে পাশে দোলাল, ফলে ছোট ছোট পদক্ষেপে সেটি সামনে এগিয়ে গেল।

ps.e: The experiment succeeded, which suggests that the old accounts may preserve a memory of a genuine method.
ps.b: পরীক্ষাটি সফল হলো, যা ইঙ্গিত দেয় যে পুরোনো বর্ণনাগুলো হয়তো সত্যিকারের একটি পদ্ধতির স্মৃতি ধরে রেখেছে।

ps.e: Another famous mystery concerns what happened to the island's society.
ps.b: আরেকটি বিখ্যাত রহস্য হলো দ্বীপের সমাজের কী হয়েছিল।

ps.e: A popular story, told in many books, holds that the settlers cut down all of the trees in order to move the statues, destroyed their own environment and then died out.
ps.b: অনেক বইয়ে বলা একটি জনপ্রিয় গল্প বলে যে বসতি স্থাপনকারীরা মূর্তি সরানোর জন্য সব গাছ কেটে ফেলেছিল, নিজেদের পরিবেশ ধ্বংস করেছিল এবং তারপর নিঃশেষ হয়ে গিয়েছিল।

ps.e: Some scientists now consider this account to be an oversimplification, and they have challenged its main conclusions.
ps.b: কিছু বিজ্ঞানী এখন এই বিবরণকে অতিসরলীকরণ মনে করেন, আর তাঁরা এর মূল সিদ্ধান্তগুলোকে চ্যালেঞ্জ করেছেন।

ps.e: They point out that rats, which arrived with the first settlers, probably ate the seeds of the palm trees and prevented the forest from recovering.
ps.b: তাঁরা দেখান যে ইঁদুর, যেগুলো প্রথম বসতি স্থাপনকারীদের সঙ্গে এসেছিল, সম্ভবত পাম গাছের বীজ খেয়ে ফেলেছিল এবং বনকে আবার গজাতে দেয়নি।

ps.e: Evidence from excavations suggests that the population was not as large as was once believed, and that the people adapted to the loss of the forest by using stones to protect their crops.
ps.b: খননকাজের প্রমাণ ইঙ্গিত দেয় যে জনসংখ্যা একসময় যতটা বড় বলে বিশ্বাস করা হতো ততটা ছিল না, আর বনের ক্ষতির সঙ্গে মানুষ ফসল রক্ষায় পাথর ব্যবহার করে খাপ খাইয়ে নিয়েছিল।

ps.e: Whatever the true explanation, the island's population fell dramatically after Europeans arrived.
ps.b: আসল ব্যাখ্যা যা-ই হোক, ইউরোপীয়রা আসার পর দ্বীপের জনসংখ্যা নাটকীয়ভাবে কমে গিয়েছিল।

ps.e: Diseases, slave raids and conflict reduced the number of inhabitants to only about a hundred by 1877.
ps.b: রোগব্যাধি, দাস-ধরার অভিযান আর সংঘর্ষ ১৮৭৭ সাল নাগাদ বাসিন্দার সংখ্যা মাত্র প্রায় একশোয় নামিয়ে এনেছিল।

ps.e: Nevertheless, the descendants of the original settlers survived, and today the people of Rapa Nui have kept their language and their traditions alive.
ps.b: তবু আদি বসতি স্থাপনকারীদের বংশধরেরা টিকে গিয়েছিল, আর আজ রাপা নুইয়ের মানুষ তাদের ভাষা ও ঐতিহ্য বাঁচিয়ে রেখেছে।

ps.e: The statues themselves have also found a new role.
ps.b: মূর্তিগুলোও এখন একটি নতুন ভূমিকা পেয়েছে।

ps.e: Many of them have been restored and are protected as part of a national park, which attracts visitors from all over the world.
ps.b: এগুলোর অনেকটি সংস্কার করা হয়েছে এবং একটি জাতীয় উদ্যানের অংশ হিসেবে সুরক্ষিত, যা সারা বিশ্ব থেকে দর্শনার্থী টানে।

ps.e: They remain a powerful reminder that a small community, cooperating with limited resources, can accomplish remarkable things, and that the achievements of ancient societies deserve our respect.
ps.b: এগুলো এক শক্তিশালী স্মারক যে সীমিত সম্পদ নিয়ে একসঙ্গে কাজ করে একটি ছোট সম্প্রদায়ও অসাধারণ কিছু করতে পারে, আর প্রাচীন সমাজের কীর্তি আমাদের শ্রদ্ধার যোগ্য।

ps.e: They also teach us to be careful about accepting a single dramatic story as the whole truth.
ps.b: এগুলো আমাদের এটাও শেখায় যে একটিমাত্র নাটকীয় গল্পকে পুরো সত্য বলে মেনে নেওয়ার ব্যাপারে সতর্ক থাকতে হবে।

cmp/129.title: Marie Curie: A Life in Two Sciences
cmp/129.src: Nobel Foundation biographies; Quinn, Marie Curie: A Life (1995)
p: In 1903, a Polish scientist working in Paris became the first woman ever to win a Nobel Prize. Eight years later, she won a second one, in a different subject, and no one has since repeated that achievement in two different sciences. Her name was Marie Curie, and her story is one of extraordinary determination, intellectual courage and personal sacrifice.

She was born in Warsaw in 1867, at a time when Poland was ruled by foreign powers and women were excluded from higher education there. Marie worked as a governess to accumulate enough money, and in 1891 she travelled to Paris to study physics and mathematics at the Sorbonne. She lived in a tiny room, often went hungry and endured bitterly cold winters, but she graduated at the top of her class.

In Paris she met Pierre Curie, a respected physicist, and they married in 1895. Together, they began to investigate a mysterious kind of energy that had recently been detected in the mineral uranium. Marie hypothesised that other substances might emit the same rays, and she coined the term for the phenomenon: radioactivity. Working in a poorly equipped, leaking shed, the couple spent years processing tonnes of rock to extract tiny amounts of new elements. In 1898, they announced two discoveries, which they called polonium, after her homeland, and radium.

In 1903, Marie and Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with another scientist, Henri Becquerel. Three years later, tragedy struck when Pierre was killed in a street accident in Paris. Marie was devastated, but she resolved to continue their research, and she became the first woman to teach at the Sorbonne. In 1911, she received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for her discovery and study of radium and polonium.

When the First World War began, she saw a different way of using her knowledge. Surgeons needed X-rays to locate bullets and fractures, but the machines were installed in hospitals far from the battlefields. Curie helped to equip vehicles with X-ray machines, and these mobile units, which people nicknamed little Curies, travelled to the front line. She also trained women to operate the machines, and it is estimated that more than a million wounded soldiers were examined with the assistance of her equipment.

At that time, nobody fully appreciated how hazardous radiation was. Marie carried small tubes of radioactive material in her pockets and kept them in her desk drawer, admiring the pale glow they gave off in the dark. She died in 1934 of a serious disease of the blood, which was almost certainly caused by years of exposure to radiation. Her notebooks are still radioactive today, and they are kept in lead-lined boxes, so that visitors who wish to read them must sign a form first.

Her legacy extends far beyond her own discoveries, and it has transformed modern medicine and physics. Radiation is now used to treat cancer and to take medical images, and the institute that she founded in Paris continues to carry out research. Marie Curie demonstrated that a determined person could overcome poverty and prejudice, and her example still inspires young scientists around the world.

ps.e: In 1903, a Polish scientist working in Paris became the first woman ever to win a Nobel Prize.
ps.b: ১৯০৩ সালে প্যারিসে কর্মরত এক পোলিশ বিজ্ঞানী নোবেল পুরস্কার জয়ী প্রথম নারী হলেন।

ps.e: Eight years later, she won a second one, in a different subject, and no one has since repeated that achievement in two different sciences.
ps.b: আট বছর পরে তিনি আলাদা একটি বিষয়ে দ্বিতীয় পুরস্কারটিও জিতলেন, আর এরপর কেউ দুটি ভিন্ন বিজ্ঞানে এই কীর্তির পুনরাবৃত্তি করেননি।

ps.e: Her name was Marie Curie, and her story is one of extraordinary determination, intellectual courage and personal sacrifice.
ps.b: তাঁর নাম মারি কুরি, আর তাঁর গল্প অসাধারণ দৃঢ়তা, বুদ্ধিবৃত্তিক সাহস ও ব্যক্তিগত ত্যাগের গল্প।

ps.e: She was born in Warsaw in 1867, at a time when Poland was ruled by foreign powers and women were excluded from higher education there.
ps.b: তিনি ১৮৬৭ সালে ওয়ারশতে জন্মেছিলেন, এমন সময়ে যখন পোল্যান্ড বিদেশি শক্তির শাসনে ছিল আর নারীদের সেখানে উচ্চশিক্ষা থেকে বাদ রাখা হতো।

ps.e: Marie worked as a governess to accumulate enough money, and in 1891 she travelled to Paris to study physics and mathematics at the Sorbonne.
ps.b: মারি পর্যাপ্ত টাকা জমানোর জন্য গৃহশিক্ষিকার কাজ করলেন, আর ১৮৯১ সালে প্যারিসে গিয়ে সোরবনে পদার্থবিদ্যা ও গণিত পড়তে শুরু করলেন।

ps.e: She lived in a tiny room, often went hungry and endured bitterly cold winters, but she graduated at the top of her class.
ps.b: তিনি একটি ছোট্ট ঘরে থাকতেন, প্রায়ই অভুক্ত থাকতেন, কনকনে শীত সহ্য করতেন, তবু ক্লাসে সবার সেরা হয়ে স্নাতক হলেন।

ps.e: In Paris she met Pierre Curie, a respected physicist, and they married in 1895.
ps.b: প্যারিসে তিনি পিয়ের কুরির সঙ্গে পরিচিত হলেন, একজন সম্মানিত পদার্থবিদ, আর ১৮৯৫ সালে তাঁরা বিয়ে করলেন।

ps.e: Together, they began to investigate a mysterious kind of energy that had recently been detected in the mineral uranium.
ps.b: একসঙ্গে তাঁরা ইউরেনিয়াম খনিজে সদ্য শনাক্ত হওয়া এক রহস্যময় শক্তি নিয়ে গবেষণা শুরু করলেন।

ps.e: Marie hypothesised that other substances might emit the same rays, and she coined the term for the phenomenon: radioactivity.
ps.b: মারি অনুমান করলেন যে অন্য পদার্থও একই রশ্মি ছড়াতে পারে, আর তিনিই ঘটনাটির নাম দিলেন: তেজস্ক্রিয়তা।

ps.e: Working in a poorly equipped, leaking shed, the couple spent years processing tonnes of rock to extract tiny amounts of new elements.
ps.b: খারাপ সরঞ্জামওয়ালা, চুঁইয়ে পড়া একটি চালাঘরে কাজ করে দম্পতি বছরের পর বছর টনের পর টন পাথর প্রক্রিয়া করে নতুন মৌলের সামান্য পরিমাণ আলাদা করলেন।

ps.e: In 1898, they announced two discoveries, which they called polonium, after her homeland, and radium.
ps.b: ১৮৯৮ সালে তাঁরা দুটি আবিষ্কারের ঘোষণা দিলেন, যার নাম দিলেন পোলোনিয়াম, তাঁর জন্মভূমির নামে, এবং রেডিয়াম।

ps.e: In 1903, Marie and Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with another scientist, Henri Becquerel.
ps.b: ১৯০৩ সালে মারি ও পিয়ের আরেক বিজ্ঞানী অঁরি বেকেরেলের সঙ্গে পদার্থবিদ্যায় নোবেল পুরস্কার ভাগ করে নিলেন।

ps.e: Three years later, tragedy struck when Pierre was killed in a street accident in Paris.
ps.b: তিন বছর পরে প্যারিসে একটি সড়ক দুর্ঘটনায় পিয়ের মারা গেলে বিয়োগান্ত ঘটনা ঘটল।

ps.e: Marie was devastated, but she resolved to continue their research, and she became the first woman to teach at the Sorbonne.
ps.b: মারি ভেঙে পড়লেন, কিন্তু তাঁদের গবেষণা চালিয়ে যাওয়ার সংকল্প করলেন, এবং সোরবনে পড়ানো প্রথম নারী হলেন।

ps.e: In 1911, she received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for her discovery and study of radium and polonium.
ps.b: ১৯১১ সালে তিনি রেডিয়াম ও পোলোনিয়াম আবিষ্কার ও গবেষণার জন্য রসায়নে নোবেল পুরস্কার পেলেন।

ps.e: When the First World War began, she saw a different way of using her knowledge.
ps.b: প্রথম বিশ্বযুদ্ধ শুরু হলে তিনি তাঁর জ্ঞান ব্যবহার করার একটি আলাদা উপায় দেখতে পেলেন।

ps.e: Surgeons needed X-rays to locate bullets and fractures, but the machines were installed in hospitals far from the battlefields.
ps.b: সার্জনদের গুলি ও হাড় ভাঙার জায়গা খুঁজে বের করতে এক্স-রে দরকার ছিল, কিন্তু যন্ত্রগুলো ছিল যুদ্ধক্ষেত্র থেকে বহু দূরের হাসপাতালে বসানো।

ps.e: Curie helped to equip vehicles with X-ray machines, and these mobile units, which people nicknamed little Curies, travelled to the front line.
ps.b: কুরি যানবাহনে এক্স-রে যন্ত্র বসাতে সাহায্য করলেন, আর এই চলমান ইউনিটগুলো, যাদের মানুষ ডাকত ছোট কুরি, সম্মুখ সারিতে ছুটে যেত।

ps.e: She also trained women to operate the machines, and it is estimated that more than a million wounded soldiers were examined with the assistance of her equipment.
ps.b: তিনি নারীদের যন্ত্র চালানোর প্রশিক্ষণও দিলেন, আর অনুমান করা হয় যে তাঁর সরঞ্জামের সাহায্যে দশ লাখেরও বেশি আহত সৈনিকের পরীক্ষা করা হয়েছিল।

ps.e: At that time, nobody fully appreciated how hazardous radiation was.
ps.b: সেই সময় তেজস্ক্রিয়তা কতটা বিপজ্জনক তা কেউ পুরোপুরি বুঝত না।

ps.e: Marie carried small tubes of radioactive material in her pockets and kept them in her desk drawer, admiring the pale glow they gave off in the dark.
ps.b: মারি ছোট ছোট তেজস্ক্রিয় পদার্থের নল পকেটে নিয়ে ঘুরতেন আর ডেস্কের ড্রয়ারে রাখতেন, আর অন্ধকারে সেগুলোর ফ্যাকাশে আভা দেখে মুগ্ধ হতেন।

ps.e: She died in 1934 of a serious disease of the blood, which was almost certainly caused by years of exposure to radiation.
ps.b: তিনি ১৯৩৪ সালে রক্তের একটি গুরুতর রোগে মারা যান, যা প্রায় নিশ্চিতভাবেই বহু বছরের তেজস্ক্রিয়তার সংস্পর্শের ফল।

ps.e: Her notebooks are still radioactive today, and they are kept in lead-lined boxes, so that visitors who wish to read them must sign a form first.
ps.b: তাঁর নোটবইগুলো আজও তেজস্ক্রিয়, আর সেগুলো সিসার আবরণে ঢাকা বাক্সে রাখা হয়, ফলে যাঁরা সেগুলো পড়তে চান তাঁদের আগে একটি ফর্মে সই করতে হয়।

ps.e: Her legacy extends far beyond her own discoveries, and it has transformed modern medicine and physics.
ps.b: তাঁর উত্তরাধিকার তাঁর নিজের আবিষ্কারের চেয়েও অনেক বেশি বিস্তৃত, আর এটি আধুনিক চিকিৎসা ও পদার্থবিদ্যাকে বদলে দিয়েছে।

ps.e: Radiation is now used to treat cancer and to take medical images, and the institute that she founded in Paris continues to carry out research.
ps.b: বিকিরণ এখন ক্যানসারের চিকিৎসায় ও চিকিৎসা-ছবি তুলতে ব্যবহৃত হয়, আর তিনি প্যারিসে যে ইনস্টিটিউট প্রতিষ্ঠা করেছিলেন তা এখনো গবেষণা চালিয়ে যাচ্ছে।

ps.e: Marie Curie demonstrated that a determined person could overcome poverty and prejudice, and her example still inspires young scientists around the world.
ps.b: মারি কুরি দেখিয়েছেন যে একজন দৃঢ়প্রতিজ্ঞ মানুষ দারিদ্র্য ও কুসংস্কার জয় করতে পারে, আর তাঁর উদাহরণ আজও সারা বিশ্বের তরুণ বিজ্ঞানীদের অনুপ্রাণিত করে।

cmp/130.title: Why Is the Sky Blue?
cmp/130.src: Rayleigh (1871, 1899); Bohren and Huffman, Absorption and Scattering of Light
p: On a clear day, the sky above us is an intense blue, yet at sunset the same sky can turn orange, pink and red. Inquisitive children often ask why, and the answer turns out to be an elegant piece of physics that anyone can understand. The explanation begins with the nature of sunlight itself.

Sunlight appears white, but it is actually a combination of all the colours of the rainbow, each of which has a different wavelength. Blue light has a short wavelength, while red light has a much longer one. When sunlight penetrates the Earth's atmosphere, it collides with the gases that make up the air, mainly nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules are far smaller than the wavelength of light, and they scatter the light in all directions, a process known as Rayleigh scattering. The British physicist Lord Rayleigh worked out the mathematics of this effect in the nineteenth century, and his explanation has remained fundamentally unchanged.

The crucial point is that short waves are scattered far more strongly than long waves. Blue light is scattered about five or six times more than red light, so the atmosphere is filled with blue light travelling in every direction. When you look at any part of the sky away from the sun, a portion of that scattered blue light reaches your eyes. This accounts for the blue sky, but it leaves a question unanswered.

Violet light has an even shorter wavelength than blue, so in theory it should be scattered even more. There are two main reasons why we do not perceive a violet sky. First, the sun emits less violet light than blue light. Second, some of it is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are considerably less sensitive to violet in any case. The combination of these factors makes the sky appear blue rather than violet.

At sunrise and sunset, the sun is low on the horizon, and its light has to travel through a considerably thicker layer of air before it reaches us. Along that extended path, most of the blue light is scattered away from our line of sight, and only the longer wavelengths of orange and red remain. That is why the sun appears red when it is close to the horizon, and why the clouds around it glow with colour. Dust, smoke and microscopic particles of pollution can make a sunset even more spectacular. After a major volcanic eruption, the additional particles in the upper atmosphere have sometimes produced vivid red sunsets in places thousands of kilometres away.

The same principle can be used to explain other familiar sights. Clouds appear white because the water droplets in them are much larger than air molecules and scatter all colours of light almost equally. The sea often appears blue for a different reason, because water absorbs red light and transmits more blue, although it also reflects the colour of the sky.

On other planets, the sky may look strikingly different. On Mars, for example, the fine dust suspended in the atmosphere gives the daytime sky a butterscotch colour, and sunsets there are blue. A simple question from a child therefore leads us towards the nature of light, the structure of the atmosphere and even the appearance of distant worlds.

q.q: Which statement best sums up the passage?
q.e: The passage explains scattering and its effects.
o: A. The sky is blue because it reflects the colour of the sea.
B. The sky changes colour only because of pollution.
C. The sky is blue because air molecules scatter short-wavelength light, and the same principle explains red sunsets and other sights.
D. The sky is blue because of the dust in the atmosphere.

q.q: What is sunlight actually made of?
o: A. Only blue and red light.
B. Only white light.
C. A mixture of all the colours of the rainbow.
D. Light of one single wavelength.

q.q: Which colour is scattered more strongly, blue or red?
o: A. Blue, because it has a shorter wavelength.
B. Neither is scattered at all.
C. Both are scattered equally.
D. Red, because it has a longer wavelength.

q.q: Why is the sky not violet?
o: A. Violet light cannot travel through air.
B. Violet light is blocked by the clouds.
C. The sun emits less violet light, some is absorbed, and our eyes are less sensitive to it.
D. Violet light is scattered less than red.

q.q: Why does the sun look red at sunset?
o: A. Its light passes through more air, and most of the blue is scattered away.
B. The sea reflects red light upward.
C. The clouds paint the sun red.
D. The sun becomes hotter at sunset.

q.q: In paragraph 1, the word "intense" is closest in meaning to
q.e: The sky is a deep, strong blue.
o: A. very strong.
B. very rare.
C. very pale.
D. very sudden.

q.q: What point does the writer make in the final sentence?
o: A. Children understand physics better than adults.
B. Distant worlds have no atmosphere at all.
C. A child's simple question can lead to big ideas about light and the atmosphere.
D. Only scientists can explain the colours of the sky.

q.q: Rayleigh scattering is named after a British physicist.
Clouds appear white because their droplets scatter all colours almost equally.
The daytime sky on Mars is blue.
The gases in the air are mainly nitrogen and ____.
After a volcanic eruption, extra ____ in the upper atmosphere have produced vivid red sunsets.
Sunsets on Mars are ____.

ps.e: On a clear day, the sky above us is an intense blue, yet at sunset the same sky can turn orange, pink and red.
ps.b: পরিষ্কার দিনে আমাদের মাথার ওপরের আকাশ গাঢ় নীল, অথচ সূর্যাস্তের সময় একই আকাশ কমলা, গোলাপি ও লাল হয়ে যেতে পারে।

ps.e: Inquisitive children often ask why, and the answer turns out to be an elegant piece of physics that anyone can understand.
ps.b: কৌতূহলী শিশুরা প্রায়ই জিজ্ঞেস করে কেন, আর উত্তরটি পদার্থবিদ্যার এমন এক মার্জিত ব্যাখ্যা, যা যে-কেউ বুঝতে পারে।

ps.e: The explanation begins with the nature of sunlight itself.
ps.b: ব্যাখ্যাটি শুরু হয় সূর্যের আলোর প্রকৃতি দিয়ে।

ps.e: Sunlight appears white, but it is actually a combination of all the colours of the rainbow, each of which has a different wavelength.
ps.b: সূর্যের আলো সাদা দেখায়, কিন্তু আসলে এটি রংধনুর সব রঙের একটি মিশ্রণ, যার প্রতিটির তরঙ্গদৈর্ঘ্য আলাদা।

ps.e: Blue light has a short wavelength, while red light has a much longer one.
ps.b: নীল আলোর তরঙ্গদৈর্ঘ্য ছোট, আর লাল আলোর তরঙ্গদৈর্ঘ্য অনেক বড়।

ps.e: When sunlight penetrates the Earth's atmosphere, it collides with the gases that make up the air, mainly nitrogen and oxygen.
ps.b: সূর্যের আলো যখন পৃথিবীর বায়ুমণ্ডলে প্রবেশ করে, তখন বাতাস গঠনকারী গ্যাসগুলোর সঙ্গে, প্রধানত নাইট্রোজেন ও অক্সিজেনের সঙ্গে, ধাক্কা খায়।

ps.e: These molecules are far smaller than the wavelength of light, and they scatter the light in all directions, a process known as Rayleigh scattering.
ps.b: এই অণুগুলো আলোর তরঙ্গদৈর্ঘ্যের চেয়ে অনেক ছোট, আর তারা আলোকে সব দিকে ছড়িয়ে দেয়, যে প্রক্রিয়াকে বলা হয় রেলে বিক্ষেপণ।

ps.e: The British physicist Lord Rayleigh worked out the mathematics of this effect in the nineteenth century, and his explanation has remained fundamentally unchanged.
ps.b: ব্রিটিশ পদার্থবিদ লর্ড রেলে উনবিংশ শতাব্দীতে এই প্রভাবের গণিত বের করেছিলেন, আর তাঁর ব্যাখ্যা মূলত অপরিবর্তিত রয়েছে।

ps.e: The crucial point is that short waves are scattered far more strongly than long waves.
ps.b: মূল কথাটি হলো, ছোট তরঙ্গ বড় তরঙ্গের চেয়ে অনেক বেশি জোরে বিক্ষিপ্ত হয়।

ps.e: Blue light is scattered about five or six times more than red light, so the atmosphere is filled with blue light travelling in every direction.
ps.b: নীল আলো লাল আলোর চেয়ে প্রায় পাঁচ-ছয় গুণ বেশি বিক্ষিপ্ত হয়, ফলে বায়ুমণ্ডল সব দিকে ছুটে চলা নীল আলোয় ভরে যায়।

ps.e: When you look at any part of the sky away from the sun, a portion of that scattered blue light reaches your eyes.
ps.b: সূর্য থেকে দূরে আকাশের যেকোনো অংশে তাকালে সেই বিক্ষিপ্ত নীল আলোর একটি অংশ আপনার চোখে এসে পৌঁছায়।

ps.e: This accounts for the blue sky, but it leaves a question unanswered.
ps.b: এটি নীল আকাশের ব্যাখ্যা দেয়, কিন্তু একটি প্রশ্ন অমীমাংসিত রেখে যায়।

ps.e: Violet light has an even shorter wavelength than blue, so in theory it should be scattered even more.
ps.b: বেগুনি আলোর তরঙ্গদৈর্ঘ্য নীলের চেয়েও ছোট, তাই তত্ত্বে এটি আরও বেশি বিক্ষিপ্ত হওয়ার কথা।

ps.e: There are two main reasons why we do not perceive a violet sky.
ps.b: আমরা কেন বেগুনি আকাশ দেখি না তার দুটি প্রধান কারণ আছে।

ps.e: First, the sun emits less violet light than blue light.
ps.b: প্রথমত, সূর্য নীলের চেয়ে কম বেগুনি আলো নির্গত করে।

ps.e: Second, some of it is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are considerably less sensitive to violet in any case.
ps.b: দ্বিতীয়ত, এর কিছু অংশ বায়ুমণ্ডলের ওপরের দিকে শোষিত হয়ে যায়, আর আমাদের চোখও যেকোনোভাবে বেগুনির প্রতি অনেক কম সংবেদনশীল।

ps.e: The combination of these factors makes the sky appear blue rather than violet.
ps.b: এই কারণগুলোর সম্মিলিত ফলে আকাশ বেগুনি নয়, নীল দেখায়।

ps.e: At sunrise and sunset, the sun is low on the horizon, and its light has to travel through a considerably thicker layer of air before it reaches us.
ps.b: সূর্যোদয় ও সূর্যাস্তের সময় সূর্য দিগন্তের কাছে থাকে, আর তার আলোকে আমাদের কাছে পৌঁছানোর আগে অনেক পুরু বাতাসের স্তর পেরোতে হয়।

ps.e: Along that extended path, most of the blue light is scattered away from our line of sight, and only the longer wavelengths of orange and red remain.
ps.b: সেই দীর্ঘ পথে নীল আলোর বেশিরভাগই আমাদের দৃষ্টিরেখা থেকে ছড়িয়ে সরে যায়, আর কেবল কমলা ও লালের দীর্ঘ তরঙ্গদৈর্ঘ্যগুলো অবশিষ্ট থাকে।

ps.e: That is why the sun appears red when it is close to the horizon, and why the clouds around it glow with colour.
ps.b: সে কারণেই সূর্য দিগন্তের কাছে থাকলে লাল দেখায়, আর তার চারপাশের মেঘ রঙে জ্বলজ্বল করে।

ps.e: Dust, smoke and microscopic particles of pollution can make a sunset even more spectacular.
ps.b: ধুলো, ধোঁয়া ও দূষণের অতি ক্ষুদ্র কণা সূর্যাস্তকে আরও দর্শনীয় করে তুলতে পারে।

ps.e: After a major volcanic eruption, the additional particles in the upper atmosphere have sometimes produced vivid red sunsets in places thousands of kilometres away.
ps.b: একটি বড় আগ্নেয়গিরির অগ্ন্যুৎপাতের পর ওপরের বায়ুমণ্ডলের বাড়তি কণা কখনো কখনো হাজার হাজার কিলোমিটার দূরের জায়গায় উজ্জ্বল লাল সূর্যাস্ত তৈরি করেছে।

ps.e: The same principle can be used to explain other familiar sights.
ps.b: একই নীতি দিয়ে অন্যান্য পরিচিত দৃশ্যও ব্যাখ্যা করা যায়।

ps.e: Clouds appear white because the water droplets in them are much larger than air molecules and scatter all colours of light almost equally.
ps.b: মেঘ সাদা দেখায়, কারণ তাদের ভেতরের পানির ফোঁটা বাতাসের অণুর চেয়ে অনেক বড় আর সব রঙের আলোকে প্রায় সমানভাবে ছড়িয়ে দেয়।

ps.e: The sea often appears blue for a different reason, because water absorbs red light and transmits more blue, although it also reflects the colour of the sky.
ps.b: সাগর প্রায়ই নীল দেখায় একটি আলাদা কারণে, কারণ পানি লাল আলো শোষণ করে আর বেশি নীল আলো পার হতে দেয়, যদিও এটি আকাশের রংও প্রতিফলিত করে।

ps.e: On other planets, the sky may look strikingly different.
ps.b: অন্যান্য গ্রহে আকাশ চোখে পড়ার মতো আলাদা দেখাতে পারে।

ps.e: On Mars, for example, the fine dust suspended in the atmosphere gives the daytime sky a butterscotch colour, and sunsets there are blue.
ps.b: যেমন মঙ্গলে বায়ুমণ্ডলে ভাসমান সূক্ষ্ম ধুলো দিনের আকাশকে বাটারস্কচের রং দেয়, আর সেখানকার সূর্যাস্ত নীল।

ps.e: A simple question from a child therefore leads us towards the nature of light, the structure of the atmosphere and even the appearance of distant worlds.
ps.b: একটি শিশুর সরল প্রশ্ন তাই আমাদের আলোর প্রকৃতি, বায়ুমণ্ডলের গঠন, এমনকি দূরের জগৎগুলোর চেহারার দিকে নিয়ে যায়।

cmp/131.title: How Chocolate Became Sweet
cmp/131.src: Coe and Coe, The True History of Chocolate (1996); Grivetti and Shapiro, Chocolate: History, Culture, and Heritage (2009)
p: Chocolate is one of the most popular foods on Earth, enjoyed by millions of people every day, but its original form would be almost unrecognisable to anyone who enjoys a bar today. For most of its history, chocolate was a bitter drink, and it was not sweet at all. The story begins in Central and South America, where people first discovered how to use the beans of the cacao tree thousands of years ago.

The ancient Maya and later the Aztecs ground the roasted beans, mixed them with water, and sometimes added chilli, vanilla or honey. They drank the mixture cold and thick, and they considered it a sacred drink, which was reserved for rulers, warriors and religious ceremonies. The beans were so valuable that they were also used as a form of currency, and people even used them to pay taxes.

Spanish explorers encountered chocolate in the early sixteenth century, and they took it back to Europe. At first, they found the taste too harsh, but the Spanish soon discovered that adding sugar and warming the drink made it far more pleasant. For many years, Spain managed to keep the recipe a secret, but it eventually spread across the continent, and drinking chocolate became popular in many courts. By the seventeenth century, drinking chocolate had become a fashionable luxury among the wealthy in cities such as Paris and London. Specialised chocolate houses opened, where wealthy customers could meet, talk and drink the expensive beverage.

Chocolate remained a drink until the nineteenth century, when new inventions transformed it. In 1828, a Dutch chemist named Coenraad van Houten developed a press that removed most of the fat, or cocoa butter, from the beans, leaving a fine powder that mixed more easily with liquid. Then, in 1847, a British company, Fry's, discovered that by adding the cocoa butter back to the powder and sugar, they could make a paste that could be moulded. This was the first solid chocolate bar for eating.

Milk chocolate came later, in 1875, after a Swiss man named Daniel Peter, who lived near a manufacturer of condensed milk, found a way to combine milk with chocolate. His neighbour, Henri Nestlé, helped him to improve the process, and the creamy, sweeter taste proved immensely popular. Soon, factories across Europe and the United States were producing chocolate in enormous quantities, and it became an affordable treat for ordinary families.

Today, chocolate is a global industry worth tens of billions of dollars, but this success has a hidden cost. Most of the world's cocoa is grown by small farmers in West Africa, many of whom earn very little, and there have been serious concerns about child labour on some farms. In response, some companies have started to purchase cocoa that is certified as ethically produced, and consumers are increasingly paying attention to where their chocolate comes from. The next time you unwrap a bar, you may enjoy it more by remembering that it is the result of thousands of years of history.

cmp/132.title: Why Do We Dream?
cmp/132.src: Walker, Why We Sleep (2017); Hobson and McCarley (1977); Stickgold (2005)
p: Every night, while we lie motionless in bed, our minds construct entire worlds, in which we fly over cities, sit examinations we have not prepared for or meet people who died years ago. Dreams have fascinated humanity for thousands of years, and scientists are still debating their purpose. What is certain is that we all dream, even if we seldom remember doing so.

Most vivid dreams occur during a particular stage of sleep known as rapid eye movement sleep, or REM sleep. During this stage, the eyes move rapidly beneath the eyelids, the heart rate rises and the brain becomes almost as active as it is when we are awake. A person who is woken during REM sleep will usually report a dream, whereas a person woken at other times is far less likely to do so. Over a lifetime, we spend several years of our lives dreaming, and the amount of REM sleep in a typical night totals around two hours.

Why do we dream at all? One popular theory holds that dreaming helps the brain to organise memories. During the day, we absorb enormous quantities of information, and sleep seems to play a crucial role in determining which of it should be retained. Experiments have shown that people who sleep after learning a new task often perform considerably better than those who remain awake for the same period. According to this view, dreams may be a by-product of the brain reviewing and reorganising the day's experiences.

A different theory suggests that dreams help us to deal with emotions. Many dreams contain intense emotions such as fear, joy or embarrassment, and some researchers believe that the brain uses REM sleep to reduce the intensity of painful memories. This might explain why a distressing event often seems easier to endure after a good night's sleep.

Other scientists have proposed that dreaming is a kind of rehearsal for dangerous situations. Dreams are full of chases, falls and threats, and rehearsing how to respond to them in a safe environment could have been advantageous for our ancestors. Not every researcher is convinced, and a few argue that dreams have no function whatsoever, but are simply the incidental result of random activity in the brain. Even if that is true, the experience can still be meaningful for the dreamer.

Dreams are bizarre for a reason that is now reasonably well understood. During REM sleep, the parts of the brain responsible for emotion and imagery are very active, whereas the region responsible for logic and planning is much quieter. As a result, impossible events seem perfectly normal while we are dreaming, and only after we wake up do we appreciate how absurd they were. Most people forget the majority of their dreams within minutes of waking. The chemicals that help the brain to form lasting memories are less abundant during REM sleep, which may be why dreams fade so quickly. Writing down a dream immediately after waking is the best way to remember it.

Dreams have also inspired many famous people. The musician Paul McCartney has said that the melody of the song Yesterday came to him in a dream, and the chemist August Kekulé claimed that a dream about a snake biting its own tail helped him to understand the shape of the benzene molecule. These stories may have been exaggerated, but they illustrate how imaginative the sleeping brain can be. Whatever their true purpose, dreams remind us that the mind is never completely at rest. Obtaining sufficient sleep, which for most adults means seven to nine hours, gives the brain the time it requires to carry out its hidden work.

q.q: Which statement best sums up the passage?
q.e: The passage reviews several theories and explains why dreams are strange.
o: A. Scientists have proved that dreams predict the future.
B. Scientists believe that people who do not remember dreams never dream.
C. Scientists agree that dreams are only the result of eating late at night.
D. Scientists have several theories about why we dream, but no single explanation is certain.

q.q: What happens to the body during REM sleep?
o: A. The eyes move rapidly and the brain becomes very active.
B. The brain stops working completely.
C. The body temperature falls sharply.
D. The heart stops for a short time.

q.q: What did experiments show about sleep and learning?
o: A. People who slept after learning often performed better than those who stayed awake.
B. Sleep had no effect on memory.
C. People forgot more after sleeping.
D. People who stayed awake learned faster.

q.q: Why might a bad event seem easier to bear after sleep?
o: A. The brain may reduce the intensity of painful memories during REM sleep.
B. The brain deletes every memory of the event.
C. The dreams show the event in a different way.
D. The body creates new chemicals every morning.

q.q: Why do impossible events seem normal in a dream?
o: A. The dreamer has taken medicine.
B. The dream lasts for a very long time.
C. The eyes are open during the dream.
D. The part of the brain for logic and planning is much quieter.

q.q: In paragraph 5, the word "advantageous" is closest in meaning to
q.e: Practising reactions could have helped our ancestors.
o: A. helpful.
B. unusual.
C. harmful.
D. unnecessary.

q.q: What does the writer say about the stories of McCartney and Kekulé?
o: A. They may have been exaggerated, but they show the sleeping brain's creativity.
B. They are completely false.
C. They show that only famous people dream.
D. They prove that dreams solve scientific problems.

q.q: Most vivid dreams happen during REM sleep.
All researchers agree that dreams have an important function.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says some argue they have none.

q.q: Paul McCartney wrote the melody of Yesterday while he was awake and working.
q.e: Paragraph 7 says it came to him in a dream.

q.q: In a typical night, REM sleep totals around two ____.
Most people forget the majority of their dreams within ____ of waking.
Most adults need seven to nine hours of ____.

ps.e: Every night, while we lie motionless in bed, our minds construct entire worlds, in which we fly over cities, sit examinations we have not prepared for or meet people who died years ago.
ps.b: প্রতি রাতে আমরা যখন বিছানায় নিশ্চল শুয়ে থাকি, তখন আমাদের মন পুরো একেকটি জগৎ গড়ে তোলে, যেখানে আমরা শহরের ওপর দিয়ে উড়ি, যে পরীক্ষার প্রস্তুতি নিইনি তাতে বসি, বা বহু বছর আগে মারা যাওয়া মানুষদের সঙ্গে দেখা করি।

ps.e: Dreams have fascinated humanity for thousands of years, and scientists are still debating their purpose.
ps.b: স্বপ্ন হাজার হাজার বছর ধরে মানবজাতিকে মুগ্ধ করে রেখেছে, আর বিজ্ঞানীরা এখনো এর উদ্দেশ্য নিয়ে বিতর্ক করছেন।

ps.e: What is certain is that we all dream, even if we seldom remember doing so.
ps.b: যা নিশ্চিত তা হলো, আমরা সবাই স্বপ্ন দেখি, এমনকি যদিও কদাচিৎ মনে রাখি।

ps.e: Most vivid dreams occur during a particular stage of sleep known as rapid eye movement sleep, or REM sleep.
ps.b: বেশিরভাগ স্পষ্ট স্বপ্ন ঘুমের এমন একটি নির্দিষ্ট পর্যায়ে ঘটে, যাকে বলা হয় র‍্যাপিড আই মুভমেন্ট ঘুম বা আরইএম ঘুম।

ps.e: During this stage, the eyes move rapidly beneath the eyelids, the heart rate rises and the brain becomes almost as active as it is when we are awake.
ps.b: এই পর্যায়ে চোখের পাতার নিচে চোখ দ্রুত নড়ে, হৃদস্পন্দন বাড়ে, আর মস্তিষ্ক জেগে থাকার সময়ের প্রায় সমান সক্রিয় হয়ে ওঠে।

ps.e: A person who is woken during REM sleep will usually report a dream, whereas a person woken at other times is far less likely to do so.
ps.b: আরইএম ঘুমের সময় জাগানো হলে একজন মানুষ সাধারণত একটি স্বপ্নের কথা বলে, অথচ অন্য সময়ে জাগানো হলে বলার সম্ভাবনা অনেক কম।

ps.e: Over a lifetime, we spend several years of our lives dreaming, and the amount of REM sleep in a typical night totals around two hours.
ps.b: সারা জীবনে আমরা বেশ কয়েক বছর স্বপ্ন দেখে কাটাই, আর একটি সাধারণ রাতে আরইএম ঘুমের মোট পরিমাণ প্রায় দুই ঘণ্টা।

ps.e: Why do we dream at all?
ps.b: আমরা আদৌ কেন স্বপ্ন দেখি?

ps.e: One popular theory holds that dreaming helps the brain to organise memories.
ps.b: একটি জনপ্রিয় তত্ত্ব বলে যে স্বপ্ন মস্তিষ্ককে স্মৃতি গুছিয়ে নিতে সাহায্য করে।

ps.e: During the day, we absorb enormous quantities of information, and sleep seems to play a crucial role in determining which of it should be retained.
ps.b: দিনের বেলায় আমরা বিপুল পরিমাণ তথ্য গ্রহণ করি, আর কোনটি ধরে রাখা হবে তা ঠিক করতে ঘুম গুরুত্বপূর্ণ ভূমিকা রাখে বলে মনে হয়।

ps.e: Experiments have shown that people who sleep after learning a new task often perform considerably better than those who remain awake for the same period.
ps.b: পরীক্ষায় দেখা গেছে, নতুন কাজ শেখার পর যারা ঘুমায়, তারা প্রায়ই একই সময় জেগে থাকা মানুষদের চেয়ে অনেক ভালো করে।

ps.e: According to this view, dreams may be a by-product of the brain reviewing and reorganising the day's experiences.
ps.b: এই মত অনুযায়ী, স্বপ্ন হতে পারে মস্তিষ্ক দিনের অভিজ্ঞতাগুলো পর্যালোচনা ও নতুন করে সাজানোর একটি আনুষঙ্গিক ফল।

ps.e: A different theory suggests that dreams help us to deal with emotions.
ps.b: আরেকটি তত্ত্ব বলে যে স্বপ্ন আমাদের আবেগ সামলাতে সাহায্য করে।

ps.e: Many dreams contain intense emotions such as fear, joy or embarrassment, and some researchers believe that the brain uses REM sleep to reduce the intensity of painful memories.
ps.b: অনেক স্বপ্নে ভয়, আনন্দ বা লজ্জার মতো তীব্র আবেগ থাকে, আর কিছু গবেষক বিশ্বাস করেন যে মস্তিষ্ক আরইএম ঘুম ব্যবহার করে কষ্টদায়ক স্মৃতির তীব্রতা কমায়।

ps.e: This might explain why a distressing event often seems easier to endure after a good night's sleep.
ps.b: এটি ব্যাখ্যা করতে পারে কেন একটি কষ্টদায়ক ঘটনা এক রাতের ভালো ঘুমের পর প্রায়ই সহ্য করা সহজ মনে হয়।

ps.e: Other scientists have proposed that dreaming is a kind of rehearsal for dangerous situations.
ps.b: অন্য বিজ্ঞানীরা প্রস্তাব করেছেন যে স্বপ্ন দেখা বিপজ্জনক পরিস্থিতির এক ধরনের মহড়া।

ps.e: Dreams are full of chases, falls and threats, and rehearsing how to respond to them in a safe environment could have been advantageous for our ancestors.
ps.b: স্বপ্ন তাড়া, পতন ও হুমকিতে ভরা, আর নিরাপদ পরিবেশে সেগুলোর সামনে কীভাবে সাড়া দিতে হয় তার মহড়া দেওয়া আমাদের পূর্বপুরুষদের জন্য সুবিধাজনক হয়ে থাকতে পারে।

ps.e: Not every researcher is convinced, and a few argue that dreams have no function whatsoever, but are simply the incidental result of random activity in the brain.
ps.b: সব গবেষক নিশ্চিত নন, আর কয়েকজন যুক্তি দেন যে স্বপ্নের কোনো কাজই নেই, এটি কেবল মস্তিষ্কের এলোমেলো কার্যকলাপের আনুষঙ্গিক ফল।

ps.e: Even if that is true, the experience can still be meaningful for the dreamer.
ps.b: তা সত্যি হলেও অভিজ্ঞতাটি স্বপ্নদ্রষ্টার কাছে অর্থবহ হতে পারে।

ps.e: Dreams are bizarre for a reason that is now reasonably well understood.
ps.b: স্বপ্ন উদ্ভট হওয়ার একটি কারণ এখন মোটামুটি ভালোভাবে বোঝা গেছে।

ps.e: During REM sleep, the parts of the brain responsible for emotion and imagery are very active, whereas the region responsible for logic and planning is much quieter.
ps.b: আরইএম ঘুমের সময় আবেগ ও চিত্রকল্পের দায়িত্বে থাকা মস্তিষ্কের অংশগুলো খুব সক্রিয় থাকে, অথচ যুক্তি ও পরিকল্পনার দায়িত্বে থাকা অঞ্চলটি অনেক শান্ত থাকে।

ps.e: As a result, impossible events seem perfectly normal while we are dreaming, and only after we wake up do we appreciate how absurd they were.
ps.b: ফলে স্বপ্ন দেখার সময় অসম্ভব ঘটনাকেও পুরোপুরি স্বাভাবিক মনে হয়, আর জেগে ওঠার পরই আমরা বুঝতে পারি সেগুলো কতটা অযৌক্তিক ছিল।

ps.e: Most people forget the majority of their dreams within minutes of waking.
ps.b: বেশিরভাগ মানুষ জেগে ওঠার কয়েক মিনিটের মধ্যে তাদের বেশিরভাগ স্বপ্ন ভুলে যায়।

ps.e: The chemicals that help the brain to form lasting memories are less abundant during REM sleep, which may be why dreams fade so quickly.
ps.b: যেসব রাসায়নিক মস্তিষ্ককে স্থায়ী স্মৃতি গড়তে সাহায্য করে, আরইএম ঘুমের সময় সেগুলো কম থাকে, যা সম্ভবত ব্যাখ্যা করে স্বপ্ন কেন এত দ্রুত মিলিয়ে যায়।

ps.e: Writing down a dream immediately after waking is the best way to remember it.
ps.b: জেগে ওঠার সঙ্গে সঙ্গে স্বপ্নটি লিখে রাখাই সেটি মনে রাখার সবচেয়ে ভালো উপায়।

ps.e: Dreams have also inspired many famous people.
ps.b: স্বপ্ন অনেক বিখ্যাত মানুষকেও অনুপ্রাণিত করেছে।

ps.e: The musician Paul McCartney has said that the melody of the song Yesterday came to him in a dream, and the chemist August Kekulé claimed that a dream about a snake biting its own tail helped him to understand the shape of the benzene molecule.
ps.b: সংগীতশিল্পী পল ম্যাককার্টনি বলেছেন যে ইয়েস্টারডে গানের সুরটি স্বপ্নে তাঁর কাছে এসেছিল, আর রসায়নবিদ আউগুস্ট কেকুলে দাবি করেছিলেন যে নিজের লেজ কামড়ানো একটি সাপের স্বপ্ন তাঁকে বেনজিন অণুর আকৃতি বুঝতে সাহায্য করেছিল।

ps.e: These stories may have been exaggerated, but they illustrate how imaginative the sleeping brain can be.
ps.b: এই গল্পগুলো হয়তো অতিরঞ্জিত, তবু এগুলো দেখায় ঘুমন্ত মস্তিষ্ক কতটা কল্পনাপ্রবণ হতে পারে।

ps.e: Whatever their true purpose, dreams remind us that the mind is never completely at rest.
ps.b: এদের আসল উদ্দেশ্য যা-ই হোক, স্বপ্ন আমাদের মনে করিয়ে দেয় যে মন কখনোই সম্পূর্ণ বিশ্রামে থাকে না।

ps.e: Obtaining sufficient sleep, which for most adults means seven to nine hours, gives the brain the time it requires to carry out its hidden work.
ps.b: পর্যাপ্ত ঘুম, যার মানে বেশিরভাগ প্রাপ্তবয়স্কের জন্য সাত থেকে নয় ঘণ্টা, মস্তিষ্ককে তার লুকানো কাজটি সারার জন্য প্রয়োজনীয় সময় দেয়।

cmp/133.title: How Bats See with Sound
cmp/133.src: Griffin, Listening in the Dark (1958); Spallanzani (1790s)
p: There is an old expression, as blind as a bat, but it could hardly be more mistaken. Bats can see perfectly well, and some species have excellent eyesight. What makes them truly remarkable, however, is their ability to find their way and to catch tiny insects in complete darkness by using sound. This ability is called echolocation, and it has fascinated scientists for more than two hundred years.

The first person to investigate how bats navigate in the dark was an Italian scientist named Lazzaro Spallanzani, in the 1790s. He discovered that bats could still fly safely around a room when their eyes were covered, but not when their ears were blocked. His conclusions puzzled many of his contemporaries, who could not imagine how an animal could perceive objects with its ears. The explanation was not discovered until the twentieth century, when new equipment made it possible to detect sounds that are too high for people to hear.

In 1938, a student at Harvard named Donald Griffin used such a device and proved that bats emit rapid pulses of ultrasonic sound. He later invented the word echolocation to describe the process. The principle is simple, although the details are astonishing.

A bat sends out a high-pitched sound through its mouth or nose, and the sound travels through the air until it hits an object, such as a moth. Part of the sound bounces back as an echo, and the bat detects it with its large, sensitive ears. By measuring how long the echo takes to return, the bat can calculate the distance to the object. Differences between the echoes arriving at each ear reveal the direction, and changes in pitch show whether the object is moving. Some bats can even detect the beating of an insect's wings.

When a bat is searching for food, it may produce about ten calls every second. As it gets closer to its target, the calls become faster and faster, until they merge into a rapid buzz of up to two hundred calls per second. This provides a constantly updated picture of the prey's position.

Insects have not remained helpless, and over millions of years some of them have evolved defences. Certain moths can hear the calls of bats and drop suddenly towards the ground to escape. Tiger moths go further, and they produce clicks of their own that appear to jam the bat's system or warn it that the moth tastes unpleasant. The bats, in turn, have responded with new tactics, and some species use calls at frequencies that the moths cannot hear. This ancient competition has produced some of the most sophisticated sensory systems in nature.

The same principle has inspired remarkable human inventions. Ships use sonar to detect the seabed, and doctors use ultrasound to examine unborn babies. Engineers have also developed walking sticks that help blind people to sense obstacles by sending out sound waves. Studying bats has therefore taught us that an animal's senses can function in ways that we find difficult to imagine, and that nature often provides ingenious solutions to technical problems.

q.q: Which statement best sums up the passage?
q.e: The passage explains echolocation, discovery and uses.
o: A. Bats can hear the sounds that insects make.
B. Bats are blind and find food by smell.
C. Bats use echoes of their own sounds to find their way and hunt, and this ability has inspired human technology.
D. Bats use sight in the dark and hearing only in daylight.

q.q: What is wrong with the expression "as blind as a bat"?
o: A. Bats are not blind but cannot hear.
B. Bats see only the colour red.
C. Bats cannot see in the dark.
D. Bats can see well, and some have excellent eyesight.

q.q: What did Spallanzani discover?
o: A. Bats could not fly at all in a room.
B. Bats could fly safely with their eyes covered but not with their ears blocked.
C. Bats used smell to find insects.
D. Bats could fly safely with their ears blocked.

q.q: Why was the explanation not found until the twentieth century?
o: A. Scientists did not study bats earlier.
B. The sounds were too low to record.
C. Equipment was needed to detect sounds too high for people to hear.
D. Bats only began to use echolocation then.

q.q: What happens to the calls as a bat gets close to its target?
o: A. They change into a low hum.
B. They stop completely.
C. They become faster and faster until they merge into a buzz.
D. They become quieter and slower.

q.q: In paragraph 6, the word "sophisticated" is closest in meaning to
q.e: The sensory systems are advanced and complex.
o: A. very noisy.
B. very simple.
C. very old.
D. highly developed.

q.q: What does the writer conclude about animal senses?
o: A. They can work in ways that are hard for us to imagine.
B. They are the same in all animals.
C. They are weaker than human senses.
D. They cannot be copied by engineers.

q.q: Spallanzani carried out his experiments in the 1790s.
Donald Griffin invented the word echolocation.
All moths are able to produce clicks of their own.
Bats can catch tiny ____ in complete darkness by using sound.
The buzz can reach up to two hundred ____ per second.
Ships use ____ to detect the seabed.

ps.e: There is an old expression, as blind as a bat, but it could hardly be more mistaken.
ps.b: একটি পুরোনো প্রবাদ আছে, বাদুড়ের মতো অন্ধ, কিন্তু এটি আর বেশি ভুল হতে পারত না।

ps.e: Bats can see perfectly well, and some species have excellent eyesight.
ps.b: বাদুড় পুরোপুরি ভালো দেখতে পায়, আর কিছু প্রজাতির দৃষ্টিশক্তি চমৎকার।

ps.e: What makes them truly remarkable, however, is their ability to find their way and to catch tiny insects in complete darkness by using sound.
ps.b: তবে যা তাদের সত্যিই অসাধারণ করে তোলে তা হলো শব্দ ব্যবহার করে সম্পূর্ণ অন্ধকারে পথ খুঁজে নেওয়া ও ছোট ছোট পোকা ধরার ক্ষমতা।

ps.e: This ability is called echolocation, and it has fascinated scientists for more than two hundred years.
ps.b: এই ক্ষমতার নাম প্রতিধ্বনি-অবস্থান নির্ণয়, বা ইকোলোকেশন, আর দুই শতাব্দীরও বেশি সময় ধরে এটি বিজ্ঞানীদের মুগ্ধ করে রেখেছে।

ps.e: The first person to investigate how bats navigate in the dark was an Italian scientist named Lazzaro Spallanzani, in the 1790s.
ps.b: বাদুড় অন্ধকারে কীভাবে পথ চলে তা প্রথম অনুসন্ধান করেছিলেন লাৎসারো স্পাল্লানজানি নামের একজন ইতালিয়ান বিজ্ঞানী, ১৭৯০-এর দশকে।

ps.e: He discovered that bats could still fly safely around a room when their eyes were covered, but not when their ears were blocked.
ps.b: তিনি আবিষ্কার করলেন যে চোখ ঢেকে দিলেও বাদুড় ঘরের ভেতর নিরাপদে উড়তে পারে, কিন্তু কান বন্ধ করলে পারে না।

ps.e: His conclusions puzzled many of his contemporaries, who could not imagine how an animal could perceive objects with its ears.
ps.b: তাঁর সিদ্ধান্ত তাঁর সমসাময়িকদের অনেককে ধাঁধায় ফেলেছিল, যারা কল্পনাই করতে পারেননি একটি প্রাণী কান দিয়ে বস্তু অনুভব করে কীভাবে।

ps.e: The explanation was not discovered until the twentieth century, when new equipment made it possible to detect sounds that are too high for people to hear.
ps.b: এর ব্যাখ্যা বিংশ শতাব্দীর আগে আবিষ্কৃত হয়নি, যখন নতুন যন্ত্রপাতি এমন শব্দ শনাক্ত করা সম্ভব করল যা মানুষের শোনার জন্য খুব উঁচু।

ps.e: In 1938, a student at Harvard named Donald Griffin used such a device and proved that bats emit rapid pulses of ultrasonic sound.
ps.b: ১৯৩৮ সালে হার্ভার্ডের এক ছাত্র ডোনাল্ড গ্রিফিন এমন একটি যন্ত্র ব্যবহার করে প্রমাণ করলেন যে বাদুড় অতিস্বনক শব্দের দ্রুত স্পন্দন ছাড়ে।

ps.e: He later invented the word echolocation to describe the process.
ps.b: তিনি পরে প্রক্রিয়াটিকে বোঝাতে ইকোলোকেশন শব্দটি উদ্ভাবন করেন।

ps.e: The principle is simple, although the details are astonishing.
ps.b: নীতিটি সহজ, যদিও খুঁটিনাটি বিস্ময়কর।

ps.e: A bat sends out a high-pitched sound through its mouth or nose, and the sound travels through the air until it hits an object, such as a moth.
ps.b: বাদুড় মুখ বা নাক দিয়ে একটি তীক্ষ্ণ শব্দ ছাড়ে, আর শব্দটি বাতাসে ছুটে চলে যতক্ষণ না কোনো বস্তুতে, যেমন একটি মথে, ধাক্কা খায়।

ps.e: Part of the sound bounces back as an echo, and the bat detects it with its large, sensitive ears.
ps.b: শব্দের একটি অংশ প্রতিধ্বনি হয়ে ফিরে আসে, আর বাদুড় তার বড়, সংবেদনশীল কান দিয়ে সেটি ধরে।

ps.e: By measuring how long the echo takes to return, the bat can calculate the distance to the object.
ps.b: প্রতিধ্বনি ফিরতে কত সময় লাগে তা মেপে বাদুড় বস্তুটির দূরত্ব হিসাব করতে পারে।

ps.e: Differences between the echoes arriving at each ear reveal the direction, and changes in pitch show whether the object is moving.
ps.b: দুই কানে পৌঁছানো প্রতিধ্বনির পার্থক্য দিক জানিয়ে দেয়, আর সুরের পরিবর্তন দেখায় বস্তুটি নড়ছে কি না।

ps.e: Some bats can even detect the beating of an insect's wings.
ps.b: কিছু বাদুড় এমনকি পোকার ডানার স্পন্দনও টের পেতে পারে।

ps.e: When a bat is searching for food, it may produce about ten calls every second.
ps.b: খাবার খোঁজার সময় বাদুড় প্রতি সেকেন্ডে প্রায় দশটি ডাক ছাড়তে পারে।

ps.e: As it gets closer to its target, the calls become faster and faster, until they merge into a rapid buzz of up to two hundred calls per second.
ps.b: লক্ষ্যের যত কাছে পৌঁছায়, ডাক তত দ্রুত হতে থাকে, শেষে মিশে যায় সেকেন্ডে দুইশো ডাক পর্যন্ত একটি দ্রুত গুঞ্জনে।

ps.e: This provides a constantly updated picture of the prey's position.
ps.b: এটি শিকারের অবস্থানের একটি ক্রমাগত হালনাগাদ ছবি জোগায়।

ps.e: Insects have not remained helpless, and over millions of years some of them have evolved defences.
ps.b: পোকারা অসহায় থাকেনি, আর লক্ষ লক্ষ বছরে তাদের কেউ কেউ আত্মরক্ষার উপায় বিবর্তিত করেছে।

ps.e: Certain moths can hear the calls of bats and drop suddenly towards the ground to escape.
ps.b: কিছু মথ বাদুড়ের ডাক শুনতে পায় এবং পালাতে হঠাৎ মাটির দিকে নেমে যায়।

ps.e: Tiger moths go further, and they produce clicks of their own that appear to jam the bat's system or warn it that the moth tastes unpleasant.
ps.b: টাইগার মথ আরও এগিয়ে যায়, আর তারা নিজেরাই ক্লিকের শব্দ করে, যা বাদুড়ের ব্যবস্থাকে বিভ্রান্ত করে বা সতর্ক করে যে মথের স্বাদ খারাপ বলে মনে হয়।

ps.e: The bats, in turn, have responded with new tactics, and some species use calls at frequencies that the moths cannot hear.
ps.b: বাদুড়েরাও পাল্টা নতুন কৌশল নিয়েছে, আর কিছু প্রজাতি এমন কম্পাঙ্কে ডাক ছাড়ে যা মথেরা শুনতে পায় না।

ps.e: This ancient competition has produced some of the most sophisticated sensory systems in nature.
ps.b: এই প্রাচীন প্রতিযোগিতা প্রকৃতির সবচেয়ে অত্যাধুনিক ইন্দ্রিয়-ব্যবস্থাগুলোর কয়েকটি তৈরি করেছে।

ps.e: The same principle has inspired remarkable human inventions.
ps.b: একই নীতি মানুষের চমৎকার উদ্ভাবনকেও অনুপ্রাণিত করেছে।

ps.e: Ships use sonar to detect the seabed, and doctors use ultrasound to examine unborn babies.
ps.b: জাহাজ সমুদ্রতল শনাক্ত করতে সোনার ব্যবহার করে, আর চিকিৎসকেরা অনাগত শিশুদের পরীক্ষা করতে আল্ট্রাসাউন্ড ব্যবহার করেন।

ps.e: Engineers have also developed walking sticks that help blind people to sense obstacles by sending out sound waves.
ps.b: প্রকৌশলীরা এমন হাঁটার লাঠিও বানিয়েছেন, যা শব্দতরঙ্গ পাঠিয়ে অন্ধ মানুষদের বাধা টের পেতে সাহায্য করে।

ps.e: Studying bats has therefore taught us that an animal's senses can function in ways that we find difficult to imagine, and that nature often provides ingenious solutions to technical problems.
ps.b: বাদুড়কে অধ্যয়ন করে তাই আমরা শিখেছি যে একটি প্রাণীর ইন্দ্রিয় এমনভাবে কাজ করতে পারে যা কল্পনা করা আমাদের কাছে কঠিন, আর প্রকৃতি প্রায়ই প্রযুক্তিগত সমস্যার চতুর সমাধান জোগায়।

cmp/134.title: The Sea Where You Cannot Sink
cmp/134.src: Israel Ministry of Environmental Protection; Gertman and Hecht (2002)
p: Imagine floating effortlessly on your back in a sea with a newspaper in your hands, as relaxed as if you were sitting in an armchair. This is exactly what visitors do at the Dead Sea, a lake on the border between Israel, Jordan and the West Bank, where nobody can sink. The secret lies in the extraordinary salinity of its water.

The Dead Sea is roughly ten times saltier than the ocean, and about one third of its weight is dissolved minerals. This makes the water so dense that the human body floats in it with minimal effort. The lake is also remarkable for its position. It lies about 430 metres below sea level, which makes the shore the lowest point of dry land on Earth.

The explanation for the salt lies in the geography of the region. Water flows into the lake, predominantly from the River Jordan, but there is no outlet through which it can drain away. The only way for water to escape is by evaporation, and in the hot, arid desert climate, an enormous quantity is lost every day. When the water evaporates, the salts and other minerals remain behind and become more concentrated over thousands of years. Because of this high concentration, hardly any organism can survive in the water, which explains the name. A few simple microorganisms are able to survive, but there are no fish, no plants and no larger animals.

Despite its name, the Dead Sea has been popular for thousands of years. The ancient Egyptians collected valuable substances from its shores for use in embalming, and the lake was famous in the ancient world for its natural asphalt. Many people believe that its mud and water have therapeutic benefits for the skin, and visitors from all over the world come to cover themselves with the dark mud before they float. Scientists have confirmed that the air near the lake contains slightly more oxygen than elsewhere, because of its low altitude, and that the sunlight is gentler, as the thick air filters out some harmful rays.

Today, however, the Dead Sea is facing a serious environmental crisis. Its level has been falling by about one metre every year, and the shoreline has retreated by hundreds of metres in some places. The principal cause is that people divert the water of the River Jordan for farming and drinking before it reaches the lake. Factories that extract minerals from the water have also contributed to the decline. As the water level drops, the ground beneath the dry shores becomes unstable, and thousands of dangerous holes, known as sinkholes, have opened up.

Several governments have discussed plans to save the lake, including a proposal to pipe water from the Red Sea. These projects are expensive and controversial, because moving water from one sea to another might change the chemistry of the lake. Meanwhile, tourists continue to arrive, increasingly aware that the experience may not last for many more generations. The Dead Sea is a vivid illustration of how a natural wonder can be shaped, and endangered, by human decisions.

q.q: Which statement best sums up the passage?
q.e: The passage covers the saltiness, history and decline.
o: A. The Dead Sea is growing larger every year.
B. The Dead Sea is the deepest lake in the world.
C. The Dead Sea has many fish that live in its salty water.
D. The Dead Sea's extreme saltiness lets people float, but the lake is shrinking and under threat.

q.q: How salty is the Dead Sea compared with the ocean?
o: A. Twice as salty.
B. Slightly less salty.
C. About ten times saltier.
D. About the same.

q.q: Why does the lake have so much salt?
o: A. Rivers flow out of it every day.
B. Water flows in but can leave only by evaporation, so minerals stay behind.
C. Salt is added by ships from other seas.
D. Underground springs fill it with pure salt.

q.q: What kinds of living things can survive in the Dead Sea?
o: A. Large plants and trees.
B. Many kinds of fish.
C. Shellfish and turtles.
D. A few simple microorganisms.

q.q: Why are sinkholes appearing near the shore?
o: A. Heavy rain has washed away the soil.
B. Earthquakes have broken the surface.
C. Tourists have dug deep holes.
D. The water level is dropping, so the ground beneath becomes unstable.

q.q: In paragraph 5, the word "divert" is closest in meaning to
q.e: People use the river's water before it reaches the lake.
o: A. send in a different direction.
B. clean carefully.
C. store for later.
D. protect from harm.

q.q: Why are the plans to save the lake controversial?
o: A. They are too cheap to be reliable.
B. They would make the lake too fresh to float in.
C. Moving water from one sea to another might change the chemistry of the lake.
D. They would flood the nearby towns.

q.q: The shore of the Dead Sea is the lowest point of dry land on Earth.
Scientists say the air near the lake contains slightly less oxygen.
The plan to bring water from the Red Sea has already been completed.
q.e: Paragraph 6 says only that it was discussed.

ps.e: The explanation for the salt lies in the geography of the region.
ps.b: লবণের কারণটি এই অঞ্চলের ভূগোলে নিহিত।

ps.e: Water flows into the lake, predominantly from the River Jordan, but there is no outlet through which it can drain away.
ps.b: পানি হ্রদে ঢোকে, প্রধানত জর্ডান নদী থেকে, কিন্তু বেরিয়ে যাওয়ার কোনো পথ নেই।

ps.e: The only way for water to escape is by evaporation, and in the hot, arid desert climate, an enormous quantity is lost every day.
ps.b: পানির পালানোর একমাত্র উপায় বাষ্পীভবন, আর গরম, শুকনো মরু-আবহাওয়ায় প্রতিদিন বিপুল পরিমাণ পানি হারিয়ে যায়।

ps.e: Because of this high concentration, hardly any organism can survive in the water, which explains the name.

ps.e: Despite its name, the Dead Sea has been popular for thousands of years.
ps.b: নামের মৃত সত্ত্বেও ডেড সি হাজার হাজার বছর ধরে জনপ্রিয়।

ps.e: The ancient Egyptians collected valuable substances from its shores for use in embalming, and the lake was famous in the ancient world for its natural asphalt.
ps.b: প্রাচীন মিশরীয়রা এর তীর থেকে মূল্যবান পদার্থ সংগ্রহ করত মমি তৈরির কাজে ব্যবহারের জন্য, আর প্রাচীন বিশ্বে হ্রদটি এর প্রাকৃতিক অ্যাসফল্টের জন্য বিখ্যাত ছিল।

ps.e: Many people believe that its mud and water have therapeutic benefits for the skin, and visitors from all over the world come to cover themselves with the dark mud before they float.
ps.b: অনেকে বিশ্বাস করেন যে এর কাদা ও পানি ত্বকের জন্য উপকারী, আর সারা বিশ্ব থেকে দর্শনার্থীরা ভাসার আগে গায়ে গাঢ় কাদা মাখতে আসেন।

ps.e: Scientists have confirmed that the air near the lake contains slightly more oxygen than elsewhere, because of its low altitude, and that the sunlight is gentler, as the thick air filters out some harmful rays.
ps.b: বিজ্ঞানীরা নিশ্চিত করেছেন যে নিচু উচ্চতার কারণে হ্রদের কাছের বাতাসে অন্য জায়গার চেয়ে সামান্য বেশি অক্সিজেন থাকে, আর সূর্যের আলোও নরম, কারণ পুরু বাতাস কিছু ক্ষতিকর রশ্মি ছেঁকে নেয়।

ps.e: Today, however, the Dead Sea is facing a serious environmental crisis.
ps.b: তবু আজ ডেড সি এক গুরুতর পরিবেশগত সংকটের মুখোমুখি।

ps.e: Its level has been falling by about one metre every year, and the shoreline has retreated by hundreds of metres in some places.
ps.b: এর স্তর প্রতি বছর প্রায় এক মিটার করে নামছে, আর কিছু জায়গায় তীররেখা শত শত মিটার পিছিয়ে গেছে।

ps.e: The principal cause is that people divert the water of the River Jordan for farming and drinking before it reaches the lake.
ps.b: প্রধান কারণ হলো মানুষ জর্ডান নদীর পানি হ্রদে পৌঁছানোর আগেই চাষ ও পানের জন্য অন্যদিকে সরিয়ে নেয়।

ps.e: Factories that extract minerals from the water have also contributed to the decline.
ps.b: পানি থেকে খনিজ আহরণ করা কারখানাগুলোও এই ক্ষয়ে অবদান রেখেছে।

ps.e: As the water level drops, the ground beneath the dry shores becomes unstable, and thousands of dangerous holes, known as sinkholes, have opened up.
ps.b: পানির স্তর নামতে থাকায় শুকিয়ে যাওয়া তীরের নিচের মাটি অস্থির হয়ে পড়ছে, আর হাজার হাজার বিপজ্জনক গর্ত, যাদের বলা হয় সিঙ্কহোল, দেখা দিয়েছে।

ps.e: Several governments have discussed plans to save the lake, including a proposal to pipe water from the Red Sea.
ps.b: কয়েকটি সরকার হ্রদটি বাঁচানোর পরিকল্পনা নিয়ে আলোচনা করেছে, যার মধ্যে লোহিত সাগর থেকে পাইপে করে পানি আনার একটি প্রস্তাবও আছে।

ps.e: These projects are expensive and controversial, because moving water from one sea to another might change the chemistry of the lake.
ps.b: এই প্রকল্পগুলো ব্যয়বহুল ও বিতর্কিত, কারণ এক সাগর থেকে আরেক সাগরে পানি আনলে হ্রদের রসায়ন বদলে যেতে পারে।

ps.e: Meanwhile, tourists continue to arrive, increasingly aware that the experience may not last for many more generations.
ps.b: এদিকে পর্যটকেরা আসতেই থাকছেন, ক্রমশ সচেতন হয়ে যে অভিজ্ঞতাটি আর বেশি প্রজন্ম টিকে নাও থাকতে পারে।

ps.e: The Dead Sea is a vivid illustration of how a natural wonder can be shaped, and endangered, by human decisions.
ps.b: ডেড সি এর একটি উজ্জ্বল দৃষ্টান্ত যে মানুষের সিদ্ধান্তে একটি প্রাকৃতিক বিস্ময় কীভাবে গড়ে ওঠে, আবার বিপন্নও হয়।

cmp/135.title: Who Built the Great Pyramid?
cmp/135.src: Lehner, The Complete Pyramids (1997); Tallet, The Red Sea Scrolls (2017)
p: More than four and a half thousand years ago, a pharaoh named Khufu ordered the construction of a tomb that would remain the tallest human-made structure in the world for nearly four thousand years. The Great Pyramid at Giza, in Egypt, was originally about 146 metres high, and it contains an estimated 2.3 million blocks of stone. The average block weighs about two and a half tonnes, and some weigh many times more.

How did people with copper tools, wooden sledges and no wheels or cranes manage to build it? For many years, the popular answer was that slaves were forced to do the work under the whip of cruel overseers. This idea was repeated by a Greek writer centuries later and then in films, but modern archaeology has shown that it is not correct.

In the 1990s, archaeologists discovered the remains of a town near the pyramids where the builders had lived. They found bakeries, breweries, sleeping quarters and a cemetery, and the skeletons showed that the workers had received medical treatment. Some of the bones had healed after serious injuries, which suggests that the workers were cared for by doctors. The evidence indicates that most of the labourers were Egyptian farmers and skilled craftsmen who were paid in food and housing. Experts estimate that the permanent workforce was around twenty thousand people, with additional crews arriving in rotation. Many probably considered the work an honour, because it was a way of serving their king and of securing a place in the afterlife.

The question of how the stones were moved has also become clearer. Most of the limestone was cut from quarries near the site, and the stones were dragged across the sand on wooden sledges. Paintings from a later Egyptian tomb show workers pouring water on the sand in front of a sledge, and modern experiments have shown that wet sand makes the sledge much easier to pull. The finer white limestone for the outer casing came from quarries across the river, and was brought by boat.

In 2013, archaeologists made an astonishing find at an ancient harbour on the Red Sea coast. They discovered the world's oldest known papyrus documents, which included the diary of an official named Merer. The diary describes how his team transported blocks of limestone by boat along the Nile to Giza, and it even mentions the pharaoh's pyramid by name. It gives us a rare first-hand account from a person who actually took part in the work.

Scientists are still debating how the blocks were lifted to the higher levels. Many believe that a system of ramps was used, but there is disagreement about whether they were straight, spiral or inside the pyramid itself. Whatever the method, the precision of the result remains impressive. The base is almost perfectly level, and its sides are aligned with the compass directions with only a tiny error. The pyramid is therefore not only an impressive monument to a king, but also a testimony to organisation, mathematics and the skill of thousands of ordinary people.

ps.b: ডায়েরিতে বর্ণনা আছে কীভাবে তাঁর দল নীল নদ ধরে নৌকায় চুনাপাথরের খণ্ড গিজায় নিয়ে গিয়েছিল, আর এতে ফারাওয়ের পিরামিডের নামও উল্লেখ আছে।

ps.b: পদ্ধতি যা-ই হোক, ফলাফলের নিখুঁত মাপ এখনো চমকপ্রদ।

ps.b: ভিত্তিটি প্রায় নিখুঁতভাবে সমতল, আর এর পাশগুলো কম্পাসের দিকের সঙ্গে সামান্যতম ভুল নিয়ে সারিবদ্ধ।

cmp/136.title: Songs That Travel Across Oceans
cmp/136.src: Payne and McVay (1971); Garland et al., Current Biology (2011)
p: Deep in the ocean, a sound rises and falls in long, mysterious phrases, which can last for twenty minutes before they are repeated. It is the song of the humpback whale, and it is one of the most complex sounds produced by any animal. Scientists have been studying these songs since the 1960s, when a recording called Songs of the Humpback Whale became a surprising best-seller and helped to inspire a worldwide campaign to protect whales. Only the males sing, and they do so mainly in the breeding season, which suggests that the songs are related to attracting a mate or competing with rivals.

Each song is built from units of sound, which are combined into phrases and repeated in themes, and the pattern follows rules that are comparable to the structure of language. Researchers who analysed the songs mathematically found that they contain patterns similar to those in human speech.

The most surprising discovery is that the songs are not fixed. Every few months, the whales within a group slowly alter their song, and all the males in the population adopt the new version, so that the song is constantly changing. Within a few years, the song may be completely different from the original. This means that humpbacks, like humans, are capable of learning from one another and passing on a tradition.

In 2011, a research team compared songs from groups of whales in the South Pacific Ocean over more than a decade. They found that a new song would appear in the west, near Australia, and then spread eastward from group to group, until it reached whales thousands of kilometres away, near French Polynesia. The whales did not meet face to face, because they lived in different areas, and so they presumably learned the song by listening to the sound travelling through the water. In some cases, a new song replaced the old one within a few years, which was an unexpectedly rapid change. Scientists describe this as cultural transmission, and it was once thought to be limited to humans and a few other animals.

Humpbacks are not the only whales that communicate with sound. Blue whales, the largest animals that have ever lived, produce deep calls that travel for hundreds of kilometres. Sperm whales use patterns of clicks, and some groups appear to have their own dialect, which they teach to their young.

Unfortunately, the ocean is becoming increasingly noisy. Ships, drilling and military sonar fill the water with sound, and this can disturb the whales and make it harder for them to hear one another. Conservationists are calling for quieter ships, stricter regulations and the protection of important breeding areas, so that the animals can communicate without constant interference. Understanding how whales communicate may help us to protect them, and it reminds us that we share the planet with other minds that are only beginning to be understood.

cmp/137.title: Why Do Onions Make Us Cry?
cmp/137.src: Imai et al., Nature (2002); Eady et al., Plant Physiology (2008)
p: Almost everyone has cried while chopping an onion, yet few people stop to ask why it happens. The tears are not a sign of sadness but the result of an ingenious chemical defence. Onions grow underground, where they are exposed to hungry insects and animals, and over millions of years they have developed ways of deterring their enemies.

Inside the cells of an onion, two kinds of substances are isolated from each other. One is a group of compounds containing sulphur, which the plant extracts from the soil. The other is a set of special proteins known as enzymes. As long as the onion remains whole, the two never meet, and nothing unusual happens.

Everything changes as soon as a knife cuts through the onion. The blade damages thousands of cells, and their contents mix together. The enzymes then begin to break down the sulphur compounds, which initiates a rapid sequence of chemical reactions. Within a few seconds, the onion has released a gas into the air.

The gas drifts upwards towards the cook's face and reaches the eyes. When it touches the thin layer of liquid that covers the surface of the eye, it irritates the nerves there. The nerves send an urgent signal to the brain, which responds by ordering the tear glands to wash the irritation away. That is why your eyes sting and fill with water.

The detailed explanation is remarkably recent. For many years, scientists believed that a different enzyme was responsible for the gas. In 2002, however, researchers in Japan discovered the real one, and this transformed the way the whole process was understood. Six years later, researchers in New Zealand used genetic engineering to switch off that enzyme in an onion, and the result was a plant that produced far fewer tears. Such onions are not yet widely available, but the experiment confirmed that the explanation was accurate.

Cooks have devised many techniques to reduce the problem, and some of them genuinely work. Chilling an onion in the refrigerator before cutting it slows down the chemical reactions, so less gas is released. A sharp knife is also helpful, because it slices cleanly and damages fewer cells than a blunt one. Cutting the onion near an open window or a fan disperses the gas, and some people wear swimming goggles to shield their eyes completely. Other popular tricks, such as chewing gum or holding a piece of bread in the mouth, lack any convincing scientific evidence.

It is ironic that the same sulphur compounds that make us cry also give onions their strong flavour and smell. Onions have been grown for thousands of years, and they are used in the cooking of almost every country in the world. Cooking an onion changes its chemistry, which is why a fried onion tastes sweet and mild instead of sharp. The next time an onion brings tears to your eyes, remember that you are watching a small demonstration of plant defence in action.
