cmp/153.title: The Bear That Lives on Bamboo
cmp/153.src: Nie et al., Science (2015); Swaisgood et al., Giant Pandas: Biology, Veterinary Medicine and Management (2006); IUCN Red List (2016)
p: Giant pandas are among the most loved animals in the world, yet they have a very strange way of life. Belonging to the bear family, pandas descend from ancestors that hunted meat, but today they spend most of their day eating a single plant: bamboo. Bamboo makes up about ninety-nine percent of their diet, and an adult panda may eat between twelve and thirty-eight kilograms of it every day.

This is surprising because the body of a panda is designed for a meat-eating animal. It has a short and simple digestive system, which cannot digest tough plants efficiently, so it takes only a small part of the energy from the bamboo that it eats. As a result, pandas must eat for ten to sixteen hours a day to obtain enough food. Unlike cows, which have several stomachs to digest grass, a panda has only one, which makes its way of life even more demanding.

Pandas have developed several clever ways to cope with this poor diet. To hold the thin stems, they use a special "thumb", which is really an enlarged wrist bone that works like an extra finger. Using their strong jaws and wide teeth, pandas crush the hard bamboo, while bacteria in their stomachs help to break it down.

Another important strategy is to save energy. Scientists in China discovered that pandas use far less energy than most animals of their size, which is more similar to the rate of a sloth than to that of other bears. For this reason, pandas move slowly, rest often and avoid unnecessary effort.

Baby pandas are even more surprising. A newborn cub is pink, almost hairless, blind and extremely small, weighing only about one hundred grams, which is roughly one nine-hundredth of its mother's weight. The mother holds it gently for the first weeks, and it needs about three months before it can crawl. Because the cub is completely helpless, the mother stays with it constantly, and during the first weeks, she hardly leaves the den, even to eat.

Although pandas live alone in the cool mountain forests of central China, their number has increased in recent years. In the 1980s, the wild population fell to about one thousand animals, but protected reserves, strict laws against hunting and the replanting of damaged forests helped them to recover. In 2016, the conservation organisation IUCN stated that the giant panda was no longer "endangered" but "vulnerable", and a survey in 2014 counted about one thousand eight hundred wild pandas.

However, the future of pandas is not completely safe. They depend on bamboo forests, and climate change may destroy much of this habitat during the century, so conservationists are creating protected connections between separate groups of pandas. The panda reminds us that even an animal with a strange diet can survive if people give it enough space and protection.

cmp/154.title: The Game That Travelled the World
cmp/154.src: Murray, A History of Chess (1913); Shannon, Philosophical Magazine (1950); International Chess Federation (FIDE); IBM Research
p: Imagine a game that is more than fifteen hundred years old, that is played by hundreds of millions of people, and that has more possible games than there are atoms in the universe. That game is chess, and its long journey across the world is as fascinating as any match played on the board. In 1950, the American scientist Claude Shannon estimated that the number of possible games is about a one followed by one hundred and twenty zeros, a figure far too large for any human to imagine.

Chess began in India in about the sixth century, and its first name was chaturanga, which means "four parts of an army". The four parts were foot soldiers, horsemen, elephants and chariots, and in the modern game, they have become the pawns, knights, bishops and rooks. The aim was already the same as today: to trap the enemy's king.

From India, the game travelled to Persia, where it was called shatranj and became popular at the royal court. The Persians also gave chess one of its most famous words, because "shah mat" meant "the king is helpless", and this phrase later became the English word "checkmate".

After the Arab conquest of Persia, the game spread across the Middle East and North Africa, and from there, it reached Spain and Italy about a thousand years ago. Traders, soldiers and travellers all carried it along the roads, and wherever it arrived, people changed the shape of the pieces and the names that they used.

In Europe, chess was played by kings, priests and ordinary families, and it was often used as a lesson in strategy and good behaviour. However, the game was still slow at that time, because the queen could move only one square at a time. Around the year 1475, players in southern Europe changed the rules, giving the queen and the bishop great power, and the fast, exciting game that we know today was born.

Since then, chess has produced some of the greatest rivalries in history. In 1972, the American Bobby Fischer defeated the Russian Boris Spassky in Iceland, and the match was followed by millions of people during the Cold War. Then, in 1997, an IBM computer called Deep Blue beat the world champion Garry Kasparov, and many people wondered whether machines would soon replace human players.

The opposite happened. Computers have become much stronger than any human, but chess is more popular than ever, because players can use them to practise, to analyse their mistakes and to play against opponents anywhere in the world. Schoolchildren, grandparents and champions now meet on the same screens, and the old game of kings has become a game for everyone. Online platforms now host millions of games every day, and several talented young players have reached the title of grandmaster before the age of fifteen.

ps.b: কল্পনা করুন এমন একটি খেলা, যার বয়স পনেরো শ বছরেরও বেশি, যা কয়েক কোটি মানুষ খেলে, আর যার সম্ভাব্য খেলার সংখ্যা মহাবিশ্বের পরমাণুর সংখ্যার চেয়েও বেশি।

ps.e: That game is chess, and its long journey across the world is as fascinating as any match played on the board.
ps.b: সেই খেলাটি হলো দাবা, আর বিশ্বজুড়ে এর দীর্ঘ যাত্রা বোর্ডে খেলা যেকোনো ম্যাচের মতোই মনোমুগ্ধকর।

ps.e: In 1950, the American scientist Claude Shannon estimated that the number of possible games is about a one followed by one hundred and twenty zeros, a figure far too large for any human to imagine.
ps.b: ১৯৫০ সালে আমেরিকান বিজ্ঞানী ক্লদ শ্যানন অনুমান করেন যে সম্ভাব্য খেলার সংখ্যা প্রায় ১ এর পর একশো বিশটি শূন্য, যা কোনো মানুষের কল্পনা করার পক্ষে অনেক বেশি বড় একটি সংখ্যা।

ps.e: Chess began in India in about the sixth century, and its first name was chaturanga, which means "four parts of an army".
ps.b: দাবার শুরু ভারতে প্রায় ষষ্ঠ শতকে, আর এর প্রথম নাম ছিল চতুরঙ্গ, যার অর্থ "সেনাবাহিনীর চার অংশ"।

ps.e: The four parts were foot soldiers, horsemen, elephants and chariots, and in the modern game, they have become the pawns, knights, bishops and rooks.
ps.b: চারটি অংশ ছিল পদাতিক, অশ্বারোহী, হাতি ও রথ, আর আধুনিক খেলায় সেগুলো হয়েছে বোড়ে, ঘোড়া, গজ (বিশপ) ও নৌকা (রুক)।

ps.e: The aim was already the same as today: to trap the enemy's king.
ps.b: উদ্দেশ্য তখনই আজকের মতোই ছিল: শত্রুর রাজাকে আটকে ফেলা।

ps.e: From India, the game travelled to Persia, where it was called shatranj and became popular at the royal court.
ps.b: ভারত থেকে খেলাটি পারস্যে গেল, যেখানে এর নাম হলো শতরঞ্জ আর তা রাজদরবারে জনপ্রিয় হয়ে উঠল।

ps.e: The Persians also gave chess one of its most famous words, because "shah mat" meant "the king is helpless", and this phrase later became the English word "checkmate".
ps.b: পারসিকরা দাবাকে এর সবচেয়ে বিখ্যাত শব্দগুলোর একটিও দিয়েছে, কারণ "শাহ মাত" মানে "রাজা অসহায়", আর এই বাক্যাংশই পরে ইংরেজি শব্দ "চেকমেট" হয়ে ওঠে।

ps.e: After the Arab conquest of Persia, the game spread across the Middle East and North Africa, and from there, it reached Spain and Italy about a thousand years ago.
ps.b: পারস্য আরবদের দখলে যাওয়ার পর খেলাটি মধ্যপ্রাচ্য ও উত্তর আফ্রিকা জুড়ে ছড়িয়ে পড়ল, আর সেখান থেকে প্রায় এক হাজার বছর আগে এটি স্পেন ও ইতালিতে পৌঁছাল।

ps.e: Traders, soldiers and travellers all carried it along the roads, and wherever it arrived, people changed the shape of the pieces and the names that they used.
ps.b: ব্যবসায়ী, সৈন্য ও পর্যটকেরা সবাই পথে পথে এটি বহন করেছে, আর যেখানেই এটি পৌঁছেছে, মানুষ ঘুঁটির আকার ও ব্যবহৃত নাম বদলে নিয়েছে।

ps.e: In Europe, chess was played by kings, priests and ordinary families, and it was often used as a lesson in strategy and good behaviour.
ps.b: ইউরোপে দাবা খেলতেন রাজা, পুরোহিত ও সাধারণ পরিবারের লোকেরা, আর কৌশল ও ভালো আচরণের শিক্ষা হিসেবেও এটি প্রায়ই ব্যবহৃত হতো।

ps.e: However, the game was still slow at that time, because the queen could move only one square at a time.
ps.b: তবে সেই সময়ে খেলাটি তখনো ধীরগতির ছিল, কারণ মন্ত্রী একবারে মাত্র একটি ঘর চলতে পারত।

ps.e: Around the year 1475, players in southern Europe changed the rules, giving the queen and the bishop great power, and the fast, exciting game that we know today was born.
ps.b: ১৪৭৫ সালের দিকে দক্ষিণ ইউরোপের খেলোয়াড়েরা নিয়ম বদলে মন্ত্রী ও গজকে বিপুল ক্ষমতা দিলেন, আর আজ আমরা যে দ্রুত ও উত্তেজনাপূর্ণ খেলাটি চিনি তার জন্ম হলো।

ps.e: Since then, chess has produced some of the greatest rivalries in history.
ps.b: তারপর থেকে দাবা ইতিহাসের কিছু শ্রেষ্ঠ প্রতিদ্বন্দ্বিতা সৃষ্টি করেছে।

ps.e: In 1972, the American Bobby Fischer defeated the Russian Boris Spassky in Iceland, and the match was followed by millions of people during the Cold War.
ps.b: ১৯৭২ সালে আইসল্যান্ডে আমেরিকান বব্বি ফিশার রাশিয়ান বরিস স্প্যাস্কিকে হারান, আর ঠান্ডা যুদ্ধের সময় ম্যাচটি লক্ষ লক্ষ মানুষ অনুসরণ করেছিল।

ps.e: Then, in 1997, an IBM computer called Deep Blue beat the world champion Garry Kasparov, and many people wondered whether machines would soon replace human players.
ps.b: তারপর ১৯৯৭ সালে ডিপ ব্লু নামের একটি আইবিএম কম্পিউটার বিশ্বচ্যাম্পিয়ন গ্যারি কাসপারভকে হারিয়ে দেয়, আর অনেকে ভাবল যন্ত্রই কি শিগগির মানুষ খেলোয়াড়দের জায়গা নেবে।

ps.e: The opposite happened.
ps.b: ঘটল ঠিক এর উল্টোটা।

ps.e: Computers have become much stronger than any human, but chess is more popular than ever, because players can use them to practise, to analyse their mistakes and to play against opponents anywhere in the world.
ps.b: কম্পিউটার যেকোনো মানুষের চেয়ে অনেক শক্তিশালী হয়ে উঠেছে, তবু দাবা আগের চেয়ে বেশি জনপ্রিয়, কারণ খেলোয়াড়েরা এগুলো দিয়ে অনুশীলন করতে, নিজেদের ভুল বিশ্লেষণ করতে এবং বিশ্বের যেকোনো জায়গার প্রতিপক্ষের বিরুদ্ধে খেলতে পারে।

ps.e: Schoolchildren, grandparents and champions now meet on the same screens, and the old game of kings has become a game for everyone.
ps.b: স্কুলের শিশু, দাদু-দিদা আর চ্যাম্পিয়নরা এখন একই পর্দায় মিলিত হয়, আর রাজাদের এই পুরোনো খেলা সবার খেলায় পরিণত হয়েছে।

ps.e: Online platforms now host millions of games every day, and several talented young players have reached the title of grandmaster before the age of fifteen.
ps.b: অনলাইন প্ল্যাটফর্মে এখন প্রতিদিন লক্ষ লক্ষ খেলা হয়, আর কয়েকজন প্রতিভাবান তরুণ খেলোয়াড় পনেরো বছর বয়সের আগেই গ্র্যান্ডমাস্টার উপাধি অর্জন করেছে।

cmp/155.title: What Is Inside a Lightning Bolt?
cmp/155.src: Rakov and Uman, Lightning: Physics and Effects (2003); Christian et al., Journal of Geophysical Research (2003); National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
p: A flash of lightning lasts for less than a second, but during that tiny moment, it releases enough energy to light a small town for a short time. The air around a bolt becomes about thirty thousand degrees Celsius, which is five times hotter than the surface of the Sun. Despite its fearsome reputation, lightning is simply a gigantic spark of electricity, with a voltage that can reach hundreds of millions of volts, and scientists now understand a great deal about how it works.

The story begins inside a storm cloud, where strong winds carry tiny particles of ice and drops of water up and down. Colliding with one another, these pieces exchange small electric charges, and gradually, the lighter pieces with positive charges accumulate at the top of the cloud, while the heavier ones with negative charges sink to the bottom. Meanwhile, the ground below the cloud develops a positive charge, because opposite charges attract each other.

Eventually, the difference becomes too large, and the air, which normally prevents electricity from passing, can no longer resist. First, zigzagging downwards from the cloud in short steps, each about fifty metres long, a faint channel of charge, called a leader, searches for a path to the ground. When it comes close to the ground, a similar channel rises to meet it, and in that instant, the circuit is complete.

Then comes the part that we actually see. Racing back up the channel at about one third of the speed of light, a powerful current produces the blinding flash. Although the bolt seems to travel downwards, the bright light moves upwards, and the whole process happens so quickly that our eyes cannot follow it.

Thunder is the sound of the same event. The enormous heat forces the air to expand explosively, sending a shock outwards as a loud crack or a long rumble. Light travels almost instantly, but sound needs about three seconds to cover a kilometre, so by counting the seconds between a flash and its thunder, you can estimate how far away the storm is.

For centuries, people believed that lightning was a punishment from the gods. In 1752, the American scientist Benjamin Franklin suggested that it was a form of electricity, and he proposed an invention to protect buildings: a metal rod placed on the roof, which carries the current safely into the ground. Lightning rods are still used today, and they have saved countless houses, churches and towers from fire.

Lightning is still dangerous, and it is worth taking simple precautions to stay safe. During a storm, you should go inside a solid building or a car, and you should never shelter under a tall tree or stand in open ground or in water. Fortunately, about nine out of every ten people who are struck by lightning survive, although many of them suffer lasting injuries. One park ranger in Virginia, Roy Sullivan, was struck seven times during his life and survived every time.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
q.e: The passage explains lightning and safety.
o: A. How lightning forms, what it does and how to stay safe.
B. Why storms happen in summer.
C. How to build a lightning rod.
D. How electricity is made in power stations.

q.q: How hot does the air around a lightning bolt become?
o: A. About the same as the Sun's surface.
B. About one hundred degrees.
C. About one thousand degrees.
D. About thirty thousand degrees Celsius.

q.q: What collects at the top of a storm cloud?
o: A. Drops of oil.
B. Lighter pieces with positive charges.
C. Pieces of rock.
D. Heavier pieces with negative charges.

q.q: What happens to the bright light of the flash?
o: A. It moves sideways.
B. It stays in one place.
C. It moves upwards, although the bolt seems to travel downwards.
D. It comes from the sun.

q.q: How can you estimate how far away a storm is?
o: A. By looking at the colour of the cloud.
B. By counting the seconds between the flash and the thunder.
C. By measuring the wind.
D. By listening to the radio.

q.q: In paragraph 7, the word "lasting" is closest in meaning to
q.e: Lasting injuries continue for a long time.
o: A. very small.
B. continuing for a long time.
C. not serious.
D. very sudden.

q.q: Why are lightning rods useful?
o: A. They make thunder quieter.
B. They carry the electric current safely into the ground.
C. They stop rain.
D. They attract storm clouds.

q.q: The air around a bolt is hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Sound travels faster than light.
q.e: Paragraph 5 says that light travels almost instantly.

The steps of the leader are each about fifty ____ long.
The American scientist ____ suggested that lightning was a form of electricity.

ps.e: The air around a bolt becomes about thirty thousand degrees Celsius, which is five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

ps.e: Despite its fearsome reputation, lightning is simply a gigantic spark of electricity, with a voltage that can reach hundreds of millions of volts, and scientists now understand a great deal about how it works.
ps.b: ভয়ংকর খ্যাতি সত্ত্বেও বজ্রপাত আসলে বিদ্যুতের একটি বিশাল স্ফুলিঙ্গ, যার ভোল্টেজ কয়েক কোটি ভোল্টে পৌঁছাতে পারে, আর বিজ্ঞানীরা এখন এটি কীভাবে কাজ করে সে সম্পর্কে অনেক কিছু জানেন।

ps.e: The story begins inside a storm cloud, where strong winds carry tiny particles of ice and drops of water up and down.
ps.b: গল্পটি শুরু হয় একটি ঝড়ের মেঘের ভেতরে, যেখানে প্রবল বাতাস বরফের ক্ষুদ্র টুকরো ও পানির ফোঁটাকে ওপর-নিচ করে বহন করে।

ps.e: Colliding with one another, these pieces exchange small electric charges, and gradually, the lighter pieces with positive charges accumulate at the top of the cloud, while the heavier ones with negative charges sink to the bottom.
ps.b: একে অপরের সঙ্গে ধাক্কা খেয়ে এই টুকরোগুলো ছোট ছোট বৈদ্যুতিক আধান বিনিময় করে, আর ধীরে ধীরে ধনাত্মক আধানের হালকা টুকরোগুলো মেঘের ওপরে জমা হয়, আর ঋণাত্মক আধানের ভারীগুলো নিচে নেমে যায়।

ps.e: Meanwhile, the ground below the cloud develops a positive charge, because opposite charges attract each other.
ps.b: এদিকে মেঘের নিচের মাটিতে ধনাত্মক আধান তৈরি হয়, কারণ বিপরীত আধান একে অপরকে আকর্ষণ করে।

ps.e: Eventually, the difference becomes too large, and the air, which normally prevents electricity from passing, can no longer resist.
ps.b: অবশেষে পার্থক্যটি অনেক বড় হয়ে যায়, আর বাতাস, যা সাধারণত বিদ্যুৎকে চলাচল করতে বাধা দেয়, আর প্রতিরোধ করতে পারে না।

ps.e: First, zigzagging downwards from the cloud in short steps, each about fifty metres long, a faint channel of charge, called a leader, searches for a path to the ground.
ps.b: প্রথমে মেঘ থেকে ছোট ছোট ধাপে আঁকাবাঁকা হয়ে নিচের দিকে নামতে নামতে, যার প্রতিটি ধাপ প্রায় পঞ্চাশ মিটার লম্বা, আধানের একটি ক্ষীণ পথ, যাকে লিডার বলা হয়, মাটিতে পৌঁছানোর পথ খোঁজে।

ps.e: When it comes close to the ground, a similar channel rises to meet it, and in that instant, the circuit is complete.
ps.b: এটি মাটির কাছাকাছি এলে একই রকম একটি পথ ওপরে উঠে একে ধরে ফেলে, আর সেই মুহূর্তেই বর্তনী সম্পূর্ণ হয়।

ps.e: Then comes the part that we actually see.
ps.b: এরপর আসে সেই অংশ, যা আমরা আসলে দেখি।

ps.e: Racing back up the channel at about one third of the speed of light, a powerful current produces the blinding flash.
ps.b: আলোর গতির প্রায় এক-তৃতীয়াংশ গতিতে পথ বেয়ে ওপরে ছুটে গিয়ে একটি শক্তিশালী প্রবাহ চোখ ধাঁধানো ঝলক সৃষ্টি করে।

ps.e: Although the bolt seems to travel downwards, the bright light moves upwards, and the whole process happens so quickly that our eyes cannot follow it.
ps.b: বজ্রটি নিচের দিকে নামছে বলে মনে হলেও উজ্জ্বল আলো ওপরের দিকে চলে, আর পুরো প্রক্রিয়াটি এত দ্রুত ঘটে যে আমাদের চোখ তা অনুসরণ করতে পারে না।

ps.e: Thunder is the sound of the same event.
ps.b: বজ্রধ্বনি হলো একই ঘটনার শব্দ।

ps.e: The enormous heat forces the air to expand explosively, sending a shock outwards as a loud crack or a long rumble.
ps.b: প্রচণ্ড তাপে বাতাস বিস্ফোরণের মতো প্রসারিত হতে বাধ্য হয়, আর একটি ধাক্কা জোরালো কড়কড় বা দীর্ঘ গুড়গুড় শব্দ হয়ে বাইরের দিকে ছড়িয়ে পড়ে।

ps.e: Light travels almost instantly, but sound needs about three seconds to cover a kilometre, so by counting the seconds between a flash and its thunder, you can estimate how far away the storm is.
ps.b: আলো প্রায় তাৎক্ষণিকভাবে চলে, কিন্তু শব্দের এক কিলোমিটার যেতে প্রায় তিন সেকেন্ড লাগে, তাই ঝলক ও বজ্রধ্বনির মাঝের সেকেন্ড গুনে আপনি ঝড়টি কত দূরে তা অনুমান করতে পারেন।

ps.e: For centuries, people believed that lightning was a punishment from the gods.
ps.b: শত শত বছর ধরে মানুষ বিশ্বাস করত যে বজ্রপাত দেবতাদের শাস্তি।

ps.e: In 1752, the American scientist Benjamin Franklin suggested that it was a form of electricity, and he proposed an invention to protect buildings: a metal rod placed on the roof, which carries the current safely into the ground.
ps.b: ১৭৫২ সালে আমেরিকান বিজ্ঞানী বেঞ্জামিন ফ্র্যাঙ্কলিন প্রস্তাব করেন যে এটি বিদ্যুতের একটি রূপ, আর তিনি ভবন রক্ষার জন্য একটি আবিষ্কারের কথা বলেন: ছাদে বসানো একটি ধাতব দণ্ড, যা প্রবাহকে নিরাপদে মাটিতে নিয়ে যায়।

ps.e: Lightning rods are still used today, and they have saved countless houses, churches and towers from fire.
ps.b: বজ্রনিরোধক দণ্ড আজও ব্যবহৃত হয়, আর এগুলো অসংখ্য বাড়ি, গির্জা ও টাওয়ারকে আগুন থেকে বাঁচিয়েছে।

ps.e: Lightning is still dangerous, and it is worth taking simple precautions to stay safe.
ps.b: বজ্রপাত এখনো বিপজ্জনক, আর নিরাপদ থাকতে সহজ সতর্কতা নেওয়া গুরুত্বপূর্ণ।

ps.e: During a storm, you should go inside a solid building or a car, and you should never shelter under a tall tree or stand in open ground or in water.
ps.b: ঝড়ের সময় আপনার কোনো মজবুত ভবনের ভেতরে বা গাড়িতে যাওয়া উচিত, আর কখনো উঁচু গাছের নিচে আশ্রয় নেওয়া বা খোলা মাঠে বা পানিতে দাঁড়ানো উচিত নয়।

ps.e: Fortunately, about nine out of every ten people who are struck by lightning survive, although many of them suffer lasting injuries.
ps.b: সৌভাগ্যবশত বজ্রাহত প্রতি দশজনের প্রায় নয়জন বেঁচে যায়, যদিও তাদের অনেকেই স্থায়ী আঘাতে ভোগে।

ps.e: One park ranger in Virginia, Roy Sullivan, was struck seven times during his life and survived every time.
ps.b: ভার্জিনিয়ার একজন পার্ক রেঞ্জার রয় সুলিভান জীবনে সাতবার বজ্রাহত হয়েছিলেন এবং প্রতিবারই বেঁচে গিয়েছিলেন।

cmp/156.title: The Day the Sun Disappears
cmp/156.src: Espenak and Meeus, Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses (2006); Dyson, Eddington and Davidson, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society (1920); NASA Eclipse Web Site
p: On a sunny afternoon, the sky begins to darken, birds stop singing, and the temperature suddenly falls. Within minutes, the Sun disappears behind a black disc, and a ghostly white light appears around it. This is a total solar eclipse, and for the people who have seen one, it is often the most unforgettable experience of their lives.

An eclipse happens when the Moon, passing exactly between the Earth and the Sun, obscures the light. By a remarkable coincidence, the Sun is about four hundred times wider than the Moon, but it is also about four hundred times farther away, so the two look almost exactly the same size in our sky. This astonishing alignment is rare, and it allows the Moon to cover the Sun completely.

Because the shadow of the Moon is small, a total eclipse can be seen only from a narrow path, which is usually about one hundred and fifty kilometres wide. People outside this path see only a partial eclipse, in which the Moon covers a part of the Sun. Total eclipses happen somewhere on Earth about every eighteen months, but at any single place, they occur only once in about three hundred and seventy years.

The total phase, called totality, lasts only a few minutes, and the longest possible is a little over seven minutes. During totality, the pale outer atmosphere of the Sun, called the corona, becomes visible, and bright planets and stars appear in the daytime sky. Just before and after totality, a tiny spot of sunlight sometimes shines through a valley on the edge of the Moon, producing a brilliant effect that is known as the "diamond ring".

For most of history, people were terrified by eclipses. In ancient China, many believed that a dragon was eating the Sun, so they made loud noises with drums and pots to frighten it away, and other cultures saw an eclipse as a sign of anger from the gods. Gradually, however, astronomers learned to predict them, because the Babylonians noticed that eclipses repeat in a pattern of about eighteen years and eleven days. According to Greek tradition, the philosopher Thales even predicted an eclipse in 585 BC that stopped a battle between two armies, and today, scientists can calculate eclipses centuries in advance.

Eclipses have also played a crucial part in the advance of science. In 1919, a British team led by Arthur Eddington travelled on an expedition to the island of Príncipe, off the coast of West Africa, to photograph the stars near the darkened Sun. The stars appeared to have moved slightly, exactly as Albert Einstein's theory of gravity had predicted, and the result made Einstein famous all over the world.

However, watching an eclipse can be hazardous if you are careless. Looking directly at the Sun, even when most of it is obscured, can permanently damage the eyes, so you must wear special eclipse glasses or make a simple viewer from a card with a small hole. Only during the few minutes of totality is it safe to look at the Sun without protection.

cmp/157.title: Are Sharks Really Dangerous?
cmp/157.src: Worm et al., Marine Policy (2013); International Shark Attack File, University of Florida; Dulvy et al., Current Biology (2021)
p: For many people, the word shark immediately brings to mind enormous teeth, dark water and a frightening piece of music. Telling the story of a giant shark attacking a seaside town, the 1975 film Jaws terrified millions of viewers, and its influence on public opinion is still felt today. The author of the original book later regretted writing it, and he spent much of his life defending sharks.

In reality, sharks are far less hazardous to humans than most people believe. There are more than five hundred species, but only a handful of them, such as the great white, the tiger shark and the bull shark, have ever been involved in serious attacks on people. Many sharks are small, shy and harmless, and the largest of all, the whale shark, which can reach twelve metres in length, feeds on tiny plankton.

The statistics support this. Every year, there are roughly seventy unprovoked shark bites worldwide, and only about five to ten of them are fatal. Most bites are probably cases of mistaken identity, since a surfboard seen from below can look like a seal. You are far more likely to be injured on the journey to the beach than by anything that swims in the water.

Humans, on the other hand, are extremely dangerous to sharks. Researchers estimate that commercial fishing fleets kill about one hundred million sharks every year, partly for their meat but also for their fins, which are used in an expensive soup in some countries. In many cases, fishermen cut off the fins and throw the living animal back into the sea, leaving it unable to swim and doomed to die slowly.

Sharks reproduce very slowly, so they cannot easily replace the animals that are lost. Some species do not produce young until they are more than ten years old, and a female may give birth to only a few pups at a time. As a result, scientists have calculated that over a third of shark and ray species are now threatened with extinction.

This matters because sharks are essential to the health of the oceans. As top predators, they remove sick and vulnerable animals, they keep the numbers of other species in balance, and they help to protect habitats such as coral reefs. When the sharks of one area disappear, the animals that they used to hunt multiply, and the damage spreads through the whole food chain.

Sharks are also remarkable survivors. They have lived in the oceans for more than four hundred million years, which is longer than trees have existed on land, and they have survived several mass extinctions. Their bodies have special senses that can detect tiny electrical signals from the muscles of other animals, and their teeth are replaced throughout life, so that a single shark may use thousands of teeth. Instead of fearing these ancient animals, perhaps we should work to protect them.

cmp/158.title: The Day Boston Was Flooded with Syrup
cmp/158.src: Puleo, Dark Tide: The Great Boston Molasses Flood of 1919 (2003); Nasr-Azadani et al., Physical Review Fluids (2013); Massachusetts Historical Commission
p: On a cold January afternoon in 1919, many people in the crowded North End of Boston were having lunch, playing in the street or working near the busy harbour, unaware that a catastrophe was about to begin. Suddenly, they heard a deep rumbling sound, like a train, and a wave of dark brown liquid, almost eight metres high, rushed down the street. It was not water but molasses, the thick, sweet syrup that is produced when sugar is refined, and it was moving with terrifying speed.

The molasses came from an enormous steel tank, standing near the harbour, that belonged to a company that made industrial alcohol, and it contained more than eight million litres, enough to fill several swimming pools. When the tank burst, the liquid travelled at about fifty kilometres an hour, knocking down buildings, damaging the supports of an elevated railway and trapping people and horses in its sticky grip.

The disaster killed twenty-one people and injured about one hundred and fifty more. Rescuers, struggling through waist-deep syrup, found it extremely hard to reach the victims, because the cold syrup became thicker and stickier, and it clung to everything that it touched. It took several days to find the last bodies, while the harbour, which had been swallowed by the spreading syrup, stayed brown for months.

Why did the tank fail? At first, the company blamed anarchists, claiming that a bomb had destroyed it. However, a long investigation found a simple and shocking explanation: the tank had been built badly. The metal walls were too thin, the builders had not tested the tank properly, and it had leaked since the day that it was filled, but instead of repairing it, the company had painted it brown to hide the leaks.

The weather also played an important part, although few people noticed it at the time. In the days before the accident, the temperature in Boston rose suddenly from very cold to unusually warm, and the warmer molasses expanded and flowed more easily, increasing the pressure on the weakened walls. Modern scientists have studied how the syrup moved, and their experiments show that the cold air made it thicker as it spread, which made it harder for victims to escape.

The legal case, which attracted enormous public attention across the country, was long and complicated. After years of hearings, a court ruled that the company was responsible, and it paid compensation to the families of the victims and to the survivors. It was one of the first major cases in the United States in which many people joined together to sue a company.

The accident also changed the rules. Before it, builders could often construct large structures without checking their calculations, but afterwards, laws required engineers and architects to approve and sign their plans. Some people in Boston still claim that on very hot summer days, you can smell molasses in the old streets of the North End.

ps.b: কোমর-সমান সিরাপের মধ্য দিয়ে এগোতে গিয়ে উদ্ধারকারীরা ক্ষতিগ্রস্তদের কাছে পৌঁছানো অত্যন্ত কঠিন বলে দেখলেন, কারণ ঠান্ডা সিরাপ আরও ঘন ও আঠালো হয়ে উঠেছিল, আর তা যা কিছু ছুঁয়েছিল সবকিছুতেই লেগে থাকছিল।

ps.e: It took several days to find the last bodies, while the harbour, which had been swallowed by the spreading syrup, stayed brown for months.
ps.b: শেষ মরদেহগুলো খুঁজে পেতে কয়েক দিন লেগেছিল, আর ছড়িয়ে পড়া সিরাপে গ্রাস হয়ে যাওয়া বন্দরের পানি কয়েক মাস ধরে বাদামি ছিল।

ps.e: Why did the tank fail?
ps.b: ট্যাংকটি কেন ভেঙে পড়ল?

ps.e: At first, the company blamed anarchists, claiming that a bomb had destroyed it.
ps.b: প্রথমে কোম্পানি নৈরাজ্যবাদীদের দোষ দিয়েছিল এবং দাবি করেছিল যে একটি বোমা সেটি ধ্বংস করেছে।

ps.e: However, a long investigation found a simple and shocking explanation: the tank had been built badly.
ps.b: তবে দীর্ঘ তদন্তে একটি সহজ ও চমকে দেওয়া ব্যাখ্যা পাওয়া গেল: ট্যাংকটি খারাপভাবে তৈরি করা হয়েছিল।

ps.e: The metal walls were too thin, the builders had not tested the tank properly, and it had leaked since the day that it was filled, but instead of repairing it, the company had painted it brown to hide the leaks.
ps.b: ধাতুর দেয়ালগুলো খুব পাতলা ছিল, নির্মাতারা ট্যাংকটি যথাযথভাবে পরীক্ষা করেননি, আর যেদিন এটি ভরা হয় সেদিন থেকেই এটি চুঁইয়ে পড়ছিল, কিন্তু মেরামত না করে কোম্পানি ফুটোগুলো লুকাতে ট্যাংকটিকে বাদামি রং করে দিয়েছিল।

ps.e: The weather also played an important part, although few people noticed it at the time.
ps.b: আবহাওয়াও এতে গুরুত্বপূর্ণ ভূমিকা রেখেছিল, যদিও সেই সময় খুব কম মানুষই তা লক্ষ করেছিল।

ps.e: In the days before the accident, the temperature in Boston rose suddenly from very cold to unusually warm, and the warmer molasses expanded and flowed more easily, increasing the pressure on the weakened walls.
ps.b: দুর্ঘটনার আগের দিনগুলোতে বোস্টনের তাপমাত্রা হঠাৎ খুব ঠান্ডা থেকে অস্বাভাবিক উষ্ণ হয়ে ওঠে, আর উষ্ণতর মোলাসেস প্রসারিত হয়ে আরও সহজে প্রবাহিত হলো, ফলে দুর্বল হয়ে পড়া দেয়ালের ওপর চাপ বাড়ল।

ps.e: Modern scientists have studied how the syrup moved, and their experiments show that the cold air made it thicker as it spread, which made it harder for victims to escape.
ps.b: আধুনিক বিজ্ঞানীরা সিরাপটি কীভাবে চলেছিল তা নিয়ে গবেষণা করেছেন, আর তাঁদের পরীক্ষা দেখায় যে ছড়িয়ে পড়ার সময় ঠান্ডা বাতাস সেটিকে আরও ঘন করে তুলেছিল, ফলে ক্ষতিগ্রস্তদের পালানো আরও কঠিন হয়েছিল।

ps.e: The legal case, which attracted enormous public attention across the country, was long and complicated.
ps.b: সারা দেশে প্রচুর জনসাধারণের মনোযোগ কাড়া আইনি মামলাটি ছিল দীর্ঘ ও জটিল।

ps.e: After years of hearings, a court ruled that the company was responsible, and it paid compensation to the families of the victims and to the survivors.
ps.b: বছরের পর বছর শুনানির পর একটি আদালত রায় দিল যে কোম্পানিটি দায়ী, আর সেটি নিহতদের পরিবার ও বেঁচে যাওয়া মানুষদের ক্ষতিপূরণ দিল।

ps.e: It was one of the first major cases in the United States in which many people joined together to sue a company.
ps.b: এটি যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের প্রথম দিকের বড় মামলাগুলোর একটি, যেখানে অনেক মানুষ একজোট হয়ে একটি কোম্পানির বিরুদ্ধে মামলা করেছিল।

ps.e: The accident also changed the rules.
ps.b: দুর্ঘটনাটি নিয়মকানুনও বদলে দিয়েছিল।

ps.e: Before it, builders could often construct large structures without checking their calculations, but afterwards, laws required engineers and architects to approve and sign their plans.
ps.b: এর আগে নির্মাতারা প্রায়ই নিজেদের হিসাব যাচাই না করেই বড় কাঠামো তৈরি করতে পারত, কিন্তু পরে আইন করে প্রকৌশলী ও স্থপতিদের নিজেদের নকশা অনুমোদন ও স্বাক্ষর করা বাধ্যতামূলক করা হলো।

ps.e: Some people in Boston still claim that on very hot summer days, you can smell molasses in the old streets of the North End.
ps.b: বোস্টনের কিছু মানুষ এখনো দাবি করে যে খুব গরম গ্রীষ্মের দিনে নর্থ এন্ডের পুরোনো রাস্তায় মোলাসেসের গন্ধ পাওয়া যায়।

cmp/159.title: The Goat Herder, the Monks and the Birth of Coffee
cmp/159.src: Pendergrast, Uncommon Grounds: The History of Coffee (2010); Hattox, Coffee and Coffeehouses (1985); International Coffee Organization
p: According to an old Ethiopian legend, the discovery of coffee began when a goat herder named Kaldi noticed that his animals, which usually slept peacefully at night, were leaping around with unusual energy after eating the bright red berries of a certain bush. Curious about the effect, Kaldi tried the berries himself, and he is said to have felt more awake than he had ever been. Historians cannot prove that the story is true, but it shows how people may have first realised that the plant was special, and people still tell it today.

The first reliable evidence of coffee being drunk as a beverage comes from Yemen in the fifteenth century, where Sufi monks, hoping to stay awake during long hours of night prayer, prepared a dark drink by roasting the seeds and boiling them in water. From the monasteries, the habit spread to merchants and pilgrims, who carried the seeds along the trade routes of the Arabian Peninsula.

By the sixteenth century, coffee had reached the great cities of the Ottoman Empire, where a new kind of public place appeared: the coffeehouse. People went there not only to drink but also to play chess, listen to musicians and discuss the news of the day, and the cafés became so popular that some rulers, fearing that critics were gathering there, tried to close them. These attempts usually failed, because the habit was already too deeply rooted in everyday life.

Coffee arrived in Europe in the seventeenth century, carried by traders from Venice and other ports. At first, some religious leaders distrusted the dark drink, but according to a popular story, Pope Clement VIII tasted it and approved, which helped to make it acceptable to Christians. Soon, coffeehouses opened in London, Paris and Vienna, and they became meeting places where merchants, writers and scientists exchanged ideas.

The Arabs had guarded their coffee trade carefully, refusing to export living plants, so that nobody else could grow the crop. Eventually, however, Dutch traders smuggled seedlings out of Yemen, and the plants were cultivated in Java, in the Caribbean and in South America.

In the eighteenth century, coffee was introduced to Brazil, where the warm climate and rich soil proved ideal for large plantations. Brazil rapidly became the biggest producer in the world, a position that it has held for more than a century and a half, although the industry grew partly through the terrible labour of enslaved people.

Today, coffee is one of the most widely traded products on Earth, and more than two billion cups, enjoyed at breakfast tables and in busy offices around the world, are drunk every day. Millions of farmers depend on it for their income, yet many of them earn very little, which is why consumers increasingly look for fairly traded beans.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
q.e: The passage follows coffee across places and centuries.
o: A. The history of the city of Vienna.
B. How to prepare the best cup of coffee.
C. How coffee spread from its legendary origins to the whole world.
D. The life of a goat herder in Ethiopia.

o: A. They ran away from the bush.
B. They refused to eat any berries.
C. They slept all day after eating.

B. To stay awake during night prayer.
C. To sell it to pilgrims.
D. To cure an illness.

o: A. They disliked the taste of coffee.

o: A. He banned it across Europe.
B. He approved it, which helped it to become acceptable to Christians.
C. He gave it to his servants.

q.q: In paragraph 5, the word "guarded" is closest in meaning to
o: A. sold.
B. protected.
C. damaged.

o: A. It banned all imports.
B. It was closer to Europe than other countries.

q.e: Paragraph 1 says that they cannot prove it.

ps.e: According to an old Ethiopian legend, the discovery of coffee began when a goat herder named Kaldi noticed that his animals, which usually slept peacefully at night, were leaping around with unusual energy after eating the bright red berries of a certain bush.
ps.b: একটি পুরোনো ইথিওপীয় কিংবদন্তি অনুযায়ী, কফির আবিষ্কার শুরু হয়েছিল যখন কালদি নামের এক ছাগলপালক লক্ষ করলেন যে তাঁর পশুগুলো, যারা সাধারণত রাতে শান্তভাবে ঘুমাত, একটি নির্দিষ্ট ঝোপের উজ্জ্বল লাল ফল খাওয়ার পর অস্বাভাবিক শক্তিতে লাফালাফি করছে।

ps.e: Curious about the effect, Kaldi tried the berries himself, and he is said to have felt more awake than he had ever been.
ps.b: প্রভাবটি নিয়ে কৌতূহলী হয়ে কালদি নিজেই ফলগুলো চেখে দেখলেন, আর বলা হয় তিনি আগে কখনো যতটা সজাগ বোধ করেননি, তার চেয়ে বেশি সজাগ বোধ করেছিলেন।

ps.e: Historians cannot prove that the story is true, but it shows how people may have first realised that the plant was special, and people still tell it today.
ps.b: ইতিহাসবিদরা প্রমাণ করতে পারেন না যে গল্পটি সত্য, কিন্তু এটি দেখায় মানুষ হয়তো প্রথমবার কীভাবে বুঝতে পেরেছিল যে উদ্ভিদটি বিশেষ, আর মানুষ আজও এটি বলে।

ps.e: The first reliable evidence of coffee being drunk as a beverage comes from Yemen in the fifteenth century, where Sufi monks, hoping to stay awake during long hours of night prayer, prepared a dark drink by roasting the seeds and boiling them in water.
ps.b: পানীয় হিসেবে কফি পান করার প্রথম নির্ভরযোগ্য প্রমাণ পাওয়া যায় পঞ্চদশ শতাব্দীর ইয়েমেন থেকে, যেখানে সুফি সন্ন্যাসীরা রাতের দীর্ঘ প্রার্থনার সময় জেগে থাকার আশায় বীজগুলো ভেজে পানিতে সেদ্ধ করে একটি গাঢ় পানীয় তৈরি করতেন।

ps.e: From the monasteries, the habit spread to merchants and pilgrims, who carried the seeds along the trade routes of the Arabian Peninsula.
ps.b: মঠগুলো থেকে অভ্যাসটি ব্যবসায়ী ও তীর্থযাত্রীদের মধ্যে ছড়িয়ে পড়ল, যাঁরা আরব উপদ্বীপের বাণিজ্যপথ ধরে বীজগুলো বয়ে নিয়ে গেলেন।

ps.e: By the sixteenth century, coffee had reached the great cities of the Ottoman Empire, where a new kind of public place appeared: the coffeehouse.
ps.b: ষোড়শ শতাব্দীর মধ্যে কফি অটোমান সাম্রাজ্যের বড় শহরগুলোতে পৌঁছে গিয়েছিল, যেখানে এক নতুন ধরনের জনসমাগমের জায়গা দেখা দিল: কফিহাউস।

ps.e: People went there not only to drink but also to play chess, listen to musicians and discuss the news of the day, and the cafés became so popular that some rulers, fearing that critics were gathering there, tried to close them.
ps.b: মানুষ সেখানে যেত শুধু পান করতে নয়, বরং দাবা খেলতে, সংগীতশিল্পীদের শুনতে এবং দিনের খবর নিয়ে আলোচনা করতেও, আর ক্যাফেগুলো এতটাই জনপ্রিয় হয়ে উঠল যে কিছু শাসক, সমালোচকরা সেখানে জড়ো হচ্ছে ভেবে ভয় পেয়ে, সেগুলো বন্ধ করার চেষ্টা করলেন।

ps.e: These attempts usually failed, because the habit was already too deeply rooted in everyday life.
ps.b: এই চেষ্টাগুলো সাধারণত ব্যর্থ হতো, কারণ অভ্যাসটি ততদিনে প্রতিদিনের জীবনে গভীরভাবে গেঁথে গিয়েছিল।

ps.e: Coffee arrived in Europe in the seventeenth century, carried by traders from Venice and other ports.
ps.b: সপ্তদশ শতাব্দীতে কফি ইউরোপে পৌঁছাল, ভেনিস ও অন্যান্য বন্দরের ব্যবসায়ীদের হাত ধরে।

ps.e: At first, some religious leaders distrusted the dark drink, but according to a popular story, Pope Clement VIII tasted it and approved, which helped to make it acceptable to Christians.
ps.b: প্রথমে কিছু ধর্মীয় নেতা গাঢ় পানীয়টিকে অবিশ্বাস করতেন, কিন্তু একটি জনপ্রিয় গল্প অনুযায়ী পোপ অষ্টম ক্লিমেন্ট সেটি চেখে দেখে অনুমোদন করেছিলেন, যা এটিকে খ্রিস্টানদের কাছে গ্রহণযোগ্য করতে সাহায্য করল।

ps.e: Soon, coffeehouses opened in London, Paris and Vienna, and they became meeting places where merchants, writers and scientists exchanged ideas.
ps.b: শীঘ্রই লন্ডন, প্যারিস ও ভিয়েনায় কফিহাউস খুলল, আর সেগুলো এমন মিলনস্থল হয়ে উঠল যেখানে ব্যবসায়ী, লেখক ও বিজ্ঞানীরা ধারণা বিনিময় করতেন।

ps.e: The Arabs had guarded their coffee trade carefully, refusing to export living plants, so that nobody else could grow the crop.
ps.b: আরবরা তাদের কফির ব্যবসা সতর্কভাবে আগলে রেখেছিল এবং জীবিত গাছ রপ্তানি করতে অস্বীকার করত, যাতে অন্য কেউ ফসলটি চাষ করতে না পারে।

ps.e: Eventually, however, Dutch traders smuggled seedlings out of Yemen, and the plants were cultivated in Java, in the Caribbean and in South America.
ps.b: তবে শেষ পর্যন্ত ডাচ ব্যবসায়ীরা ইয়েমেন থেকে চারাগাছ চোরাচালান করে বের করে আনল, আর গাছগুলো জাভা, ক্যারিবীয় অঞ্চল ও দক্ষিণ আমেরিকায় চাষ করা হলো।

ps.e: In the eighteenth century, coffee was introduced to Brazil, where the warm climate and rich soil proved ideal for large plantations.

ps.e: Brazil rapidly became the biggest producer in the world, a position that it has held for more than a century and a half, although the industry grew partly through the terrible labour of enslaved people.

cmp/160.title: Giant Drawings in the Peruvian Desert
cmp/160.src: Aveni, Nasca Lines: The Mystery of Peru's Ancient Geoglyphs (2000); UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Lines and Geoglyphs of Nasca and Palpa; Reiche, Mystery on the Desert (1949)
p: On the dry, windswept plains of southern Peru, hundreds of enormous drawings are cut into the ground, showing hummingbirds, monkeys, spiders, a condor and countless straight lines that stretch for several kilometres across the desert. Some of the figures are more than three hundred metres long, so they can be seen clearly only from the air, which is why they remained almost unknown to the outside world until aeroplanes began to fly over the region in the twentieth century.

The drawings were made by the Nazca people, who lived in the valleys near the coast of Peru between about five hundred BC and five hundred AD. Their method was surprisingly simple: the desert surface is covered with dark, rusty stones, and by removing them and piling them along the edges, the workers revealed the pale ground that lay underneath, so that the lines stood out sharply against the darker background.

The climate is among the driest on Earth, with almost no wind or rain. As a result, the pictures have survived for roughly two thousand years. Experiments have shown that a small team, using only wooden stakes and rope, could have designed a large animal in a few days.

The most famous researcher of the lines was Maria Reiche, a German mathematician who moved to Peru in the 1940s and fell in love with the desert. She spent decades sweeping the sand from the drawings with a brush, measuring them and protecting them from visitors, and she argued that some of the lines might be linked to the positions of the sun and the stars.

Nobody knows for certain why the Nazca people made the figures, and over the years several different explanations have been suggested. One theory holds that they formed a giant calendar, while another proposes that they were pathways for religious ceremonies, along which people walked to honour the gods. A more recent idea is that they were connected to the search for water, because many lines point toward places where underground springs appear.

In recent years, scientists using drones and artificial intelligence have discovered more than a hundred new figures that were previously hidden, including smaller drawings that were meant to be seen from the ground by walkers. This discovery suggests that the people who made them wanted ordinary visitors, and not only the gods, to enjoy their work as they walked across the desert.

Today, the site is protected as a World Heritage Site, which brings thousands of visitors every year, but it faces real dangers. Heavy rain, which has become more frequent because of changes in the climate, can damage the lines, and illegal buildings and trespassers threaten them as well. Authorities are therefore working to keep the desert quiet, so that the mystery can be preserved for the generations that are still to come.

cmp/161.title: The Planet That Was Taken Away
cmp/161.src: NASA, New Horizons mission pages; International Astronomical Union, Resolution B5 (2006); Tombaugh, Out of the Darkness (1980); Brown, How I Killed Pluto and Why It Had It Coming (2010)
p: For seventy-six years, children around the world learned that the Solar System contained nine planets, and the smallest and most distant of them was Pluto. Then, in 2006, a group of astronomers voted to change its status, and the little world that had been loved by millions of people suddenly stopped being called a planet.

The story began in 1930, when a young American astronomer named Clyde Tombaugh, working at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona, compared photographs of the night sky taken a few days apart. By looking carefully at pairs of images, he noticed one faint dot that moved slowly against the background of stars, which proved to be a new object far beyond Neptune. The name Pluto was suggested by an eleven-year-old schoolgirl in England, Venetia Burney, who liked the idea of naming the planet after the Roman god of the underworld.

For decades, astronomers believed that Pluto was much larger than it really is, but later measurements showed it to be smaller than Earth's Moon. Its orbit is also unusual, because it is tilted and stretched into an oval shape, so that for some years it travels closer to the Sun than Neptune does.

The real trouble began in the 1990s, when astronomers discovered many other icy bodies in the same distant region, known as the Kuiper Belt. In 2005, a team led by Mike Brown found one called Eris, which seemed to be even more massive than Pluto, and it forced scientists to ask a difficult question: if Pluto was a planet, should Eris be one too, and what about all the others that were still waiting to be found?

In 2006, the International Astronomical Union met in Prague and agreed on a formal definition. According to it, a planet must orbit the Sun, be large enough to become round, and have cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit of other objects of similar size. Pluto failed the third test, so it was reclassified as a dwarf planet, a decision that surprised many people and angered some of them.

Even so, Pluto has not been forgotten by scientists or by the public. In 2015, a spacecraft called New Horizons, which had been travelling for nine and a half years, flew past the dwarf planet and sent back astonishing photographs. They revealed mountains of water ice as high as the Rocky Mountains, a vast heart-shaped plain of frozen nitrogen and even a thin blue haze in the sky.

The debate about the word "planet" continues, with some scientists arguing that the definition should be based on what a world is like inside rather than where it travels. However the argument ends, Pluto reminds all of us that science is not a fixed list of facts, because new evidence can always change the way that we understand the universe.

ps.e: Then, in 2006, a group of astronomers voted to change its status, and the little world that had been loved by millions of people suddenly stopped being called a planet.
ps.b: তারপর ২০০৬ সালে একদল জ্যোতির্বিজ্ঞানী এর মর্যাদা বদলাতে ভোট দিলেন, আর লক্ষ লক্ষ মানুষের ভালোবাসার সেই ছোট জগৎটিকে হঠাৎ করে আর গ্রহ বলে ডাকা হলো না।

ps.e: The story began in 1930, when a young American astronomer named Clyde Tombaugh, working at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona, compared photographs of the night sky taken a few days apart.
ps.b: গল্পটি শুরু হয়েছিল ১৯৩০ সালে, যখন ক্লাইড টমবো নামের এক তরুণ আমেরিকান জ্যোতির্বিজ্ঞানী, অ্যারিজোনার লোয়েল মানমন্দিরে কাজ করতে গিয়ে, কয়েক দিনের ব্যবধানে তোলা রাতের আকাশের ছবি তুলনা করলেন।

ps.e: By looking carefully at pairs of images, he noticed one faint dot that moved slowly against the background of stars, which proved to be a new object far beyond Neptune.
ps.b: জোড়ায় জোড়ায় ছবিগুলো মনোযোগ দিয়ে দেখতে গিয়ে তিনি তারাদের পটভূমির বিপরীতে ধীরে সরে যাওয়া একটি ক্ষীণ বিন্দু লক্ষ করলেন, যা শেষ পর্যন্ত নেপচুনের অনেক ওপারের একটি নতুন বস্তু বলে প্রমাণিত হলো।

ps.e: The name Pluto was suggested by an eleven-year-old schoolgirl in England, Venetia Burney, who liked the idea of naming the planet after the Roman god of the underworld.
ps.b: প্লুটো নামটি প্রস্তাব করেছিল ইংল্যান্ডের এগারো বছর বয়সী এক স্কুলছাত্রী ভেনেশিয়া বার্নি, যে পাতালের রোমান দেবতার নামে গ্রহটির নাম রাখার ধারণাটি পছন্দ করেছিল।

ps.e: For decades, astronomers believed that Pluto was much larger than it really is, but later measurements showed it to be smaller than Earth's Moon.
ps.b: কয়েক দশক ধরে জ্যোতির্বিজ্ঞানীরা বিশ্বাস করতেন যে প্লুটো আসলে যতটা বড় তার চেয়ে অনেক বড়, কিন্তু পরবর্তী পরিমাপ দেখাল এটি পৃথিবীর চাঁদের চেয়েও ছোট।

ps.e: Its orbit is also unusual, because it is tilted and stretched into an oval shape, so that for some years it travels closer to the Sun than Neptune does.
ps.b: এর কক্ষপথও অস্বাভাবিক, কারণ এটি হেলানো ও ডিম্বাকার আকারে প্রসারিত, ফলে কয়েক বছর এটি নেপচুনের চেয়েও সূর্যের কাছাকাছি দিয়ে চলে।

ps.e: The real trouble began in the 1990s, when astronomers discovered many other icy bodies in the same distant region, known as the Kuiper Belt.
ps.b: আসল সমস্যা শুরু হলো ১৯৯০-এর দশকে, যখন জ্যোতির্বিজ্ঞানীরা একই দূরবর্তী অঞ্চলে, যা কুইপার বেল্ট নামে পরিচিত, আরও অনেক বরফের বস্তু আবিষ্কার করলেন।

ps.e: In 2005, a team led by Mike Brown found one called Eris, which seemed to be even more massive than Pluto, and it forced scientists to ask a difficult question: if Pluto was a planet, should Eris be one too, and what about all the others that were still waiting to be found?
ps.b: ২০০৫ সালে মাইক ব্রাউনের নেতৃত্বে একটি দল এরিস নামের একটি বস্তু খুঁজে পেল, যা প্লুটোর চেয়েও ভারী বলে মনে হচ্ছিল, আর এটি বিজ্ঞানীদের একটি কঠিন প্রশ্ন করতে বাধ্য করল: প্লুটো যদি গ্রহ হয়, তাহলে এরিসও কি গ্রহ হওয়া উচিত, আর যে বাকি সবগুলো এখনো খুঁজে পাওয়ার অপেক্ষায় আছে সেগুলোর কী হবে?

ps.e: In 2006, the International Astronomical Union met in Prague and agreed on a formal definition.
ps.b: ২০০৬ সালে আন্তর্জাতিক জ্যোতির্বিজ্ঞান সংঘ প্রাগে মিলিত হয়ে একটি আনুষ্ঠানিক সংজ্ঞায় একমত হলো।

ps.e: According to it, a planet must orbit the Sun, be large enough to become round, and have cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit of other objects of similar size.
ps.b: সেই অনুযায়ী একটি গ্রহকে সূর্যকে প্রদক্ষিণ করতে হবে, গোলাকার হওয়ার মতো যথেষ্ট বড় হতে হবে, এবং তার কক্ষপথের আশপাশ সমান আকারের অন্য বস্তু থেকে পরিষ্কার করে ফেলতে হবে।

ps.e: Pluto failed the third test, so it was reclassified as a dwarf planet, a decision that surprised many people and angered some of them.
ps.b: প্লুটো তৃতীয় পরীক্ষায় ব্যর্থ হলো, তাই এটিকে বামন গ্রহ হিসেবে পুনর্শ্রেণিবদ্ধ করা হলো, এই সিদ্ধান্ত অনেক মানুষকে অবাক করল আর কিছু মানুষকে রাগান্বিত করল।

ps.e: Even so, Pluto has not been forgotten by scientists or by the public.
ps.b: তবু বিজ্ঞানী বা সাধারণ মানুষ কেউই প্লুটোকে ভুলে যায়নি।

ps.e: In 2015, a spacecraft called New Horizons, which had been travelling for nine and a half years, flew past the dwarf planet and sent back astonishing photographs.
ps.b: ২০১৫ সালে নিউ হরাইজনস নামের একটি মহাকাশযান, যা সাড়ে নয় বছর ধরে ভ্রমণ করছিল, বামন গ্রহটির পাশ দিয়ে উড়ে গেল এবং বিস্ময়কর ছবি পাঠাল।

ps.e: They revealed mountains of water ice as high as the Rocky Mountains, a vast heart-shaped plain of frozen nitrogen and even a thin blue haze in the sky.
ps.b: সেগুলো প্রকাশ করল রকি পর্বতমালার মতো উঁচু পানির বরফের পাহাড়, জমাট নাইট্রোজেনের হৃদয়-আকৃতির বিশাল সমভূমি, এমনকি আকাশে একটি পাতলা নীল কুয়াশা।

ps.e: The debate about the word "planet" continues, with some scientists arguing that the definition should be based on what a world is like inside rather than where it travels.
ps.b: "গ্রহ" শব্দটি নিয়ে বিতর্ক চলছে, কিছু বিজ্ঞানী যুক্তি দিচ্ছেন যে সংজ্ঞাটি একটি জগৎ কোথায় চলে তার বদলে ভেতরে সেটি কেমন, তার ওপর ভিত্তি করা উচিত।

ps.e: However the argument ends, Pluto reminds all of us that science is not a fixed list of facts, because new evidence can always change the way that we understand the universe.
ps.b: তর্ক যেভাবেই শেষ হোক, প্লুটো আমাদের সবাইকে মনে করিয়ে দেয় যে বিজ্ঞান তথ্যের কোনো স্থির তালিকা নয়, কারণ নতুন প্রমাণ সবসময়ই মহাবিশ্বকে আমরা যেভাবে বুঝি তা বদলে দিতে পারে।
